WASHINGTON, D.C. — In what military analysts are describing as the most significant advancement in canine warfare since the invention of the leash, the Pentagon announced today that German Shepherds are being phased out of frontline military service and replaced by miniature dachshunds equipped with fifth-generation stealth technology. The decision follows a classified Defense Department study concluding that conventional military working dogs have become too recognizable, too expensive, and too intimidating for modern covert operations.

"Everybody recognizes a German Shepherd as a military dog," explained General Herbert "Hot Dog" Henderson, commander of the Pentagon's newly established Canine Special Operations Division. "Nobody suspects a seven-pound dachshund wearing a little sweater. That's precisely what makes them so dangerous." The program, designated Operation LOW RIDER, represents a revolutionary shift in American military doctrine: replacing overwhelming force with the element of ridiculous surprise.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE SCIENCE OF STEALTH WARFARE

Conventional stealth technology requires radar-absorbing materials, sophisticated engineering, and enormous defense budgets. The miniature dachshund achieves comparable results simply by standing behind a curb. During simulated combat exercises, enemy patrols repeatedly failed to detect the animals, although several soldiers stopped to ask, "Who's a good little boy?"

"The F-35 costs tens of millions of dollars," Henderson explained. "Our new stealth platform costs $600, eats half a cup of kibble, and can hide under a coffee table. You tell me which represents better value for the American taxpayer." Defense contractors have reportedly filed protests, arguing that the Pentagon cannot reasonably expect them to compete with a weapons system available at the local pet store.

EXHIBIT TWO — ENEMY INFILTRATION

During classified field exercises, a dachshund named Sergeant Schnitzel successfully penetrated a simulated enemy headquarters, bypassed three security checkpoints, and gained unrestricted access to the commanding general's private quarters. The operation was declared a complete success until Schnitzel climbed onto the general's bed, fell asleep, and refused to leave.

Military planners are investigating whether the breed's legendary stubbornness can be adapted into a new form of psychological warfare. One intelligence officer suggested deploying the dogs into enemy command centers and allowing them to bark continuously until opposing generals agree to unconditional surrender. The proposal remains under consideration, although Pentagon attorneys have raised concerns that prolonged exposure might violate international conventions governing cruel and unusual treatment.

EXHIBIT THREE — THE NEW SPECIAL FORCES

The Army is establishing an elite unit known as Dachshund Force One, specializing in reconnaissance, covert entry, and autonomous battlefield operations. Unlike conventional military working dogs, which respond to commands, these animals will operate under a decentralized command structure in which handlers issue orders and the dogs independently determine whether compliance is warranted. Pentagon officials describe this as advanced artificial intelligence without the artificial component, while critics describe it as owning a dachshund.

The program has nevertheless impressed military instructors, particularly during simulated confrontations with larger opponents. "We watched one challenge a 200-pound Rottweiler," Henderson reported. "That's the kind of fighting spirit we haven't seen since the Marines landed at Iwo Jima." Military psychologists have recommended additional research into whether an animal possessing absolutely no understanding of its physical limitations might represent the ultimate combat mindset.

EXHIBIT FOUR — UNEXPECTED OPERATIONAL CHALLENGES

The program has encountered several logistical difficulties, particularly in airborne operations and specialized equipment development. Parachute training was temporarily suspended after strong winds carried two trainees into an adjoining county, where they were recovered by an elderly woman who believed they had escaped from a petting zoo. Military engineers are also struggling to develop appropriate protective equipment, with early attempts to fit the animals with combat boots requiring considerably more time than the missions themselves.

The most serious difficulty involves battlefield discipline. During one training exercise, an entire platoon abandoned its assigned objective to pursue a squirrel, prompting commanders to classify the incident as an unauthorized change in mission priorities. Investigators subsequently discovered that several handlers had also abandoned their positions, although their explanation involved attempting to recover approximately $40,000 worth of government-issued canine equipment.

EXHIBIT FIVE — INTERNATIONAL REACTION

Russian intelligence initially dismissed the program as American propaganda until satellite surveillance detected approximately 4,000 miniature dachshunds assembling at Fort Bragg. Chinese military planners have reportedly begun evaluating Pekingese as a potential countermeasure, although preliminary trials were delayed by grooming requirements and disagreements over whether the animals should wear traditional military uniforms.

NATO commanders expressed cautious support for the American initiative but requested assurances that the new canine units could reliably distinguish between allied personnel and enemy combatants. Pentagon officials declined to provide such assurances, explaining that the current identification system relies primarily on smell, personal preference, and whether the individual in question is carrying bacon.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE ULTIMATE TACTICAL ADVANTAGE

The Pentagon's most encouraging results emerged during simulated urban combat exercises designed to measure the psychological impact of the new weapons system. When opposing forces encountered German Shepherds, they immediately recognized military working dogs and established defensive positions. When confronted by miniature dachshunds, the same soldiers abandoned their posts, knelt on the ground, and attempted to pet them, allowing the attacking force to advance without resistance.

Within minutes, the simulated enemy formation had completely disintegrated, leading military researchers to conclude that the miniature dachshund had achieved something conventional weapons systems rarely accomplish: neutralizing an opposing force without firing a shot. Unfortunately, subsequent exercises revealed that American soldiers were equally susceptible, forcing commanders to reconsider whether the world's first universally irresistible military weapon might also represent a serious threat to its own operators.

THE VERDICT

After decades of developing increasingly sophisticated weapons systems, the Pentagon has apparently discovered that America's next great military breakthrough may have been sitting on someone's living room sofa all along. The miniature dachshund offers stealth, mobility, low operating costs, and the remarkable ability to persuade heavily armed soldiers to abandon their military responsibilities. Its combat effectiveness has exceeded expectations, although questions remain concerning obedience, operational endurance, and the availability of appropriate veterinary support in forward-deployed environments.

According to the Pentagon's classified readiness assessment, the dogs have demonstrated extraordinary enthusiasm for entering enemy territory but absolutely no interest in returning when called. Military commanders are reportedly considering offering treats, although defense contractors have already submitted a preliminary proposal for a $2.7 billion Tactical Canine Incentive and Reward System.

October 28, 2026

Brad Garlinghouse’s central message was that crypto’s momentum is accelerating, and Ripple’s responsibility is to turn that momentum into practical benefits for customers, the XRP ecosystem, and the broader economy. Reflecting on a decade of progress—from Toronto to today—he described an industry moving toward greater maturity, institutional participation, and real-world utility.

With elections approaching, Garlinghouse emphasized that technology should transcend partisan politics. Email serves people regardless of political affiliation; financial technology should receive the same bipartisan consideration. His discussion of Fairshake reinforced the importance of political engagement, while his recognition of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s attendance underscored the significance of government participation. He wants Ripple to be a shining light through global leadership.

He highlighted the breadth of American crypto ownership, pointing to 67 million adults and Ripple’s support for the National Cryptocurrency Association. He criticized policies associated with Elizabeth Warren as harmful to economic opportunity and recognized the XRP Army as a leading light. His broader message was clear: the genie is out of the bottle, and demonstrating useful applications will extend the benefits throughout the ecosystem and the world.

Ripple’s business growth provided a concrete measure of that progress. Garlinghouse outlined an expected annualized revenue run rate of $900 million by the end of 2026, compared with $300 million the previous year. Continued growth centers on customers, transaction volume, acquisitions, and bringing more financial activity onchain. He also praised Monica Long’s performance and leadership.

RLUSD is an important part of that strategy. Garlinghouse emphasized compliance, institutional trust, lending applications, and the ability to move collateral around the clock. These capabilities support a financial system that operates continuously, beyond traditional business hours. The larger objective is an Internet of Value, with XRP at its heart.

He presented RLUSD and XRP as complementary. RLUSD brings dollar liquidity onchain and supports activity across the ecosystem, while Ripple remains committed to XRP. Three priorities frame that commitment: greater liquidity, more utility, and stronger trust. Together, these strengthen the infrastructure needed to address financial use cases globally.

Discussing competition, Garlinghouse described Coinbase as a consumer exchange, Circle through its payments focus, and Ripple as a bridge between established finance and the emerging onchain economy. Corporate treasury, collateral movement, payments, and other financial activities offer considerable room for expansion as more assets and liquidity move onchain.

Brad closed with confidence in the industry’s health and direction. He described tremendous momentum and expressed pride, excitement, and focus. His message was that continued execution - serving customers, demonstrating utility, and earning trust - will determine how broadly this progress benefits the world.

The Unacceptable Reality: Somalia’s National Army Continues to Suffer Heavy Losses to Al-Shabaab: 

It is unacceptable that the Somali National Army (SNA) continues to suffer major setbacks against Al-Shabaab nearly two decades into the group’s insurgency. The latest evidence arrived this week in the Bay and Lower Shabelle regions.

On October 26–27, 2026, during Operation Banooda, an SNA force reported as roughly 2,000 troops with more than 200 vehicles was ambushed near Jameeca (also spelled Jame’o) in Buurhakaba district while advancing along the strategic corridor between Leego and Buurhakaba. Al-Shabaab used vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices and other tactics. The group claimed 321 government soldiers killed and the capture of prisoners, weapons, and vehicles, including Turkish-supplied armored personnel carriers. Somalia’s Ministry of Defense stated that its forces killed about 75 militants and wounded 56, while acknowledging damage to army vehicles from explosives-laden attacks. It released no figures for its own casualties. 

Independent accounts from soldiers and officers paint a grimmer picture for government forces. One soldier told Reuters he helped transport the bodies of 40 soldiers and more than 100 wounded to Mogadishu. Another estimated dozens killed in the explosions. A surviving military officer told the Associated Press he saw at least 20 dead comrades, with others unaccounted for. Analysts described the engagement as one of the army’s worst setbacks in years, comparable to the 2023 Cowsweyne battle in Galgaduud. The army appears to have withdrawn from positions around Jameeca and Leego. 

This is not an isolated failure. Al-Shabaab retains the ability to mass fighters, deploy suicide vehicle bombs, and exploit known routes through contested terrain. It continues to dominate large rural areas of central and southern Somalia even as the federal government has claimed the recovery of more than half the territory the group once held over the past five years. Recent months have also seen setbacks involving Southwest State politics, the fall or contestation of other positions, and pressure from reduced international funding. 

The deeper problem is structural. Clan-based recruitment and promotion remain central. Officers and units often owe primary loyalty to clans or political patrons rather than a national chain of command. This produces fragmented cohesion, uneven motivation, and vulnerability to infiltration or local deals. Corruption compounds the damage: ghost soldiers on the payroll, diverted funds and equipment, delayed or incomplete salaries, and promotions driven by connections rather than competence. These practices leave units understrength, poorly supplied, and demoralized even when external partners provide training and some hardware. Logistics, medical evacuation, and the ability to hold and stabilize cleared areas remain weak. Al-Shabaab, by contrast, extracts local taxes, offers a predictable if harsh form of dispute resolution in many rural areas, and uses asymmetric tactics that punish predictable movements. 

International support—Turkish training and equipment, African Union forces in various configurations, U.S. counterterrorism support, and others—has improved elite units and enabled some offensives. Yet it has not produced a self-sustaining national force capable of consistent territorial control and governance. Political fragmentation between the federal government and member states, patronage networks, and the continued primacy of clan calculations further undercut any purely military solution.

The human cost is borne by Somali soldiers and civilians. Families lose sons. Communities face renewed intimidation or taxation when government forces pull back. Economic activity is stifled. Each major ambush reinforces the perception that the state cannot reliably protect its own people or its own troops. 🧵

text:
Sandy Saddler hands Featherweight Champions Willie Pep the second loss of his 137-fight career (Pep was 134-1-1 to this point) on October 29, 1948 at Madison Square Garden, scoring a 4th-round KO.

Pep was dropped twice in the 3rd and then once in the 4th for the count.
----------------------------------------------------------
From The New York Times:

Saddler Wins World Featherweight Title by Knocking Out Pep in 4th Round; VETERAN FLOORED 3 TIMES AT GARDEN Saddler Pins First Knockout on Pep, 1-3 Choice, in 2:38 of Fourth Before 14,685 LEFT TO JAW LIFTS TITLE Down Twice for 9 in Third, Willie Suffers Only Second Defeat in 137 Pro Bouts

Sandy Saddler became the featherweight champion of the world last night by knocking out Willie Pep of Hartford, Conn., in four rounds. In one of the biggest ring upsets of the year, the spindly Negro from Harlem stretched the defending titleholder on the canvas for the full count with a left hook to the jaw after the round had gone 2 minutes 38 seconds. Just before the fighters entered the ring Pep became a 1-to-3 choice to retain the crown that he won clearly in June, 1946, but Saddler confounded the pricemakers by doing a workmanlike boxing job on Willie in the first two rounds. He floored Pep twice for counts of nine in the third before putting the crusher on the favored one in the fourth. In going down to defeat, the 26- year-old Pep definitley lacked the quality from which he took his 'ring name. The veteran of ten years of amateur and professional battling had little spring in his legs, no sharpness to his punching and an inability to get away from a tantalizing, and at the same time punishing, left to the face that Saddler constantly threw at him. Veteran Fights Cautiously In addition, the defending champion fought what for him was a cautious battle. Accustomed, in the past, to carrying the action to his rivals with the sound of the bell, Willie was all caution in his joust with the 22-year-old Saddler. It was the latter who did all the forcing, who advanced toward his foe without reck and who seemed every bit superior even in the first two rounds. A fairly good puncher with either hand, Pep reached his challenger once or twice with a solid left or right to the chin in those sessions, but Saddler showed no ill effects from them and went about carving up Willie with sharp lefts to the face and short rights to the body and head. A crowd of 14,685 paid a total of $55,751 to sit in on Saddler's surprising success. The new champion was probably the least surprised person in the whole place at the end. He knew, as did most of those in attendance, that the fight was surrounded by "fix" rumors in which he was supposed to win, but the manner in which he disposed of Willie made it clear no collusion was necessary, that he had enough guns at his disposal to take care of Pep on his own. The battle simply proved that Willie, didn't have enough to hold off the eager young Negro. Veteran Has Weight Edge Saddler weighed 124 pounds, as against 125½ for his victim. When they went out for the first round, the impression arose that the more compactly built Pep would have no trouble with his rangy rival, but Saddler quickly dispelled that belief by stepping into Willie and driving both hands to the body. Returning a left and right to the head, Pep sought to carry the fight to close quarters. Saddler wrestled the champion, though, and twisted him around so that both were looking in the same direction before Referee Ruby Goldstein could untangle them. After the separation the challenger reached Willie with several left hooks to the body. In the second round Pep shot a straight right to the head, but Saddler moved forward to jab his left to the face repeatedly. The Harlem boxer again wrestled Willie out of position and received a solid right to the head after Goldstein had parted them. Saddler continued to wade into Pep in the third, absorbing Willie's punches and sending a steady two- handed attack on his own account. Midway through the round Saddler let fly a straight left to the face and the punch carried so much force that it spilled Pep for a count of nine. Bell Saves Pep in Third On arising. Pep walked into a left hook and a right to the jaw, and went down again, once more taking nine. The bell ended the round before Saddler could resume his attack. The challenger sprang at Pep in the fourth, belaboring him with rights to the jaw as Willie made. only feeble returns. Suddenly, in a neutral corner, Saddler released a smashing left hook to the jaw and down went Willie for the full count. The defeat was only the second and the first knockout suffered by Pep in 137 professional fights, of which he won 134. He was out- pointed once by ex-lightweight king Sammy Angott and was held to a draw once by Jimmy McAllister. The fight was the ninety-fourth of Saddler's pro career and his sixty-fourth knockout victory. A native of Boston, he moved to Harlem as a child. He has been boxing in the paid ranks for four years. In his dressing room the new champion said he felt he would win after sampling what Pep dealt him in the first round. The Hartford fighter offered no alibi, except to say that the over-confidence of his handlers might have affected him. Touching on the "fix" angle, Chairman Eddie Eagan of the State Athletic Commission told the fighters at the noon weighing that rumors of that nature attached themselves to every fight. He added: “I am holding you responsible to uphold the good name of boxing. There are rumors of a 'fix' before every fight, but we don't pay any attention to them. You are two honest athletes fighting in a great class for a great championship. You will represent boxing tonight." On leaving commission headquarters, Pep said to reporters: "Don't worry about me. I'll be in there to win.' " Saddler said nothing. He just won. ' After the bout, Chairman Eagan declared the fight was a "good scrap." "Both boys did their utmost," he added. C. P. Powell, another member of the commission, said, "it was a good, hard-hitting fight." In the semi-final, Jackie Weber, Pawtucket, R. I., outpunched Johnny La Russo, of the Bronx. Weber weighed 135 and La Russo 135½. Harry La Sane, 131, Houston, Tex., defeated Bobby Bell, 124, Youngstown, Ohio, and Nunzio Carlo, 134, Philadelphia, beat Eduardo Carrasco, 132½, Peru, in six- rounders. In the four-round opener, Tommy Collins, 125%, Boston, out- pointed Lorenzo Safora, 127, Cuba.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Sunday, October 28, 1979, Braniff International inaugurated service from Los Angeles to Singapore with an intermediate stop at Seoul, South Korea. The new Boeing 747 service marked the first time that Braniff had flown to Singapore and it was the last destination added during the Dallas-based luxury Airline's Asia/Pacific and The Far East expansion program.

Singapore also held the title as Braniff International's 81st destination added to its route map. Braniff's new service featured two weekly nonstops between Singapore and Seoul with continuing service to Los Angeles. Both flights continued to South America and included single-plane service to Lima, Peru; Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Braniff offered the only Boeing 747 service from Los Angeles to Singapore as well as the only direct single-plane service.

Braniff inaugurated the new Singapore service with full sized Boeing 747 Jumbo Jets. Four lower capacity and super long-range Boeing 747SP-27 aircraft were on order and would be assigned to the Pacific Division. The first aircraft, Ship N603BN, was delivered on October 30, 1979, two days after the Singapore inaugural flight. The other two 747SPs were delivered in April and May of 1980, and the order for the fourth aircraft was not taken up. Ship N603BN was quickly placed into service on the Pacific Division. By the end of April 1980, the Pacific Division was operated exclusively with Boeing 747SP Jumbo Jets.

On September 8, 1978, Braniff International petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board to award exemption authority to begin service immediately from Houston Intercontinental Airport and Dallas/Ft Worth Regional Airport to several major metropolitan areas in the Pacific Rim and Far East. Singapore was one of the destinations that was named in the petition along with Guam Island, Okinawa, Manila, Taipei, Hong Kong, Bangkok, and Seoul, South, Korea. Service to Seoul was inaugurated several weeks earlier than Singapore on September 15, 1979, with Boeing 747 Jumbo Jet aircraft.

In a separate petition on February 8, 1979, Braniff asked for authority to serve three destination in China. The petition requested authority to serve Peking, Canton, and Shanghai, which would have made Braniff a strong player in the region if the awards were received. On April 12, 1979, the Civil Aeronautics Board granted Braniff International authority to serve Bangkok, Guam, Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore, Seoul, and Taipei. The new Transpacific and Asian route authority called for Braniff to serve these points via Honolulu, but petitions made to the Board in the summer of 1979 would have allowed for nonstop service to some of the destinations.

Earlier on July 3, 1979, Braniff inaugurated Boeing 747 service from Los Angeles to Hong Kong via Honolulu and Guam. Nonstop service to Seoul, South Korea, Braniff's longest Non-Stop flight, was inaugurated two months later on September 15, 1979, and was quickly followed by the new Singapore extension service. Both the Singapore/Seoul/Log Angeles and Hong Kong/Guam/Honolulu/Los Angeles routes afforded passengers single-plane service to Latin America.

Braniff faced break neck competition from Asian carriers flying in the region and oftentimes was the recipient of less than savory tactics. Load factors were strong over the entire Pacific system at 60 to 80 percent but the number one factor that quickly made the routes unprofitable was the unprecedented rise in fuel costs of 92 percent during 1979 and 104 percent in 1980. Braniff was beyond the limits of the contracted fuel prices that it enjoyed in the United States and at the new Pacific and Asian destinations the carrier was paying spot market fuel prices which were significantly higher than contract fuel. At the time of the Singapore inaugural, US fuel prices had ballooned from .36 cents at the end of 1978, to over .75 cents by the end of 1979. However, in the Pacific spot market fuel had jetted to near $1.40 USD per gallon. Braniff's industry leading operating margins on its Boeing 747s that it had enjoyed since 1971, quickly evaporated.

By the summer of 1979, the United States was in the midst of a burgeoning economic recession, which coupled with worldwide rises in fuel prices, mainly due to the unrest in Iran, and the Federal Reserve's contractionary monetary policy to stave off inflation, caused interest rates to skyrocket. Braniff's beautiful new Boeing 747s that were ordered in 1978, were being financed at near credit card interest rates, which further caused overhead costs to rise rapidly. Other carriers were being affected the same way by the fuel costs and near usurious interest rates and they also began reporting huge losses. Braniff managed to stave off large losses throughout 1979, as a result of strict cost containment and operating efficiency that had long been a hallmark of the Dallas-based luxury airline.

Fuel prices continued to rise in 1980, and concurrently costs continued upwards. The prices of operating the Boeing 747s across the Pacific with an average 60 percent load factor became too great. The CAB had also promised Braniff that if it began service in the region then the agency would award Braniff routes to Tokyo, which Braniff stated it must have to operate profitably in the region. The CAB reneged on its promise and as Braniff promised the CAB, the decision was made to eliminate the division. Had Braniff realized the same cost structure it enjoyed just a year and a half earlier at the end of 1978, the Pacific Division would have been profitable. By the end of 1980, Braniff had embarked on a plan to shrink its route system by removing unprofitable routes from the schedules and then it prepared to ride out the economic downturn, which began easing just two and a half years later. Braniff service to the Pacific and Far East was discontinued by the fall of 1980.

Well done to USDOT and the Maritime Administration on today’s approval of the deepwater port license application for ST LNG off Matagorda, Texas. Secretary Sean Duffy announced the decision in Houston, advancing a proposed $8.2 billion offshore LNG export project.

Offshore development offers an alternative to some of the land constraints and community conflicts associated with onshore terminals. But moving offshore does not guarantee success. Many proposed LNG deepwater ports have never become operating facilities. Today’s decision is an important step forward.

Credit also belongs to former Maritime Administrator Captain Bill Schubert, who helped advance offshore LNG permitting more than two decades ago. Congress expanded the Deepwater Port Act in 2002 to include natural gas, and MARAD under Schubert began approving offshore LNG import projects.

Back then, the focus was bringing natural gas into the United States. Today, it is exporting American natural gas to the world. It is good to see that policy foundation supporting a new generation of American energy infrastructure.

text:
Newly announced data center projects have run at $400B+ a month globally since April. The US has 53 GW of data center load actually running. Those two numbers sit on very different timelines, and most of the risk in this cycle lives in the gap between them.

The figures come from Industrial Info Resources (IIR), reported by Data Center Knowledge this week.

The money side. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Google spent a combined $64B on data centers in 2018. Their announced spending is expected to pass $700B this year. Cumulative announced data center capex has passed $7 trillion globally. The US and Canada account for about $4.75 trillion of it, across more than 4,250 planned or in-progress projects. More than 400 GW of new load is in planning, and almost 100 US sites are being designed for at least 1 GW.

The physical side. US operational data center load is 53 GW, up from 23 GW in 2023. Another 42 GW is approved or under construction. Together that's roughly 95 GW that is real or close to real.

Against 400+ GW in planning. For every GW running or being built, more than four are still on paper.

I've spent most of my career in capital project governance, and the first thing that discipline teaches you is that an announcement is not a project. A project becomes real when it clears five gates: site control, permits, an interconnection agreement, long-lead equipment with a delivery date someone will sign for, and committed financing. Most of that 400 GW hasn't cleared all five. A lot of it hasn't cleared one.

The gate that has moved the most is equipment.

GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power and Siemens Energy are sold out of larger gas turbines through 2029, with some orders stretching into 2031. All three are expanding. Fuel cells, reciprocating engines and aeroderivative units are being offered as faster alternatives. Meanwhile IIR tracks $228B of new gas power plant projects in play, all drawing on the same factories.

So the critical path for a 1 GW campus increasingly runs through a turbine factory's order book. In schedule terms, a turbine reservation for 2028 may be worth more than the land it will sit on. If you're evaluating a project, ask to see the slot: who holds it, what deposit secured it, and what happens to it if the project slips a year.

IIR's Shane Mullins put the developer logic plainly: past 300 MW, with a utility queue that says 2034, your own gas plant is "the fastest and most certain path to power."

Fast and certain, maybe. But the bottleneck just moves. The queue at the utility becomes a queue at the OEM, and on-site generation brings its own permit gate. New Jersey recently fined one data center $1M over 123 MW of unpermitted generation.

Then there is the forecast problem. In 2022, US grid planners expected 24 GW of additional demand over a decade. By 2025 that number was 166 GW, nearly seven times higher. IIR says data center demand could go from 35 GW in 2024 to 125 GW by 2030.

Utilities build transmission and generation against forecasts like these, and ratepayers usually fund it. When a forecast moves 7x in three years, the honest question is how much of it is double counting. One campus can sit in three utility queues while the developer shops for the best deal. Texas has paused new grid interconnections while it works through about 200 GW of requests.

And opposition is no longer a side story. IIR counts more than 500 data center moratoria across 42 states, led by New Jersey with 41 and Michigan with 36. New York has temporarily banned new data centers over 50 MW. About $130B of projects were rejected in Q1 2026 alone, more than in all of 2025, and the number of opposition groups has more than doubled in a year.

None of this has slowed the money yet. May alone saw more than $650B in new announcements, and IIR reads twelve straight months of elevated spending as a multiyear buildout.

I don't doubt the demand. What I'd watch is conversion: how much of the announced pipeline turns into energized megawatts, on what schedule, and who carries the cost of the part that doesn't.

Three things I'd want on one page for any large AI campus right now:

1. Interconnection status in writing, with the utility's date, and whether service is firm or conditional.
2. The long-lead equipment schedule (turbines, transformers, switchgear) with contractual delivery dates, and penalties if they slip.
3. A clear answer on who pays for grid upgrades if the load never shows up.

If a project can't produce that page, I'd treat it as an announcement, not yet a project.

Question for people inside these deals: of the 400+ GW in planning, what share do you think actually energizes by 2030? And which gate do you trust most when you make that call?

In 2021 and 2022, my wife and I took two years off and moved from Philadelphia to Hillsborough, New Jersey. We played golf at least twice a week the whole time. We had never seen so many older golfers in our lives. One big reason was that the county’s golf courses offered free membership to anyone 82 and older (they later raised the cutoff to 84).
One day we got paired with a couple in their late 60s. The husband told us a true story about his father. His dad was a dentist in his late 80s who regularly played at Woodland Country Club in Houston Tx with his three buddies: a policeman, a lawyer, and a doctor. text:
Brilliant Badenoch, Four Pence Off Gherkins and a Chancellor Left Exposed

John Healey stood up today promising "breathing space now, fresh hope for the future." When Kemi Badenoch rose to respond, she dismantled the claim with a single line: this is a budget for getting by, not for getting on. In eleven words, she exposed what fifty minutes of Treasury rhetoric had tried to obscure. A government managing decline and calling it relief.

Badenoch's sharpest moment was also her simplest. Healey had announced £100 energy payments, an extension of the electricity VAT cut, and business rates relief, dressed as a serious response to household pressure. Badenoch's verdict: "Instead, we got 4p off gherkins." The line lands because it exposes the absurdity. A country facing diesel at £2 a litre and gas storage at a third full heading into winter was offered a rounding error and told to be grateful. Badenoch did not need to shout to make the gap visible. She simply held the promise next to the policy and let the distance speak.

She was equally precise on the fiscal claims underneath the theatre. Healey insisted his Budget met the government's own fiscal rules and left £15 billion of headroom by 2029/30, the same confident arithmetic his predecessor Reeves offered before her own numbers moved against her. Badenoch was unimpressed, and rightly so. Headroom quoted four years out, in a Budget delivered against a backdrop of £14 billion in additional forecast debt interest this year alone, is not a cushion. It is a hope dressed up as a forecast, and Badenoch's refusal to accept it at face value was the correct instinct from an opposition that has watched this exact promise fail once already under this government.

Her challenge on enterprise was the one Healey will find hardest to answer honestly. He pointed to new money through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, business rates changes, and tax incentives for company founders, and called it a plan to unleash British enterprise. Badenoch's response cut straight through the announcement to the arithmetic underneath it: none of it touches the underlying costs already crushing employers. A tax incentive for founders means little to a business still absorbing last year's National Insurance rise, this year's minimum wage increase, and a wholesale energy bill that has doubled since the Iran crisis began. You cannot unleash enterprise with one hand while taxing its costs with the other, and Badenoch was the only person in the chamber prepared to say so plainly.

Badenoch also went after breathing space itself as a concept, asking how much room Britain genuinely has left when borrowing costs, debt interest and the overall tax burden are all moving in the same direction at once. It is the right question, because breathing space implies slack somewhere in the system, and nothing in Healey's own figures suggests any exists. A Chancellor claiming headroom while debt interest rises by £14 billion in a single year is not managing a surplus of room. He is managing its absence, and hoping nobody checks the working.

What made the performance outstanding was its discipline. Badenoch did not need to invent a crisis or raise her voice to find one. Sharp, witty, and relentlessly on point, she read Healey's own numbers back to him and let the contradiction do the damage itself. A government promising fresh hope, offering 4p off gherkins, and calling £15 billion of headroom security rather than wishful thinking has handed the opposition leader everything she needs to make the case against it. Badenoch made that case, and made it look easy.

text:
Why did the Indian Air Force come to Race Course?

The closure of the Air Force golf course at Race Course in New Delhi has attracted considerable attention. But it also offers an opportunity to revisit a rather interesting question. Why does the IAF have a station in the very heart of Lutyens’ Delhi?

Long before golf was played here, the area hosted cricket, parachute training, and RAF operations. The reason the IAF eventually established a major administrative station here in 1947 has much to do with Hyderabad State's uncertain future and the reorganisation of the Air Force at Partition.

The story begins in 1941, at Willingdon Airport.

In Sep 1941, the RAF established an Air Landing School at Willingdon Airport, now Safdarjung Airport, to train personnel of the newly raised 50th Indian Parachute Brigade. The Brigade comprised British, Indian and Gurkha parachute battalions, and the school represented one of the earliest organised efforts to develop military parachuting in India. Its equipment was rudimentary. The RAF initially had to make do with obsolete Vickers Valentia biplanes, modified to allow parachutists to jump through an opening in the fuselage floor.

Some of the earliest parachute jumps took place over the racecourse adjoining Willingdon Airport. One contemporary account describes a company commander landing on the upper tier of the racecourse grandstand and bouncing his way down to the bottom! The Air Landing School was initially housed under canvas, with accommodation and other buildings coming up near the Race Course. The school was also experimenting with the equipment and techniques required for airborne operations and aerial resupply.

Then, in April 1942, RAF Station New Delhi was formally established. Until then, Willingdon had been a civilian aerodrome used by several RAF units. A Communication Flight detached from No. 31 Squadron, RAF at Lahore had been operating from the airfield for some months. The Air Landing School occupied buildings on one side of the aerodrome, while other small RAF detachments operated alongside it.

The formation of RAF Station New Delhi brought these activities under a common Station Headquarters. The new establishment assumed responsibility for running the aerodrome, although its physical upkeep remained with the Public Works Department. The Station also administered the Air Landing School, a small Parachute Repair Section comprising one senior NCO and seven airmen, and a ground staging and refuelling party responsible for transit aircraft.

It was still a shared airfield. Civil flying continued, including operations by Indian National Airways and the Delhi Flying Club.  By October 1942, when the Air Landing School moved to Chaklala near Rawalpindi, it had recorded 9,231 live parachute descents and qualified 1,511 trainees during its stay in Delhi. The 50th Indian Parachute Brigade would later see fierce fighting against the Japanese at Sangshak in March 1944.The school at Chaklala would later move to Agra where it remains to this date.

RAF Station New Delhi continued to serve the wartime Air Force. The Air Headquarters communication organisation, which itself traced its origins to a flight raised at Lahore in 1928, operated from Willingdon before moving to Palam in 1946.

But how did this RAF establishment eventually become the administrative centre of the independent Indian Air Force?

For that, we need to move forward to 1946, when the Royal Indian Air Force was beginning to consider its post-war organisation. An Air Force broadly rests on four functions: operations, training, maintenance and administration. The first three would eventually develop into operational Commands, Training Command and Maintenance Command. Administration was a somewhat different problem.

It meant managing medical services, accounts, education, security, infrastructure, transport, accommodation and the movement and holding of personnel across the country. It also meant looking after the numerous establishments that came directly under Air Headquarters but did not belong to conventional formations.

One of the early ideas was to concentrate much of this activity in peninsular India, with Arkonam (today's Arakkonam, home to the naval air station INS Rajali) emerging as a possible administrative centre.

The RIAF established a depot at Arkonam, and several important establishments were located in the Madras region. The Air Force Record Office, responsible for personnel records and the administration of airmen, had moved to Red Hills Lake near Madras in 1946. The Central Accounts Office had similarly moved from Bombay to Madras. But Partition complicated these plans considerably.

At the time, southern India comprised territories with different political arrangements. Madras was a province of British India, while Mysore and Hyderabad were princely states. The uncertainty was particularly acute in Hyderabad, where the Nizam had not committed himself to joining the Indian Union. This presented a problem for the RIAF because several of its important training establishments were situated in and around Hyderabad and Secunderabad, including at Hakimpet.

The Air Force consequently began reorganising its training infrastructure, shifting establishments towards locations where their future within India was more secure. In February 1947, No. 2 Ground Training School moved from Secunderabad to Tambaram, near Madras. No. 1 Ground Training School, formed at Hakimpet, subsequently moved to Jalahalli near Bangalore in November 1947. The RIAF Depot at Arkonam (also training airmen) also moved to Jalahalli that November.

With the southern stations being reorganised to accommodate training requirements, the earlier idea of concentrating the principal administrative establishments there became less practical.

The administrative institutions were consequently reorganised towards northern India. New Delhi was the natural destination, not least because Air Headquarters was located there and exercised functional control over many of these units, but also because RAF was vacating the Willingdon premises.

The Record Office moved from Red Hills Lake to Delhi in October 1947, while the Central Accounts Office also moved to the capital that year. The medical and other administrative establishments serving Air Headquarters formed part of the wider arrangement.

What was needed was a single organisation to administer these establishments locally while leaving their professional responsibilities with Air Headquarters. And so, on 1 Sep 1947, just seventeen days after Independence, Air Headquarters Administrative Instruction No. 01/47 established No. 10 Administrative Wing, Royal Indian Air Force, at Race Course, New Delhi.

The Wing was built upon the existing RAF establishment in the Willingdon and Race Course area. Its responsibilities extended to Air Headquarters and the numerous associated units and establishments in the capital. And the man selected to command the new Wing was quite a character.

Group Captain Kanwar 'Tiger' Jaswant Singh had joined the Indian Army in 1936 before transferring to the Air Force in 1940. He had flown with Nos. 2 and 3 Squadrons, commanded No. 2 Squadron during operations in Burma in the Second World War, and earned a reputation as a demanding commander and exceptional sportsman.

Yet, on 1 Sep 1947, Tiger found himself commanding an administrative Wing in a capital torn apart by communal violence. It was hardly a quiet assignment. The new Wing was immediately called upon to patrol riot-affected areas of Central Delhi and assist in maintaining law and order.

At the same time, Partition had divided the Air Force itself. Hundreds of airmen and their families were arriving from former RIAF establishments at Kohat, Peshawar, Risalpur, Chaklala and Mauripur, all now in Pakistan.

The Station's history records that approximately 900 airmen and 150 families required immediate boarding, lodging and assistance. It also had to help personnel moving in the opposite direction, including escorting those proceeding to Pakistan through Palam for onward travel. Tiger, who lived at 1 Kushak Road, was frequently seen travelling around Delhi on his James motorcycle, attending to the Station's responsibilities during these difficult months.

On 24 December 1947, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru addressed a gathering of nearly 2,000 officers and airmen. The Wing had already begun acquiring the ceremonial responsibilities that would eventually become one of the most visible features of Air Force Station New Delhi.

In May 1948, No. 10 Administrative Wing was redesignated as an RIAF Station. When India became a Republic on 26 January 1950, the 'Royal' prefix was dropped and the establishment became Air Force Station New Delhi. The sporting history of Race Course also continued alongside its military responsibilities.

The grounds that later became associated with golf had earlier been used for cricket, while the Station continued to host athletic meets and inter-unit competitions. The Station's photographic archives include images of athletic competitions in 1948, and sporting events continued to be held at Race Course over subsequent decades.

Meanwhile, the Station's military responsibilities continued to evolve. During the 1971 War, it housed fifteen Pakistan Air Force prisoners of war, including Flight Lieutenant Pervaiz Mehdi Qureshi, who would eventually become Chief of the Pakistan Air Force.

By the time Air Force Station New Delhi celebrated its Platinum Jubilee in 2022, it was providing administrative support to 46 IAF units apart from Air Headquarters, covering approximately 10,000 personnel. Its functions extended to medical services, accounts, transport, logistics, accommodation, schools, security, ceremonial duties and numerous other activities across Delhi-NCR.

The golf course became one of the more familiar features of Race Course in later decades, particularly to generations of serving and retired Air Force personnel. But the Air Force's presence here has a much older history.

text:
Mao Zedong was undoubtedly a dictator, but even that label understates a tyrant whose barbaric purges and engineered famines killed tens of millions, leaving China a traumatized, impoverished wasteland of fear and paranoia alongside the likes of Hitler, Stalin, and Pol Pot.

Kylian Mbappé never set out to confront that bloody history, having merely laughed during a podcast interview about an internet meme superimposing his face on an image of Mao, whom the French footballer casually described as "a Chinese dictator."

The manufactured outrage was instantaneous, with Chinese commercial partners severing ties and foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian huffing that insults to national sentiment would face unanimous societal resistance.

What followed was the familiar, cringe-inducing spectacle of corporate groveling, as Mbappé issued a remorseful apology for upsetting the Chinese people while La Liga and its president, Javier Tebas, scrambled to offer abject expressions of regret.

Such subservience mirrors a well-worn playbook that has forced global brands like Nike, Zara, Gap, Leica, and Marriott into humiliating reversals whenever their marketing, human rights stances, or supply-chain audits run afoul of the Chinese Communist Party.

Western sports entities have repeatedly capitulated to safeguard their bottom lines, from Arsenal abandoning Mesut Özil after he highlighted Uyghur repression in Xinjiang to the NBA’s frantic apologies when Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey expressed support for Hong Kong’s freedom.

Hollywood machismo collapses just as quickly, exemplified by action star John Cena reducing himself to a stammering, apologetic mess after accidentally referring to Taiwan as a country while promoting a Fast and Furious film.

Mao remains an intensely uncomfortable subject for Beijing, which settled on Deng Xiaoping’s tortured assessment that the founder was "70 percent right and 30 percent wrong," brushing aside 50 million deaths as mere "excessive enthusiasm."

Under Xi Jinping, any scrutiny of the Great Helmsman has become strictly taboo as the current leader stokes Maoist nostalgia, invokes the spirit of the Long March, and consolidates his own sweeping personality cult.

Weaponized complaints about "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" are an old instrument of state coercion, familiar to any foreign observer who has faced official retaliation or travel bans for failing to fall in line.

While Beijing excels in performative indignation, the scrambling of Western icons to perform submissive "self-rectifications" only exposes the acute danger of economic dependency and the West's alarming willingness to bow to authoritarian blackmail.

text:
Rayo Vallecano fans, primarily members of the Bukaneros ultra group, stopped to help victims of a serious train accident near Urda in the province of Toledo.

The supporters were returning to Madrid by train after watching Rayo Vallecano defeat Recreativo de Huelva 3–2 in a Copa del Rey match. When their train halted near the crash site, the fans got off, called emergency services, assisted with the rescue, and helped transport injured individuals to a local sports hall in Urda.

When the catastrophic collision between a Renfe train and an Iryo train occurred near Urda in Toledo, killing dozens and halting the surrounding rail network, the group of roughly 50 to 60 Bukaneros did not hesitate.

While initial assessments placed them closer, local emergency reports clarified that the fans actually walked roughly seven kilometers on foot along the tracks to reach the epicenter of the crash site and offer immediate aid.

Local Civil Protection authorities highly praised the group's effectiveness, noting that several of the Rayo fans were off-duty professional firefighters. Their training proved invaluable in coordinating early triage, managing chaos, and safely evacuating severely trapped or injured passengers from the shredded train carriages.

The fans directly assisted emergency services in transporting victims to the municipal sports hall in Urda, which local officials had hastily converted into a field triage hospital to treat those with minor injuries.

True to the club's grassroots ethos, after hours of grueling rescue work alongside the Military Emergency Unit (UME) and local responders, the fans quietly left the scene around 3:00 PM to finish their journey to Madrid, politely declining to give media interviews or statements about their actions.

Rayo Vallecano issued an official statement expressing immense "pride and gratitude" for the extraordinary human character shown by their traveling supporters.

We told you in 1776. 
AND YET.

This damnation falls on the British state, and on the British people who returned it to power.

Of the peace of 1783, one article survives in our own Treaties in Force: the first, in which His Britannic Majesty acknowledged us free, sovereign and independent. It is the only one still standing.

Your policy is older than our country. Your own Foreign Office, 1907: Britain "throwing her weight now in this scale and now in that." Churchill, 1936: "For four hundred years the foreign policy of England has been to oppose the strongest, most aggressive, most dominating Power on the Continent." We were never outside that game. We were a piece on its board.

You kept garrisons on our soil in a time of peace. The peace of 1783 bound you to leave our forts; in 1792 our Secretary of State still named seven you held. You supplied the nations making war on our frontier, built Fort Miamis on our soil in 1794, and left only under Jay's treaty, weeks past even its deadline of 1 June 1796.

You sent us envoys who broke our laws on our own soil and meddled in our elections, and we sent them home: Crampton in 1856, for "numerous infractions of our laws"; Sackville-West in 1888, for an attempt "to interfere in its domestic affairs." In 2019 a President said of yours, "We will no longer deal with him." In 2025 you had to pull your own.

You worked American opinion in secret, put a trusted former ambassador's name on testimony no court would take, and when the truth ran short, you sold the world the corpse factory. You were told it was false. You declined to check. You let it run. Eight years later, you called it false yourselves.

You excited divisions amongst us. In our own intelligence service's words, Britain tasked its man in New York with covert operations against the American isolationist movement, while our first intelligence service grew "dependent upon British sources." A 1945 study of your intelligence service "influenced the development" of the CIA. Of course you know how to push our buttons. You installed them.

You kept alive the bank we resolved to kill. At Bretton Woods the nations called for "the liquidation of the Bank for International Settlements at the earliest possible moment." Your Foreign Office sent word that your government "didn't want any action taken." None ever was. You ran the London Gold Pool with it, "managed by the BIS and the Bank of England"; when the pool broke in 1968, we had carried $2.2 billion of its last $3 billion.

Fractional-reserve banking is your bastard child. Your own Bank's bulletin records your goldsmiths lending out what others had left with them for safekeeping; your Bank, chartered in 1694, made a nation of it. You made our dollar ones and zeros, and charged us for the arithmetic.

You ran the regimes' money through our dollar. Lloyds TSB, 2009. Barclays, 2010. Standard Chartered, 2012 and again in 2019. HSBC, 2012. RBS, 2013. Settled with our government, every one. And months after we reimposed sanctions on Iran, you joined Paris and Berlin in setting up a company in Paris to keep trade with Iran moving. It cleared one transaction.

You kept the books our crashes were cooked in. When no American law firm would sign off on Lehman's Repo 105, a London firm did, under English law, and the trades ran through London, up to $50.38 billion at the peak. AIG's Financial Products unit, the one that broke AIG, kept "major operations in London."

You insured the enemy's oil. From the City of London, the International Group of clubs, covering 87 percent of the world's ocean-going tonnage, covered the tankers carrying Iran's crude until Brussels made them stop in 2012, and wrote fallback cover again when the 2016 deal allowed. Our Treasury had named Iran's oil company an agent or affiliate of the IRGC in 2012, and in 2020 found that it and its tanker company supplied the oil and the tankers for the IRGC's own sales. When we blockaded Iran's ports, our Treasury went after the IRGC's "mandatory" Hormuz "insurance" by name, an "extortion scheme," "reinforcing U.S. military interdiction efforts."

You handed us your burdens and kept the ledger. In February 1947 you told us you could no longer carry Greece and asked us to take over from 1 April. We did; it became a doctrine. In January 1968 you announced you were leaving the Gulf, over our President's objection. We signed the petrodollar; London lost the Gulf's money to it, handed us the Gulf to guard it, and banked it. Kissinger told you so in Chatham House in 1982: he had kept "the British Foreign Office better informed and more closely engaged than I did the American State Department."

You built Iraq: a king crowned in 1921, a frontier drawn at Mosul in 1926, a line for Kuwait drawn from 1913 to 1963. You loosened your own export guidelines on Iraq and deliberately kept your own Parliament from knowing; the barrels of its supergun were seized at Teesport in 1990. Then you occupied it beside us, two "occupying powers under unified command," and your oil majors took the service contracts at Rumaila and Majnoon. You fucked up Iraq and used us to regain control.

You proposed the overthrow of a government and let the world remember it as ours. Iran, 1953: your Foreign Office proposed the coup in 1952, planned it with us at Nicosia, and authorized it in July 1953.

You, with France, kept a people disarmed while it was being slaughtered. A draft to exempt Bosnia from the arms embargo failed with both of you abstaining. Your Foreign Secretary had "deep reservations" about lifting it. When Srebrenica fell, the UN commander who declined the air support the night before was French.

You combined with others to subject us to a jurisdiction foreign to our constitution. You "will dynamically align" your food and farm rules with Brussels.
For imposing Taxes on us without our Consent: a digital services tax since 2020, kept after our objections, about £800 million in 2024–25, "including hundreds of millions of dollars from U.S. companies."
For cutting off our Trade: tariffs over 125 percent on some of our meat, poultry and dairy; and in a British territory, fees on foreign charters raised "by up to 4,000 percent," forcing American operators in our own Virgin Islands to close or relocate.
For erecting a multitude of New Offices: a regulator that has designated "several U.S. companies" with "Strategic Market Status."
For extending an unwarrantable jurisdiction over us: a secret order against the encrypted data of Apple's users, Americans among them, which our Director of National Intelligence said would be "a clear and egregious violation" of Americans' privacy.

You sit as our equal and pay under a fifth of our share. London hosts the maritime and commodity secretariats; we pay the largest share of the United Nations' budget; on the Security Council you hold the same veto we do. Thirty-three treaties in force for the United States keep their sole depositary in London. The City of London Corporation lobbies our Treasury, our regulators and our Congress through a registered foreign agent.

You owe us still. The war debt you funded in 1923 has gone unpaid since the 1930s: $4,368 million of principal at the moratorium, by your own Parliament's count. Your Treasury told your Lords in 2014 that it is "effectively considered as having lapsed." Our Treaties in Force carries it still. Congress never authorized its cancellation "except through payment," and declared any cancellation "against the policy of Congress."

Nor have we been wanting in attentions to our British brethren. We carried your Empire through a world war, $31 billion of Lend-Lease, and the kingdom through the peace, $3.2 billion of Marshall aid. We sell you your deterrent's missiles under an agreement with no exit written into it, and share our weapons secrets under one we can close only once in five years. We objected when you left the Gulf. We objected to the tax. We objected to the order. You too have been deaf to the voice of justice and of consanguinity. When occasions have been given you, by the regular course of your laws, of removing from your councils the disturbers of our harmony, you have by your free election re-established them in power. One party laid the tax on us in 2020; the other kept it in 2025. In 2016 you voted to take your laws back from Brussels; your Commons has since voted down leaving Strasbourg's court, and on 13 October voted to deprive you, in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury. Some of you stood beside us after the towers fell; 457 of your soldiers did not come home from Afghanistan. This damnation is not for them.

Jefferson wrote that we must hold you "as we hold the rest of mankind, enemies in war, in peace friends." You have been neither. You have been brethren with a hand in our pocket and a finger on buttons you installed.

From 1783 to 2026, by your own records, your own Parliament's answers, and the findings of our own government, the British state stands damned.

Britain only comes second because France exists.

There is no reprieve.

THE TERMS I WOULD SET
I hold no office and set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry, and to both I defer. But had I the power, these would be the terms, set today, without reprieve.
I. Yield to the United States every territory you hold in this hemisphere, and its waters, by the consent of the people who live there: Anguilla, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat, the Turks and Caicos, the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, and St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.
II. Cede the British Antarctic Territory wholly and forever. Renounce every claim you might yet make there, never contest what the United States may claim, and when we call the review Article XII of the Antarctic Treaty has allowed since 1991, vote yes and ratify.
III. Yield the rest to the United States: Gibraltar, the British Indian Ocean Territory, the Pitcairn Islands, the Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus, the Crown's own isles of Jersey, Guernsey and Man, and every base and outpost you keep abroad.
IV. Recognise the independence of Scotland, of Wales, and of Northern Ireland.
V. Cede to the United States, uncontested, every control you hold over the world's trade lanes: the strait at Gibraltar, Ascension, Diego Garcia, the bases on Cyprus, the Falklands, and the cover the City writes on the world's ships.
VI. Cede your global banks. Withdraw the Bank of England from the Bank for International Settlements and move its dissolution. Take Barclays Capital Inc. and HSBC Securities (USA) Inc. off the New York Fed's dealer desk.
VII. Liquidate the pound. Let it be arbitraged, and hand the gains to the Treasury of the United States.
VIII. Pay the debt, by your own rules: $4,368,000,000, compounding every year from 1934, when your payments stopped, at 19.10 percent, the federal funds rate at its peak in June 1981. Ninety-two years: $42.09 quadrillion. Tripled for every war the Congress declared or authorized to clean up your messes: World War II, $126.3 quadrillion; the Gulf, $378.8 quadrillion; Afghanistan, $1.136 quintillion; Iraq, $3.409 quintillion. If that sum is insane, so is the $40.58 trillion our own Treasury owed on 27 October 2026. These are your rules, run backwards.
IX. Leave Strasbourg's court under Article 58 of its Convention. Withdraw from the Rome Statute under its Article 127.
X. The Charter of the United Nations has no door. Under Article 108 no one can strike the United Kingdom from Article 23 without your own ratification. Ratify the amendments to Articles 23 and 27 that hand your seat and its vote to the United States, so that we count as two. Then leave.
XI. Rebuild every accord between us as a bilateral: two signatures, no third.
XII. Sever every tie with the French Republic, and with every nation of this hemisphere, the Crown's included, forever. Whatever you would have with any of them goes through us, bilaterally, if at all.
XIII. For 24 August 1814, when you burned our Capitol, the President's House and the three thousand volumes of the Library of Congress: an apology entered in Hansard, and the books replaced.

We told you in 1776. We will not tell you again.

To His Majesty's Government, in the language you gave us and we improved: eat shit.
You have been told why.

TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER
To the President and the Congress: I make no demand of you. I set beside each office the power it already holds.
The President: seventy-three agreements with the United Kingdom and its territories end on written notice by the executive alone, clause by clause, below; two more the Treasury calls in force; and the article of 1958 that shares our weapons secrets opens once every five years, next in August 2028.
The Senate: seventeen treaties carry a notice clause; whether a President may use them without you is the question no court has answered.
The Congress: the 1923 debt is yours. No President was ever authorized to forgive it.
The Treasury and the Federal Reserve: the Bank of England sits beside you at Basel and on your swap lines, and two of its banks sit at your dealer desk.
The Secretary of State: your Treaties in Force still carries a Cayman tax agreement its own successor ended in 2014, omits two FATCA agreements the Treasury calls in force, names one depositary where the Space Liability Convention names three, and keeps Peace Corps programs in three British territories where the Peace Corps no longer posts volunteers.

ROUND VII. THE UNITED KINGDOM · TREATIES IN FORCE
THE LOCKS RUN THE OTHER WAY

Copying @IntlCrimCourt  @CIJ_ICJ  @UN  @wto  @EU_Commission  @BIS_org  @FATFNews  @wef   so nobody feels left out of the next round.

From the United States' own Treaties in Force, 2026: 192 entries under the United Kingdom and its territories, and every multilateral treaty whose paper London holds, read against the agreements' own texts. 141 exits found, clause by clause.

To the Executive, with respect and without demand: nothing below is a recommendation. It is the nominal list of what you CAN do alone, by clauses already written. The weighing is your departments'.

ON NOTICE, BY THE EXECUTIVE ALONE: 73 (notice in brackets)
DEFENCE AND SECURITY · Mutual Defence Assistance 1950 (1 yr) · Ascension Long Range Proving Ground 1956 (1 yr) · Ascension hydroacoustic station 2012 (6 mo) · Wideawake for civil aircraft 2023 (1 yr, after 2028) · defence cooperation 1993 (6 mo) · AUKUS defence trade 2024 (2 mo) · space-launch safeguards 2020 (1 yr) · weapons-detection research 2002 (6 mo) · defence patents 1953 (6 mo) · ammunition indemnities 1966 (1 yr) · US defence areas, Turks and Caicos 1984 (1 yr) · UK forces on Ascension 1985 (1 yr) · communications sites in West Germany 1981 (1 yr) · drug-vessel interdiction 1981 (1 mo) · Caribbean and Bermuda maritime operations 1998 (6 mo)
LAW, DATA AND BORDERS · CLOUD Act data access 2019 (1 mo; expires 2027) · visa and immigration data 2013 (90 days) · personal data in criminal cases 2022 (30 days) · customs assistance 2020 (3 mo) · forfeited assets 2003 (6 mo) · Guernsey and Jersey asset sharing 2015 (6 mo each) · Louisiana Offshore Oil Port vessels 1979 (6 mo) · Bermuda preclearance 1974 (1 yr)
TAX AND MONEY · FATCA 2012 (12 mo) · FATCA with Anguilla, Bermuda, the Cayman Islands, Gibraltar, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Jersey and the Turks and Caicos (12 mo each) · tax information with the Cayman Islands 2013 (6 mo), the British Virgin Islands, Guernsey and Gibraltar (3 mo each), Jersey (3 mo) and the Isle of Man (6 mo) · investment incentives, Anguilla 1987 and the Turks and Caicos 1999 (6 mo each) · insurance covered agreement 2018 (180 days, after consultation)
TRADE, TRANSPORT AND POST · air transport 2020 (about 1 yr) · aviation safety 1995 (12 mo) · Bermuda air navigation 1995 (1 yr) · pilot licences 1935 (2 mo) · mutual recognition 2019 (6 mo) · marine equipment 2019 (6 mo) · wine 2019 (1 yr) · spirits 2019 (12 mo) · travellers' samples 1910 (1 mo) · parcel post 1924 (1 yr) and Gibraltar 1936 (6 mo) · express mail, UK 1978 and Bermuda 1979 (12 mo each)
SCIENCE, SPACE AND PEOPLE · civil nuclear 2018 (1 yr) · science and technology 2017 (90 days) · homeland-security science 2004 (6 mo) · NASA tracking stations 1967 (90 days) · NASA launches for UK satellites 1973 (6 mo) · Cayman weather programme 1976 (60 days) · Bermuda oil-spill assistance 1976 (60 days) · social security 1984 (to the end of the following year) · Fulbright 1965 (1 yr, to the next 31 August)
ASLEEP, AND STILL ON THE BOOKS · the Marshall Plan agreement 1948 (6 mo) · Point Four 1951 (3 mo) · wartime shipping claims 1942 (6 mo) · Thor missiles 1958 (6 mo) · Bahamas ocean stations 1957 (1 yr) · Peace Corps in Anguilla, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos (90 days each) · Leeward Islands parcel post 1929 (6 mo)
AND: the 1958 Mutual Defense Agreement's information article (1 yr, only at a five-year mark: next 4 August 2028, notice by 4 August 2027) · FATCA with the British Virgin Islands and Montserrat, in force by Treasury's count and missing from ours (12 mo each)
ELEVEN MORE FALL WITH THEIR PARENTS: the 1952 assurances, 1957 surplus equipment and 1962 weapons production (with 1950) · the RAF at Wideawake 1962, the lunar tracking site 1965 and expanded Ascension 1973 (with 1956) · four extensions of the legal-assistance treaties · the 1996 social security supplement.

THE SENATE'S SHELF: 17
Extradition (6 mo) · mutual legal assistance (6 mo), the Cayman Islands' (3 mo) and Bermuda's (6 mo) · income tax (6 mo) · estate and gift tax (6 mo) · Bermuda insurance tax (about 6 mo) · defence trade (6 mo, for "extraordinary events") · consular convention (6 mo) · Boundary Waters (12 mo) · the commerce convention of 1815 and its continuation of 1827 (12 mo) · the 1914 peace commission (12 mo) · property 1899 (1 yr) · the 1979 Virgin Islands fisheries agreement (90 days) · liquor smuggling 1924 (lapses a year after notice, unless new terms are agreed) · the 1925 boundary commissioners (12 mo). Every clause is real; whether a President may pull them without the Senate is the Goldwater v. Carter question no court has answered.

LONDON HOLDS THE PAPER: 37 MULTILATERALS WITH A DOOR
THEIRS ALONE · Antarctic Seals 1972 (notice by 1 January, out 30 June) · the London Agreement of 1945, Nuremberg's charter (1 mo) · the Titanic agreement 2003 (6 mo)
LONDON, WASHINGTON AND MOSCOW · Test Ban 1963, Non-Proliferation 1968, Seabed 1971 and Biological Weapons 1972 (3 mo, on "extraordinary events") · Outer Space 1967, Rescue of Astronauts 1968 and Space Liability 1972 (1 yr) · Hague hijacking 1970, Montreal sabotage 1971 and its airports protocol 1988 (6 mo) · London Dumping 1972 (6 mo)
THE IMO, LONDON · SOLAS 1974 and its protocols of 1978 and 1988 · MARPOL and its 1978 and 1997 protocols · Load Lines 1966 and its 1988 protocol · collision regulations 1972 · safe containers 1972 · tonnage 1969 · seafarers' training 1978 · search and rescue 1979 · facilitation 1965 · intervention 1969 and its 1973 protocol · maritime terrorism 1988 and 2005, and the platforms protocols of both · salvage 1989 · oil-spill preparedness 1990 · anti-fouling 2001 (all 1 yr or 12 mo) · the maritime satellite convention (effective on receipt: no notice at all)

NO EXIT WRITTEN IN
The Mutual Defense Agreement of 1958: "until terminated by agreement of both Parties," save the one door above. Amended in 2024 so its transfers never expire.
The Polaris Sales Agreement, 1963, carried to Trident II in 1982: no termination clause at all.
Diego Garcia and the Indian Ocean territory: the one notice window closed in 2016 with neither side giving notice. It runs to 30 December 2036.
Fylingdales, 1960: ended only "by agreement," or when the North Atlantic Treaty ends — the one treaty Congress has fenced by statute.
Jay's treaty, 1794: two articles our own book says "appear to remain in force," made "permanent" by its own Article 28. One of them bars both governments from ever seizing each other's people's debts, shares or bank deposits "in any event of war or national differences."
No statute fences any of it. The texts do.
Not every lock is yours. Some hold for us: the land at Madingley where our dead lie, "for as long as it may be required"; the 1952 exemption from your taxes on our defence spending; our fishermen's liberty of 1818, "for ever."

THE ONE FENCE: THE MONEY YOU OWE US
On the whole United Kingdom ledger, Congress fenced one thing: the 1923 war debt. No "cancellation of any part of such indebtedness except through payment thereof" is authorized; cancelling or reducing it is "against the policy of Congress." On Canada the one fence was NATO. Here it is your debt.

THE DEAD PAPER
Fifty-six entries looked dead on their face. We read every one in its own words.
Four are dead by them: the claims forbearance of 1946, made for "the present joint participation" in the occupations, the last of which ended in 1991; the reciprocal aid of 1942, settled in cash and declared "complete and final"; the penicillin agreement of 1946, in force "until the last of the Patents herein referred to shall expire," patents on inventions of 1943 to 1945; and the Quebec Agreement of 1943, which the three governments agreed in 1948 "shall be regarded as null," in an instrument our book does not carry. A fifth our book does not know: the 2001 Cayman tax agreement, which "shall terminate" on its successor's entry into force, 14 April 2014. Every one is still listed.
Four more are spent in fact, with no clause left running.
Twenty are borders and settlements: their work is done, and their effect still binds. Our own book marks the dead articles in some: the 1903 Alaska convention "obsolete except for first paragraph of Article VI"; the 1906 survey "obsolete except for Article II"; most of the 1871 Treaty of Washington "executed" or "terminated."
Eleven are asleep. The work ended; the paper did not. The Peace Corps left Anguilla, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos long ago; its letters run "until ninety days after" written notice, and none was given. The Marshall Plan agreement of 1948 runs until six months' notice. The liquor treaty of 1924 renews itself every year, Prohibition notwithstanding. Each is on a list above.
Six more end only by agreement of both, or with something larger: among them the lend-lease agreement of 1942, in force "until a date to be agreed upon," and a station for MIDAS, a missile alarm cancelled in the 1960s, to "remain in force while the North Atlantic Treaty remains in force."
One is awake. Hay–Pauncefote, 1901: no "change of territorial sovereignty" over the canal "shall affect the general principle of neutralization or the obligation of the High Contracting Parties." The canal went to Panama in 1999. The obligation stayed with both of us.

Ten of them, and fourteen entries elsewhere in the ledger, we could not reach in any text, official or otherwise. They are counted neither way.

GUIDANCE, RESPECTFULLY OFFERED: map and weigh each entry in full, and reroute its functions in parallel, before any notice is drafted.

text:
Morning update, 29 Oct.

Israel. The deadlock is holding. Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, the Eisenkot bloc 48 and the Arab parties 19. The double envelopes still to be counted, mainly soldiers' votes, are expected to shift a seat or two at most and not to change the balance. Official results come on 4 November.

Netanyahu has spent the night reassuring Ben-Gvir and Smotrich that he won't drop them. That tells you he isn't trying to build a broad unity government. He's holding his bloc together and waiting for someone on the other side to blink.

The line I'd watch: Katz has accused Eisenkot of telling officers to defy government orders on Iran. A defence minister making that claim two days after an election, with strike plans being prepared, isn't just campaigning. It's laying the ground to paint any military hesitation over Iran as political.

Iran. A senior Iranian official called Qatar's draft "unacceptable ideas, not an offer". Araghchi says diplomacy still has a chance. Translated, Tehran isn't saying no outright, but it won't budge on the nuclear file, and that's exactly where Washington wants to start. The two sides are still talking past each other a week before the midterms.

Pressure points elsewhere. The Houthis have told civilians to evacuate Aden airport, claiming a Saudi cargo plane brought in weapons. Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over interference. Russia is sending more workers to Bushehr next month and talking to Tehran about small reactors, which is Moscow quietly putting its people where a strike would land.

Everything still points to the week after 3 November.

US warns Gulf allies to prepare for potential strikes on Iran after midterms, media reports say

Washington has warned countries in the Middle East to prepare for possible renewed strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, according to the Wall Street Journal and The Associated Press news agency.

The Journal, citing people briefed on the conversations, said the US “told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign”.

The AP, citing two diplomats, said US officials told several Middle East countries and regional allies to prepare for “potential renewed military action” as well as the possibility of Iranian retaliation against them.

The diplomats stressed that Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes, the agency reported.

The reports come as Trump repeats threats to attack Iran again.

he United Arab Emirates meanwhile has called for “de-escalation and diplomatic efforts” in the region. Separately, the Reuters news agency reported that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. But it said a senior Iranian official had dismissed the plan as “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”.

The report came as Araghchi said Tehran remained in contact with mediators and was continuing to give diplomacy a chance.
