FIRST LOOK AT RAINFALL TOTALS FOR THIS WEEKEND! 🌧️ But first, let's talk about the TOASTY day we have ahead! We're looking at mostly sunny skies with afternoon highs climbing into the upper 70s and lower 80s for most of us OFF the Cumberland Plateau. For those of you living the "high life" up on the Plateau, temperatures should stay in the lower 70s. Our average high for October 29th is around 68 degrees, so we're running a good 10–12 degrees ABOVE NORMAL in many locations. A little on the toasty side for sure!

NOW, LET'S TALK ABOUT SOME MUCH-NEEDED RAIN! We're FINALLY getting close enough to our first rain system in more than two weeks that we can begin discussing potential rainfall totals! That's been the BIG question lately, and I've got some good news... along with a little bit of a reality check. Remember earlier this week when I said we needed to "pump the brakes" on some of those model-generated rainfall maps showing widespread totals of 2–3+ inches? THIS is exactly why! Things change. They ALWAYS do! And unfortunately, if you were getting your hopes up for a BIG soaking rain this weekend based on some of those maps being shared around, you might want to lower those expectations just a bit.

MY FIRST CALL FORECAST shows widespread rainfall totals of around 0.25–0.50 inches across Southern Middle Tennessee through Sunday night. A few locations COULD pick up as much as an inch, especially if some heavier pockets of rain develop. However, with limited instability (storm fuel) available and thunderstorms looking pretty unlikely, I'm leaning more toward a nice, steady, moderate rain for most of us rather than widespread heavy downpours.

Now, before you get too disappointed, THERE IS STILL HOPE! I'm actually becoming more encouraged about a SECOND, potentially more impressive rain system heading our way NEXT WEEK! That system could bring some better rainfall totals to complement whatever we manage to pick up this weekend. And remember, we're still JUST outside that sweet spot for some of our more reliable short-range weather models, so adjustments to these totals may still be needed!

WHAT ABOUT HALLOWEEN? 🎃 As of right now, I'm still feeling pretty good about most Halloween activities, especially those taking place BEFORE 9 PM Saturday. Rain chances will gradually increase Saturday evening and overnight, with our southern and western counties likely seeing rain FIRST and our northern and eastern counties seeing it LAST. I'm continuing to watch for any shifts toward an earlier arrival, so don't completely let your guard down just yet! Sunday, on the other hand, is looking QUITE rainy as we officially "fall back" into Central Standard Time! And hey, look at the bright side... we get an extra hour of sleep AND some much-needed rainfall! That's a win-win, right? RIGHT?! 😂

I'll continue fine-tuning both the rainfall totals and Halloween timing as new weather data comes in. Stay tuned!

text:
Clara Belle Williams dedicated her life to education as a teacher, life-long student, and devoted mother. She went on to receive many honors during her lifetime and was an inspiration as she succeeded despite significant obstacles of discrimination placed before her while pursuing her higher education.

. . . 

In 1937, Clara Belle Williams was ready to graduate from college. She was 51 years old, a mother of three, and a longtime teacher. She had spent summers studying for the degree she had finally earned.

But some of her white classmates refused to walk in a commencement ceremony with a Black woman. The ceremony was canceled. Williams received her diploma through the registrar's window.

She had faced that same exclusion for years. In 1928, Williams enrolled at New Mexico College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts, now New Mexico State University, while teaching at a segregated school in Las Cruces. Some professors would not allow her inside their classrooms. She stood in the hallway, listened to lectures and took notes outside the door.

Williams was no novice student. Born in Texas in 1885, she had graduated as valedictorian from Prairie View and devoted much of her adult life to teaching. She and her husband Jasper were raising three sons. College classes were offered to her during summers, and she returned year after year.

In 1937, she became the school's first Black graduate, earning a bachelor's degree in English. She later recalled that only 13 students were due to graduate. Their objections meant there was no procession for her to join.

She continued teaching Black children in Las Cruces. She also helped later Black college students secure housing when they were barred from campus dormitories. Her own three sons became physicians and established a medical clinic in Chicago.

Then, in 1980, the university invited Williams back. It awarded her an honorary doctorate, 43 years after she had been denied a proper commencement. At 94, she finally walked in a graduation ceremony.

The university later named its English building Clara Belle Williams Hall. Williams died in 1994 at 108.

The first time she earned a degree there, the school passed it to her through a window. The second time, it asked her to cross the stage.

A family doctor in the Chicago area is warning that hospitals are vaccinating children while they are under anesthesia, often without clear, informed consent from parents.
In his own words: “I'm a family doctor who practices in the suburbs and the city of Chicago. I wanted to offer some practical advice tonight to those of you who, like me, might be angry and very concerned about the news reports detailing the rise of what one hospital is calling, close your eyes, we'll immunize. This is a growing practice, perhaps pioneered at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia... where children are undergoing elective and emergency medical surgeries and being immunized while they're away from their parents in the operating room.”
He adds that parents have often given consent unknowingly or under duress, and that true informed consent is rarely being provided the way it should be. Flu shots are the most common, but RSV, COVID, and other vaccines are also being given while kids are sedated.
Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia has run its official “Close Your Eyes, We’ll Immunize” program since 2023 and reported giving 2,054 influenza doses this way in the 2025–2026 season alone. Children’s Hospital Colorado has done it for more than 18,000 patients since 2020. Lurie Children’s in Chicago and other facilities have similar offers, with staff raising the option on the day of surgery.
Imagine taking your child in for appendicitis. You sign a form saying the team can do what’s necessary to help your child. Fifteen minutes later, before the first incision, your child gets a flu shot you never specifically approved. That is the scenario the doctor is describing.
Ask, in writing, before your child goes under. Do not assume a general surgical consent covers vaccines.

text:
***BOOK REVIEW***

Few episodes in Tudor history had consequences as far-reaching as King Henry VIII’s ‘Great Matter’. Determined to annul his marriage to Katherine of Aragon so that he could marry Anne Boleyn, Henry set in motion events that would transform England’s relationship with Rome and reshape its religious and political future. Yet there is a delicious irony at the heart of the story: the king so desperate for a male heir could never have imagined that his daughter Elizabeth would one day become one of England’s most celebrated monarchs.

Having read numerous books and articles on the subject over the years, I was intrigued by Helene’s fresh approach to this familiar chapter of Tudor history. Her central argument is that the ‘Great Matter’ should be understood as a much longer process than is generally assumed, rather than simply an attempt to annul Henry’s marriage to Katherine so that he could marry Anne Boleyn. She makes a convincing case for looking beyond the immediate question of the annulment to explore the wider developments that shaped the story.

The early chapters examine Henry’s marriage to Katherine before turning to a subject that is too often overlooked: Henry did, in fact, have a son, Henry FitzRoy, Duke of Richmond and Somerset, born outside his marriage. Helene explores the implications of his existence and considers what might have happened had FitzRoy lived.

I was also interested in Helene’s examination of Thomas Cromwell’s role in the Great Matter. Anne Boleyn and Cromwell are often presented as political allies, but how much evidence actually supports this assumption? Helene offers a different interpretation, carefully examining the evidence to provide a fresh perspective on their relationship and its significance.

The book is thoroughly referenced, with primary sources examined closely and translations analysed for their potential meanings. I particularly appreciated this attention to detail, which encourages readers to look beyond familiar narratives and consider how our understanding of the period is shaped by the surviving evidence.

Readers with a passion for Tudor history will find plenty here to challenge their assumptions and provide food for thought.

Many thanks to Pen and Sword for sending me a copy of this book

text:
French involvement in the #WarsoftheRoses is often overlooked. The French Regent Anne of Beaujeu funded Henry Tudor’s 1485 invasion against #RichardIII, but this wasn’t an isolated intervention.

OTD in 1480 - the Milanese embassy in France reported that the French paid the Scots to invade England. According to a despatch sent to Milan:  "the Scots have attacked the English & I think it is the handiwork of the king here [France]I am confirmed in this opinion because I chance to have seen a letter of the King of Scotland to the king here, in which he advises him that the English made an incursion into his country, but his people had forthwith cast them out, & they had done but little harm & gone away with the worst of it... | am practically certain that the king here has a hand in it, since he asks him for help against the English.’

The King of France referred to in the letter was Louis XI, known variously as ‘the Prudent’ or the ‘Universal Spider.’ His many schemes included playing an active role in the Wars of the Roses.

Louis had been negotiating with Warwick the Kingmaker to marry Princess Bona to #EdwardIV when the news of Edward’s secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville was revealed in 1464. He brokered the reconciliation between Warwick & Margaret of Anjou, which led to the brief restoration of Henry VI in 1470-71. He also paid Edward IV off in 1475 to end the English invasion of France. 

The Scottish attacks on northern England in 1480 were short lived, but in Louis’s eyes they served a purpose. They deflected English attention from France  & reduced the risk of another English invasion by giving England trouble through its back door. It is no coincidence that Edward IV had sought to secure this back door by making an agreement with James III of Scotland in 1474 as part of the preparations for his 1475 invasion of France. 

These attacks became part of a context of deteriorating Anglo-Scottish relations, doubtless as Louis had intended. James’s failure to follow through on the proposed marriage of his heir to Edward’s daughter Cecily (agreed as part of the 1474 treaty)  or to return her dowry then became a key catalyst for the 1482 English invasion of Scotland led by Edward’s brother Richard, Duke of Gloucester (later Richard III.) Louis must have been delighted. With the English forces engaged in Scotland there was no prospect of them attacking France any time soon.

After Louis’s death in August 1483 his daughter Anne served as regent for her younger brother Charles VIII. She funded Henry Tudor’s 1485 invasion of England because of the threat which the French believed Richard remaining as King posed to them. Richard was well known to be a foreign policy hawk who wanted to pursue England’s claim to France & restart the Hundred Years War. Within weeks of Richard becoming King in June 1483, Isabella of Castile made an offer to him in August 1483 to open her ports & provide military support for an English invasion of France.

text:
Name a prime minister in three hundred years who truly served the people 🤔 The two most people reach for are Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee, and both prove the same thing.

Half a century after he left office, Harold Wilson, Labour prime minister from 1964 to 1970 and again from 1974 to 1976, only looks like a man who put the people first because the bar has been dragged so low. When you've spent the winter choosing between heating and eating, a one-off energy rebate feels like generosity, and being grateful for the rebate is how you stop asking who owns the power.

The security of those years wasn't his doing. It was the tail of the post-war boom, and Wilson managed its surpluses without touching the foundations: who owns the land, who holds the wealth, the City of London, and power centralised at Westminster. When the boom ended, everything he had handed out was stripped away, because nothing underneath had changed.

He spent three years squeezing the economy to defend the value of the pound for the City, then devalued it anyway in 1967. His promised "white heat of technology" brought new ministries and committees, not a shift of power.

The coal industry was already shrinking. Wilson turned that into policy and paid for it: his Redundancy Payments Act of 1965 was sold to the Commons as "reducing resistance to change", and 212,000 mining jobs went in six years. Branch plants like the Linwood car factory near Paisley, owned from Detroit and kept alive on bail-outs, were gone by 1981. That is subsidised decline, managed from the centre.

When working people organised, his 1969 plan to curb the unions, In Place of Strife, treated them as a problem to be legally restrained, not the foundation of anything. When Scotland and Wales stirred, he offered assemblies with the real powers kept at Westminster, a safety valve. All the while his administration kept the McCrone report buried. Written in 1974 by Gavin McCrone, the Scottish Office's chief economic adviser, it found that Scotland's own oil would leave her in "chronic surplus to a quite embarrassing degree". It stayed hidden for thirty years, and Scots are still choosing between heating and eating on top of it.

The Welsh village of Capel Celyn was drowned in 1965 on his watch to give Liverpool a reservoir, under an Act that 35 of 36 Welsh MPs had opposed. Troops went onto the streets of Derry and Belfast in 1969, and by 1974 his officials were drafting secret plans to cut the north of Ireland adrift. His resignation honours, the so-called Lavender List, went to his business friends.

None of this lets the man off. Wilson was the managerial class at its most polished, and every time the choice came, he served the machine and managed the people. The machine is Crown-in-Parliament: the doctrine that the monarch in Parliament at Westminster holds unlimited power, so sovereignty sits there and not with the people. Whichever party wins office holds the whole machine between elections on a mandate it treats as a blank cheque. Wilson never had to ask the miners, the Welsh valleys, or Scotland about any of it, because the system never requires it. Scotland's most senior judge, Lord President Cooper, said as much in 1953: the unlimited sovereignty of Parliament is "a distinctively English principle which has no counterpart in Scottish constitutional law". In Scotland sovereignty sits with the people, and it was never in the loan they give a party at the ballot box.

Clement Attlee, prime minister from 1945 to 1951, is the best most can offer in the three hundred years since Robert Walpole became the first, and he built the NHS. His government still binned the 1949 Scottish Covenant, two million signatures asking for a parliament of their own. That is the system's ceiling: in a hierarchy built to keep power at the top, even the best of them can do only as much good as the machine allows.

Those who lived through the 1970s watched the turn: the post-war settlement unravelling, the oil found and hidden, the industries run down. Ask them now and they will tell you it has been one long climb since, in greed, in extraction, and in class, each decade amplifying the last. Wilson did not start that climb, but he built the stairs.

That is the Crown-in-Parliament model, run from Westminster for the extraction class, the few who take the wealth out of the places that make it, and it has been for three hundred years: give working people just enough to keep them quiet, teach them to look to managers instead of to their own communities, and keep the owners of the wealth in charge. That is why nobody can name a good one. Calling it the good old days is how the cycle carries on. We don't need a better manager. We need to stop lending the manager what was never his to hold, and decide for ourselves, directly, on our own ground.

One more thing. Ask an Irish republican to name a good prime minister and they can't, because the Irish state doesn't have one. It has a Taoiseach, and Article 6 of its Constitution says the people have the right "in final appeal, to decide all questions of national policy". They use it. In March 2024 the Taoiseach put two amendments to them and they threw both out, 67.7 and 73.9 per cent No, the heaviest defeat in the state's history. He called it "two wallops" and said, "Clearly, I was incorrect." They refused to abolish the Seanad in 2013, rejected the Lisbon Treaty in 2008, and when a government tried to ratify a European treaty without them in 1987, the Supreme Court said it could not. No prime minister at Westminster has to answer to the people like that. The question was never who was a good leader. It is who gets the final say, and in Scotland that has always been the people too; the Irish just kept the habit of using it.

text:
PRESS BRIEFING BY MALLAM ALWAN HASSAN (@yesmylo) IN KANO STATE ON THE CASE FOR NORTHERN NIGERIA TO REELECT PRESIDENT BOLA AHMED TINUBU FOR A SECOND TERM IN OFFICE
Thursday, 29 October 2026

Distinguished members of the press, ladies and gentlemen,

Good morning.
I want to begin today's briefing by extending my warm congratulations to the leadership, members and supporters of the All Progressives Congress (APC) on the successful campaign rally held at the Ranchers Bees Stadium in Kaduna.

I congratulate the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, His Excellency Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, the leadership of our great party, the organisers of the rally and the thousands of Nigerians who came out to participate in what was a remarkable political gathering.

The turnout was impressive. The enthusiasm was unmistakable. From the stadium to the surrounding communities, Kaduna witnessed an extraordinary demonstration of political mobilisation.

For those of us who have followed political developments across Northern Nigeria, the significance of such a gathering cannot be overlooked.
It tells us something about the strength of party organization, the willingness of supporters to participate in the political process and the importance of Kaduna as a center of political activity in Northern Nigeria.

But rallies are only one part of the democratic process. The real test of political leadership is what happens beyond the stadium: in our communities, in our schools, in our markets, on our farms and in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

Three days ago, I gathered members of my ward in Dakata, Kano State, for a door-to-door engagement with residents. We visited homes, spoke with families and discussed the policies and programmes of the Federal Government.

It was an opportunity to hear directly from people about their experiences, their expectations and the challenges they continue to face. These conversations are important because the success of government policy cannot be measured by official announcements alone. It must also be measured by its effects on the people.
And this brings me to the central issue I want to address today: the economic and development record of the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Ladies and gentlemen,

When President Bola Ahmed Tinubu assumed office in May 2023, Nigeria faced serious economic challenges. The country was struggling with substantial fiscal pressures, a fragmented foreign exchange market, rising inflation and a public finance system under strain.
According to the Federal Government's State of the Economy presentation delivered to the Federal Executive Council on 28 October 2026, Nigeria's economy grew by only 2.74 per cent in 2023.

At the beginning of the administration, the country had net usable external reserves of approximately $859 million, despite gross reserves of about $35 billion.
The foreign exchange market was characterized by multiple windows and a spread exceeding 60 per cent.
The tax-to-GDP ratio stood at approximately 7 per cent, while debt servicing consumed about 97 per cent of government revenue. These were substantial economic challenges.

The administration responded with reforms intended to address the structural weaknesses in public finance, foreign exchange management and the allocation of national resources.

The removal of petrol subsidy and the restructuring of the foreign exchange market were among the most consequential decisions. They also imposed significant adjustment costs on Nigerians.

However, nearly three and a half years into the administration, the available economic indicators provide an opportunity to assess the progress that we have made.

The Nigerian economy recorded real GDP growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with annual growth of 2.74 per cent in 2023.

Headline inflation stood at 14.63 per cent in September 2026, according to the latest figures presented by the Federal Government.

Nigeria's gross external reserves reached $55.1 billion on 9 October 2026, with net reserves reported at approximately $46 billion.

The Federal Government also reported that our foreign exchange market spread had narrowed to less than 5 per cent.

The tax-to-GDP ratio increased from approximately 7 per cent to 12.5 per cent, while the ratio of debt service to government revenue declined to approximately 65 per cent in the first half of 2026.

These figures point to changes in the country's fiscal and macroeconomic position. They are evidence that President Tinubu’s economic policies are putting Nigeria in the right direction and affirm that we are achieving economic stability.

This economic stability we are achieving is providing the foundation for investment, business expansion, employment creation and sustainable public expenditure.

One important consequence of the economic reforms has been the increase in resources available to the three tiers of government.

According to official records of the Federal Government, net Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) distributions increased from N15.2 trillion in 2024 to N21.9 trillion in 2025. That is an increase of approximately 44 per cent.

The share of state government expenditure devoted to capital projects increased from 46 per cent in 2023 to 61 per cent in 2025.

Improved allocations to states is providing our sub-regional governments with greater fiscal capacity to invest in roads, schools, healthcare facilities, water infrastructure and other essential public services.

Ladies and gentlemen,

I will never get tired of speaking about NELFUND. It is one of the most impactful programmes of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's administration.

For years, many Nigerian parents have struggled to pay their children's tuition fees. Some have had to borrow money, sell their possessions or make difficult sacrifices just to keep their children in school. Others have watched helplessly as their children abandoned their education because the family could no longer afford it.

Today, NELFUND is helping to change that story.
As at September 2026, N372.6 billion has been disbursed in student loans, with 1.66 million applications processed. Behind these figures are Nigerian families who now have access to financial support for their children's education.

But the President's interventions in education do not end with students. They extend to the welfare of those who teach them and the institutions in which they learn.
Across the country, we continue to receive testimonies from teachers and academic staff about improvements in their welfare under this administration. Recently, President Tinubu cleared all outstanding Consolidated Academic Tools Allowance (CATA) arrears for academic staff across the country. ALL!

This is significant because the welfare of our teachers and lecturers is fundamental to the quality of education we provide. We cannot demand excellence from our educational institutions while neglecting the people responsible for training the next generation of Nigerians.

The administration has also continued to address infrastructure deficits in our tertiary institutions. So far, N38.93 billion has been disbursed to 166 public tertiary institutions through the Needs Assessment Revitalisation Funds to improve teaching and learning facilities and address longstanding infrastructure challenges.

Today, under this administration, we can see an approach that addresses three important pillars of education: access for students, welfare for academic staff and infrastructure for institutions.

These are investments in the future of Nigeria.

The administration's economic interventions also extend to vulnerable households and small businesses.
As of today, more than 10 million households have been reached through its cash transfer programme, with over N600 billion disbursed. The programme provides N75,000 per beneficiary household in three instalments.

Similarly, more than 800,000 micro, small and medium enterprises have reportedly benefited from Bank of Industry financing schemes.

These interventions address different but related challenges. Cash transfers provide immediate assistance to vulnerable families, while affordable business financing can help enterprises purchase equipment, expand production and create employment.

I must also speak about the remarkable achievements of the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), whose Board is chaired by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and which is led by a proud son of Kano State, Khalil Halilu.

Today, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the United States is partnering with NASENI and the Presidential Implementation Committee on Technology Transfer (PICTT) to establish regional acceleration programmes for innovation and entrepreneurship. The first agricultural hub, located in Adamawa State has been established. It covers approximately 40,000 hectares of land and is designed to provide a complete agricultural ecosystem, from production to processing and commercialisation. This is an initiative that brings together technology, agriculture and enterprise to create opportunities and unlock the enormous economic potential of our country.

Under President Tinubu, NASENI is also training thousands of engineers, equipping a new generation of Nigerians with the skills to drive our country's technological and industrial future. The agency is assemblying Made-in-Nigeria vehicles. It is building drones and training thousands of Nigerians to operate them. These are practical investments in our industrial capacity, our young people and our ability to develop and manufacture the technologies we need.

This is the kind of government that is building for the future. A government that is not merely talking about innovation but investing in it. A government that is not content with importing technology but is developing the capacity to produce it here in Nigeria. A government that understands that the future of our economy must be built on the ingenuity, skills and productive capacity of Nigerians.
Ladies and gentlemen,

In Northern Nigeria, the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has undertaken significant investments in road infrastructure, education and regional connectivity.

Across the region, federal road projects are being constructed, rehabilitated and completed to address longstanding infrastructure deficits and improve economic activities.

These interventions are particularly important to the North, where agriculture, commerce and the movement of goods depend heavily on reliable transportation networks.

More than 6,000 road projects are ongoing or have been completed across northern Nigeria under President Bola Tinubu. In the North West alone, 348km of roads have been completed, out of 1,016km that have been completed nationwide.

Among the major projects is the Akwanga–Jos–Bauchi–Gombe–Biu–Maiduguri Superhighway, a strategic road corridor connecting the North-Central and North-East geopolitical zones.

In July this year, the Federal Government flagged off construction of the first section of this approximately 700-kilometre highway. The initial phase covers about 125 kilometres from Akwanga in Nasarawa State to Jos in Plateau State. When completed, this highway will improve connectivity between communities, facilitate the movement of agricultural produce, reduce transportation difficulties and strengthen economic integration across the region.

We have also achieved the completion of the first 118-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria corridor, including 81 kilometres constructed with reinforced concrete pavement. Work continues on other sections of the highway, while President Tinubu has directed the installation of solar-powered streetlights along the entire 375-kilometre corridor.

This is one of the country's most important transportation routes. It connects the Federal Capital Territory with Kaduna and Kano, two major centres of commerce, industry and population in Northern Nigeria.
Its rehabilitation is important not only for motorists but also for traders, manufacturers, transport operators and businesses that depend on the movement of goods between these cities.

The President @officialABAT administration is equally pursuing other major projects, including the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, Kano Northern Bypass, Kano–Katsina Road, Zaria–Funtua–Gusau–Sokoto Road and sections of the Kano–Maiduguri Road.

These projects represent substantial investments in the transportation infrastructure required to support agriculture, commerce and industrial development particularly in Northern Nigeria.

Infrastructure development does not end with roads. Under President Tinubu it also extends to the classrooms where the next generation of Nigerians is being educated.

In Kano State alone, the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) has undertaken interventions to improve learning conditions in our public primary schools.

These include the renovation of more than 50 primary schools across 15 local government areas, the rehabilitation of classroom blocks and the provision of over 16,000 furniture items.

In July 2026, the Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, confirmed to Nigerians that the Commission had delivered nearly 4,000 classrooms across Kano State as part of efforts to expand access to quality basic education.

These important investments in our basic education mean improved learning environments for children, better facilities for teachers and additional support for communities where inadequate educational infrastructure has remained a longstanding challenge.

Ladies and Gentlemen of the Press,

I will conclude by expressing my disgust at the former Vice President, who served Nigeria from 1999 to 2007 and has since been desperate to become President, despite having nothing to offer.

It is extremely offensive that Atiku, who served in an administration and was a member of the Party that created and left many of Nigeria's longstanding problems unresolved, now presents himself as the answer to those same problems.

Atiku has run for the presidency again and again, and Nigerians keep turning him down. They know he is not the solution. He is the problem. He has no ideas.

He went from customs officer to billionaire without ever explaining how. That unexplained wealth has bankrolled him election after election, and he is now reportedly selling off properties to keep his campaign alive. Nigerians are right to worry: if such a man reached office, would he not spend his first four years recouping his investment?

Atiku should retire and enjoy whatever is left of his customs-days largesse!

Public office is not a place to recover political investments. Nigeria’s treasury belongs to the Nigerian people!

And on the North, Atiku must account for his record. The people of the North deserve more than declarations of his pretentious concern. What has he done for the North in 27 years? Where are his investments? In Dubai! Yet he wants us to believe he has the North’s interest at heart?

@atiku, go and retire! You have nothing to offer!

Thank you, ladies and gentlemen.

God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

$KYMR Q3 2026 earnings: Kymera's new autoimmune pill passes human tests, while trial costs rise

Kymera Therapeutics, a biotech developing daily pills that destroy disease-causing proteins, cleared a key human test while its trial costs climbed. Chief executive Nello Mainolfi reported that its second pill, KT-579, cut its target protein by at least 90% in healthy volunteers with side effects matching placebo. Meanwhile, research spending rose 73% from a year ago to $129 million as partner revenue dropped to zero.

• KT-579 Phase 1 IRF5 protein reduction: >=𝟗𝟎% (target: >90% reduction)
• Research and development spending: $𝟏𝟐𝟖.𝟓𝐌 (+73% from a year ago)
• Cash and marketable securities: $𝟏.𝟔𝟓𝐁 ($1.50B last quarter)
• Full-year collaboration revenue outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (zero revenue planned for Q4)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the company proved its second autoimmune pill works in humans ahead of schedule and finished patient visits in its main eczema trial. That removes the early human translation doubt on KT-579 before the year-end readout for its lead drug, KT-621. One caution: the quarterly loss reached $132 million as late-stage trial prep ramped up.

The question now is whether KT-621 can match the skin clearance of injectable drugs in its year-end eczema readout without a high placebo response blurring the result. Either the pill delivers clear shot-like relief that justifies a large Phase 3 program, or a modest gap over placebo leaves it vulnerable to rival pills. Top-line data from the BROADEN2 eczema trial by the end of 2026 will decide it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐊𝐓-𝟓𝟕𝟗 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐇𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲
KT-579 is Kymera's daily pill designed to destroy IRF5, a protein that drives autoimmune diseases such as lupus. Chief executive Nello Mainolfi had promised initial healthy-volunteer results in the fourth quarter, and the key question was whether animal results would hold up in people. "These findings exceed our expectations in terms of depth of degradation, safety and pathway suppression measured by downstream cytokines and gene transcripts," Mainolfi said.

• IRF5 protein reduction in blood: 90% or more across multiple doses, reaching maximum effect by the third dose level
• Inflammatory marker reductions at Day 14: 88% for TNF-alpha, 87% for IL-12/23p40, 94% for IL-1-beta, and 98% for IFN-beta
• Safety: "The safety profile of KT-579 was comparable to placebo", with no serious side effects or dropouts

These results beat the 50% to 80% marker reduction target that management set last quarter, and the drug lowered IRF5 in skin as well as blood. Because healthy volunteers do not have active autoimmune disease, this trial softens the translation risk rather than settling it. The biotech company now plans to test KT-579 in about 30 lupus patients over 16 weeks in the LUMORA trial, starting by early 2027.

What to watch: the start of the LUMORA Phase 1b lupus study by early 2027 and its first patient data later on. Strong marker and symptom improvements in lupus patients would prove the pill works in sick people, not just stimulated blood samples.

🟢 𝐄𝐜𝐳𝐞𝐦𝐚 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐄𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐮𝐭
KT-621 is Kymera's lead daily pill, built to clear STAT6, the protein behind allergic inflammation in eczema and asthma. The drug maker wants KT-621 to offer shot-like relief in a pill for over 140 million patients with Type 2 inflammatory diseases. In October, the last patient finished the 16-week visit in the BROADEN2 Phase 2b eczema trial, after the company hired chief medical officer Terence Rooney and program leader Elizabeth Laws in July.

Finishing all patient visits locks in the timeline for the company's biggest catalyst, which management already pulled forward by about six months earlier this year. The Massachusetts group remains on track to report top-line eczema results by the end of 2026 and start Phase 3 testing by mid-2027, while its BREADTH Phase 2b asthma trial continues enrolling for a late-2027 readout.

What to watch: top-line week-16 skin clearance and safety results from the BROADEN2 eczema trial by the end of 2026. Clear skin improvement over placebo without new side effects would support starting Phase 3 trials in mid-2027.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐉𝐮𝐦𝐩𝐬 𝟕𝟑% 𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐬
Kymera has no commercial drugs on the market, so it funds its trials with cash on hand and occasional milestone payments from partners Sanofi and Gilead Sciences. After collecting $99.4 million of partner revenue in the first half of 2026, the company booked zero revenue in the third quarter and confirmed that "The Company does not expect to recognize additional collaboration revenue in 2026".

• Research and development (R&D) spending: $128.5 million, up 73.4% from a year ago and up 7.6% from last quarter
• Cash R&D spending, excluding stock pay: $117.6 million by our math, up 79.0% from a year ago
• Net loss: $132.0 million, or $1.32 per share, compared with $82.2 million a year ago

The company said R&D rose because it spent more on the STAT6 clinical trials, early discovery work, and hiring across the research team. Because partner revenue dropped to zero while trial costs climbed, the quarterly net loss widened by 60.6% from a year ago. By our math, total cash operating expenses excluding stock pay reached $128.4 million this quarter, and Phase 3 trials have not even started yet.

What to watch: fourth-quarter R&D spending and the first-half 2027 budget when Phase 3 eczema preparations begin. Another large step-up in quarterly spending would eat into the cash buffer faster than the current 2029 outlook assumes.

🔴 𝐊𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐚 𝐐𝐮𝐢𝐞𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐓𝐞𝐧-𝐃𝐫𝐮𝐠 𝐆𝐨𝐚𝐥
At the end of 2024, Kymera told investors it was on a path to put a total of 10 experimental degrader drugs into human trials by the end of 2026. In this quarter's release, Mainolfi called KT-579 "our 7 th degrader to enter the clinic", and the company now states "a goal to deliver at least one new development candidate per year".

With two months left in 2026 and no other drug ready to start human dosing this year, the biotech firm will finish 2026 at seven clinical programs rather than 10. Management never announced that it was dropping the 10-drug target after shelving earlier cancer and immune programs. Shifting the goal to one preclinical candidate a year lowers the pace of new shots on goal from its research engine.

What to watch: whether Kymera names a new development candidate for human testing by the end of 2026. Missing the one-candidate-per-year goal would show that the early research pipeline is slowing while money shifts to late-stage trials.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing risks around the year-end eczema readout, rival drugs, and the balance sheet could not be tested from the third-quarter press release alone.

• BROADEN2 trial bar and placebo rate: management has not shared the statistical powering or baseline patient severity, which the year-end 2026 readout will test.
• Safety in 16-week eczema dosing: whether KT-621 causes eye inflammation or other side effects in patients remains open until the year-end 2026 data release.
• STAT6 competition: how Kymera positions KT-621 against Pfizer's Phase 2 inhibitor and the Nurix and Sanofi degrader requires the conference call Q&A.
• Source of the third-quarter cash increase: cash rose by $141 million despite a $132 million net loss, and the quarterly filing's cash flow statement will show how much came from share sales.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟔𝟒𝟓.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities rose by $141.0 million from last quarter and grew 68.2% from a year ago. Even with $128.4 million in cash operating costs by our math and a $20 million Sanofi milestone collection, the balance climbed, pointing to financing inflows not detailed in the release.

𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟎𝟎.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
The average share count rose 14.7% from a year ago and 2.0% from last quarter, adding about 1.9 million shares sequentially. That 2.0% sequential increase helps explain why cash on the balance sheet rose during a quarter with no revenue, though the exact proceeds await the quarterly filing.

𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐝𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟖.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Overhead costs — spending on legal fees, executives, and office space — rose 8.0% from a year ago but fell 11.4% from $21.1 million last quarter. Stock-based pay made up $7.9 million of the total, leaving cash overhead at $10.8 million by our math.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟑.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Accrued expenses — bills for clinical trials and services that Kymera has recorded as costs but not yet paid in cash — jumped 49.8% from $42.3 million at the end of 2025. Delaying cash payments on those rising trial bills kept more cash on the balance sheet at quarter-end.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟗𝟗.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝)  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $99.4 million (implied)
Unchanged. The biotech group reiterated that it does not expect to book any more partner revenue in 2026 after recording $99.4 million in the first half. By our math, that leaves fourth-quarter collaboration revenue at zero, compared with $2.9 million in the fourth quarter of last year, until a partner hits a new clinical milestone in 2027 or later.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟗  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Into 2029
Unchanged. Management still expects its $1.65 billion cash pile to fund operations into 2029, past the upcoming eczema, asthma, and lupus readouts. By our math, funding the next 10 quarters into early 2029 allows an average net cash draw of about $165 million per quarter, well above this quarter's $128.4 million in cash operating expenses.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐛𝐲 $𝟏𝟒𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Cash and investments climbed from $1.50 billion to $1.65 billion even though Kymera posted a $132 million net loss and zero revenue. The release omits a cash flow statement, leaving unclear how much came from ATM share sales versus working capital.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐜𝐲 𝐠𝐚𝐩 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐛𝐨 𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐊𝐓-𝟔𝟐𝟏 𝐡𝐢𝐭?
With the BROADEN2 eczema trial now finished dosing and top-line data due by year-end, management still has not shared the trial's statistical powering or the placebo-adjusted skin clearance score it views as a commercial win.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐊𝐓-𝟔𝟐𝟏 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟑 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭?
R&D spending already hit $128.5 million this quarter before any Phase 3 study has begun. Investors need to know how many Phase 3 studies are included inside the 2029 cash runway and when a partner or new financing would be needed.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐊𝐓-𝟓𝟕𝟗 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐛𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭?
Following strong Phase 1 healthy-volunteer data, Kymera outlined a 30-patient lupus trial starting by early 2027. Management also listed rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease as targets, but gave no timeline for testing outside lupus.

PRESS BRIEFING BY MALLAM ALWAN HASSAN IN KANO STATE ON THE CASE FOR NORTHERN NIGERIA TO REELECT PRESIDENT BOLA AHMED TINUBU FOR A SECOND TERM IN OFFICE

Thursday, 29 October 2026

Distinguished members of the press, ladies and gentlemen,
Good morning.
I want to begin today's briefing by extending my warm congratulations to the leadership, members and supporters of the All Progressives Congress (APC) on the successful campaign rally held at the Ranchers Bees Stadium in Kaduna.

I congratulate the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, His Excellency Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, the leadership of our great party, the organisers of the rally and the thousands of Nigerians who came out to participate in what was a remarkable political gathering.
The turnout was impressive. 
The enthusiasm was unmistakable. 

From the stadium to the surrounding communities, Kaduna witnessed an extraordinary demonstration of political mobilisation.
For those of us who have followed political developments across Northern Nigeria, the significance of such a gathering cannot be overlooked.
It tells us something about the strength of party organisation, the willingness of supporters to participate in the political process and the importance of Kaduna as a centre of political activity in Northern Nigeria.

But rallies are only one part of the democratic process. The real test of political leadership is what happens beyond the stadium: in our communities, in our schools, in our markets, on our farms and in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

Three days ago, I gathered members of my ward in Dakata, Kano State, for a door-to-door engagement with residents. We visited homes, spoke with families and discussed the policies and programmes of the Federal Government.

It was an opportunity to hear directly from people about their experiences, their expectations and the challenges they continue to face. These conversations are important because the success of government policy cannot be measured by official announcements alone. It must also be measured by its effects on the people.
And this brings me to the central issue I want to address today: the economic and development record of the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Ladies and gentlemen,
When President Bola Ahmed Tinubu assumed office in May 2023, Nigeria faced serious economic challenges. The country was struggling with substantial fiscal pressures, a fragmented foreign exchange market, rising inflation and a public finance system under strain.
According to the Federal Government's State of the Economy presentation delivered to the Federal Executive Council on 28 October 2026, Nigeria's economy grew by only 2.74 per cent in 2023.

At the beginning of the administration, the country had net usable external reserves of approximately $859 million, despite gross reserves of about $35 billion.
The foreign exchange market was characterised by multiple windows and a spread exceeding 60 per cent.
The tax-to-GDP ratio stood at approximately 7 per cent, while debt servicing consumed about 97 per cent of government revenue.

These were substantial economic challenges.
The administration responded with reforms intended to address the structural weaknesses in public finance, foreign exchange management and the allocation of national resources.

The removal of petrol subsidy and the restructuring of the foreign exchange market were among the most consequential decisions. They also imposed significant adjustment costs on Nigerians.

However, nearly three and a half years into the administration, the available economic indicators provide an opportunity to assess the progress that we have made.

The Nigerian economy recorded real GDP growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with annual growth of 2.74 per cent in 2023.
Headline inflation stood at 14.63 per cent in September 2026, according to the latest figures presented by the Federal Government.

Nigeria's gross external reserves reached $55.1 billion on 9 October 2026, with net reserves reported at approximately $46 billion.
The Federal Government also reported that our foreign exchange market spread had narrowed to less than 5 per cent.

The tax-to-GDP ratio increased from approximately 7 per cent to 12.5 per cent, while the ratio of debt service to government revenue declined to approximately 65 per cent in the first half of 2026.
These figures point to changes in the country's fiscal and macroeconomic position. They are evidence that President Tinubu’s economic policies are putting Nigeria in the right direction and affirm that we are achieving economic stability.

This economic stability we are achieving is providing the foundation for investment, business expansion, employment creation and sustainable public expenditure.

One important consequence of the economic reforms has been the increase in resources available to the three tiers of government.

According to official records of the Federal Government, net Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) distributions increased from N15.2 trillion in 2024 to N21.9 trillion in 2025. That is an increase of approximately 44 per cent.

The share of state government expenditure devoted to capital projects increased from 46 per cent in 2023 to 61 per cent in 2025.
Improved allocations to states is providing our sub-regional governments with greater fiscal capacity to invest in roads, schools, healthcare facilities, water infrastructure and other essential public services.

Ladies and gentlemen,
I will never get tired of speaking about NELFUND. It is one of the most impactful programmes of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's administration.

For years, many Nigerian parents have struggled to pay their children's tuition fees. Some have had to borrow money, sell their possessions or make difficult sacrifices just to keep their children in school. Others have watched helplessly as their children abandoned their education because the family could no longer afford it.
Today, NELFUND is helping to change that story.

As at September 2026, N372.6 billion has been disbursed in student loans, with 1.66 million applications processed. Behind these figures are Nigerian families who now have access to financial support for their children's education.

But the President's interventions in education do not end with students. They extend to the welfare of those who teach them and the institutions in which they learn.

Across the country, we continue to receive testimonies from teachers and academic staff about improvements in their welfare under this administration. Recently, President Tinubu cleared all outstanding Consolidated Academic Tools Allowance (CATA) arrears for academic staff across the country. ALL!

This is significant because the welfare of our teachers and lecturers is fundamental to the quality of education we provide. 
We cannot demand excellence from our educational institutions while neglecting the people responsible for training the next generation of Nigerians.

The administration has also continued to address infrastructure deficits in our tertiary institutions. So far, N38.93 billion has been disbursed to 166 public tertiary institutions through the Needs Assessment Revitalisation Funds to improve teaching and learning facilities and address longstanding infrastructure challenges.

Today, under this administration, we can see an approach that addresses three important pillars of education: access for students, welfare for academic staff and infrastructure for institutions.
These are investments in the future of Nigeria.
The administration's economic interventions also extend to vulnerable households and small businesses.
As of today, more than 10 million households have been reached through its cash transfer programme, with over N600 billion disbursed. The programme provides N75,000 per beneficiary household in three instalments.

Similarly, more than 800,000 micro, small and medium enterprises have reportedly benefited from Bank of Industry financing schemes.
These interventions address different but related challenges.

Cash transfers provide immediate assistance to vulnerable families, while affordable business financing can help enterprises purchase equipment, expand production and create employment.

I must also speak about the remarkable achievements of the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), whose Board is chaired by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and which is led by a proud son of Kano State, Khalil Halilu.

Today, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the United States is partnering with NASENI and the Presidential Implementation Committee on Technology Transfer (PICTT) to establish regional acceleration programmes for innovation and entrepreneurship. The first agricultural hub, located in Adamawa State has been established. 
It covers approximately 40,000 hectares of land and is designed to provide a complete agricultural ecosystem, from production to processing and commercialisation. This is an initiative that brings together technology, agriculture and enterprise to create opportunities and unlock the enormous economic potential of our country.

Under President Tinubu, NASENI is also training thousands of engineers, equipping a new generation of Nigerians with the skills to drive our country's technological and industrial future. 
The agency is assemblying Made-in-Nigeria vehicles. It is building drones and training thousands of Nigerians to operate them. These are practical investments in our industrial capacity, our young people and our ability to develop and manufacture the technologies we need.
This is the kind of government that is building for the future. A government that is not merely talking about innovation but investing in it. 

A government that is not content with importing technology but is developing the capacity to produce it here in Nigeria. A government that understands that the future of our economy must be built on the ingenuity, skills and productive capacity of Nigerians.

Ladies and gentlemen,
In Northern Nigeria, the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has undertaken significant investments in road infrastructure, education and regional connectivity.

Across the region, federal road projects are being constructed, rehabilitated and completed to address longstanding infrastructure deficits and improve economic activities.
These interventions are particularly important to the North, where agriculture, commerce and the movement of goods depend heavily on reliable transportation networks.

More than 6,000 road projects are ongoing or have been completed across northern Nigeria under President Bola Tinubu. In the North West alone, 348km of roads have been completed, out of 1,016km that have been completed nationwide.

Among the major projects is the Akwanga–Jos–Bauchi–Gombe–Biu–Maiduguri Superhighway, a strategic road corridor connecting the North-Central and North-East geopolitical zones.

In July this year, the Federal Government flagged off construction of the first section of this approximately 700-kilometre highway. The initial phase covers about 125 kilometres from Akwanga in Nasarawa State to Jos in Plateau State. When completed, this highway will improve connectivity between communities, facilitate the movement of agricultural produce, reduce transportation difficulties and strengthen economic integration across the region.

We have also achieved the completion of the first 118-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria corridor, including 81 kilometres constructed with reinforced concrete pavement.

Work continues on other sections of the highway, while President Tinubu has directed the installation of solar-powered streetlights along the entire 375-kilometre corridor.

This is one of the country's most important transportation routes. It connects the Federal Capital Territory with Kaduna and Kano, two major centres of commerce, industry and population in Northern Nigeria.
Its rehabilitation is important not only for motorists but also for traders, manufacturers, transport operators and businesses that depend on the movement of goods between these cities.

The President Bola Tinubu administration is equally pursuing other major projects, including the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, Kano Northern Bypass, Kano–Katsina Road, Zaria–Funtua–Gusau–Sokoto Road and sections of the Kano–Maiduguri Road.

These projects represent substantial investments in the transportation infrastructure required to support agriculture, commerce and industrial development particularly in Northern Nigeria.
Infrastructure development does not end with roads. Under President Tinubu it also extends to the classrooms where the next generation of Nigerians is being educated.

In Kano State alone, the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) has undertaken interventions to improve learning conditions in our public primary schools.
These include the renovation of more than 50 primary schools across 15 local government areas, the rehabilitation of classroom blocks and the provision of over 16,000 furniture items.

In July 2026, the Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, confirmed to Nigerians that the Commission had delivered nearly 4,000 classrooms across Kano State as part of efforts to expand access to quality basic education.

These important investments in our basic education mean improved learning environments for children, better facilities for teachers and additional support for communities where inadequate educational infrastructure has remained a longstanding challenge.

Ladies and Gentlemen of the Press,
I will conclude by expressing my disgust at the former Vice President, who served Nigeria from 1999 to 2007 and has since been desperate to become President, despite having nothing to offer.

It is extremely offensive that Atiku, who served in an administration and was a member of the Party that created and left many of Nigeria's longstanding problems unresolved, now presents himself as the answer to those same problems.

Atiku has run for the presidency again and again, and Nigerians keep turning him down. They know he is not the solution. He is the problem. He has no ideas.
He went from customs officer to billionaire without ever explaining how. 

That unexplained wealth has bankrolled him election after election, and he is now reportedly selling off properties to keep his campaign alive. Nigerians are right to worry: if such a man reached office, would he not spend his first four years recouping his investment?

Atiku should retire and enjoy whatever is left of his customs-days largesse!
Public office is not a place to recover political investments. Nigeria’s treasury belongs to the Nigerian people!

And on the North, Atiku must account for his record. The people of the North deserve more than declarations of his pretentious concern. What has he done for the North in 27 years? Where are his investments? In Dubai! Yet he wants us to believe he has the North’s interest at heart?

Atiku, go and retire! You have nothing to offer!

Thank you, ladies and gentlemen.

God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

text:
Let’s get right to the point for all you cliff notes readers: 

Imagine a high school association that didn’t take 80 percent of the gate revenue from high schools hosting games like the IHSA does in Illinois.

“We lost money being in the playoffs,” said Bill Thomas, head football coach at Snead High School in Florida. “The FHSAA took 25 percent of the playoff gate here. 

“With the SSAA, they don’t take a dime of your playoff gate unless you play for the state championship.”

Wait: FHSAA only takes 25 percent? Wait, wait, wait: SSAA doesn’t take any until state-championship games?

Illinois high schools leaders continue to hurt kids, families, schools and communities by not creating a second high school association in the massive Midwest state.

Just ask Stuart Weiss.

“All schools are not the same, and a one-size-fits-all approach doesn’t work in high school sports anymore,” said Weiss, who is president of the Sunshine State Athletic Association (SSAA).

**Full story below with details**

Imagine a high school athletic association that didn't control the overwhelming majority of postseason gate revenue generated at stadiums it doesn't own, didn't build and doesn't maintain.

Sound impossible?

Welcome to Florida.

Here’s a history lesson every Illinois superintendent, principal, athletic director and school board member should study.

In 2008, eight Florida schools decided the existing model wasn't serving their student athletes. They didn't wait for permission, didn't spend decades complaining. 

They created a second association.

Eighteen years later, the SSAA reports more than 160 member schools across 12 sports.

More competitive opportunities, meaningful games, financial flexibility and more control for schools.

Illinois continues operating under a high school model where 100s of schools enter postseason tournaments knowing their chances of winning even a regional or sectional championship are extremely limited.

Why?

Who benefits from sending overmatched teams into predictable postseason eliminations? How does that build participation, strengthen programs or create meaningful opportunities for kids?

Why should schools continue providing facilities, employees, security, utilities and community support, while surrendering control of so much postseason revenue?

These are schools - not IHSA franchises.

Here’s what makes Florida’a story so important: They didn't need to destroy the FHSAA to create something better.

They created competition, choices and another pathway for kids and schools.

Now consider Illinois.

There are 100s of high schools, 1,000s of experienced coaches and administrators, tremendous athletic facilities and communities that invest millions into school sports.

But somehow we’re supposed to believe these same adult school leaders couldn’t organize a second athletic association?

Seriously?

A second model could offer competitive divisions based on actual program strength, modernized eligibility rules, student broadcasting rights and a significantly larger share of postseason revenue returning to schools.

Imagine championship opportunities that give more kids something meaningful to play for.

The biggest obstacle isn’t money, facilities, talent or opportunity. It’t adult leadership willing to challenge the status quo.

Too many school leaders have become comfortable running on the same hamster wheel, complaining about the IHSA privately while defending the system publicly.

Imagine what 20, 40 or 60 Illinois schools could accomplish if their leaders stopped asking what the IHSA would allow and started asking what was best for their students.

The IHSA doesn’t own Illinois high school sports. Schools don’t owe the IHSA a thing.

Always remember: The kids provide the purpose. The schools provide the product. The communities provide the investment.

Illinois doesn’t need another “committee” studying what’s wrong. 

It needs leaders willing to build what's next.

#MoreThanJUSTGames

text:
The IHSA takes 80 percent of playoff football gate revenue from games played in stadiums it didn’t build, doesn’t own and didn’t pay for.

Think about that. Brother Rice is begging donors for money, maybe the IHSA should donate to its capital fund? 

Taxpayers, donors and school districts invest millions in facilities. Schools provide the athletes, coaches, staff and communities.

The IHSA collects the money.

We also have retired athletic directors entering the vendor and consulting business, and current school ADs consistently promoting sidehustling  consulting services on LinkedIn during the day.

That’s not a knock, it leads to this: We’re supposed to believe there aren’t enough smart, experienced people in Illinois to create an independent, stipend-supported board to operate a statewide football playoff?

Why are schools surrendering millions in potential revenue to a private third-party business, while asking taxpayers and donors for more money every school year?

And here’s another question: Why couldn't mid-tier and lower-tier football programs organize their own postseason championships?

Their own brackets, sponsors, media rights and revenue. You think TV stations, streaming platforms and sponsors wouldn't be interested?

Of course they would.

Why do these schools continue to be used by the one-size system that doesn’t help all?

We have plenty of talented administrators, retired ADs and business-minded people who could build a better model.

Schools keep running on the same hamster wheel, some blindly defending a system that sends money away from the very institutions creating the product.

The IHSA doesn’t own high school football. 

The schools are high school football.

It’s time school leaders stopped asking what the IHSA will allow and started asking what they could accomplish without it.

More revenue for schools, more opportunities for kids and less money flowing to a middleman.

IHSA was needed 100 years ago.

It’s not today.

#MoreThanJUSTGames

text:
What if the most revealing evidence about Nixon's position on Taiwan was never published in the 1972 Shanghai Communique?

A TOP SECRET White House briefing prepared for his historic China visit contained language far more explicit than the carefully negotiated public statement.

It said Washington would not claim Taiwan's status was undetermined. It would not encourage other countries to make that claim either.

And then there was a handwritten note:
"Taiwan will be settled."

I examined this document at the Nixon Presidential Library about a decade ago.

Now, let's uncover what this remarkable document reveals about one of the most consequential diplomatic agreements of the Cold War.

On February 28, 1972, as President Richard Nixon's historic visit to China drew to a close, Washington and Beijing issued the Shanghai Communique, the first of the three foundational joint communiques that would come to define China-US relations.

Without question, the most important part of the communique was its language on Taiwan.

The US side declared: The United States acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China and that Taiwan is a part of China. The United States Government does not challenge that position.

When I was studying US foreign policy at Cornell, I discussed this particular wording with two of my instructors. Both interpreted it as meaning that the United States had been committed to the One China principle and that Taiwan was part of China.

Yet many of Washington's subsequent actions appeared inconsistent with the language of the communique. So they viewed this as a failure by the United States to honor its commitments.

Later, however, while studying at Stanford, I heard a strikingly different interpretation from another professor. She was also a renowned fellow at Hoover and a longtime China specialist who had been reading the People's Daily (人民日报) consistently since the 1970s. And she spent most of her career researching in DC.

She pointed out that Washington's diplomats were often far more deliberate in their choice of words than most people might imagine.

And the key, she explained, lay in just two English words: Acknowledge and Recognize.

In everyday English, acknowledge can mean admitting that something is true, but it can also simply mean being aware of, taking note of, or recognizing the existence of a particular position.

In diplomatic language, however, recognize often carries a stronger implication of formal recognition.

This is why some diplomats in DC confidently claim that the United States has never broken its promises. Their argument is that acknowledge does not go as far as recognize. In their interpretation, Washington merely "heard" that the Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait maintained there was one China and that Taiwan was part of China, without formally endorsing that position as its own.

What did the White House really think about Taiwan behind closed doors? Let's take a closer look at this memo.
-- Neither of us should allow the Taiwan issue to color unduly our developing relationship. There are many areas in which cooperation between our two countries would be to our mutual benefit, and the absence of diplomatic relations due to Taiwan ought not to prevent such cooperation.

In the Legal Status of Taiwan part, A section headed "Your Position" explicitly laid out the stance President Nixon was advised to take on Taiwan.
-- You hope that the assurances which you have already given regarding our policy not to support "two Chinas," "one China, one Taiwan," or the Taiwan independence movement will convince the Chinese of your good intentions.

-- Regarding the status of Taiwan, you have noticed that Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait agree that there is only one China and that Taiwan is a part of it. In this sense we do not maintain that the status of Taiwan is undetermined. There will be no statements from US officials about Taiwan's status being undetermined. Nor will we encourage other countries to take such a position. (Note: This is the approach which the British - completely independently and coincidentally - are taking in their efforts to upgrade their Peking diplomatic mission from Charge to Embassy.)

This was far more specific than the language the United States publicly used in the 1972 Shanghai Communique. It also makes clear that the theory of Taiwan’s "undetermined status," which certain irresponsible scholars have enthusiastically promoted in recent years, was not supported by the White House.

Those commitments that had already been articulated behind closed doors, only to disappear between the lines of the final Shanghai Communique.

When Nixon had already expressed certain principles so explicitly in private, it seems to me that, interpreting "acknowledge" as merely "I hear you" is far less than a tenable reading.

Public diplomatic language is crafted for the entire world to hear. But those few words in top-secret memo may offer a far more revealing glimpse into what the White House truly believed.
author: zhaixiang5
authorBio: Stanfordian, Cornell'11 Scholar on China-US Relations Member of China's National Cultural Relics Society

text:
48 hours before Nixon landed in China, Kissinger sent him a TOP SECRET memo.

Dated February 19, 1972, it offered a remarkably candid psychological and strategic assessment of Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai.

A few lines caught my eye:

"They see history on their side."

In the previous pages, Kissinger recognized something remarkable about China's leaders: they were deeply ideological, yet extraordinarily pragmatic. They understood the long game of history.

But Kissinger also understood something crucial: both men were in their seventies. Time was running out, and they wanted to secure their country's future before leaving the political stage.

He warned Nixon that China would judge America not merely by its words, but by its seriousness, reliability, and willingness to deliver on its commitments.

And then came his chilling final warning:

History might remember Nixon's visit as "a gallant but stillborn venture."

Nixon himself underlined numerous passages in this classified memo.

Two days later, he walked into Mao's study in Beijing's Zhongnanhai.

By the end of the visit, the two countries had issued the Shanghai Communique.

Kissinger had warned of a historic failure. Instead, Nixon, Mao, and Zhou helped achieve one of the most consequential diplomatic breakthroughs of the Cold War.

Nixon had the courage to reach out. Mao had the strategic vision to respond. And Zhou had the diplomatic skill to help turn that opening into reality.

History wasn't merely on anyone's side that week. It was being made, by both sides.

text:
Before Nixon met Mao in 1972, White House advisers were studying something rather unexpected:

Mao's favorite novels. 

Water Margin (水浒传).
Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义).
Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦).
Why?

Because they believed these ancient Chinese stories might offer clues to Mao's personality, military instincts, and even how he would deal with the United States.

I came across the original briefing memo at the Nixon Presidential Library ten years ago.

And those handwritten underlines and annotations you see in the photos? They're Nixon's own.

And some of its conclusions were fascinating. Now take a closer look at the pages. What do you think caught the President's eye?

text:
What does intellectual hypocrisy wear for Halloween?

Quite the collection of ad hominem attacks you've assembled. Yet you've offered no explanation of why Jewish national self-determination is inherently incompatible with liberalism. Calling liberal Zionists cruel and dishonest doesn't establish that contradiction. Invective is not an argument, however enthusiastically delivered.

A liberal Zionist can believe in Jewish national self-determination while opposing particular policies of the Israeli government. Just as support for Palestinian self-determination does not require endorsement of Hamas or Abbas. Do you recognize that distinction for both peoples, or only for Palestinians?

You condemn Jewish national self-determination as inherently incompatible with liberalism, while conspicuously avoiding the same judgment of Palestinian nationalism. Are we to infer that Palestinian national aspirations enjoy a moral exemption from the liberal standards you demand of Jews? Does opposition to Israel, in your view, excuse conduct that would otherwise violate the liberal principles you profess?

Let's examine the distinction. Is Hamas's record of political repression in Gaza compatible with your understanding of liberal democracy? What about Mahmoud Abbas, elected to a four-year term in 2005, who has remained in office without another presidential election for more than two decades?

And what of freedom of speech, religious liberty, women's rights, and the treatment of LGBT Palestinians? Are these liberal principles you defend universally, or only when politically convenient?

National self-determination and liberal democracy are not inherently contradictory. The relevant question is whether a state protects equal civil rights, political participation, and individual liberties. That standard should apply equally to Jewish and Palestinian national aspirations.

Liberalism is a universal principle, not a political convenience to be invoked or discarded according to one's sympathies. Perhaps you could explain why Jewish national self-determination and liberal democracy are inherently incompatible, rather than merely declaring it so.
