text:
Let me try to give my perspective as an ordinary citizen without any function, never a member or activist of any political party, having spent my entire life in Serbia.

We’ll skip the nineties, because that would lead to a catastrophic debate.

The year 2000 brought a "color revolution" and the overthrow of Slobodan Milošević. To be clear, I am not defending him, nor am I saying he was good, but those events were orchestrated by foreign intelligence agencies. Since then, no government in Serbia has existed that wasn't controlled from the outside, and not just the government, but the opposition as well. Anyone can verify this by examining the political scene over the last 26 years, where the same people rotate through positions across various parties, but fundamentally remain the same individuals and their successors. Plus, a few remnants from the nineties, such as Aleksandar Vučić himself, then Ivica Dačić, and similar figures.

The goal of the people brought to and maintained in power is to shape Serbia's foreign and domestic policy in such a way that Serbia becomes a colony of cheap labor and resources, economically exploited and politically directed to serve its new masters. In return, the local governors are granted the opportunity to plunder their own people and the state under foreign protection. For example, Chief Public Prosecutor Zagorka Dolovac took that position in 2010, before Vučić came to power, and has been kept in office to this very day, and nobody even remembers her acting on anything until yesterday.

The first set of politicians brought in after 2000, once they realized how much there was to steal, slowed down the execution of their masters' orders. Additionally, the charismatic Zoran Đinđić emerged into the foreground (they weren't as centralized as Aleksandar Vučić's regime) with speeches and ideas that could have actually been good for Serbia. The consequence was what happened to him. I know the official version is that he was assassinated by criminals, but hardly anyone here believes that anymore. Those same criminals were engaged in 2000 to help overthrow the regime, and it was well known that afterward, they received police badges, which made it easier for them to carry out their criminal activities. Through this, they infiltrated the police, gained serious finances and contacts, and eventually went rogue. They were the perfect fall guys for an act meant as a warning to others.

Then came the problem for both the ruling establishment at the time and their foreign masters, the most painful issue for Serbs: Kosovo and Metohija. All these years, there has been a demand for Serbia to officially sign and recognize the secession of that part of its territory. But every politician here knows that doing so is political suicide, with a serious risk of not being able to remain in the country due to the backlash it would inevitably trigger among the people.

Losing patience, the foreign masters replaced the previous rulers with new governors led by Tomislav Nikolić and Aleksandar Vučić, where the latter soon removed the former, because sharing power is undesirable and dangerous. Vučić was previously a member of the Serbian Radical Party and had been in politics since the nineties. He doesn't have a single day of regular work experience; he has never done anything other than politics, living his entire life at the expense of the state and the citizens of Serbia. However, he was there the entire time in high circles, knowing what was happening and what to expect. With that in mind, he slowly and gradually de facto handed over Kosovo, that is, the very last institutions and influence Serbia had there, short of an official recognition and explaining it to the public.

Before continuing, let’s add the information that most high-ranking members of his party currently are people who were in power in the set of politicians after 2000. This even causes rage inside the party among many members who have been there from the beginning and rarely advanced, while these newcomers arrived later and now make the decisions. Generally, I speak here of "Vučić doing this or that," but let's understand that the apparatus is too big for one person, so it is an entire organization; he is merely the leader. This is proven by individual scandals and accusations among themselves where even criminal acts are mentioned, yet no one is held accountable, and during every election, they are back together as best friends.

Let’s continue with Vučić. Knowing how things happen and work, over time he brought the police, prosecution, judiciary, and criminals under his control. Not just for easier plunder and covering up corruption, but also trying to protect himself from an internal strike that could bring him down. Now, my view of things is that in that area, he made a catastrophic mistake that brought him to this current situation. To secure control of a now large and powerful organization, he recruited people who are incapable of achieving anything on their own and who know that without him, they are nobodies. In working for him, they grew richer than they had ever dreamed. That’s where the problem arises: their level of intelligence wasn’t high enough for them to stay quiet, do what they were told, and be happy; instead, extremely arrogant and violent behavior began, all without any punishment because they were "protected." That's when it started becoming too much for the people, who are in a daily struggle for survival.

Then we arrive at the now widely known tragedy: the collapse of the canopy in Novi Sad and the deaths of 16 people. From a moment of shock, disbelief, and grief, the people snapped into anger. "We want those responsible held accountable," and protests began (by the general public, not the students yet). Now we run into a problem: those responsible are part of a state machinery that has functioned for years at a serious level. If they are handed over to the law according to the will of the people, they could expose a lot of things the public isn't aware of or only suspects, so no one was held accountable for 16 dead bodies. Let me emphasize, this is not the only case with fatal consequences for which this regime is considered guilty, but it is the largest.

Further on, protests started with a complete majority of the people. The regime waited for the situation to quiet down and hush everything up, as had been done for decades. That’s where the problem arose: a portion of the people didn't stop, and among them, the students led the charge. Not knowing what to do, the regime lost self-control and attempted to stop it through violence.

Next comes the student story, which from my perspective, in its shortest version, would require another text as long as this already lengthy one.

Now, what connects to the students and this video: The student blockades of universities. Posts on social media, their only form of communication with the people, asking for items at a specific university anywhere in the country resulted in local people, ordinary citizens, coming to the university to bring them supplies (food, water, toilet paper, shampoo...). It went to such an extent that they had to call on people to stop because they had too much. I know business owners who were never interested in politics secretly donating money out of fear of regime repression. The protests were the largest in decades; I know many people who went, including myself a few times, but no one was there who didn't finance it themselves. The regime didn't change its stance, escalating tension and violence, which led to politicization and the creation of a movement whose motto from the start of the protests was "the smart one doesn't stay silent, the smart one organizes." The point is, they had VERY LARGE support from the people in every aspect.

The trust and support of the people were perhaps shown most at the elections themselves, where turnout was unprecedented, resulting in a convincing majority victory for candidates who, for the most part, people had generally never even heard of until two months prior, when the "student list" was first publicly presented, introducing those people. Summary: People voted for 250 almost unknown individuals, trusting their youth, who had worked for two years to earn that trust.

Now, no one is naive in a world driven by money, but their campaign was reduced to social media, protests (where people came on their own), and traveling through Serbia by bicycle and on foot, sleeping where they were hosted, and sometimes outside, but without paying for anything. The students operated without a leader. In media appearances, the same person never spoke more than twice. At rallies, there were a large number of stewards and organizers who had to possess a lot of information to execute their jobs so perfectly. Conclusion: if it's a scam, a LOT of students participated in it (since all of them were verified active university members, while those previously politically active were rejected).

On the other hand, videos were seen of Vučić's "loyalists" gathering in Belgrade on the evening before polls closed, alongside heavy police and gendarmerie forces. Suddenly, Vučić conceded defeat, and all of them abruptly dispersed, criminals and police alike. The regime's thesis that they were there as a routine measure during elections to prevent riots falls apart right there, because they left, and there were no riots, only celebration. Vučić is not a man who concedes defeat, so I leave the conclusion for everyone to draw for themselves.

The Finale: We have around 140 professionals with established careers entering parliament to lead the country, and likely a few more will appear since a prime minister, ministers, and others are needed. They were selected (according to the students' explanation, which matches their biographies) from various parts of Serbia so Belgrade wouldn't hold primacy as it did for decades, and from various fields of expertise so that whatever is decided tomorrow, someone among them possesses the knowledge and extensive experience to speak on it and explain the situation.

For now, they haven't taken power yet, but through various congratulations and questions, huge pressure is mounting from all sides externally, which is by no means good for them. All of you who say they are heartily congratulated know that this creates a negative effect among the people in Serbia, so the perception of those congratulations can vary. In the meantime, they face serious internal sabotage from the previous regime, which still officially holds all positions, even if at a reduced capacity. For now, they firmly stand behind statements that the Constitution of Serbia must be respected, whoever understands knows the answer regarding Kosovo and Metohija is right there, and consequently tied to the EU. To pick fights with anyone right at the start before even consolidating the government and institutions would make them fools and poorly chosen.

Conclusion: We were already a colony; whether we have exchanged one set of governors for another, time will tell. Even if that is the case, if there is at least somewhat less plunder of the people, at least basic respect for the law, then the people living here have already made progress. For Serbia, the most important thing is to start changing the regime and the people in office, as that is the only way to reach good ones. Up until now, for decades, it was practically impossible to break out of the vicious cycle of the same proven bad people.

All of this is strictly my view. I am not an expert in any aspect to speak on this (other than having lived through all of it), with very little interest in and knowledge of politics and geopolitics, I offer no proof for anything I said.

text:
“There are no untypical stories in the USSR!”

That’s what a furious Soviet general reportedly shouted down the phone to Mosfilm studio when he heard the title of a new war film: An Untypical Story.

The film was renamed Tryasina (The Quagmire). Its director, Grigory Chukhray, knew exactly what he was up against.

Chukhray was a frontline soldier who fought at Stalingrad and was wounded three times. 
After the war he became one of the most celebrated directors in the world: The Forty-First won a special prize at Cannes in 1957, and Ballad of a Soldier (1959) won the BAFTA for Best Film and was nominated for an Oscar.

For Tryasina he took on a story he had every reason to reject. He had read a short newspaper item about a man who hid from conscription for 12 years during the war. Chukhray despised deserters. But as an artist, he turned the story around and told it through the mother.

In the film, a village woman loses her husband at the front, and her eldest son goes missing. When her youngest is called up, she hides him in the attic. Out of love, she saves his life, and destroys his soul, and her own.

The role went to Nonna Mordyukova, one of the great Soviet actresses. The story goes that after three years without work she wept in a small village church, and that same evening the phone rang with the offer.

The authorities did not see a tragedy. They saw a threat.

General Yepishev, head of the Army’s Main Political Directorate, was outraged. He insisted there were no deserters in the army during the war, and he was offended “for our Soviet mother.” In his words: a mother is associated with the Motherland, so showing her in a negative light means Chukhray “defames our Motherland.”

Red Star, the army newspaper, ran a devastating attack. Positive reviews were pulled. A Party commission descended on the studio to find out who had allowed such a harmful film to be made.

The film was re-cut and scenes were removed, but it was still shelved. It reached Soviet cinemas only in November 1978, and went on to draw nearly 20 million viewers.

The officials had hoped audiences would condemn the mother. Instead, people pitied her.

Chukhray had also dreamed for years of making a film about the Battle of Stalingrad, which he had survived. He was never allowed to.

Today marks 25 years since his death. Some stories about war and what it does to ordinary families never stop finding new relevance.

If you have never seen Tryasina, it is worth seeking out.

text:
📖 DAILY SCRIPTURE

Birthing of A Nation
Faith • Family • Freedom

THURSDAY, OCTOBER 29, 2026

WHEN COMPASSION CROSSES THE ROAD

📖 Luke 10:33 (NLT)

“Then a despised Samaritan came along, and when he saw the man, he felt compassion for him.”

🔥 LOVE THAT REFUSES TO WALK PAST

Jesus told of a traveller beaten, robbed, and left beside the road. A priest passed him. Then a Levite passed him. Both saw the need, but neither stopped.

Finally, a Samaritan—someone the injured man’s community would have looked down upon—came near.

He didn’t ask whether the man deserved help. He saw his suffering and responded with mercy.

The Samaritan interrupted his journey, tended the man’s wounds, and paid for his care. His compassion cost him time, comfort, and money.

That’s the difference between feeling sorry for someone and loving them as Jesus taught.

📖 A STORY FOR TODAY

Imagine a woman leaving work after a long shift. She’s exhausted and eager to get home.

At the grocery-store entrance, she notices a father trying to carry bags while comforting a crying child.

People hurry past. She nearly does too.

Then she remembers Jesus’ words about loving our neighbour.

She turns around, offers to carry the bags, and walks with them to the car.

It takes only a few minutes, but the father’s relief is unmistakable.

She didn’t preach a sermon. She lived one.

✝️ JESUS AT THE CENTRE

The religious men in Jesus’ story knew the law, yet the outsider showed mercy.

Jesus was challenging the belief that loving our neighbour stops at the boundaries of our comfort, circle, or culture.

When He asked who had been a neighbour, the answer was the one who showed mercy.

Jesus told His listener to go and do likewise (Luke 10:36–37).

Christ didn’t love us from a distance. He came near, entered our brokenness, and gave Himself for us.

We cannot earn His grace through good deeds, but receiving His love should change how we treat people.

🔥 PRACTICAL APPLICATION

It’s easy to discuss what’s wrong with our communities while overlooking the person hurting right in front of us.

The stranger, the lonely neighbour, the struggling parent, even the person who disagrees with us—each is someone we can treat with dignity.

Faith • Family • Freedom begins with hearts willing to love beyond words.

A nation is strengthened when neighbours refuse to leave one another behind.

🎯 TODAY’S MISSION

Notice one person you would normally pass by.

Offer practical help, encouragement, or a listening ear.

Don’t wait for a convenient moment.

Be the neighbour Jesus calls you to be.

🙏 PRAYER

Lord Jesus, give me eyes to see the hurting and a heart that moves with compassion. Forgive me when busyness or prejudice makes me walk past. Help me love with courage, humility, and action. Let others see Your mercy through my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

#BirthingOfANation #DailyScripture #FaithFamilyFreedom #Luke1033 #GoodSamaritan #LoveYourNeighbour #FaithInAction #JesusChrist #Alberta

text:
📜Austerlitz Campaign, 29 October 1805

Braunau falls to a party small enough to arrive in a boat.

Colonel Kirgener, the engineer sent ahead to repair the crossing, takes a few chasseurs across the Inn under fire. They enter the fortress, scatter its defenders and turn the guns on the ramparts against an approaching Austrian detachment.

Lannes arrives, followed by Murat and Davout. Their meeting brings together columns that have approached by different roads.

But the commanders are ahead of much of their army. Lannes can initially bring only four companies of grenadiers into Braunau, while other units remain across the river or farther behind.

The fortress offers something the pursuit badly needs: a protected place for stores, hospitals and supplies. Capturing it gives Napoleon a base from which to push deeper into Austria.

text:
This is the reason I left Facebook for the first time in 2018. Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion for deceiving Facebook users regarding their personal data in connection with the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Digital giants promise to protect user privacy while simultaneously profiting from targeted advertising. The American justice system has just served as a reminder that such commitments come at a price. The ruling against Meta in the Cambridge Analytica case penalizes years of falsehoods concerning the protection of user accounts—a situation that persists to this day. I have no faith left in anything Zuckerberg says!

On October 21, 2026, in New Mexico, Judge Francis Mathew ordered the owner of Facebook to pay $25 billion following a trial regarding its privacy practices, as reported by *The Verge*. The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which broke in 2018 and severely damaged user trust in the social network. The judgment against Meta is based on more than 43 million individual violations, as determined by a jury after years of litigation.

The ruling against Meta brings a five-year standoff to an end.

New Mexico filed a lawsuit in 2021 and chose to proceed to trial—unlike almost every other state, which opted for an $18 billion settlement reached in August. This solitary gamble paid off. In September, a jury in Santa Fe found the company guilty of lying about how it collected and protected the personal data of its members.

In determining the penalty, the court took into account the intentional and repetitive nature of the false statements made by the company’s executives, as well as the duration over which these deceptions occurred. The jurors reviewed dozens of public statements made by the company regarding privacy and content moderation, deeming the majority of them to be misleading. The resulting penalty far exceeds the fines that platforms typically absorb without a second thought.

How Cambridge Analytica siphoned data from Facebook!

In the late 2010s, a simple personality questionnaire offered on the social network served as a Trojan horse. The application harvested the profiles of approximately 87 million users—extending well beyond just those who took the quiz—and passed the data on to Cambridge Analytica, all without genuine consent. This political consulting firm, which has since ceased operations, used these profiles to craft election advertisements tailored to the specific personality traits of individual users—most notably for Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign.

A fine that Meta deems disproportionate...

Where does such a figure come from? Under New Mexico consumer protection law—which prohibits deceiving buyers—each individual violation could carry a penalty of up to $5,000. When multiplied by the tens of millions of identified breaches, the theoretical total reached nearly $219 billion, a figure the judge subsequently adjusted to $25 billion. The state had sought between $35 billion and $40 billion, while the company argued that the amount should not exceed $3.4 billion.

Meta considers the sanction indefensible, disputing the notion that any residents actually saw these statements or suffered any harm as a result. The company also points out that it has overhauled its practices since 2021 and now removes 99% of problematic content. State Attorney General Raúl Torrez intends to dedicate the entire sum to public schools and is seeking an injunction to put an end to these practices. However, nothing is guaranteed. The appeal announced by Meta could reduce the number of established violations—and the associated financial penalty—all while interest continues to accrue.

text:
Christian Haynes.  RG #64

I have watched all 200+ of his offensive snaps from 2026. Here are my thoughts.

2024 3rd round pick out of UConn. 31 career games with all 5 starts coming in 2026.

It's worth noting that Miami takes over Haynes' contract from Seattle which goes through 2027, which means there's another full year of team control at a minimal rate.

Obviously no longer a start for the Seahawks after the Quentin Nelson trade and Grey Zabel manning the other side. 

My GUESS as to why Haynes got released vs. the other IOL reserves on the roster is versatility.  Haynes is strictly a guard and may only be a RG since that's where he played both in college and for Seattle in 2026 (I'm not sure if Seattle has tried him on the left). 

The Seahawks have a defensive minded HC who arrived in 2024, an OL coach who arrived in 2025, and an OC who joined the team in 2026.  So he likely wasn't a 'my guy' for anyone who would have a voice for keeping him on the roster.

His 2026 film for me backs up what I thought of him coming out of college.  I don't think his play lives up to his athletic scores, which I think is why many people were high on him.  Stylistically I still think my Rob Jones comparison is valid.

He lacks the functional athleticism that we have seen Kadyn Proctor and Jonah Savaiinaea put on display.  He's got a mix of solid reps and ugly reps, but is generally steady.  High FBI guy that understands where and how to get where he needs to be in all run concepts, but at times just isn't capable of it.  Doesn't get a ton of movement in the run game. 

My opinion, in the end, is that this is a guy that you can 'get by' with as your 5th offensive lineman - but if he would break into the starting lineup, he'd always be the guy you're looking to replace.

This is MAYBE a move that would give credit to the thought of moving KP to RT because reserve OL must have multi-position versatility - and I'm not sure Haynes offers that.  So maybe it's a chance to get another body in the door to compare to someone like Jarrett Kingston and see if they can fill LG organically without having to invest in the offseason?  Just a thought.

In the end, this is likely a guy that Sully liked in the draft process and saw an opportunity to get a closer look.  DJ Campbell has kind of been what I expected and isn't even active on the gameday roster (again, lack of position versatility).

I expect Campbell to clear waivers and to be brought back on the practice squad - likely at the expense of James Ester.

I like the move, love the process.  Keep churning the bottom of this roster and if you can find one or two guys that fall off the tree elsewhere and can be 2027 contributors for the Miami Dolphins - then it's another feather in the cap for JES.

text:
Ah, there he sits again, the professional soothsayer of other men’s suitcases, peering into a crystal ball that has shown him nothing but his own reflection for the better part of two decades.

He has observed that a certain “fakeer” may one day collect his jhola and seek a friendly foreign shore. One is tempted to applaud the optimism. After all, the same gentleman has been announcing the imminent collapse, the flight, the reckoning, and the grand unmasking with the regularity of a monsoon that never quite arrives. The electorate, meanwhile, has displayed a most uncooperative habit of returning the “fakeer” and his party with majorities large enough to make even the most inventive conspiracy theorist pause and check his arithmetic. In 2014, 2019, and again in 2024 the numbers refused to cooperate with the prophecy; the villagers, it seems, prefer their own lanterns to the borrowed ones offered by those who specialise in predicting darkness.

India’s traditions, for better or worse, have never been especially hospitable to the idea that a leader who has governed for over a decade, won successive mandates, and left the opposition in electoral ruins will suddenly pack a bag and request asylum from a “phrand.” The country has absorbed far larger shocks—partition, emergency, economic near-collapse, pandemics—without the executive boarding a private jet for Miami. Its institutions, noisy and imperfect as they are, have a tiresome way of remaining in place long after the press conferences predicting their overthrow have concluded. The conspirators, on the other hand, tend to remain exactly where they began: drafting the next urgent affidavit, sharing the next forged notice, and wondering why the jhola never quite leaves the ground.

One might almost feel a twinge of sympathy. It is a hard life, watching the same dream fail to materialise for a quarter-century while the land continues, stubbornly and with its usual contradictions, to go about its business. The suitcase remains unclaimed. The flight is never booked. And the soothsayer, undeterred, polishes his crystal ball once more and announces that next time, surely, the monsoon will finally stay.

text:
Rabbit is the one meat that punishes you for being impatient, careless, or distracted.

Pork forgives you. Chicken forgives you most of the time. Beef lets you hide behind a good sear. Rabbit forgives nothing.

It is so lean that a few extra minutes over the wrong heat turns it into something you chew politely and never order again. Which is exactly why the cooks who get it right tend to get it very right, and why a rabbit handled properly over real fire is a different animal from the one most people think they have tasted.

This is not a recipe post. It is about what happens when someone picks the least forgiving meat, the least forgiving heat, and the least forgiving setting (outdoors, wind and all) and then commits without flinching.

The video is attached. Read this before you press play or after. Either way, there is a decent chance you will watch it twice.

THE MEAT THAT HAS NO SAFETY NET

Here is a fact that surprises people: you can starve to death while eating rabbit.

Not because it is poisonous. Because it is almost pure lean protein. Arctic explorers and frontier trappers had a grim name for it, "rabbit starvation," a condition that shows up when someone lives on very lean meat with no fat to go with it. The body needs fat. Rabbit barely brings any.

That one biological quirk explains nearly every rabbit tradition on earth. The Maltese stew it slowly and call the dish a national treasure. The French wrap it, lard it, braise it in mustard. Italians roast it with olive oil and rosemary until the kitchen smells like a hillside. Spanish cooks pair it with rice and rich stock. Look closely and you will notice the same hidden theme everywhere: every great rabbit dish is really a clever plan for supplying the fat and moisture the animal never had.

Now remove the stove. Remove the oven door with its tidy temperature dial. Remove the timer that beeps. Move the whole operation outside, where the only controls are fire, distance and the cook's own judgment.

That is the territory this video lives in. And the margin for error out there is measured in minutes.

A FIRE DOES NOT HAVE A DIAL

People who cook on gas or electric forget how much of cooking is simply outsourcing attention to a machine. You set a number. The machine holds it. You walk away.

A live fire never holds a number. Coals brighten when the wind picks up and sulk when it drops. Fresh wood spikes the heat and then lets it collapse. Two spots six inches apart can be a hundred degrees different. Old fire cooks have a test that is almost embarrassingly simple: hold your hand over the coals and count how long you can stand it. Two seconds means hot. Five means gentle. That is the entire instrument panel, and it has fed people for longer than writing has existed.

Think about what that demands. A cook working over coals is not following instructions. He is reading a living system in real time, adjusting by feel, by smell, by the sound fat makes when it hits something hot. Skill like that cannot be downloaded. It is built from burnt dinners, and the cooks who have it rarely talk about the burnt dinners.

Every time you watch someone work a fire with total calm, you are watching a pile of failures turned into confidence.

THE OLDEST OVEN IN THE WORLD IS A HOLE

Long before anyone invented a metal pot, people discovered that heat could be trapped.

Dig a pit. Fill it with hot stones or coals. Add food. Cover it. Leave. Polynesian cooks developed the imu. Maori families have the hangi. In Mexico it became the foundation of barbacoa. New England turned it into the clambake. Archaeologists keep finding ancient burned-rock features in places that have nothing to do with each other, on different continents, left by people who never met, all arriving at the same answer: enclosed heat plus patience equals food worth remembering.

What is strange is how little the principle has changed. Covered heat cooks from every direction at once. It holds moisture in. It pushes the meat toward tenderness through time rather than force. And it demands something that modern life increasingly refuses to ask of us: trust.

Because once the lid is on, you cannot check. You cannot poke it. You cannot taste it. You made your decisions earlier, and now there is only waiting and the quiet suspicion that you may have made a mistake.

Holding that suspicion for hours is its own kind of courage.

WHAT HEAT ACTUALLY DOES TO MEAT

There are two chemical stories happening inside anything cooked well, and they want opposite things.

The first is browning. Once surfaces pass roughly 140 degrees Celsius, sugars and amino acids start reacting into hundreds of new flavor compounds. This is the Maillard reaction, and it is the reason roasted things smell like a promise. It is fast, it likes dry heat, and it is greedy: leave it alone too long and the promise turns bitter.

The second is softening. Connective tissue in meat is mostly collagen, tough and rubbery when raw, but over time and moderate heat it melts into gelatin, which is the silky texture people travel across cities for. This process is slow, and it likes gentleness and moisture.

So here is the cook's riddle. One reaction needs punishing heat. The other needs patience. A lean animal gives you almost no room to satisfy both, because it has so little fat to cushion mistakes.

Real fire cooking resolves the riddle in odd, beautiful ways: hot where you need color, shielded where you need softness, enclosed where you need moisture. It is physics performed with instinct. Nobody at an open fire is calculating anything, but everyone who is good at it has somehow solved the same equation.

THE QUIET POWER OF A MARINADE

Anyone can season a piece of meat. Fewer people understand what seasoning is for.

Salt does more than flavor. Given time, it pulls moisture out of the surface, dissolves into it, and then draws it back inside, carrying flavor deeper than any quick sprinkle ever could. Oil is not decoration either. It is a thermal blanket, a carrier for fat-soluble spice, and for lean meat it is insurance. Acid, like citrus, brightens and loosens, but it is a double-edged tool. Too little and nothing changes. Too much and the texture turns chalky. The window is narrow, and it moves with the cut, the temperature and the clock.

This is why marinating is not a preliminary step but an argument you make with the meat hours before anyone is hungry. You are deciding, in advance, how it will behave under heat. You are placing a bet.

The best cooks I have watched treat the prep as the real performance and the fire as the final exam. By the time the heat arrives, most of the result is already decided. The fire only reveals whether you were right.

WHY A WHOLE ANIMAL CHANGES THE CONVERSATION

There is a part of whole-animal cooking that polite food content tends to skip.

Most of us now meet meat as a rectangle under plastic. No face, no shape, no history. It arrives anonymous, and in that anonymity it becomes very easy to waste. People throw out staggering amounts of edible food without a flicker of guilt, because nothing about it ever looked like a living thing.

Cooking a whole animal rearranges that relationship. It cannot be anonymous. It has a shape you recognize. It asks whether you are going to honor it or squander it. Cooks who work this way often describe the same shift: they become more careful, more thrifty, more respectful of every part, not less. The old phrase "nose to tail" sounds trendy now, but it started as plain economics and plain decency. If something gave its life to feed people, the least you owe it is a meal done properly.

You can feel that tension sitting quietly inside this video. It does not lecture you. It does not need to. It just refuses to pretend food comes from nowhere, and that refusal is more honest than most food content you will scroll past today.

Whether that makes you comfortable is a separate question. It is worth asking yourself why.

THE THING WE FORGOT WE WERE GOOD AT

There is a serious theory in anthropology, championed by Harvard primatologist Richard Wrangham, that cooking did not merely accompany human evolution. It drove it. Cooked food is easier to chew, easier to digest, and delivers more usable energy. Spend less of the day chewing and digesting, the argument goes, and you free up energy for a bigger, hungrier brain. The theory is debated, but it is taken seriously for a reason.

If that is even partly true, then fire cooking is not a hobby. It is the oldest shared skill our species has. It is how a group of tired people became a community that sat in a circle facing the same light.

And notice what happens when someone cooks over open flame today. People drift toward it. Strangers stand closer than they normally would. Conversation softens. Phones come out of pockets, but they go back in. Something very old in us switches on, a memory that has nothing to do with taste.

Maybe that is why videos like this travel so far. We are not only watching dinner. We are watching a hundred thousand years of instinct switch on in someone else, and recognizing it as our own.

THE QUESTION BEFORE THE REVEAL

Every serious cook knows the strange hush that falls before food is revealed.

It is the point where preparation is over and judgment has not begun. The cook has made every decision he can make. The fire has done what it was going to do. Nothing can be added, nothing can be taken back, and every person waiting has already imagined the best version of what they are about to eat.

That gap, between expectation and reality, is where the real tension in cooking lives. It is why unveiling a dish feels almost theatrical. It is why a quiet nod from a guest can outweigh a hundred compliments. And it is why watching someone else go through that moment, with no way to hide, is oddly compelling.

You do not need to like rabbit to feel it. You do not even need to like cooking. You only need to remember a time you made something for someone you cared about and waited, trying to look casual, to see their face.

That is the whole show. Everything else is fire and timing.

THE MEAT THAT DISAPPEARED FROM THE TABLE

Rabbit used to be ordinary.

Across wartime Britain, families were encouraged to raise rabbits in backyards because they were cheap to feed, quick to breed and needed very little space. In many parts of Europe and the Mediterranean it never stopped being everyday food. In Malta, stewed rabbit is practically a point of national pride. Yet in much of the English-speaking world it drifted out of sight, replaced by cuts that were easier to standardize and market, and then quietly forgotten by whole generations.

Something odd happened along the way. A meat that once symbolized thrift and self-reliance started to symbolize either nostalgia or squeamishness. People who happily eat chicken wince at rabbit, not because of anything about the meat itself, but because of a story about what rabbits are supposed to be.

I am not here to tell you what your story should be. I am saying that the story is worth noticing. It reveals how much of what we call taste is really culture, and how quickly a normal thing can become exotic simply by being left alone for two generations.

Seeing it cooked with real confidence, as food and not as a stunt, is a small act of reclaiming a lost ordinary.

PATIENCE IS BECOMING A LUXURY

Consider the arithmetic of what you are about to watch.

A cook invests hours of preparation, waiting and fire management. The video compresses it into moments. Everything slow gets squeezed into something you can swallow between two notifications. There is a small paradox in that: we consume patience at high speed.

And yet that paradox is exactly why this kind of content works. In a world engineered for instant everything, watching someone commit to slowness feels like standing in front of an open window. You do not have to live that way. You just want to feel the air for a minute.

I think this is the real reason people send videos like this to friends. Not to say "look at this food." To say "remember when we used to do things this way?" or "someday we should."

Slow cooking is a time machine that runs on charcoal. It drags you out of the present tense and into the one where a meal takes a day, a day takes a whole life, and nobody is checking a phone because the fire needs watching.

COOKING AS A LANGUAGE

In many cultures, the first question a host asks a guest is whether they have eaten. Not how they are. Not what they do for work. Have you eaten.

It is hospitality as a reflex, and it says something profound: feeding someone is the most basic way of telling them they matter. When a person spends an entire day preparing a meal for others, with fire, and effort, and risk of failure, he is saying something no sentence could carry as well.

Large outdoor cooking has always carried that weight. Feasts mark weddings, harvests, reunions, funerals and the end of long journeys. The amount of food is never about hunger. It is about saying that there is enough here, for everyone, and that you were thought of.

Watch the faces around a table when a meal like that begins. Not the food. The faces. You will see something that is almost impossible to fake and almost impossible to buy: people who feel looked after.

That is what is being cooked. The rabbit is the vehicle.

WHY WE WATCH OTHER PEOPLE COOK

The modern internet runs on strange appetites. Millions of people watch strangers cook meals they will never taste, in kitchens they will never enter, and still feel satisfied afterwards.

Psychologists point toward a few reasons. One is vicarious competence: watching a skilled person do something well produces its own small reward, the same way watching a craftsman or a athlete does. Another is sensory simulation. The brain responds to the sight and sound of sizzling, chopping and pouring as if some of it were real. A third is plain relief. In a chaotic world, a process with clear steps and a visible result is soothing.

But outdoor fire cooking adds something extra. It is physical, unpredictable, and slightly dangerous. Heat is real. Mistakes are visible. There is no editing out a collapsing fire or a misjudged hour. The stakes are small but honest, and honesty is rarer on screens than any recipe.

So when something like this shows up in your feed between arguments and advertisements, it lands differently. It is one of the few things that asks nothing of you except attention, and gives back something that feels like it was made by hand.

WHAT SEPARATES A STUNT FROM A CRAFT

Plenty of food videos are spectacle. Huge fires, giant portions, dramatic music, a face of fake astonishment at the end. Spectacle is cheap, and the audience knows it.

Craft has a different signature. It is in the small unglamorous decisions: how something is prepared before it ever touches heat, how the fire is managed instead of just lit, how patiently the cook leaves things alone. Craft does not need to announce itself. It shows up as calm.

When you watch, look for calm. Look for the absence of panic. Look for the moment where the cook has clearly done this before, and clearly respects the process too much to rush it. That quiet is the sound of experience, and it cannot be faked with editing.

If you only take one thing from a video like this, let it be that. Confidence is not loud. It is the thing that remains when nothing is left to prove.

THE SMELL THAT BYPASSES YOUR DEFENSES

Of all the senses, smell has the shortest road to memory. Signals from the nose travel to the brain regions tied to emotion and recollection with almost no detour, which is why a single whiff can drop you into a kitchen you left thirty years ago while your conscious mind is still trying to name what you smelled.

Woodsmoke may be the most powerful trigger of all. It is not one smell but a layered chord: resin, char, sweetness from caramelizing sugars, the savory edge of rendering fat. Billions of people share a deep, wordless association with it. Fire meant warmth. Warmth meant safety. Safety meant someone had cooked and you were about to be fed.

This matters for a simple reason. A video cannot transmit smell, and yet the best fire-cooking videos somehow make you remember it. You catch yourself leaning toward the screen. Your mouth reacts before your opinion does.

That is not a trick of editing. It is evidence that the memory is already inside you, waiting for almost any excuse. Someone, somewhere in your past, stood near a fire and fed you. You may have forgotten the face. The smell never forgot.

THE NUMBER THAT SEPARATES DINNER FROM A MISTAKE

For all the romance of fire, there is one unromantic number every responsible cook respects.

Food safety guidance for rabbit, like poultry, points to an internal temperature of about 74 degrees Celsius, or 165 Fahrenheit. Below that, you are gambling with something far more serious than texture. Above it by too much, a lean animal dries out and the whole day of work collapses into sawdust.

Look at how narrow that corridor is. Undercook, and you risk making people sick. Overcook, and you waste an animal and a day. The target sits in a thin strip between two failures, and the only way through is attention.

This is where experienced outdoor cooks quietly separate themselves from enthusiastic amateurs. Amateurs trust the fire. Veterans trust the fire and verify the meat. They touch it, they probe it, they learn how it feels at each stage, and over the years that feel hardens into something close to a sixth sense.

Pride and humility live in the same hand here. The best cooks know exactly how good they are, and they still check.

THE REST NOBODY WANTS TO WAIT FOR

There is a step in cooking that almost everyone rushes, and it may be the most important one: resting.

When meat comes off the heat, its juices are driven toward the center and loosely held. Cut immediately and they run out onto the board, taking the best of the dish with them. Give it a few minutes and the fibers relax, the temperature evens out, and the moisture settles back into the meat where you wanted it all along. Heat also keeps moving inward after the fire is gone, which is why a piece can finish cooking in its own warmth.

Resting is also the hardest instruction in cooking to follow, because it comes at the exact moment when the food smells best, everyone is hungry, and doing nothing feels like punishment.

That is why it is such a good measure of a cook. Anyone can light a fire. Anyone can season a piece of meat. Very few can stand beside a finished dish, with hungry people watching, and wait.

Discipline is mostly the ability to keep your hands still when everything in you wants to move.

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE ACTUALLY LIVES

Ask a skilled fire cook how long something needs and you will often get a strange answer. Not a number. A description. Until it smells like this. Until the color looks like that. Until it feels a certain way under the fingers.

That is not vagueness. It is a kind of knowledge that does not fit neatly into recipes, because it was never written down. It lives in hands, in eyes, in decades of watching someone older do it and being quietly corrected. Anthropologists call it tacit knowledge, the type you can demonstrate far more easily than you can explain.

It is also fragile. Every time a generation grows up without standing next to a fire, a little of it disappears. Not dramatically. Just one quiet afternoon at a time, until one day nobody remembers how the old hands knew.

Which gives a video like this a second job beyond entertainment. It is a small act of preservation. Somebody is doing something with their hands, in the open, in a way that others can learn simply by watching. It is not a lecture or a lesson. It is a demonstration, and demonstration was how every important human skill was passed on for most of history.

So watch it the way an apprentice would. Not for the ending. For the hands.

THE LOGISTICS NOBODY APPLAUDS

Cooking for a crowd is a logistics puzzle wearing the costume of a meal.

Somebody has to decide how much fuel, how much time, how many mouths. Something must be prepared a day early so it can be ready at the right hour. Everything has to arrive hot at roughly the same moment, even though each part wants a different heat and a different clock. Professional kitchens call this timing. Home cooks call it chaos. Outdoor cooks call it Tuesday.

What makes it remarkable is how invisible it is when done well. Nobody at the table thinks about the planning. They think the food simply appeared. The better the cook, the more effortless it looks, and the less credit the effort receives.

That is one of the quiet injustices of craft: mastery erases the evidence of itself. If you want to appreciate what you are seeing, do the opposite of what the final result invites. Imagine the version where something went wrong, then notice how everything went right.

THE COST OF ONE WRONG CHOICE

In most areas of modern life, a mistake can be reversed. You edit the draft. You refund the order. You undo the change.

Fire does not offer an undo button. Once meat has been cooked too far, no clever correction restores it. Once a day has been spent, it has been spent. That finality is exactly what gives outdoor cooking its weight. Every choice is real because it cannot be retracted.

There is something strangely refreshing about that. A life full of undo buttons makes everything feel provisional. A fire makes decisions count. You season once. You place the food once. You wait, and you live with what you did.

Maybe that is the deepest reason these videos hold people. Not the food. The stakes. A small, honest, irreversible stake, set against an afternoon, with nobody pretending it does not matter.

A SMALL ARGUMENT ABOUT RESPONSIBILITY

There is a version of this conversation that ends with a lecture, and I want to avoid it.

But I do think there is a fair question hiding in any story where an animal ends up on a table: what do we owe the thing that feeds us? Not sentimental guilt. Not a performance of discomfort. Just seriousness.

Some people answer by eating less meat. Some answer by buying from people they can look in the eye. Some answer by learning to cook an animal so well that nothing is wasted and nothing is cheapened. All of those are real responses, and none of them is available to someone who has stopped thinking about it.

Maybe that is the quiet gift of watching whole-animal cooking done with care. It does not tell you what to believe. It only makes it harder to look away from the question.

WHAT TO NOTICE WHEN YOU WATCH

You do not need me to explain a video. But if you are going to give it your attention, give it the right kind.

Notice how much of the work happens before the dramatic part. Notice what is left to time. Notice who is paying attention to whom. Notice the point where the cook stops doing and starts trusting, because that point is the heart of every cooking story ever told.

And notice your own reaction. Appetite, curiosity, discomfort, nostalgia, a sudden hunger for a simpler afternoon. Each one is information about you. Few things on the internet hold up a mirror this small and this honest.

WHY SIMPLE IDEAS HIT HARDEST

Strip this story down and it has almost no moving parts: an animal, a fire, a long wait, and people who are hungry. No plot twists. No villain. No soundtrack the plot depends on.

That simplicity is deliberate on nature's part, not ours. The most durable stories humans tell are the ones built on needs older than language. Hunger. Warmth. Skill. Sharing. They do not expire, because the need does not expire.

So if a post like this makes you feel something you cannot quite name, do not overthink it. You are responding to a pattern your ancestors rehearsed around countless fires, and your body still knows the steps.

THE LAST WORD

We live in a time that rewards speed, and food made over fire is a rebuke to it.

It says some things cannot be hurried. It says that the best results come from preparation nobody applauds and waiting nobody films. It says that feeding people is serious, that skill is built from failure, and that trust, in a fire, in a process, in each other, is still the only way to make anything worth sharing.

The rabbit is just the excuse.

Some meals are eaten in minutes and remembered for years. That ratio is the whole point: hours of work, minutes of eating, and a memory that quietly outlasts both of them by whole decades.

So when you finally watch, ask yourself a simple question: when was the last time you made something that took all day and could not be rushed, for people you wanted to feed?

If the answer is "too long ago," then you already know what this video is really about.

Watch it. Then tell me the best thing you have ever eaten that was cooked over fire, and who taught you how.

$APH KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM AMPHENOL’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Amphenol’s October 28 call supports a selective broadening of the electronics-investment cycle, not an indiscriminate bullish view across technology and industrials. The strongest positive signals are accelerating interconnect demand, sustained investment in data-center power infrastructure, broad industrial-electronics growth and increasing defense-electronics content. The clearest negative signal is the divergence between AI infrastructure and traditional broadband spending. A less obvious competitive implication is that CommScope’s acquired connectivity business now has the capital and operating support to compete more effectively. The most actionable incremental information concerns companies still awaiting results, particularly Belden, Eaton, ADTRAN and Curtiss-Wright. For Corning, TE Connectivity and Vertiv, which had already reported by the time of Amphenol’s call, the evidence primarily corroborates existing disclosures and informs subsequent-quarter expectations. Country labels below identify primary equity-listing markets; impact magnitudes describe business exposure, not predicted share-price moves.

INDUSTRIAL CONNECTIVITY

BROAD INDUSTRIAL ELECTRONICS STRENGTH SUPPORTS BELDEN AHEAD OF ITS REPORT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Belden (BDC: United States) and TE Connectivity (TEL: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: moderate at the consolidated-company level, with potentially greater significance for industrial-connectivity operations. Confidence is high in the demand direction, but lower in the size of any earnings surprise.

Call evidence: Amphenol’s industrial revenue increased 25% organically and 7% sequentially, with sequential performance materially exceeding expectations. Management stated that the “vast majority” of its industrial applications were growing at double-digit organic rates, citing building automation, instrumentation, oil and gas, alternative energy, electrification, factory automation and heavy equipment. Crucially, management said that data-center construction was “not the predominance” of industrial growth. Organic growth excluding AI was in the high teens.

The transmission mechanism is increased demand for the physical networking, connectors, sensors and communications infrastructure embedded in industrial equipment and facilities. Greater electronic content increases connectivity requirements even when equipment-unit growth is modest. Stronger production and project activity provide an additional volume driver. This is a more direct read-through for Belden’s industrial networking and TE’s industrial connectivity than for broad machinery manufacturers, whose sales depend more heavily on equipment replacement cycles and capital-budget decisions.

Belden is the most immediate catalyst. Its Q3 results are scheduled for October 29, before the market opens. Belden entered the quarter with record orders of $836 million, a 1.11 book-to-bill ratio and 8% organic revenue growth in Q2. Amphenol’s subsequent evidence of broad industrial strength supports continued order conversion and reduces the likelihood that Belden’s earlier improvement was confined to isolated customers or AI projects. The relevant tests are organic growth, industrial orders and the outlook beyond the initial RUCKUS consolidation.

The earnings-quality distinction is important. Belden’s Q2 adjusted EPS included approximately $0.25 of net tariff-related benefit, while Amphenol’s headline sequential margin decline concealed underlying improvement because tariff recoveries fell. A softer reported sequential EPS or margin comparison at Belden would therefore not necessarily invalidate the positive demand signal. RUCKUS also changes Belden’s business mix, making consolidated growth less informative than organic performance.

For TE, the call is corroboration rather than a fresh earnings forecast. TE’s October 28 results already showed 18% organic growth in Automation and Connected Living across all regions. Agreement between the companies strengthens the case for a broader industrial-electronics recovery into 2027. The longer-duration implication is that electronic content growth can sustain connectivity suppliers through uneven industrial production, although Amphenol’s 25% growth rate should not be transferred directly to either peer.

DATA-CENTER INTERCONNECT

PASSIVE OPTICAL INFRASTRUCTURE IS PARTICIPATING IN THE AI BUILDOUT AT MATERIAL SCALE (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Corning (GLW: United States). Direction: positive overall. Magnitude: high for Optical Communications and material for consolidated earnings. Confidence is high in the demand read-through; incremental supplier allocation and pricing remain unquantified.

Call evidence: Amphenol raised the acquired CommScope business’s 2026 revenue expectation to $5.1 billion from $4.6 billion. Management expects CommScope’s IT datacom sales to more than double and represent approximately 50% of its annual revenue, versus approximately 33% in the prior year. Management specifically attributed progress to “advanced optical interconnect solutions” and described efforts to secure materials, “including glass.”

The transmission mechanism extends beyond optical transceivers. Larger AI clusters require fiber, cable assemblies, high-density termination, patching and connectivity infrastructure. Higher connection density and more demanding installation requirements increase the value of engineered optical solutions. Corning participates through optical fiber, cable and connectivity products, making the call directly relevant to its enterprise optical business.

The scale is meaningful. Applying management’s approximate mix to the $5.1 billion CommScope forecast implies approximately $2.55 billion of annual IT datacom revenue within that acquired business. This is not incremental revenue available to Corning, nor is it a disclosure of Corning’s supply relationship with Amphenol. It demonstrates that optical infrastructure demand is large enough to materially reshape an established connectivity business.

Corning’s October 27 results already reported 44% Optical Communications growth, 84% Enterprise Networks growth and more than 100% growth in Gen AI products. Optical Communications represented approximately 47% of core sales. Amphenol therefore provides independent confirmation of an already-reported growth engine rather than advance evidence of an undisclosed Corning quarterly beat.

The near-term implication is greater confidence in continued demand and capacity utilization through Q4 and into 2027. The longer-duration implication is that optical content can grow faster than accelerator units as cluster architecture and connectivity density evolve. Neither Amphenol’s 77% organic IT datacom growth nor CommScope’s doubling should be interpreted as an equivalent increase in GPU shipments.

The glass-supply discussion also requires restraint. It supports the existence of procurement constraints and the importance of qualified capacity, but does not establish a particular Corning order, higher fiber prices or guaranteed margin expansion. Amphenol’s effort to diversify sourcing could spread procurement across suppliers. The high-conviction conclusion is stronger optical-infrastructure demand, not a quantified transfer of Amphenol’s growth into Corning’s earnings.

COPPER AND OPTICS ARE EXPANDING TOGETHER, REDUCING THE FORCE OF A NEAR-TERM COPPER-OBSOLESCENCE THESIS (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: Credo Technology Group (CRDO: United States) and TE Connectivity (TEL: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high strategic relevance for Credo’s connectivity portfolio and moderate consolidated relevance for TE. Confidence is high in the coexistence of copper and optics, but not in platform-specific content or market-share outcomes.

Call evidence: When questioned about future AI architectures, management stated that customers “need more interconnect period,” adding that this means “more copper high-speed interconnect,” “more optical interconnect” and “more power interconnect.” IT datacom revenue increased 30% sequentially, predominantly from AI, and management said “it wasn’t that anything was pulled in.”

The transmission mechanism is differentiated by reach and electrical requirements. Copper remains economically attractive where distance, power consumption, reliability and signal integrity support its use, while optics addresses other reach and density requirements. Expansion in optical connectivity does not require an immediate decline in the absolute number of high-speed electrical connections.

Credo’s verified portfolio includes active electrical cables, optical transceivers, optical DSPs, silicon-photonics components and retimers. The call therefore supports the demand backdrop for its existing copper products while also validating the relevance of its optical expansion. This is shared end-market evidence, not confirmation that Credo supplies a specific Amphenol assembly or wins a particular customer program.

The near-term catalyst is Credo’s next fiscal Q2 update, for which its published revenue outlook is $525 million to $535 million. Amphenol’s physical shipment acceleration supports the deployment environment behind that outlook. It does not establish a Credo beat, because customer mix, fiscal timing, product qualification and vendor share differ. A confirmed reporting date was not established in the reviewed disclosures.

For TE, management had already outlined more than $1 billion of incremental Digital Data Networks revenue in fiscal 2027, predominantly from AI, with more than 50% of that increase expected in the fiscal second half. Amphenol’s commentary reinforces the architectural basis for that opportunity, but does not justify pulling TE’s expected second-half ramps into earlier quarters.

The principal limitation is architecture specificity. Amphenol declined to discuss named customers or validate the proposed NVIDIA backplane-to-midplane transition raised by an analyst. The call weakens a blanket copper-displacement thesis, but does not resolve content on any particular future NVIDIA system. Moreover, Amphenol’s Q4 IT datacom guidance slows to mid-single-digit sequential growth. The positive conclusion is durability of participation, not continued 30% sequential growth across the interconnect supply chain.

A BETTER-FUNDED COMMSCOPE REMOVES A COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE ENJOYED BY OTHER CONNECTIVITY SUPPLIERS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies: Corning (GLW: United States) and Belden (BDC: United States). Direction: negative competitive read-through, distinct from the positive demand backdrop. Magnitude: modest immediate earnings relevance but potentially material over several years in overlapping optical and building-connectivity markets. Confidence is high that the competitor’s capabilities have strengthened; actual share loss or pricing pressure at peers is not established.

Call evidence: Management contrasted CommScope’s former capital constraints with its position inside Amphenol, citing investment in technology, additional manufacturing resources, diversified material supply and support for geographic expansion. The business’s revenue expectation increased by $500 million from the preceding forecast. Its operating margin had reached the “low 20s,” and management expressed confidence in eventual convergence toward Amphenol’s corporate average.

The transmission mechanism is improved competitive execution. A supplier with greater access to capital can expand capacity, fund product development, secure materials and support customer ramps more reliably. Those capabilities can influence design awards and customer allocation, particularly when timely delivery and engineering support matter more than nominal unit price.

Corning competes with the acquired business in optical cable and connectivity, although its upstream fiber capabilities provide a different economic exposure. Belden overlaps in passive network infrastructure and building connectivity. A more capable CommScope can reduce opportunities created by a financially constrained competitor and increase the investment required to defend customer relationships.

The implication is not that either company has already lost share. Both can grow in an expanding market, and Corning’s latest results demonstrate substantial growth. The negative conclusion is narrower: forecasts should not continue to assume that CommScope remains limited by its former parent’s financial condition. The relevant longer-term evidence will be design wins, delivery performance, competitive pricing and changes in customer allocation.

Ownership distinctions are essential. The CommScope business discussed on Amphenol’s call is the acquired Connectivity and Cable Solutions operation. RUCKUS Networks is separately owned by Belden following its July 1 acquisition. CommScope’s optical growth should not be counted again as Belden revenue, while Belden’s RUCKUS exposure should not be confused with Amphenol’s acquired assets.

For near-term trading, this is principally a qualification to optimistic connectivity-sector assumptions, not evidence supporting an immediate peer earnings cut. Over a longer horizon, it increases the importance of proprietary technology, customer qualification and capital efficiency as sources of competitive advantage.

DATA-CENTER POWER INFRASTRUCTURE

POWER DENSITY SUPPORTS ELECTRICAL-CONTENT GROWTH, BUT 800-VOLT REVENUE TIMING MUST REMAIN SEPARATE (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Eaton (ETN: United States) and Vertiv Holdings (VRT: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high relevance for Vertiv’s core market and material for Eaton’s data-center electrical businesses. Confidence is high in rising power-delivery requirements, but lower in the timing and profitability of specific architecture transitions.

Call evidence: Amphenol characterized power interconnect as a meaningful component of its AI business and identified higher chip power consumption and “new power formats like 800 volt and beyond” as growth drivers. Management emphasized efficiency and safety as the central customer requirements.

The transmission mechanism is increased engineering and equipment requirements throughout the power-delivery chain. Higher rack density creates demand for power conversion, distribution, protection, energy storage, busway and rack-level infrastructure. Eaton and Vertiv sell equipment at these layers; their exposure is to common customer infrastructure requirements, not a demonstrated supplier relationship with Amphenol.

The important economic distinction is between rising infrastructure value and rising material volume. Higher-voltage distribution reduces current for a given power level and can lower conductor requirements and electrical losses. The positive read-through therefore rests on system complexity, power capacity, protection and conversion needs, not a simplistic assumption that every architecture consumes more copper.

Eaton’s November 3 earnings release is the nearest unreported catalyst. Amphenol’s commentary supports the demand environment for data-center electrical equipment, while Eaton’s own technical roadmap includes high-density DC infrastructure and a sidecar platform targeting manufacturing readiness in Q1 2027. The relevant earnings questions are orders, backlog conversion, delivery capability and margin performance, rather than whether 800-volt systems already contribute materially to revenue.

Vertiv had already reported on October 28, so Amphenol provides corroboration rather than a new forecast of that quarter. Vertiv’s own call described initial revenue and customer validation for full native 800-volt DC systems during 2027, with broader deployment in 2028. Amphenol’s enthusiasm should not be used to accelerate that disclosed timetable.

The longer-duration opportunity is substantial because suppliers must accommodate multiple infrastructure configurations during the transition. Existing AC installations, intermediate rack-level conversion and eventual native DC systems can coexist. However, architectural change can also alter equipment content and challenge legacy products. The positive thesis requires successful product migration, not merely exposure to current power infrastructure.

TELECOMMUNICATIONS AND BROADBAND EQUIPMENT

AI CONNECTIVITY STRENGTH DOES NOT VALIDATE A RESIDENTIAL BROADBAND RECOVERY (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: ADTRAN Holdings (ADTN: United States). Direction: negative for near-term access-network recovery assumptions. Magnitude: potentially material for access-related profitability, but moderated at the consolidated level by ADTRAN’s optical-networking and cloud-related growth. Confidence is high in the adverse end-market signal, not in a specific revenue miss.

Call evidence: Amphenol’s communications networks revenue declined 28% organically and 13% sequentially. Management expects another sequential decline in Q4, citing “continued softness and spending, particularly in broadband.” The 25% reported revenue increase was acquisition-driven and therefore obscured the underlying contraction.

The transmission mechanism is slower operator deployment and purchasing. Reduced broadband investment can defer access equipment, subscriber-network upgrades and related infrastructure. For ADTRAN, that risk applies most directly to its access-oriented operations rather than uniformly to its entire portfolio.

Operating leverage makes this important. ADTRAN’s latest reported non-GAAP operating margin was only 3.8%, and its Q3 margin outlook was 1.5% to 5.5%. A business operating at those margins has limited room to absorb additional shipment delays, unfavorable mix or underutilization. Even modest revenue disruption can have a disproportionate effect on earnings.

The immediate catalyst is ADTRAN’s November 2 results release and November 3 call. Amphenol’s warning increases the importance of access-project timing and the outlook for Q4 deployment. However, ADTRAN had already incorporated timing and supply issues into its outlook. The call does not prove that those assumptions were insufficient.

Counterevidence prevents an indiscriminate bearish conclusion. ADTRAN’s August release described strong optical-networking demand and 47% growth from cloud, enterprise and government customers. Amphenol itself reported exceptional AI connectivity growth. The same supplier can therefore experience weak residential-access spending and strong data-center interconnect demand simultaneously.

The actionable implication is to separate access-network exposure from AI-related optical transport when evaluating telecom-equipment companies. A broad “networking recovery” thesis is insufficient. Customer category, project type and product mix determine the outcome. This is a negative read-through for access-recovery upside, not evidence that all optical networking or all carrier investment is contracting.

DEFENSE ELECTRONICS

ELECTRONICS MODERNIZATION AND REPLENISHMENT SUPPORT A DEMAND CYCLE LONGER THAN CURRENT CONFLICTS (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: Curtiss-Wright (CW: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high relevance for Defense Electronics and moderate consolidated relevance. Confidence is high in the structural demand direction, while quarterly shipment timing remains program-specific.

Call evidence: Amphenol’s defense revenue increased 30% organically and 12% sequentially. Management described double-digit growth across nearly all tracked defense applications, including space, unmanned vehicles, communications, avionics, land systems, munitions and naval equipment. It also identified replenishment as a “multi-year, if not multi-decade initiative,” alongside increased electronic content and a broader set of defense customers.

The transmission mechanism is demand for embedded computing, tactical communications, control systems, sensing and other electronics required by modern defense platforms. Curtiss-Wright participates through embedded computing, communications and defense-electronics products. More electronically intensive platforms can increase its addressable content even without a proportionate increase in platform units.

The geographic evidence is also relevant. Amphenol cited growing investment in indigenous defense technology across NATO countries, South Asia and the Middle East. Curtiss-Wright’s latest disclosures identified international turret-drive and radar-system demand alongside domestic fighter and unmanned-aircraft computing programs. These are overlapping market exposures, not evidence that Amphenol has identified a specific Curtiss-Wright contract.

The near-term catalyst is Curtiss-Wright’s November 4 results release and November 5 call. Its Q2 release already described record demand for defense-electronics products, yet Defense Electronics sales declined 3% because of tactical-communications timing. Amphenol’s broad shipment strength increases confidence in the underlying market but does not eliminate that timing risk. Orders, backlog conversion and program schedules are more useful than applying Amphenol’s 30% growth rate to Curtiss-Wright.

The longer-duration implication is that a reduction in active conflict would not necessarily cause an immediate collapse in electronics demand. Inventory replenishment, modernization and development of newer platforms can continue after current consumption moderates. This supports a more durable demand framework than a thesis based solely on wartime replacement spending.

The qualification is fiscal and contractual. Management’s multi-decade replenishment characterization is not funded backlog, and procurement priorities can change. The high-conviction positive is sustained electronics intensity across a broad set of defense applications, not guaranteed budget growth or immunity from program delays.

Across the portfolio, the distinction between economic diversification and ticker diversification remains critical. Corning, Credo, Vertiv and the AI-facing portions of TE and Eaton share substantial exposure to the same infrastructure-investment cycle. Belden’s industrial networking and Curtiss-Wright’s defense electronics offer more differentiated demand drivers, while ADTRAN demonstrates why traditional broadband exposure should not be treated as interchangeable with AI connectivity.

text:
🕰️ The Clock is Ticking 

Canada is undergoing a massive shift as provinces abandon the twice-yearly time change. 

British Columbia moved to permanent Pacific Time earlier this year, and Alberta and Manitoba are stopping the clock change on November 1. 

Saskatchewan and Yukon already watch the clocks stay still year-round.

The Northwest Territories and parts of Northwestern Ontario are also planning to align with their neighbours to stop shifting. 

Meanwhile, Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces are still set to fall back this November, though Quebec has recently signaled plans for change.

This patchwork rollout means Canada is splitting into different time zones. The policy momentum across most provinces has favoured permanent Daylight Saving Time, driven by public and political preference for brighter winter evenings and avoiding business disruption.

However, the medical and scientific community is strongly pushing back. 

A landmark analysis in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, alongside position statements from the Canadian Sleep Society, warns that permanent Daylight Saving Time comes with severe biological costs.

Sleep researchers emphasize that human biological clocks rely strictly on morning sunlight to reset daily and stay alert. 

Under permanent Daylight Saving Time, Canada's northern latitude means winter sunrises will happen brutally late, past 9:00 AM or even 10:00 AM in some cities.

When the sun rises very late but school and work hours stay fixed, it forces people into social jet lag. 

Without morning light to anchor the circadian rhythm, individuals naturally drift into later sleep patterns while still being forced to wake up early.

Chronobiologists warn this leads to chronic sleep deprivation, which carries long-term health risks. 

Epidemiological data links permanent circadian misalignment to higher rates of cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, and depression.

History also offers a warning. 

When the United States tried permanent Daylight Saving Time in 1974, and Russia tried it in 2011, both experiments were quickly repealed because winter mornings became too dangerous for school children and commuters.

While sleep experts agree that ending the twice-yearly clock switch is good for public health, they argue that choosing permanent Daylight Saving Time over Permanent Standard Time is a step backward for long-term Canadian health and safety. 

What do you prefer?
