text:
The temple you see is Vaitheeswaran Koil, the abode of Lord Vaidyanatha Swamy, a form of Lord Shiva worshipped as the divine healer.

I don't know how many generations this tradition goes back in our family, but whenever a boy or girl is born, we take the child to this temple at a very young age and tonsure their head as an offering to the Lord.

There is also a ritual in which we offer salt and black pepper in the kulam (குளம்), the sacred temple tank, and pray for good health.

This February, there was no family occasion or particular reason to visit Vaitheeswaran Koil. I was about to return to Delhi when, quite unexpectedly, I felt a strong urge to visit the temple. It was almost a last-minute decision. I hired a cab, went there, prayed to the Lord and offered salt and black pepper in the sacred tank.

I returned to Delhi, and life went on as usual.

Three months later, in May, my family insisted that I undergo a health check-up. The tests revealed multiple plaques in my left coronary artery, with one blockage measuring around 60% on angiography.

I was devastated. Life changed overnight. Medicines became part of my daily routine, severe leg cramps made even climbing ten steps difficult, and my diet became restricted. The normal, carefree life I had taken for granted suddenly seemed to have disappeared.

In those moments of helplessness, I kept asking God, “Why me?”

Then, slowly, I began to look back at that unexpected visit to Vaitheeswaran Koil.

There had been no plan to go there. No occasion. No reason that I could explain. Yet something within me had drawn me to the temple just before I returned to Delhi.

Perhaps that was my answer.

Maybe Lord Vaidyanatha Swamy had called me to His abode, not to promise that I would never face difficulties, but to reassure me that I would not have to face them alone.

In my heart, I could almost hear Him saying:

“Son, I called you, and you came to Me. Now do not be afraid. Take care of your health, have faith, and leave the rest to Me. I am with you.”

I may never know why I felt that sudden calling in February. Nor do I know what lies ahead. But today, I choose to see that visit as a moment of grace, a reminder that even when life takes an unexpected turn, faith can give us the strength to carry on.

Perhaps God's care does not always mean removing our troubles. Sometimes, it means giving us the courage to face them.

I went to Vaitheeswaran Koil without knowing what awaited me. I returned with a faith that, whatever awaits me now, I am not alone. 🙏

text:
Medical schools accused of rebranding DEI programs to evade Trump administration scrutiny | Fox News

Medical schools across the U.S. are rebranding their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) departments as the Trump administration increases scrutiny of DEI programs in higher education and medicine, according to a new report by https://t.co/4t7HTNv4C0.

The report, which examined six medical schools, found that although the departments have been renamed, their programming has remained largely unchanged, despite some softened language since President Donald Trump began his second term in 2025.

"The rebranding is not really meaningful in a sense," William Jacobson, a Cornell Law School professor and founder of the Equal Protection Project, told Fox News Digital. "The programming hasn't changed and a lot of the examples, and I think there's a couple in our report, they simply shift programs over to a different department or under a different name, but the programming hasn't really changed."

The medical schools profiled in the report include Drexel University College of Medicine, Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell, Saint Louis University School of Medicine, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University, and the University of Nevada-Reno School of Medicine (UNR Med). https://t.co/4t7HTNv4C0's report notes that the schools often used terms such as "belonging," "engagement" and "excellence" in names of what appeared to be rebranded DEI departments.

"You see all of these euphemisms for critical race theory, all of the euphemism, frankly, for race discrimination popping up, and that's the rebranding that we're talking about, and that is what we've documented at six particular medical schools," Jacobson told Fox News Digital. "Medical schools are the worst when it comes to DEI."

Drexel University College of Medicine, according to the report, described its Office of Community Health and Inclusive Excellence in an announcement, saying it "incorporates the functions of the Office of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion and the former Office of Community Health & Health Equity, to better align and strengthen the College’s resources to address inclusivity across missions." The office, according to Drexel's website, supports a Diversity Week and the college's Diversity in Medicine Research Symposium.

The Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell did something similar, rebranding its DEI office as the "Office of Engagement & Excellence," according to the report. The office's list of featured events includes student-led "Safe and Brave Spaces" and "Diversity Night."

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, Terry Coniglio, spokesperson for Hofstra University, said, "The Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell supports all students while remaining consistent with its institutional values and applicable law."

At Northwestern University, the Feinberg School of Medicine once had a DEI office, but the report says it has since been replaced by the Office of Health Equity, which offers "Safe Space Training." https://t.co/4t7HTNv4C0's report notes that the training is open to students, trainees, staff and faculty and aims to educate LGBTQIA+ allies.

The Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University also rebranded its DEI office, according to https://t.co/4t7HTNv4C0, which cited a Campus Reform report on the matter. Campus Reform reported in November 2025 that the school renamed its Office of Health Equity, Diversity and Inclusion to the Office of Strategic Partnership in Health, Education and Resources (SPHERE), which still promoted "equity" programs.

Meanwhile, UNR Med appeared to have moved its DEI programs to another department, taking them from the Office of Diversity and Inclusion to the Multicultural Center, according to the report. The university's website describes the Multicultural Center as "a critical hub of cultural, LGBTQIA+, gender-focused services, programs and social justice initiatives that support student success and increase graduation rates of students at the University of Nevada, Reno." The website page for the Multicultural Center's webpage also features a DEI statement.

In response to a question about what happened to its Office of Diversity and Inclusion, UNR Med told Fox News Digital that "in line with multiple unit reorganizations within the University of Nevada, Reno School of Medicine the dean’s staff currently includes an associate dean for inclusive excellence but does not include a named office."

Additionally, UNR Med clarified that the Multicultural Center serves the entire university and acts as "a student support and engagement center dedicated to fostering belonging, cultural understanding and student success."

"The Multicultural Center does not conduct student recruitment, admissions or enrollment services; its primary focus is supporting students once they are part of the university community and helping create an inclusive environment," UNR Med told Fox News Digital.

UNR Med said that it "abides by accreditation standards related to curricular programming, student admissions and faculty recruitment" and that it "remains compliant with all federal laws and guidelines, as well as state law, the Nevada Constitution and the U.S. Constitution."

Fox News Digital reached out to Drexel University College of Medicine, Saint Louis University School of Medicine, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University for comment but did not immediately receive responses.

Upon his return to office in 2025, Trump signed several executive orders aimed at eliminating DEI from various aspects of American life. Jacobson said that while these orders have had an impact, many in academia are not ready to let go of DEI, which he called a "religion on campuses." The Cornell Law School professor believes that many are biding their time until the Democrats return to power, hoping that it will mean a return to DEI.

"The schools, particularly the medical schools, are hanging on to DEI, like survivors on a shipwreck, and they're hoping for a rescue, and they think their rescue is going to be Democrats getting control of the federal government again, because then all the DEI will come back. They're not giving it up," Jacobson told Fox News Digital.

Jacobson argued that, while DEI is an issue in academia, it presents a different set of risks when introduced in the medical field. He explained that it "destroys confidence in the system," as patients may question whether their physicians were admitted to medical school and trained fairly, as well as whether they will receive fair treatment.

"When this sort of race-based focus, when this sort of identity group focus happens in medicine, it's extremely destructive," he added.

In 2022, Jacobson was named as the plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging New York guidance that instructed healthcare providers to consider race and ethnicity when prioritizing scarce COVID-19 treatments. He argued that the policy was discriminatory and violated federal civil rights laws. Courts dismissed the case after finding that he lacked standing. However, Jacobson told Fox News Digital that the case was a prime example of the dangers of having DEI influence the medical field.

"This has a real world impact," Jacobson told Fox News Digital. "This is not just the crazy dance therapy department or the crazy gender ideology department or the sociology department where the most harm they can really do is to the minds of young people. Here we're talking about healthcare decisions are being made, access to healthcare because of the DEI infusion in medical schools is being rationed and affected by these ideologies. So this is life and death. This is serious stuff."

While Trump's executive orders did not categorically prohibit DEI programming at medical schools, a January 2025 order pointed to the medical industry and institutions of higher education as areas in which race- and sex-based preferences could violate federal civil rights laws.

The order, titled "Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity," called on the Justice Department and the Education Department to issue guidance to federally funded institutions on complying with the Supreme Court's 2023 decision restricting the use of race in college admissions.

Jacobson argued that many medical schools had changed the language used in programs without necessarily changing their intent.

"I think it's less blatant. I think, again, they don't use the terminology of color in their programming like they used to, but it's the same programming," Jacobson said.

There is one major difference when it comes to DEI in medical schools, according to Jacobson. The law professor told Fox News Digital that, while in most areas of academia the push for DEI is driven by professors, in medical schools it tends to come from administrators rather than instructors.

"If you'd asked me four years ago, I would have said, wait five years, and DEI will have captured STEM, the sciences, and we're now four to five years and it's captured a lot of STEM, not as bad as the humanities and the social sciences, but there is a real problem in the sciences with DEI," Jacobson said. "Unlike the other aspects of the universities where it's professor-driven, in medicine, it's mostly administration-driven."

He said that this could mean the policies may be easier to address once identified, but that medical schools remain "extremely resistant to change."

Jacobson believes states could play a significant role in challenging DEI policies at public medical schools, particularly as federal officials and accrediting organizations increase their scrutiny of race-based requirements. He also noted that the federal government has played a role in the accrediting stage, adding that some DEI practices were required by accreditors, who are now under pressure.

Ultimately, Jacobson believes that government action has to be accompanied by a significant cultural shift in academia.

"The federal and state governments can help, but we need a long-term effort over many years to change the culture on campuses to a culture of equality, not a culture of diversity, equity, and inclusion," he told Fox News Digital.

THOMAS EVENSTAD FOR PRESIDENT BLASTS MAYOR JACOB FREY AND MINNEAPOLIS CITY COUNCIL FOR REFUSING TO PLATFORM THE ONLY CANDIDATE WITH A REAL SOLUTION TO MINNEAPOLIS VIOLENCE
City Leadership Continues to Prioritize Politics and Failed Status-Quo Approaches While Families, Neighborhoods, and Children Remain Under Threat
MINNEAPOLIS, MN — Thomas Evenstad, candidate for President of the United States in 2028 and lifelong Minnesota public-safety advocate, today issued a strong condemnation of Mayor Jacob Frey and the Minneapolis City Council for systematically refusing to give him a platform to present the only proven framework capable of meaningfully reducing the city’s violence crisis.
Evenstad charged that Frey and the Council have chosen political insulation over public safety by declining invitations, forums, briefings, and direct engagement on the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act), also known as Mariah’s Law. He described this refusal as a dereliction of duty at a time when Minneapolis continues to suffer from gang violence, carjackings, shootings, and the release of high-risk offenders back into the community.
“Mayor Frey and the Minneapolis City Council have made a deliberate choice,” Evenstad stated. “They will platform the same failed approaches, the same press conferences, the same task-force theater, and the same soft-on-violence orthodoxy that have left Minneapolis bleeding. What they will not do is platform the one person who has put forward a concrete, measurable solution designed to identify and remove the most violently dangerous persons from our streets. That is not leadership. That is avoidance.”
Evenstad emphasized that the VDP Act expands existing civil-commitment tools already used for the highest-risk sex offenders under Minnesota’s MSOP framework and applies them to the subset of violently dangerous individuals who drive a disproportionate share of serious crime. He has repeatedly offered to brief city officials, appear at public forums, and submit detailed modeling showing substantial projected reductions in violence. Those offers, he said, have been met with silence or outright refusal.
“The people of Minneapolis do not need more photo-ops or more rhetoric about ‘root causes’ while the same dangerous actors cycle through the system,” Evenstad continued. “They need leadership willing to look at the only tool that targets the actual problem instead of managing decline. I am that candidate. I have the plan. Frey and the City Council have chosen not to hear it. The blood that continues to be spilled is on their hands as long as they refuse to engage.”
Evenstad called on residents, neighborhood groups, business owners, and faith leaders to demand that the Mayor and City Council schedule a public hearing or open forum specifically to hear the VDP Act proposal and related public-safety solutions. He reiterated his willingness to appear anytime, anywhere, under any format, without conditions.
“This is not about politics. This is about whether Minneapolis will keep pretending that more of the same will somehow produce different results,” Evenstad said. “I am running for President because the failure is not limited to one city. But Minneapolis is ground zero for the refusal to face reality. Platform the solution or own the continued violence. Those are the only two options left.”

text:
American Cruise Lines' Southeast Alaska Cruise: An Intimate Journey Through the Last Frontier

For travelers seeking Alaska's majestic glaciers, abundant wildlife, and frontier towns without the crowds associated with large cruise ships, American Cruise Lines' Southeast Alaska itinerary offers one of the most immersive ways to experience the region. Sailing aboard small American-built vessels carrying only a fraction of the passengers found on mainstream cruise ships, guests enjoy a highly personalized journey through the spectacular waterways of Alaska's famed Inside Passage.

The American Cruise Lines Difference

Founded in 1973, American Cruise Lines has built its reputation around small-ship cruising exclusively within the United States. Today, the company operates the nation's only 100% U.S.-flagged fleet of riverboats and coastal cruise ships, focusing on domestic destinations ranging from New England and the Mississippi River to the Pacific Northwest and Alaska.

Unlike conventional mega-ships carrying thousands of passengers, American Cruise Lines' Alaska vessels accommodate fewer than 200 guests, creating a more intimate atmosphere and allowing access to ports and waterways that larger ships often cannot visit.

The emphasis is not on water parks, casinos, or Broadway-style productions. Instead, the line focuses on:

Regional enrichment and education
Personalized service
Scenic cruising
Authentic local experiences
Comfortable accommodations
Small-group shore excursions

This approach appeals particularly to travelers who value destination immersion over onboard spectacle.

Best Time to Take the Southeast Alaska Cruise

The Alaska cruise season generally runs from May through September, with the sweet spot being mid-June through late August.

June

Many experienced Alaska travelers consider June among the best months to visit. Snow-capped mountains remain dramatic, days are exceptionally long, and wildlife activity is increasing.

July

The warmest month of the season, July offers excellent opportunities for whale watching, glacier viewing, and outdoor activities. Expect the highest demand and premium pricing.

August

Wildlife viewing peaks as salmon runs attract bears and bald eagles. Weather remains relatively mild, and the scenery is lush and vibrant.

September

Fewer crowds and beautiful autumn colors make September appealing. While temperatures are cooler, travelers may enjoy lower fares and a quieter Alaska.

For first-time visitors seeking optimal weather and wildlife viewing, July and August are often considered ideal.

How Far in Advance Should You Book?

Because American Cruise Lines operates relatively small ships with limited capacity, booking early is highly recommended.

A general rule is:

12 to 18 months in advance for preferred summer sailings
18 months or more for premium balcony accommodations and suites
6 to 12 months minimum even for less popular departure dates

The Alaska season is short, and the small-ship nature of the experience means availability often disappears earlier than on larger cruise lines.

Accommodations: Spacious Staterooms and Suites

One of the most appreciated aspects of American Cruise Lines is its unusually large accommodations.

Many staterooms feature:

Private balconies
Floor-to-ceiling glass doors
Sitting areas
Spacious bathrooms
Ample storage

Suites offer additional living space and enhanced views, making scenic cruising through Glacier Bay and Endicott Arm particularly enjoyable.

Unlike many large cruise ships, guests often spend significant time relaxing in their cabins because the scenery outside is constantly changing and spectacular.

Cuisine and Dining

American Cruise Lines includes all meals in the cruise fare and emphasizes regionally inspired cuisine.

In Alaska, menus commonly showcase:

Fresh salmon
Halibut
Dungeness crab
Local shellfish
Seasonal produce

Dining is typically open seating, encouraging social interaction among fellow travelers. The atmosphere is refined but not formal, reflecting the line's relaxed small-ship philosophy.

According to the cruise line, fares include fine dining, cocktails, gratuities, Wi-Fi, and shore excursions, creating a largely all-inclusive experience.

All-American Crew

A distinctive feature of American Cruise Lines is its American crew members.

Because the ships are U.S.-flagged, crew members are primarily American citizens. This creates a different onboard atmosphere than many international cruise lines and often leads to engaging conversations with staff members who are passionate about both hospitality and American destinations.

Guests frequently remark upon the friendly, personalized service that naturally develops on smaller vessels.

Enrichment and Education

Education plays a major role in the Southeast Alaska experience.

Throughout the voyage, guests enjoy presentations covering:

Alaska Native cultures
Russian influence in Alaska
Gold Rush history
Wildlife ecology
Glaciology
Maritime traditions

Naturalists and historians frequently accompany the cruise, providing expert commentary during scenic passages through Glacier Bay, Endicott Arm, and other wilderness areas.

Shore Excursions

American Cruise Lines includes at least one complimentary excursion in each port.

Possible experiences include:

Wildlife expeditions
Glacier viewing
Bald eagle observation
Alaska Native cultural experiences
Historic walking tours
Gold Rush heritage sites
Small-group nature excursions

Because passenger counts are lower, excursions tend to feel more personal and less crowded than those offered on large ships.

The Southeast Alaska Itinerary

One of American Cruise Lines' signature Southeast Alaska voyages is the 9-day roundtrip sailing from Juneau. The cruise begins and ends in Alaska's capital while exploring many of the region's most celebrated destinations.

Embarkation Port: Juneau, Alaska

Your journey begins in Juneau, the only U.S. state capital inaccessible by road. Guests typically enjoy a hotel stay and guided city experience before boarding the ship.

Highlights include:

Alaska State Capitol
Mendenhall Glacier
Historic downtown
Gold Rush heritage
Haines

Nestled between towering mountains and the Lynn Canal, Haines is famous for its extraordinary wildlife and breathtaking scenery.

Visitors often enjoy:

Chilkat Valley excursions
Bald eagle viewing
Cultural attractions
Scenic photography opportunities

The region hosts one of the world's largest concentrations of bald eagles.

Glacier Bay National Park

For many travelers, this is the highlight of the cruise.

Glacier Bay encompasses millions of acres of protected wilderness and is both a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Biosphere Reserve. Ships sail among massive tidewater glaciers while guests often observe:

Humpback whales
Sea otters
Harbor seals
Mountain goats
Bald eagles

National Park rangers and onboard naturalists provide expert narration throughout the day.

Petersburg

Known as "Little Norway," Petersburg was founded by Norwegian fishermen and remains one of Alaska's most authentic fishing communities.

Highlights include:

Working fishing harbor
Norwegian heritage
Nearby LeConte Glacier
Local seafood culture

Unlike larger tourist ports, Petersburg offers a genuine glimpse into everyday life in Southeast Alaska.

Wrangell Narrows

The ship navigates the famous Wrangell Narrows, a winding 21-mile channel known for its tight passages and navigational markers. This scenic transit is often one of the voyage's most memorable cruising experiences.

Wrangell

One of Alaska's oldest communities, Wrangell features a rich history shaped by Native cultures, Russian traders, and Gold Rush prospectors.

Visitors can explore:

Historic sites
Totem traditions
Wildlife habitats
Coastal rainforest landscapes
Endicott Arm and Dawes Glacier

The voyage culminates with spectacular cruising through Endicott Arm, where sheer granite walls rise from icy waters filled with floating bergs. At the head of the fjord lies Dawes Glacier, a magnificent tidewater glacier flowing from the Stikine Icefield.

Passengers frequently spot:

Harbor seals
Mountain goats
Waterfalls cascading hundreds of feet
Ice calving from the glacier face
Disembarkation: Return to Juneau

The cruise concludes back in Juneau, allowing guests additional time to explore Alaska's capital before flying home.

Final Thoughts

American Cruise Lines' Southeast Alaska itinerary is ideally suited for travelers who want to experience Alaska in a more intimate and educational setting. Rather than focusing on entertainment complexes and crowded ports, the line emphasizes authentic exploration, personalized service, regional cuisine, and close-up encounters with some of North America's most spectacular wilderness.

For guests seeking Glacier Bay's towering ice, Haines' wildlife, Petersburg's maritime heritage, and the extraordinary scenery of Endicott Arm, few Alaska experiences combine comfort, enrichment, and accessibility quite as effectively as a small-ship voyage with American Cruise Lines.

text:
Everything that happened in the data center world today (Oct 29, 2026)

Alphabet just burned $9B of free cash in a quarter and is down 11% premarket. Microsoft spent less than it planned and is up. Same AI boom, two very different reactions.

HYPERSCALERS
- Alphabet Q3: Cloud +103% to $30.7B. Capex $51.4B vs ~$55.1B expected. Free cash flow -$9.1B. 2026 capex guide held at $195-205B, 2027 to rise "significantly." Stock -11% premarket (Alphabet, CNBC)

- Alphabet's long-term debt is now $125.1B vs $21.6B a year ago. Purchase commitments hit $924B. It started renting third-party compute late in Q3 and says that will hurt cloud margins near term (Alphabet, CNBC)
- Microsoft: Azure +48% to $33.2B, Q2 Azure guide 49-50%. Capex $45.2B, under its own $50B+ guide because third-party capacity arrived late. Q2 capex seen over $50B, calendar 2026 ~$170B. Stock +2% premarket (Microsoft, Reuters)
- Oracle at investor day: FY2030 revenue $225B+, capex peaks this year and next, outside funding capped at $20B more through FY2030, FCF positive in 2H FY2028. Stock +10.7%. CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN up 2-5% (Reuters)

MEMORY
- Samsung Q3: operating profit 107.4T won, the first company over 100T in a quarter. Chips made 106.5T, a hair under the ~107.3T estimate. HBM4 revenue more than tripled q/q. DRAM average prices up ~20% q/q (Samsung, Yonhap)
- Samsung says 2027 HBM is sold out and the shortage lasts through 2028, a shorter call than SK hynix. Long-term deals with 10 customers, 10 more in talks. Chip capex 76.8T won this year, up 62%, rising sharply in 2027 (Reuters)
- Samsung pushed its new shareholder return plan to January. Shares -4.1% to 232,000 won while SK hynix rose 2.6% (Yonhap)
- Samsung foundry says it won 2nm orders from hyperscalers and starts mass production at Taylor, Texas next year (Reuters)

CHIPS AND OPTICS
- Marvell is reportedly in advanced talks to buy Lumentum, worth ~$83B, with a deal possible as soon as next week. Lumentum +5%, Marvell -11% premarket (Bloomberg via Reuters, CNBC)
- KLA: revenue $4.14B, above guide. December quarter guided to $4.7B. It says AI, memory and packaging all keep driving demand (KLA)
- Advantest raised its full-year operating profit forecast 14% to 967B yen on AI chip test demand. Stock +6% (Advantest, Kyodo)

POWER
- DOE offered Constellation $5B in loans to add 1.1GW at eight nuclear plants. Most of the added power at seven of them is already sold to Google, Amazon or Meta. Not final yet (TechCrunch, Constellation)

MARKETS
- Wednesday: Fed held at 3.75-4%, two dissents wanted a hike. Nasdaq +0.27%, chip index +1.8%, Micron +5.9% (Reuters)
- KOSPI -1.24% to 5,937. Nikkei +1.10% on Advantest. Taiwan -1.42%, TSMC -0.4%, UMC limit-down. Amazon and Intel report tonight (Yonhap, Kyodo, CNA)

What it all means: The market is grading capex on cash flow now, not growth. Google posted 103% cloud growth and still got hit because the cash went negative and debt is up almost 6x. Microsoft spent less and got paid. Oracle got a 10% pop for promising to stop raising money. Memory is still the strongest data point, but Samsung shows the bar is now "beat SK hynix," not "beat estimates." Marvell-Lumentum tells you optics is where the next fight is. Amazon tonight decides the tone.

JUST IN: The nation’s first detransition clinic has opened.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced on Tuesday that Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston opened the clinic for people who have undergone transgender procedures and want to reverse them.

For patients through age 21, the hospital will provide detransition-related medical care; for those over 21, it will offer related obstetric and gynecologic care. Services include surgery, psychiatry, endocrinology, primary care, fertility counseling, speech pathology, and psychology, with care plans individualized to each patient.

The opening of the clinic is part of a settlement between the hospital, Paxton’s office, and the DOJ. As part of the settlement, the hospital is required to pay $10 million and fund the clinic at no cost to patients for five years. The settlement resolved a federal investigation into allegations the hospital submitted false billings to obtain Medicaid coverage for pediatric “sex-rejecting” procedures, the Department of Justice said.

Background

Texas banned transgender surgeries, puberty blockers, and hormone therapy for minors with gender dysphoria in 2023. The clinic opening comes amid a broader federal crackdown on transgender procedures for minors: CMS has ended federal Medicaid and CHIP funding for these procedures on children, and other hospitals have agreed with the DOJ to stop providing them to minors.

text:
🚨BREAKIMG: ATTENTION PARENTS!

A family doctor in the Chicago area is warning that hospitals are vaccinating children while they are under anesthesia, often without clear, informed consent from parents.

In his own words: “I'm a family doctor who practices in the suburbs and the city of Chicago. I wanted to offer some practical advice tonight to those of you who, like me, might be angry and very concerned about the news reports detailing the rise of what one hospital is calling, close your eyes, we'll immunize. This is a growing practice, perhaps pioneered at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia... where children are undergoing elective and emergency medical surgeries and being immunized while they're away from their parents in the operating room.”

He adds that parents have often given consent unknowingly or under duress, and that true informed consent is rarely being provided the way it should be. Flu shots are the most common, but RSV, COVID, and other vaccines are also being given while kids are sedated.

Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia has run its official “Close Your Eyes, We’ll Immunize” program since 2023 and reported giving 2,054 influenza doses this way in the 2025–2026 season alone. Children’s Hospital Colorado has done it for more than 18,000 patients since 2020. Lurie Children’s in Chicago and other facilities have similar offers, with staff raising the option on the day of surgery.

Imagine taking your child in for appendicitis. You sign a form saying the team can do what’s necessary to help your child. Fifteen minutes later, before the first incision, your child gets a flu shot you never specifically approved. That is the scenario the doctor is describing.

Ask, in writing, before your child goes under. Do not assume a general surgical consent covers vaccines.

text:
Scientists Found a Blood Signature Linked to 23% Lower Risk of Death | Esra Öz, ScienceAlert

Remembering everything you ate last week can be difficult, but your blood may keep its own record: traces of how your body processed those meals.

Scientists have found that a blood signature tied to Mediterranean-style eating is linked to risk of dying years later. In a study involving 14,584 people in Spain and the United States, groups with higher signature scores had a lower risk of death during follow-up.

The research, involving scientists from the University of Navarra, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and other institutions, offers a way to study diet without relying only on what people remember eating.

Mediterranean-style eating emphasizes vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, fish, and olive oil, while limiting red and processed meat. This pattern has been linked to various health benefits, but measuring how closely someone follows it usually involves dietary questionnaires.

"Questionnaires depend on what people remember and report, so they are prone to misclassification," University of Navarra epidemiologist Estefanía Toledo told ScienceAlert.

As the body processes food, it produces or transforms small molecules called metabolites. These can carry information about both what we eat and how our bodies respond to it.

The researchers examined a pattern of 67 metabolites, mostly lipids (fat-related molecules). Developed in 2020, the signature had previously been associated with Mediterranean diet adherence and cardiovascular disease risk. The new study investigated its relationship with long-term mortality.

Many of those fats echo the diet's staples. In earlier work, some tracked closely with olive oil intake, while others are long-chain fatty acids found in nuts and fish.

The team started with blood samples collected from 1,880 participants upon joining a Spanish dietary trial called PREDIMED. These were older adults who had no cardiovascular disease when they enrolled but were at high risk of developing it.

Over roughly 13 years of follow-up, people in the highest third of signature scores had a 23 percent lower risk of death than those in the lowest third, after accounting for factors including age, smoking, body mass index, and existing health conditions.

The researchers then examined data from 12,704 participants in three long-running US studies, followed for an average of 25 years.

The association appeared again: Participants in the highest fifth of signature scores had a 23 percent lower risk of death than those in the lowest fifth.

In the Spanish group, the association remained largely intact after accounting for self-reported adherence to the Mediterranean diet. Toledo explained that the signature may also capture how each person's body absorbs and handles food.

The authors suggest a blood test like this might eventually help doctors spot the people who stand to gain most from changing how they eat.

The results can't, however, tell someone how many years they have left.

"It indicates differences in risk between groups, not an individual's lifespan," Toledo said.

Although PREDIMED was a randomized dietary trial, this analysis of the blood signature and mortality was observational, comparing people's existing scores with what happened to them later. It cannot establish that raising someone's signature score would extend their life.

Scores measured at the start of the trial and after one year, along with their average, were associated with mortality, while changes in the signature over that first year of intervention were not.

The findings suggest the signature may reflect longer-term eating habits and metabolic health, although it's uncertain whether one year is too short to capture the effects of dietary changes.

Before the approach could become a routine blood test, it would need to be tested in more diverse populations, including people of different ages and health backgrounds.

The US participants were health professionals "who are mostly white and relatively healthy," Toledo told ScienceAlert.

Researchers would also need to show that the signature improves risk prediction beyond established risk factors.

He assured prayers for everyone affected and for the eternal rest of those who lost their lives. He offered comfort to their families and wished the injured a speedy recovery. He also encouraged the rescue teams to keep going in their work, and he gave them his Apostolic Blessing.

Srinath Ravichandran, CEO of @AgnikulCosmos, explains how small rockets are similar to Uber for Space

"Let's build the best rocket possible to take today's small satellites to orbit. Customers should be able to launch them quickly, without long waiting times, and at the price they want, not at an extremely high cost. That's why a customer would come to us."

"We offer flexibility in every aspect of transportation: price, waiting time, and the exact drop-off destination in space. Today, no one else does that, because rockets are big."

"At best, you get dropped at a bus stop. You are still at the mercy of everyone else who has to board before the bus leaves. You may also end up with a difficult co-passenger. All of these problems exist in the rocket industry as well. We eliminate all of that."

"We tell customers we can give them a dedicated ride on their own terms, at the same price, and essentially let them own the mission. Just because the satellite is small does not mean the mission is small."

Robert Lee Kessler is charged in the 2021 de*th of Stephanie Crone-Overholts, whose dismembered remains were found in McKay Bay after she had been staying at his home. Prosecutors allege he st*bbed her in the neck multiple times, cut her body into pieces, and dumped the parts in the water.
⠀
"I'll do that for a Philly cheesesteak, and an order of fries and a Pepsi," Kessler told Hillsborough Circuit Judge Nick Nazaretian, later specifying onions, mayonnaise, and a 20-ounce Pepsi to "save the taxpayers."
⠀
The judge rejected it outright. "I've never, in my almost 40 years, ever heard that request before," Nazaretian said, adding that exchanging a meal for a plea would be "wrong in a thousand ways." He promised Kessler standard lunch but not the specific order.
⠀
Kessler replied, "Just pick the jury," and later confirmed he did not want an open plea unless he got the sandwich. The case had been delayed for years over questions of his mental fitness and visual impairment.

text:
Let’s get right to the point on how to build a second high school sports association in Illinois for all you cliff notes readers: 

Imagine a high school association that didn’t take 80 percent of the gate revenue from high schools hosting games like the IHSA does in Illinois.

“We lost money being in the playoffs,” said Bill Thomas, head football coach at Snead High School in Florida. “The FHSAA took 25 percent of the playoff gate here. 

“With the SSAA, they don’t take a dime of your playoff gate unless you play for the state championship.”

Wait: FHSAA only takes 25 percent? Wait, wait, wait: SSAA doesn’t take any until state-championship games?

Illinois high schools leaders continue to hurt kids, families, schools and communities by not creating a second high school association in the massive Midwest state.

Just ask Stuart Weiss.

“All schools are not the same, and a one-size-fits-all approach doesn’t work in high school sports anymore,” said Weiss, who is president of the Sunshine State Athletic Association (SSAA).

**Full story below with details**

Here’s a history lesson every Illinois superintendent, principal, athletic director and school board member should study.

In 2008, eight Florida schools decided the existing model wasn't serving their student athletes. They didn't wait for permission, didn't spend decades complaining. 

They created a second association.

Eighteen years later, the SSAA reports more than 160 member schools across 12 sports.

More competitive opportunities, meaningful games, financial flexibility and more control for schools.

Illinois continues operating under a high school model where 100s of schools enter postseason tournaments knowing their chances of winning even a regional or sectional championship are extremely limited.

Why?

Who benefits from sending overmatched teams into predictable postseason eliminations? How does that build participation, strengthen programs or create meaningful opportunities for kids?

Why should schools continue providing facilities, employees, security, utilities and community support, while surrendering control of so much postseason revenue?

These are schools - not IHSA franchises.

Here’s what makes Florida’a story so important: They didn't need to destroy the FHSAA to create something better.

They created competition, choices and another pathway for kids and schools.

Now consider Illinois.

There are 100s of high schools, 1,000s of experienced coaches and administrators, tremendous athletic facilities and communities that invest millions into school sports.

But somehow we’re supposed to believe these same adult school leaders couldn’t organize a second athletic association?

Seriously?

A second model could offer competitive divisions based on actual program strength, modernized eligibility rules, student broadcasting rights and a significantly larger share of postseason revenue returning to schools.

Imagine championship opportunities that give more kids something meaningful to play for.

The biggest obstacle isn’t money, facilities, talent or opportunity. It’t adult leadership willing to challenge the status quo.

Too many school leaders have become comfortable running on the same hamster wheel, complaining about the IHSA privately while defending the system publicly.

Imagine what 20, 40 or 60 Illinois schools could accomplish if their leaders stopped asking what the IHSA would allow and started asking what was best for their students.

The IHSA doesn’t own Illinois high school sports. Schools don’t owe the IHSA a thing.

Always remember: The kids provide the purpose. The schools provide the product. The communities provide the investment.

Illinois doesn’t need another “committee” studying what’s wrong. 

It needs leaders willing to build what's next.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

In 2003, Microsoft sent a massive 25-page legal cease-and-desist letter to a 17-year-old Canadian high school student named Mike Rowe over his domain name MikeRoweSoft. com, and eventually settled the case by giving him an Xbox and a trip to Microsoft headquarters. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

1. ​The Name Game and the $10 Insult:
​In late 2003, high school student Mike Rowe registered the domain MikeRoweSoft. com to host his part-time web design business. He added "Soft" onto the end of his name as a clever phonetic pun on "software" and his own moniker.  
​It didn't take long for Microsoft’s legal team to spot the domain.

Fearing phonetic trademark confusion, Microsoft’s lawyers sent Rowe a demand letter ordering him to surrender the web address.  When Rowe asked to be compensated for the work he put into the site, Microsoft’s lawyers offered him $10, the exact out-of-pocket cost to register a new domain. Offended by the $10 offer, Rowe jokingly countered by demanding $10,000.

Microsoft responded by doubling down, sending a formal 25-page legal threat and accusing the teenager of illegal "cybersquatting".

2. The "David vs. Goliath" Public Relations Disaster:
​Realizing he was facing off against a multi-billion-dollar tech titan, Rowe took the legal documents and went straight to the news media.
 
​The story exploded worldwide as the ultimate internet "David vs. Goliath" struggle. The public backlash against Microsoft was swift and brutal. 
​Rowe received over $6,000 in public donations to help cover a legal defense fund (which he ended up donating to a children's hospice charity). 

​So many curious internet users rushed to see the site that the web traffic crashed Rowe’s servers after receiving over 250,000 page views in 12 hours. 

3. ​The Xbox Settlement:
​Realizing their aggressive defense of a trademark was morphing into a public relations nightmare, Microsoft backed down and admitted they had perhaps taken the matter "a little too seriously". 

​Rather than fighting in court, Microsoft agreed to an out-of-court settlement in exchange for the domain:

A. ​An Xbox console bundled with a selection of popular video games.  

B. ​An all-expenses-paid family trip to Microsoft’s Tech Fest at their headquarters in Redmond, Washington.  

C. ​Full payment for Microsoft Developer Network (MSDN) subscriptions and certification training courses.  

D. ​Full reimbursement for setting up a new website under a different domain. 

​SUMMARILY! 
​The saga of MikeRoweSoft. com remains one of the most famous domain disputes in internet history. While trademark law legally obligated Microsoft to protect its brand name, the company's heavy-handed response against a teenager named Mike Rowe proved that sometimes taking a softer approach in matters may lead to a better conclusion.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

text:
The money Microsoft saved by laying off 4,800 people this year pays for about two days of its AI data center spending.

Half the internet is passing around a one-minute office vlog as proof Microsoft employees just eat snacks all day, so I ran the numbers. (Also, if you squeeze a 9.5-hour day into a minute, you're going to see the snack machine. Nobody films themselves reviewing a pull request for 40 minutes.)

Microsoft told investors it'll spend at least $175 billion on capex in 2026. Spread across the year, that's about $480 million a day, mostly on data centers, chips and memory. They spent $41 billion last quarter alone, up 69% from a year ago.

Now the layoffs. Say each role costs $200K a year with benefits, which is generous since a big chunk of Microsoft's workforce sits in India and Europe. 4,800 people comes out to around $960 million a year. So roughly two days of servers.

Profit was up 31% last fiscal year, to $133.7 billion, and free cash flow still went down, from about $72 billion to $67 billion. The buildout is eating cash faster than Azure can bring it in. Microsoft now plans to spend more on capex than the $155 billion its entire business earned from operations.

When you're spending more than your whole company makes, you go looking for money everywhere, and payroll is the easiest place on the spreadsheet to find it.

Luck is not the key ingredient to success. 

Here is just some of the bad luck I have had and recovered from:

1. Joined a startup that sent out a press release on 9/11 and had our office across the street from the Empire State Building. I should have known then that this was a really stupid career choice. But I kept going.

2. I had early shares in a startup that never raised much money, and I negotiated a buyout offer with a giant public company, but the founders passed on it. That sale would have made me very rich. Ouch.

3. I was promoted 3 times and was finally promoted to VP, only to have COVID hit, have to lay off half of a very large team in a single day, and then struggle in misery for 12 months building the business back. Then left. Honestly, this still brings tears to my eyes.

4. Took an Uber early in the morning to the airport. I arrived only to enter the building and realize the ticket said LGA, not EWR, so I had to call another Uber and ride to the airport. But I made the flight, so it wasn't that bad, really. This was on me. LOL.

The point is, hard work and resiliancey in the face of hardship are what it takes to be successful, and for some reason, these stories aren't popular anymore. 

It's much more convenient to blame the rich, the corporations, the boomers (I am Gen X BTW), than to look at yourself and accept your situation and just do something about it.

In Seattle, there is this ridiculous notion that this tiny group of wealthy business owners has Stockholm syndrome and we can hold them hostage, steal their wealth, and use it to fund a massive, inefficient government bureaucracy. 

Well, it's already backfiring spectacularly. 

The rich aren't stupid. That is how they go so rich. Bezos left, so did the founder of Starbucks and the entire corporation. And many other wealthy people. Supporters of these idiotic socialist policies have no problem lying about this. And will tell you it's not true that people are leaving. But they are.

Please join me in voting Yes on I-645 because we need to make this place the very best place in the nation to start and operate a business. It once was that. That is why two massively successful corporations are here.

Let's be real, Amazon and Microsoft didn't pick Washington State for the weather.

My mom was a hippie. My dad was a beatnik.

I was so poor that at one point I worked two jobs and shared a bed with a friend. I got home at 8 AM from a night shift at a bakery, got into his bed, and slept while he went to his day job.

I bought my first computer with my own credit card at age 20 and taught myself HTML. At the time, I worked nights in a giant, city block-sized printing plant in Queens, NY. I took the 7 train home at 2 AM most nights and was spit on and beaten up for being Irish on that train. Like GD Gangs of New York. I got up at 7 AM and coded websites until 11 AM and went to my printing plant job until the wee hours of the morning.

My first website was featured in a book from Japan in 1997 as one of the 100 best-designed websites in the world. That opened doors and eventually brought me to San Francisco in 2004. And you know the rest of the story. It's on my website.

I never begged for money, expected handouts, or called for government intervention in markets because of my difficult existence when I was young.

I worked so hard my eyeballs fell out. And then I worked even more.

And I succeeded well beyond anyone’s expectations because THIS IS AMERICA.

So yes, I have a problem with politicians looking at what someone earns today and deciding they deserve a bigger piece of it. They see a fattened pig ready for the slaughter. I see the decades of sacrifice it took to build it. Even if it's modest.

Calling it a so-called “millionaires tax” doesn't settle the argument. They already admitted it will apply to everyone. But I want the person cleaning the bakery at 4 AM to build something worth a fortune and keep the rewards. That is what America is about.

Besides, we all pay plenty of tax as it is.

I am voting YES on Initiative 645 to repeal Washington’s new income tax. 

I will never apologize for believing everyone should keep more of what they worked for and earned

text:
Iran Hasn’t Rebuilt Nuclear Sites, According To Nuclear Watchdog | Daily Caller News Foundation

International nuclear inspectors have detected no attempts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged by American and Israeli airstrikes.

Monitoring efforts have uncovered no reconstruction activity at Iranian nuclear facilities damaged in military operations during 2025 and 2026, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Director General Rafael Grossi, told the United Nations (UN) on Tuesday. However, inspectors remain unable to verify the whereabouts of hundreds of kilograms of highly enriched uranium, raising questions about Tehran’s remaining nuclear capabilities.

“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct,” Grossi told the Security Council, according to the UN transcript.

This assessment is in line with previous statements from the Pentagon and other U.S. officials.

Iran’s nuclear facilities suffered extensive damage during American strikes in June 2025, including attacks on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, according to the Pentagon.

Former Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Tulsi Gabbard previously declared Iran’s nuclear enrichment program had been “obliterated” by American strikes in June 2025, according to her March 18 congressional testimony. Gabbard also said Tehran had made no attempts to restore its enrichment capabilities, with entrances to bombed underground facilities buried and sealed with cement.

Gabbard reaffirmed those findings when Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff questioned whether American intelligence agencies believed Iran’s enrichment program had been destroyed and whether Tehran had attempted to rebuild it. She answered “Yes” to both assessments, according to the Senate hearing.

However, Gabbard declined to say whether American intelligence agencies believed Iran posed an imminent nuclear threat before the U.S. launched its February offensive. She argued that President Donald Trump alone could determine whether a threat was imminent, while acknowledging that Iran retained the intention to rebuild its enrichment capabilities, according to the Senate hearing.

The U.S. launched another major military campaign against Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, targeting its missile capabilities, naval forces and military infrastructure, according to the Pentagon. President Donald Trump’s administration identified preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons as a central objective.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth subsequently claimed American operations struck nearly 80% of Iran’s nuclear industrial base, further undermining Tehran’s ability to develop atomic weapons, according to an April 8 Pentagon briefing.

The findings suggest Iran has not visibly attempted to restore its damaged nuclear infrastructure despite repeated American warnings about Tehran’s nuclear ambitions. However, Grossi cautioned that monitoring cannot replace physical inspections, according to the UN transcript.

The IAEA has been unable to verify the location of approximately 970 pounds (440 kilograms) of highly enriched uranium previously declared by Iran, Grossi told the Security Council. Inspectors have lacked access to most Iranian nuclear facilities since American and Israeli strikes disrupted inspections in June 2025.

Iran possessed an estimated 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity before those attacks, according to a September 2025 IAEA report. Uranium enriched to that level is approaching the 90% purity generally associated with nuclear weapons.

The IAEA also cannot verify whether previously declared nuclear material has been diverted from civilian purposes, Grossi told the UN.

However, the latest IAEA findings offer no confirmation that Iran has permanently abandoned its nuclear ambitions. The agency cannot independently establish the current condition of many nuclear facilities without inspectors on the ground, according to the UN.

Grossi specifically requested access to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, a new uranium enrichment facility Iran announced plans to establish on June 12, 2025. The IAEA scheduled an inspection for the following day, but the visit was canceled when Israeli airstrikes began, according to a September 2025 IAEA report.

The Bushehr nuclear power plant remains an exception, with inspectors conducting verification activities there, Grossi told the Security Council.

The findings follow a September decision by the IAEA Board of Governors to refer Iran to the Security Council over continued violations of nuclear safeguards obligations, according to the British government.

Russia and China opposed Tuesday’s meeting, arguing that the Security Council lacked grounds to revisit Iran’s nuclear program under the existing agenda. Their objections failed in an 11-2 procedural vote, with two countries abstaining, according to the UN.

Iranian Deputy Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi condemned the American and Israeli strikes, accusing Washington of aggression and insisting Tehran’s nuclear activities remain peaceful, according to the UN transcript.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz rejected Iran’s arguments, demanding that Tehran explain its continued failure to comply with nuclear inspection obligations, according to the UN transcript.

Grossi urged Iran to cooperate with inspectors and pursue gradual diplomatic measures to restore international confidence in its nuclear program. A lasting resolution would require credible inspections and verification rather than military action alone, he told the Security Council.

text:
In 1979, a woman who was seven months pregnant opened a children's book inside her Washington, D.C. home and found a handwritten note that was never meant for her.

It was intimate, unmistakable, and left no room for explanation.

Her husband was Carl Bernstein, the famous investigative journalist who had helped bring down a presidency by exposing Watergate. He was celebrated across the nation for revealing hidden truths, yet the truth inside his own house had been hiding in plain sight.

The other woman was a BBC journalist, the daughter of the British Prime Minister, and a frequent guest who had sat at their dinner table.

Her name was Nora Ephron.

As Washington began to whisper, Nora didn't stay to listen.

Heartbroken, she flew to New York and sat across from her therapist, admitting a thought millions have felt in moments of deep personal betrayal: "I will never be the same."

Her therapist offered a quiet perspective: "You were going to leave him eventually."

Days later, on August 15, 1979, she went into labor and gave birth to their second son, Max, bringing a newborn into the quiet wreckage of a collapsed marriage.

She packed up her life, gathered her two young sons and their nanny, and left Washington behind. Her editor, Robert Gottlieb, opened his Upper West Side apartment to give them a safe place to land.

Most people in her position might have chosen silence, discretion, and a quiet withdrawal from public attention.

Nora chose sentences.

In 1983, she published Heartburn, a razor-sharp, 179-page novel so thinly disguised that anyone who had attended a Washington dinner party immediately recognized the real-life figures involved.

She filled the pages not just with the raw details of the affair, but with her actual home recipes, potatoes Anna, linguine alla cecca, and the exact vinaigrette she had made for her husband.

She embedded her core philosophy directly into the book: "If I tell the story, I control it."

Bernstein was far from pleased, later publicly admitting, "Obviously, I wish Nora hadn't written it."

But the narrative was no longer his to shape.

In 1986, Heartburn was adapted into a major film starring Meryl Streep and Jack Nicholson. Nora was no longer framed by the public as the betrayed spouse; she was the author, the storyteller, and the owner of her own narrative.

She didn't stop there.

Over the next decade, she wrote and directed some of the most celebrated films of modern cinema, including When Harry Met Sally..., Sleepless in Seattle, and You've Got Mail. The woman whose marriage had broken apart under public scrutiny became the defining cinematic voice on love, relationships, and human connection for an entire generation.

She eventually remarried writer Nicholas Pileggi, building a steady life together that lasted until her death in 2012 from complications of leukemia, an illness she kept private until the end.

Years after her passing, her son Jacob directed a documentary about her life, titling it Everything Is Copy, a reference to the rule Nora lived by.

She understood that while we cannot always prevent people from breaking our hearts, we retain absolute ownership over what we do with the pieces.

Mahdi Mohammadi (@mmohammadii61), an adviser to Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led Iran's diplomatic efforts with the US to end the war, offers a noteworthy assessment of Vance's reported letter to Mohsen Rezaei and the motivations of Iran's postwar leadership.

Discussing the letter, which he neither confirms nor denies, Mohammadi suggests that Washington is, in part, trying to stimulate rivalries within Tehran by reaching out to different senior officials.

He argues, however, that the US fundamentally misunderstands Iran's current leadership if it believes personal ambitions or competition for power can be exploited to create divisions at this stage.

Mohammadi makes a particularly striking argument about the psychology of Iran's postwar leadership.

He portrays figures such as Ghalibaf, Rezaei, and Pezeshkian as men who have survived a war that killed many of their colleagues, recognize that they themselves could be assassinated, and have come to terms with the possibility of death.

"At this point, nobody at this level has any desire left to fight for power. They're all looking to depart [this world]," he says.

"They know that, God willing, martyrdom will eventually be their destiny. It's only a question of sooner or later."

He adds: "Today, all these men are holding their lives in their hands and are ready for martyrdom. They're even prepared to put their reputations on the line to do something for this country."

In Mohammadi's telling, these leaders have moved past personal political ambitions, accepted the possibility of being killed, and are therefore less susceptible to efforts to exploit internal rivalries.

This is, of course, a self-serving portrayal of the leadership's motivations and cohesion, and whether it ultimately accurately reflects the calculations of individual officials is of course another question.

But it raises a broader question about the efficacy, and  counterproductive consequences, of campaigns to assassinate senior Iranian leaders.

Iran's political system emerged from a mass revolutionary movement in which sacrifice and martyrdom became central sources of political legitimacy, drawing on deeply embedded traditions of Shia political and religious thought. Within that framework, the killing of senior leaders does not necessarily produce the political fragmentation or capitulation its perpetrators might anticipate. Instead, it can reinforce narratives of resistance, elevate those killed into symbols of legitimacy, and strengthen the resolve of surviving officials.

Ultimately, Mohammadi's remarks offer insight into the mindset of Iran's postwar leadership and raise broader questions about the strategy of assassinating senior officials to weaken or fracture the political system—a model that has not borne out as seemingly anticipated and merits greater scrutiny.

Some are struggling themselves. Others are watching friends and family fall behind. Increasingly, he said, people who supported President Donald Trump in 2024 are considering voting differently, even if their underlying political beliefs haven’t changed.

text:
The Windmill Family Who Shared Water With the Whole Community — Kansas, 1935. During the severe drought years of the Great Depression, clean water became one of the most valuable resources across parts of rural Kansas. Wells dried up, crops withered under relentless heat, and many families struggled simply to secure enough water for daily survival. In several farming communities, neighbors depended on one another more than ever before.

The Bennett family lived on a modest farm outside Dodge City where an aging windmill powered one of the few dependable wells in the area. While many nearby water sources failed, the Bennett well continued producing enough water for livestock, gardens, and household needs.

Each morning before sunrise, William Bennett inspected the windmill and pump while his wife Sarah helped organize water collection for neighboring families. Wagons, buckets, barrels, and milk cans lined the road as residents arrived to gather what they needed.
No payment was required. Some neighbors offered vegetables, eggs, or firewood in return, but the Bennetts never demanded compensation. They believed that during difficult times, access to water should not depend on a person's ability to pay.

Children from surrounding farms often spent hours helping fill containers and load wagons. The daily routine became a community effort that strengthened relationships across the countryside. As the drought continued, the farm became known as a place where people could always find help. Travelers stopped for water, struggling families received assistance, and neighbors worked together to keep the windmill operating.

Years later, one local resident remembered: "The well gave us water, but the family gave us hope." The drought eventually ended and better seasons returned to the plains. Yet many residents never forgot the farm where generosity flowed as freely as the water itself.

text:
🚨THE MAN THEY BURIED TWICE, IVAN SEMWANGA, THE RICH GANG DON WHO MAY NEVER HAVE DIED.

Ivan Semwanga was born on 12 December 1977 in Nakaliro, Kayunga. His father, George Semwanga Pinto Lutaaya, died of a stroke when Ivan was 6. He was raised by relatives, including his uncle Jimmy Luyinda. He attended Bishop Brown Primary School, Kanjuki Secondary School, and Central Academy for A-levels, then earned a degree from Sokoine University of Agriculture in Tanzania.

In 1999, at the invitation of his cousin Ed Cheune, he traveled to South Africa and enrolled at Damelin College in Pretoria for a diploma in business management. He later founded Brooklyn City College, which grew to around 10 campuses across Durban, Pretoria, and Johannesburg, offering courses in IT, mining, and policing. He also owned student hostels, apartments, and luxury homes in Sandton and Pretoria. Back in Uganda, he built a mansion in Munyonyo and was developing a hotel on Sir Apollo Kagwa Road.

He met Zari Hassan around 2000. They had 3 sons, Pinto, Raphael, and Quincy, and held their traditional introduction ceremony on 24 December 2011 at a cost of over 1 billion shillings. They separated around 2013, and Zari later married Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz. At the time of his death, Ivan reportedly had another wife.

In Uganda, he became the self-styled president of the Rich Gang alongside Ed Cheune and King Lawrence. Every December they returned to Kampala and turned the city into a money-splashing carnival. In December 2012, he and Zari became the first to import a Lamborghini into Uganda. He was known as the modern father of Ugandan showbiz, famous for driving Hummers, Mercedes-Benzes, and BMWs.

His final months were turbulent. In early 2017, a newspaper ad showed his Munyonyo house for sale, sparking rumors he was broke. He flew back to Uganda, hired a state helicopter, and partied at Blankets and Wine on 30 April. About a week before his death, he suffered a stroke linked to high blood pressure. He was admitted to Steve Biko Academic Hospital in Pretoria, underwent surgery for bleeding in the brain, slipped into a coma for roughly 10 to 12 days, and died on the morning of 25 May 2017 at age 39. Zari announced it, calling him Ivan the Great.

His body was flown back to Uganda on 28 May under the name Ali Sennyomo. A vigil was held at his Muyenga home, prayers at Namirembe Cathedral, and burial on 30 May at his ancestral home in Nakaliro. The funeral was pure Rich Gang theater — champagne poured on the casket, cash tossed instead of soil, police guarding the tomb.

Almost immediately, rumors spread that he faked his death. The theories: he allegedly defrauded a South African of over $200 million in cash, diamonds, and gold, and faking death was his escape. Voice notes claimed he was hiding in the Middle East getting plastic surgery. His casket was never opened for public viewing, and photos were banned.

In late October 2026, journalist Simon Kaggwa Njala reopened the case. He said he could not establish where Semwanga's vigil was held in South Africa. Namirembe Cathedral told him the body had never been viewed. Steve Biko Hospital said there was never any patient named Semwanga, not even under other names. Uganda's High Commission in South Africa never saw an autopsy report. He demanded the postmortem be released and asked for any Ugandan who actually saw the body to come forward. Pastor Mondo Mugisha offered 10 million shillings for a photo of Ivan in a casket, insisting nobody ever saw him in one and that they buried a dummy. Zari Hassan fired back, saying the family handled the postmortem in Uganda. Njala later posted that he can now confirm Ivan is alive. His sister Ritah appeared on Sanyuka TV, and one circulating claim says Ivan is now working as a car mechanic in Germany under a new identity.

Nine years after they lowered him into red soil in Nakaliro, half the country is still arguing about whether the soil was ever his.
