text:
🚨 We need to talk about Sir Ian Cheshire...

In June 2026, he became chair of @Ofcom, the regulator responsible for broadcasting, telecoms, the post and, increasingly, the online world. Four months later, he gave MPs a revealing glimpse of how he sees the job.

I’m concerned. I think you should be too.

On 20 October, appearing before the Commons culture committee for the first time in the role, he was asked why the regulator seemed unable to get to grips with GB News. Labour’s @RupaHuq named some of the channel’s critics: Andrew Neil, its founding chairman, who walked away from it; the former ITN editor Stewart Purvis; and Chris Banatvala, Ofcom’s founding director of standards and the author of its first broadcasting code.

None of them, she pointed out, is of the left.

Cheshire replied that Ofcom also has a duty to protect free speech. When Huq pressed him, he said he would encourage “Stewart and the others to set up a left-wing version of GB News”. Huq said she would oppose that channel too. Later in the session the Conservative MP Nigel Huddleston returned to the remark: “God help us if that happens.”

It was a very revealing moment.

Faced with concerns from a former ITN editor and the man who wrote Ofcom’s own rulebook, the regulator’s new chair treated a question of law and evidence as a quarrel between left and right, to be settled by giving each side its own channel. Due impartiality, the principle Ofcom exists to uphold, has no place in that picture.

It was also, frankly, an embarrassing thing for the chair of a regulator to say. Britain’s national press is concentrated in very few hands: according to the Media Reform Coalition, three companies, DMG Media, News UK and Reach, control 90 per cent of national newspaper circulation. From the Harmsworths and Beaverbrook to Murdoch, the Barclay brothers and now Paul Marshall, proprietors have almost always leaned right and used their titles to court and influence those in power.

Proprietors have very occasionally backed Labour when it suited them, most famously Murdoch’s Sun under Tony Blair. The best-known proprietor of recent decades to call himself a socialist was Robert Maxwell, a former Labour MP who owned the Mirror from 1984 until his death in 1991. Yet Paul Foot, who wrote for the Mirror under him, said he “broke the unions like a Tory”, and he went on to raid his own papers’ pension funds.

Inviting critics to set up a left-wing GB News assumes a left-wing Paul Marshall is waiting in the wings. There isn’t one. Cheshire’s answer treats an imbalance of ownership and capital as if it were simply an imbalance of opinion.

In my view, Cheshire’s appointment was a mistake, made at the worst possible moment. His background gives little reason to expect a robust approach to broadcasting standards, his attention is spread across too many boards, and what he has said about GB News since taking office suggests nothing will change.

Cheshire is what the Financial Times, reporting him as frontrunner in April, called a “City grandee”. He ran Kingfisher, the owner of B&Q, from 2008 to 2015, and has since chaired Barclays UK, Debenhams, Spire Healthcare and the property giant Landsec, as well as sitting on the board of BT. He was knighted in the 2014 New Year Honours, on David Cameron’s list.

His only substantial broadcasting experience is three years as chair of Channel 4, from 2022 to 2025. He has never held an executive role at a broadcaster or a technology platform.

In fairness, his Channel 4 record deserves credit. Nadine Dorries approved his appointment while she was pushing to privatise the broadcaster, and Labour’s Lucy Powell accused her of installing a “yes man” for the sell-off. He is instead generally seen to have helped Channel 4 see off privatisation, and, according to the Telegraph, Michael Grade, then chair of Ofcom and a Conservative peer until he resigned the whip to take that job, declined to give him a second term. Defending a public broadcaster you chair is a different task, though, from holding a partisan commercial channel to account.

He got the Ofcom job after being sounded out by someone at No 10, as he told MPs in May, though he would not say who. He beat Labour’s Margaret Hodge and the former Conservative culture secretary Sir Jeremy Wright. The science committee endorsed him but urged him to prioritise improving his knowledge of online safety. At that hearing he admitted he had not even read the Rycroft review, which warns that too little is known about dark money in British media, and when Liam Byrne asked whether that was Ofcom’s responsibility, he replied that he did not know yet.

For £120,000 a year and three days a week, the public is entitled to expect more preparation.

Cheshire is no party politician. I can find no record of party membership or donations, and he was described as pro-Remain at the time of the referendum. His career has instead been spent moving between boardrooms and Whitehall.

Conservative-led governments have turned to him again and again. In 2011 Iain Duncan Smith appointed him lead non-executive at the Department for Work and Pensions, as it embarked on the coalition’s welfare reforms. David Cameron made him the government’s lead non-executive in 2015, a job designed to bring boardroom governance into Whitehall, and Theresa May reappointed him in 2018.

In 2022 Nadine Dorries approved him as chair of Channel 4. In 2024 he was the Conservative government’s preferred candidate to chair the Climate Change Committee, in what the Telegraph described as an attempt to install more moderate leadership after Lord Deben. Ministers in all three devolved governments refused to approve the shortlist, saying its candidates were too close to the Conservatives and lacked diversity, and the Guardian reported accusations that Westminster was trying to “blunt the teeth” of the watchdog. The government insisted it had found a credible chair.

His other public work points the same way: in 2013 he sat on Cameron’s business taskforce on cutting EU “red tape”, and he chaired the Ecosystem Markets Task Force, which looked for business opportunities in valuing and protecting nature.

His boardroom career fits the pattern: from 2021 until this autumn he chaired Spire Healthcare, Britain’s biggest private hospital group, which earns around 30% of its hospital revenue treating #NHS patients.

Taken together, it is the record of a market-minded businessman whom Conservative ministers trusted, repeatedly, to bring business methods into government.

That role raises at least one question that has never been answered. In 2018 Michael Gove appointed Ben Goldsmith, a donor to the Conservatives and occasionally the Greens, to Defra’s board after a selection process overseen by Cheshire. Goldsmith ran Menhaden Capital Management, which managed the investment trust Menhaden Capital plc, and the Cabinet Office’s register of interests listed Cheshire as that trust’s chairman. I have found no public record of whether he declared the connection or stood aside.

None of this makes him a Conservative placeman. But it does place him in a small circle of business figures whom governments of every colour reach for, and Labour deserves as much criticism for that as the Conservatives.

In 2022 Labour’s frontbench accused the Conservatives of cronyism over his Channel 4 appointment. Four years later, a Labour government chose him to chair the regulator itself, over one of its own peers. It fell to a Labour backbencher, Rupa Huq, to press him in public on GB News.

Then there is the question of time. The Ofcom chair is expected to commit just three days a week. Cheshire joined the board on 9 June. On 14 July he was appointed chair of Anglian Water.

He has since given up the chair of Spire Healthcare and will leave the Mountbatten hospice charity in December. He still chairs Landsec, the Institute for Government and the King Charles III Charitable Fund. When Chi Onwurah, chair of the science committee, asked him in May how he would manage Ofcom alongside his other chairs, he had not yet taken on a water company.

Anglian is a company under intense scrutiny. LBC reported in July that it recorded more than 1,000 pollution incidents in 2025, the highest total for any water company in more than a decade. In September 2025 it agreed a £62.8m enforcement package with Ofwat over failures in running its sewage works and networks, and in July it introduced its first hosepipe ban since 2012, three days before he arrived. Its chief executive received an extra £1.3m, including a £500,000 retention payment, despite the ban on bonuses at failing water firms; the company says shareholders funded it and that it complies with the rules.

Cheshire inherited all of this and is not responsible for it. Even so, at a time when Ofcom needs its chair’s full attention, he chose to take on a company in a sector that has become a byword for regulatory failure.

On GB News, the evidence so far points to continuity. 

GB News’s parent company, All Perspectives Ltd, has two main owners: the Dubai-based Legatum group and Sir Paul Marshall, the hedge fund co-founder who also owns The Spectator and UnHerd. Each owns around 40% of the company. In May, Liam Byrne noted that its presenters included the leader of a political party and seven sitting MPs, all from one side.

The senior world of broadcasting and regulation is a small one, and Ofcom’s leaders inevitably have ties within it. Grade, as he told the Telegraph, came out as a Tory only in 2010, the year before he became a Conservative peer.

Dame Melanie Dawes, Ofcom’s chief executive since 2020, is a career civil servant, and there is no evidence that her decisions reflect anything other than her own judgement. Her husband, Benedict Brogan, was political editor of the Daily Mail and later deputy editor of the Telegraph. Since leaving journalism in 2014 he has worked in corporate public affairs, including at the firm co-founded by Peter Mandelson, and since April has advised financial services clients at FTI Consulting, a sector Ofcom does not regulate.

None of this proves bias, and I make no such claim. Ofcom’s register of interests already covers partners, and that kind of transparency is what keeps such connections from becoming a story.

A month before stepping down, Michael Grade told the Telegraph there was “no blurring of news and comment” on GB News, and that politician presenters were a matter for Parliament. In my view that claim is absurd, and Ofcom’s own lawyers had argued the opposite: in the High Court in 2025, Ofcom’s case, as the judge summarised it, was that challenger broadcasters such as GB News were “blending news and comment content, in an unprecedented manner”. Ministers reportedly wanted a successor with a different profile.

Six months later, Ofcom under Cheshire is saying much the same. At the October hearing he argued that Ofcom regulates individual programmes rather than whole channels, and that this has been tested in law. Dawes added that whether serving politicians should present current affairs is for politicians to decide.

That is a retreat. In May he told MPs that GB News was “literally the second question on my induction plan”, suggested that with the code last revised five years earlier this “may be the time to ask ourselves again”, and asked whether the rules on politician presenters were “something we should address”. By October, programme-level regulation “currently works”, and anything more is for Parliament.

In my view, handing the question to Parliament is an abdication. Parliament gave Ofcom, not ministers or MPs, the duty under the Communications Act 2003 to set the Broadcasting Code and “from time to time to review and revise” it, so that news is presented with due impartiality. It also gave Ofcom the power to report questions of general broadcasting policy to the Secretary of State.

Dawes herself told the same committee that Ofcom’s primary duty is to further the interests of citizens, and that this is written into the Act. Ofcom must weigh freedom of expression and editorial independence: weighing them is its job.

Leaving politicians to decide whether politicians may front television programmes hands the question to the interested party.

When Huq listed GB News’s critics, Cheshire’s first reply was that Ofcom also has a duty on free speech. Earlier in the session, Dawes had said Ofcom sets very few rules in advance “because of freedom of expression”. Nobody should want a censorious regulator, and freedom of expression is a duty Ofcom must take seriously. Too often, though, the argument is reduced to a simplistic, unhelpful binary in which any rule is censorship and any restraint an attack on liberty.

Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the basis of free expression in UK law, says the right “carries with it duties and responsibilities”, and expressly allows states to license broadcasters. Impartiality rules silence no one: they set conditions on how a licensed broadcaster presents news and political controversy, and anyone unwilling to meet them is free to publish online.

As George Lakoff has long argued, whoever sets the frame shapes the debate, and a regulator that treats “free speech” as a trump card has let one side set it. The harder and more honest question is how to protect open debate while limiting the partisan distortion that can drive people further apart.

Perhaps most revealing was what Cheshire volunteered about the broadcaster itself. He told MPs he had taken time out to meet GB News to understand its compliance effort. He conceded it had started “very chaotically”, with its technical transmissions all over the place, but said it had invested in compliance and was “moving in the right direction”. “Right”, critics might say, being the operative word. He offered that public reassurance while Ofcom was still investigating one of the channel’s interviews with Donald Trump, and still defending its £100,000 fine against GB News in court.

He did not say when the meeting took place or who attended, no MP asked, and I can find no public record of it. A regulator’s chair who meets a broadcaster, then vouches for it in Parliament while his own organisation is still investigating it, owes the public a full account of that meeting.

In May, when MPs complained that Ofcom would not say whom it meets, he promised to take the point on board. This would be a good place to start. In May he also told MPs he intended to meet @arusbridger, whose investigation for The New World had criticised Ofcom’s handling of GB News; I can find no record of whether he did.

In 2025 GB News overturned Ofcom’s rulings on two episodes of Jacob Rees-Mogg’s State of the Nation, after the High Court found errors in how Ofcom had interpreted its rules on politicians presenting news. That judgment turned on the difference between news and current affairs programmes; it did not rule on whether Ofcom can judge a channel as a whole. The judge pointed to Ofcom’s duty to revise its own code as the proper route for any change. Ofcom consulted on tightening the rules on politician presenters, then kept them as they were and strengthened only its guidance.

Ofcom points to 24 investigations into GB News as proof it is not asleep, and the courts have narrowed its room for manoeuvre: the Telegraph reported that GB News’s win was the first time Ofcom had lost a legal challenge to one of its broadcasting decisions. The programme-by-programme approach is long-standing. The problem is a chair who treats it as the whole answer, when it cannot capture what a channel adds up to.

In my view, GB News is something close to a British Fox News: built around opinion, fronted by politicians from one party, and owned by one of the country’s most influential right-wing media proprietors.

Ofcom regulates the tech platforms under the Online Safety Act and broadcasters under the Communications Act, so the two jobs are not identical, and the courts have already narrowed the broadcasting rules. Even so, the difference in his tone is striking. 

According to Computing’s report of an interview Cheshire gave the Financial Times in August, he argued for greater digital sovereignty, so that what British citizens see online is not shaped mainly by American or Chinese interests, and indicated that Ofcom would seek new powers where necessary. Pressed on free speech, he said Ofcom was “protecting our citizens”. In October he called Ofcom’s legal battles with Meta “a great calling card to recruit new lawyers”. Faced with GB News, co-owned by Paul Marshall, the same chair treated free speech as a reason to hold back. Yet the concern behind his sovereignty argument, a few powerful owners shaping what citizens see and hear, applies whatever the owners’ nationality, and GB News is a case in point. The framing is telling.

Ownership is not someone else’s problem, either. Newspapers sit largely outside Ofcom’s day-to-day regulation, but it has a statutory duty to secure sufficient plurality in television and radio, must review the media ownership rules at least every three years, and advises ministers when media mergers raise public interest concerns. The press barons own broadcasters too.

Murdoch’s News UK runs TalkRadio and talkSPORT, as well as Talk, which left linear television for streaming in 2024. Marshall co-owns GB News and also owns The Spectator and UnHerd, giving one man a stake across television, a political weekly and online commentary. 

Ofcom itself recommended, in 2021 and again in 2024, widening the public interest test for media mergers beyond newspapers and broadcasters. When Liam Byrne raised the opacity of GB News’s funding in May, Cheshire said that as a citizen he would be worried, but that he had not yet done the homework. Five months into the job, he should have.

The rules also stop at the edge of the television. The Broadcasting Code covers licensed TV and radio services. When Talk left linear television in 2024, its online video ceased to be covered by the Broadcasting Code, although much of its schedule still airs in TalkRadio’s slot, which remains licensed. Ofcom’s existing rules for on-demand services, where they apply, contain no impartiality requirements. Clips of GB News programmes on @X or @YouTube are not broadcasts at all. A segment balanced within a programme on air can be clipped, stripped of that balance and shared widely, and the code does not follow it. The Online Safety Act also excludes qualifying news publisher content from the user-generated content that platforms’ safety duties cover, and that can include a licensed broadcaster’s own clips, provided the statutory conditions are met.

Print and online titles are blurring the line from the other direction. At the time of writing, SpectatorTV, The Spectator’s YouTube channel, has more than half a million subscribers and nearly 4,000 videos, and the magazine’s own media pack describes daily shows and calls its newest programmes “broadcast shows”. UnHerd’s channel also has more than half a million subscribers, and national newspapers have followed on a far larger scale: the Telegraph’s channel has more than six million subscribers and some 37,000 videos, including long-form political interviews and livestreamed debates.

None of it falls under the Broadcasting Code, and political podcasts and YouTube shows that look and sound like news face no impartiality rules at all, as Dawes acknowledged in October. Reform UK’s planned “Reform TV”, a YouTube-based channel financed by a recent £72 million donation windfall and intended to feature interviews, documentaries and party-aligned programming, would sit entirely outside the Broadcasting Code for the same reason.

The Media Act 2024 will bring the biggest streamers under a new code, with impartiality rules for news. Ofcom consulted on it this summer and plans to publish the final version in late 2026; it will apply to services with more than 500,000 monthly UK users, such as Netflix and ITVX, and services will have a year to comply. Whether it will reach Talk, The Spectator’s video shows or political channels on YouTube is unclear. 

Cheshire himself spotted the problem in May, telling MPs that clipped content on social media raised the question of whether the rules hang together “as a coherent piece of regulation”. But he did not return to it in October.

The stakes are real. In the United States, the abolition of the fairness doctrine in 1987 removed a duty on licensed broadcasters to air contrasting views. It never applied to cable channels such as Fox News, which launched in 1996, but it was part of a wider shift towards a media system in which millions live inside partisan information.

In Hungary, Viktor Orbán’s government spent years capturing public-service media and building a network of loyal private outlets, through ownership, regulatory pressure and state advertising. Britain is not Hungary, and GB News is a privately owned channel with no state control. Both examples still show that media pluralism cannot be judged one programme at a time.

Here, MPs on the science committee have examined how online misinformation fed the riots that followed the Southport murders in 2024. Broadcast regulation is one of the few levers a democracy has over the quality of its information, and Ofcom holds it.

Cheshire can still prove me wrong, and I sincerely hope he does. First, he should publish the online safety review he told MPs in October was finished, and deliver the performance measures the science committee asked to see within six months of his appointment. 

Ofcom already publishes his outside interests, but he ought to go further, explaining how conflicts between those roles and Ofcom’s work are managed and recording any occasion on which he has stood aside. 

Every meeting he holds with a broadcaster Ofcom is investigating should be published, with its date and attendees, beginning with GB News.

On the bigger questions, he should use Ofcom’s next review of the media ownership rules, due by 2027, to argue for a plurality regime fit for an era of billionaire-owned broadcasters, and tell Parliament how licensed broadcasters’ own online output can be held to the standards that apply on air.

Above all, Ofcom should use its own power to revise the Broadcasting Code for an age of politician presenters. If it will not, and keeps telling MPs that channel-wide impartiality and politician presenters are matters for Parliament, then Parliament should take it at its word and legislate.

A regulator’s chair who answers serious criticism by inviting the critics to start a partisan channel of their own has misunderstood the job. What Britain needs is a watchdog that believes accurate, impartial news is essential for a well-functioning democracy and worth defending, led by a chair with the time and the conviction to defend it.

text:
1. Baird Middle School / Ludlow Public Schools (Massachusetts) — Foote v. Ludlow
Parents Stephen Foote and Marissa Silvestri sued after school staff socially transitioned their 11-year-old (who identified as “genderqueer”) and 12-year-old without parental knowledge or consent. A school librarian assigned sixth-graders a project encouraging them to announce pronouns; a counselor then directed staff to use a different name and nonbinary pronouns, allowed bathroom choice, and followed a non-disclosure protocol based on state guidance. Staff used the preferred identity at school but the legal name/pronouns with parents. The parents alleged this amounted to mental-health intervention and concealment. A federal district court dismissed the case; the First Circuit affirmed in 2025; the U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari in 2026. 
Background and ADF summary: https://t.co/QtPzGgZSnu
2. Sierra View Elementary / Chico Unified School District (California) — Regino v. Staley
Mother Aurora Regino sued after a school counselor facilitated the social transition of her then-11-year-old fifth-grader. The child, experiencing depression and anxiety, told the counselor she “felt like a boy”; the counselor offered a different name and male pronouns, and the student requested that her mother not be informed. Staff used the male name/pronouns at school. Later accounts indicated the counselor discussed topics such as top surgery and breast binding and advised against telling the mother. The child eventually disclosed via a grandparent. The district’s policy barred notification without student consent. A district court initially dismissed the case; the Ninth Circuit revived aspects of it on appeal (finding the lower court applied incorrect standards regarding parental rights); it was later dismissed again on remand and is under further appeal.

NEW RESEARCH: As Americans prepare to vote in next week's midterm elections, new research from Merrill College suggests political distrust may be motivating some citizens to become more engaged rather than driving them away from democratic involvement. 

A study funded by #UMD's Maryland Democracy Initiative found residents interviewed in Frederick County, Maryland, expressed deep frustration with politicians, skepticism toward news media and anxiety about the future of the American Dream. Yet many remained committed to voting, volunteering, following local news and holding elected officials accountable. 

Frederick County offers a revealing setting for understanding political divisions as a “purple” county — one of Maryland’s most evenly split electorates between Republicans and Democrats.

Conducted by researchers Jodi McFarland Friedman and Sarah Oates, the study involved in-depth interviews with 18 Frederick County residents from April through June 2026 about how citizens experience American democracy.

text:
👏 More momentum for human-based research! Here are some recent news articles from @NIH:

Funded by NIAID and NIGMS, @Dr_ASingh, @KrishRoyLab, and colleagues combined a human lymphoid organoid with a bone marrow-on-a-chip to study aspects of immune function that have been difficult to investigate directly in humans. The platform can incorporate cells from specific patient populations to study aging, infections, autoimmune disease, and allergies while providing “opportunities to gather new insights that existing models do not offer,” said John H. Powers III, acting director of NIAID. https://t.co/kEdcxk7t3K

NCATS highlighted a new project funded by Complement_ARIE to develop non-animal methods to better understand fibrotic diseases and accelerate the discovery of potential treatments: the 3D MultiOrgan Models of Fibrosis (3D-MOFIB) technology development center. Researchers from NCATS, NIEHS, NIAAA, NHGRI, and the University of Michigan are bringing together human 3D tissue models, high-throughput drug screening, multi-omics, and AI-driven computational models.
https://t.co/syOazvqASB

Nine papers by @CDNeurogenomics, funded by NIA, showed how scientists are using donated human brain tissue, single-cell technologies, and AI to build high-resolution molecular maps of Alzheimer’s and related brain disorders. By analyzing more than 6.3 million nuclei from 1,494 human donors, researchers identified shared and disease-specific molecular processes that could inform new biomarkers and precision treatments.
https://t.co/MXIHF2ElWl

Funded by NIAID, NHLBI, NIGMS, NIDDK, and NCI, Calvin Kuo’s team developed human lung organoids using samples from more than 220 patient volunteers. The organoids retain key immune cells and mount virus-specific immune responses, creating a promising platform for studying respiratory infections and testing interventions. The platform “may provide a replacement for animal models for some types of evaluations and may provide insights that tests in animal models could not capture.” https://t.co/8sLsM7vK3v

🚀 This exciting progress exemplifies the possibilities that emerge when funding agencies embrace technologically sophisticated human-based methods designed around the biology we ultimately need to understand: our own.

text:
Today, the 18th of Cheshvan, is the 8th tragic Hebrew anniversary of the massacre at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh. Here is a niggun composed in memory of the eleven women and men murdered there.

https://t.co/JgNk6ewe1B

A brief explanation of the lyrics:

The words reflect the outpouring of love that followed this horror. People of all backgrounds streamed to the site to offer sympathy, reflecting the sentiment of the Psalmist, We are with you in your distress – Imo anochi be’tzara. The overflowing light of the millions who came forward to share in the grief echoed the Hassidic teaching, A little bit of light pushes away an abundance of darkness – k’tzat min ha’or doheh harbeh min ha-hoshech.

The names of the slain are called out amidst the collage of ancient holy words, in an ultimate tribute. And who can ever forget the headline of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, in large Hebrew letters: Yitgadel Ve’yitkadesh Shmeih Rabbah – the text of the Kaddish, the Memorial Prayer for the dead.

And then, a final cry. Ad matai, Ad matai – When will it end?

In tribute to Congregation Tree of Life, and its then rabbi Jeffrey Myers, the melody shifts midway to the tune of the prayer Etz Hayim Hi (it is a tree of life), sung when returning the Torah to the Ark.

Coming from the heart, the niggun is melancholy yet hopeful – the hope that soon, soon, the light will push away the darkness.

Credits: Chaim Fruchter: vocals, guitar | Yoshie Fruchter: guitars, bass, banjo, mandolin, percussion | Jeremy Brown: violin | Avi Bloom: visual montage | The melody was composed and paired to words by Avi Weiss

text:
TODAY IN NAVAL HISTORY

1814

The first American steam-powered warship, the harbor defense ship Fulton—also called Demologos by its designer, Robert Fulton—is launched in New York. Advanced for its time, the ship is a catamaran with a paddle wheel located in the center of the vessel between the hulls, and carries only auxiliary sails. Much of its machinery is below the water line, a favorable feature in preventing damage from enemy shot. The ship is not delivered to the U.S. Navy until 1816.

1861

A Union expedition consisting of 77 ships, under Flag Officer Samuel DuPont, sails from Fort Monroe, Virginia. The largest U.S. fleet assembled to date, its vessels carry some 16,000 Union troops for an assault against Port Royal, South Carolina, which DuPont considers “the most important point to strike, and the most desirable to have first and hold,” because of its ability to admit large ships and its value as a coaling station.

1870

The side-wheel steamer Saginaw breaks up on a reef off Ocean Island in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. The remote location offers little hope of rescue, prompting five volunteers under the command of Lieutenant John G. Talbot to man a ship’s gig and attempt to reach Hawaii. After sailing some 1,500 miles, the crew reach Kauai on 20 December after 31 days at sea. Tragically, Talbot and four sailors are drowned in heavy surf as they come ashore. Only Coxswain William Halford survives to bring help to his shipmates. He receives the Medal of Honor and a promotion to the rate of Acting Gunner.

1968

In a surprise attack in the Lon-Bo De River area of South Vietnam, Navy patrol boats join South Vietnamese Air Force A-1 Skyraiders, tank landing ship Washoe County (LST-1165) and Coast Guard cutter Wachusett (WHEC-44) in destroying 242 enemy watercraft and 167 structures during a period of five hours.

2012

To support relief efforts in New York and New Jersey following Hurricane Sandy, the U.S. Navy deployed USS Wasp (LHD-1), USS San Antonio (LPD-17), and USS Carter Hall (LSD-50). The Navy also provided the 26th Marine Expeditionary Unit, Construction Battalion Maintenance Unit 202, Naval Mobile Construction Battalion 11, Composite Riverine Squadron 4, Mobile Diving and Salvage Unit 2, and the Underwater Construction Team. Naval efforts consisted of repairing infrastructure, rescuing citizens, and clearing debris.

The end.

text:
Excerpts from Part 3 of the interview.

Our recently conducted interview with Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, Chief of the Air Staff, Indian Air Force

Topic: Capability enablers like AWACS Netra Mk.1A and Mk.II and refuellers + plans.

Strengthening both is a clear priority for the IAF and concrete steps are under way on each. To bridge the capability gap, we are processing cases for the AEW&C Mk-IA and Mk-II, both of which will carry indigenous systems on selected platforms. Our approach builds on a real strength: we already have the knowledge and expertise to integrate indigenous mission systems on aerial platforms. Both programmes are planned to perform significantly better than the existing Netra, with longer radar ranges and upgraded mission system avionics.

Under the AEW&C Mk-II programme, six A321 aircraft will be modified for the AEW&C role. They will carry mission systems developed indigenously by DRDO’s Centre for Airborne Systems. The contracts are now in place:
Green aircraft conversion: a contract to convert the commercial aircraft before modification, finalised on 8 July 2026.
Modification: a contract signed by DRDO in December 2025 for modifying the aircraft.
Mission systems: a contract signed by DRDO with its Development-cum-Production Partner, which will manufacture the mission systems in India.
Under the contract timelines, the mission aircraft are expected to be delivered to the IAF from 2032–33. To complement these programmes, the IAF is also exploring innovative solutions offered by Indian and foreign OEMs, and the induction of further suitable platforms is under active consideration.
Flight refuelling aircraft-Aerial refuelling has been identified as a key focus area. As an interim measure, the IAF has contracted a wet leased flight refuelling aircraft, used jointly by the IAF and the Indian Navy for training; it was operationalised in December 2025. For the longer term, the Defence Acquisition Council accorded Acceptance of Necessity for six flight refuelling aircraft on 16 February 2024. The contract is expected to be finalised shortly, with deliveries likely between 2028 and 2030. A case for additional flight refuelling aircraft is at the pre-AoN stage.
Together, these programmes will substantially enhance the IAF’s situational awareness, command and control, reach and endurance. They are anchored in indigenous mission systems wherever possible. The IAF is committed to taking each of them forward with urgency, so that our combat fleet is backed by the force multipliers that turn individual aircraft into a complete, networked combat system.

text:
Could a prayer keep speaking after you left?

Ptah could be addressed as “One Who Hears Prayers.” At Memphis, devotees left stelae carved with ears in a chapel dedicated to him. Ear stelae sometimes carry hundreds of ears: the repeated image evokes the act of hearing itself. Many were roughly made and had no inscription, suggesting that this way of approaching the divine reached a broad circle of society. They offered a lasting presence for a very personal appeal. A person’s voice might fall silent, yet a small offering could remain in the god’s sacred space, asking to be heard.

A prayer could outlast the voice that spoke it. Do you think an ancient Egyptian trusted Ptah to hear the words they never dared say aloud?

Image: Ptah, original painting in Nefertari’s tomb (QV66), 19th Dynasty. Photo: Onceinawhile / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; square close-up crop. https://t.co/cqLVY8zkrg

text:
Panerai’s watches have never been designed to disappear on the wrist. Size and presence are fundamental elements of the brand’s identity, from the historic Radiomir and Luminor designs through today’s Submersible collection.

Panerai has long offered its Submersible dive watch in both imposing 47mm and more compact 42mm formats. The new Submersible QuarantaQuattro splits the difference, introducing a 44mm case size designed to preserve the collection’s unmistakable character in a three-watch collection. The Submersible’s design draws directly on the brand’s long association with the maritime world and the precision instruments it historically supplied to the Italian Navy and its specialist diving units.

The QuarantaQuattro does not attempt to reinvent that formula. Instead, the 44mm case adds another set of proportions to the established Submersible architecture. The signature Safety Lock crown-protection system remains prominently positioned at 3 o’clock, while a unidirectional rotating bezel with graduated diving scale provides the means to track elapsed immersion time.

The significance of the QuarantaQuattro isn’t that Panerai has made the Submersible small; it hasn’t. The 44mm format occupies what may prove to be an appealing middle ground. It retains the broad bezel, oversized luminous indications, substantial crown-protection bridge, and muscular proportions that make a Submersible immediately recognizable, while sitting between the established 42mm and 47mm offerings.

And with three very different treatments available at launch — lightweight Carbotech and deep blue, steel and stark black, or steel with white and military green — Panerai isn’t merely introducing another case diameter. It’s turning 44mm into a new pillar of the Submersible family.

Discover the Submersible QuarantaQuattro collection now over on aBlogtoWatch.

text:
The auto sector has done well over the last few years.
And it will continue to do well over the next 3-5 years.

𝗪𝗵𝘆?

India has just 33 cars per 1,000 people, the lowest among major economies.
Incomes are rising, and Indians are shifting from hatchbacks to SUVs.
The government is pushing EVs, with a 30% target by 2030.

Here's the entire auto value chain, in 5 stages:

Raw materials → Tier 2 suppliers → Tier 1 suppliers → Vehicle makers → After-sales

———

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝟭: 𝗥𝗔𝗪 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗔𝗟𝗦

Steel is more than 50% of a car's weight. Then plastics, aluminium, cast iron, rubber, glass and copper.

• SAIL
• JSW Steel
• Tata Steel
• Hindustan Copper
• Hindalco Industries
• National Aluminium Company

These are commodity businesses. Their profits move with the commodity cycle.

———

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝟮: 𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗥 𝟮 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗘𝗥𝗦

Make basic parts and sell them to Tier 1 suppliers, not to vehicle makers. Most are unlisted or SME. A few listed ones:

• Rishi Laser: cuts and welds sheet metal into parts
• Rolex Rings: forged steel rings that become bearings
• Triton Valves: the small air valve on a tyre
• Kranti Industries: precision-machined metal parts
• Tube Investments of India: steel tubes and chains

———

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝟯: 𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗥 𝟭 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗘𝗥𝗦

Make major components and full systems, and sell them directly to vehicle makers. 13 groups:

𝟭. 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀
Metal parts shaped under high pressure.

• Bharat Forge
• M M Forgings
• Kalyani Forge
• Kross Limited
• Ramkrishna Forgings

𝟮. 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
Engine blocks and housings, cut to exact size.

• Uniparts India
• Alicon Castalloy
• Rico Auto Industries
• CIE Automotive India
• Pritika Auto Industries

𝟯. 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀
Parts that make power and send it to the wheels.

• RACL Geartech
• Precision Camshafts
• Sansera Engineering
• Craftsman Automation
• SPR Auto Technologies

𝟰. 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀
Let moving parts rotate smoothly.

• SKF India
• Timken India
• NRB Bearings
• Menon Bearings
• Schaeffler India

𝟱. 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀
The nuts, bolts and screws that hold it all together.

• Sterling Tools
• Sundram Fasteners

𝟲. 𝗧𝘆𝗿𝗲𝘀
You already know what a tyre is 😊

• CEAT
• Tolins Tyres
• Apollo Tyres
• Balkrishna Industries

𝟳. 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀
Start the engine, or power the whole EV.

• Exide Industries
• Amara Raja Energy & Mobility

𝟴. 𝗘𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
Wiring, sensors, switches and control systems.

• Pricol
• UNO Minda
• Minda Corporation
• Dhoot Transmission
• SEDEMAC Mechatronics
• Motherson Sumi Wiring India

𝟵. 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
Headlights, tail lights and interior lights.

• Fiem Industries
• Lumax Industries
• Varroc Engineering

𝟭𝟬. 𝗕𝗼𝗱𝘆, 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
Seats, panels, mirrors and door parts.

• S.J.S. Enterprises
• NDR Auto Components
• Sandhar Technologies
• Lumax Auto Technologies
• Samvardhana Motherson International

𝟭𝟭. 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝘅𝗵𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘁
Send power from the engine or motor to the wheels.

• Bosch
• Greaves Cotton
• Tenneco Clean Air India
• Sharda Motor Industries
• Divgi TorqTransfer Systems
• Sona BLW Precision Forgings

𝟭𝟮. 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝘀𝘂𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝘅𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗲𝗹𝘀
Help the vehicle turn, stop and ride smoothly.

• JTEKT India
• Wheels India
• Carraro India
• Gabriel India
• Rane (Madras)
• ASK Automotive
• Automotive Axles
• Belrise Industries
• Steel Strips Wheels
• Suprajit Engineering
• Endurance Technologies

𝟭𝟯. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴
Keep the car cool.

• Subros
• PPAP Automotive
• Talbros Automotive Components

———

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝟰: 𝗩𝗘𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗟𝗘 𝗠𝗔𝗞𝗘𝗥𝗦 (𝗢𝗘𝗠𝘀)

They don't build a vehicle from scratch. They design it, make some parts, buy the rest from Tier 1 suppliers and assemble it.

Compare them only within the same segment. A car maker is not a two-wheeler maker.

𝟭. 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀
Top 4 hold about 79% of the market.

• Tata Motors
• Maruti Suzuki
• Hyundai Motor India
• Mahindra & Mahindra

𝟮. 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀
Top 4 hold about 88.5%.

• Tata Motors
• Ashok Leyland
• Eicher Motors
• Mahindra & Mahindra

𝟯. 𝗧𝘄𝗼-𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀
Top 4 listed hold about 63%.

• Bajaj Auto
• Hero MotoCorp
• Eicher Motors
• TVS Motor Company

𝟰. 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲-𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀
Top 4 listed hold about 49%.

• Atul Auto
• Bajaj Auto
• TVS Motor Company
• Mahindra & Mahindra

𝟱. 𝗢𝗳𝗳-𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝘃𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀
Tractors, construction and mining equipment.

• Escorts Kubota
• AJAX Engineering
• Mahindra & Mahindra
• Action Construction Equipment

———

𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝟱: 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥-𝗦𝗔𝗟𝗘𝗦

The value chain doesn't end when the vehicle is sold.

𝟭. 𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴
Oil, parts and repairs.

• Castrol India
• Studds Accessories

𝟮. 𝗗𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀
Sell vehicles, in showrooms or online.

• Landmark Cars
• CarTrade Tech
• Popular Vehicles and Services

𝟯. 𝗩𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴
80% of cars are bought on credit.

• Shriram Finance
• Cholamandalam Finance
• Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services

———

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸?

Stage 4 is the most important stage. But it is full of large, well-known companies with slower growth.

As you move backwards in the value chain, you find lesser-known companies with faster growth and attractive valuations.

That's why Stage 3 offers better opportunities than Stage 4.

text:
Ted Bundy confessed to 30 murders in 7 states, and almost no woman who got into his car ever got out alive. Rhonda Stapley is one of the very few who did. He strangled her until she blacked out, brought her back and did it again, then she ran, fell into a freezing river and let the current carry her away from him. She survived Ted Bundy. And then she didn’t tell a single person for almost 40 years.

In the video below, she tells the story of the ride that should have been her last.

October 1974. She was a pharmacy student at the University of Utah, waiting for a late bus. A tan Volkswagen rolled by slowly. The driver looked at her, stopped, backed up and rolled down the window.

“Me too, hop in.”

The first thing she noticed: the inside door handle was missing. He leaned over her and pulled the door shut himself. She figured it was just a broken college car.

He was cute. Green sweater. Nice slacks. Said his name was Ted and he was a law student. He politely asked if she minded a quick detour near the zoo.

He drove right past the zoo. Then into a canyon. Then turned left when the city was to the right.

He stopped talking. His eyes started scanning side roads and empty parking spots.

She thought he wanted to make out. She was already planning how to turn him down without embarrassing him.

He pulled over. Turned off the engine. Leaned in close, like he was about to kiss her.

“Do you know what? I’m going to kill you.”

Then his hands were on her throat.

For a split second she thought it was a sick joke. Then she realized he was squeezing too hard. No door handle. No way out. She fought until she ran out of air and everything went black.

She was sure she would die in that Volkswagen. He had other plans.

When he finally turned his back for a moment, she ran. Into the river. The current swept her downstream, out of his reach.

She never went to the police. She told no one. Not her friends, not her family. She watched Bundy’s face on the news for years, through his escapes, his trials and his execution, and stayed silent.

She became a pharmacist and lived an ordinary life with the most terrifying secret in America.

Nearly 4 decades later, she finally said it out loud and wrote a book called I Survived Ted Bundy.

The scariest killers don’t look like monsters. They look like the cute guy who offers you a ride.

Some lessons are written in other people’s mistakes. Watch it once. Remember it forever.

VIRGINIA MENTAL HEALTH EXECUTIVE ARRESTED IN $49 MILLION MEDICAID FRAUD CASE: WHAT THE RECORDS SHOW

On October 28, the Department of Justice announced the arrest of Mikia Antoneice Noble, 37, of North Chesterfield, Virginia.

Noble was the co-owner and Chief Operating Officer of Advancing Communities Everywhere (ACE), a mental health provider in the Richmond area.

Federal prosecutors allege she helped run a Medicaid fraud scheme involving nearly $50 million in false claims between January 2022 and April 2026.

Here's what the official records show.

WHAT IS THE ALLEGED SCHEME?

ACE provided services intended to help people experiencing serious mental health crises.

According to prosecutors, the company billed Virginia Medicaid for services that were not provided as claimed.

The allegations include:

• FALSE TEAM BILLING: Charging Medicaid for treatment supposedly provided by teams that included licensed professionals, when only one less-qualified worker actually provided care.

• HOTEL PAYMENTS: Spending more than $2 million on hotel rooms offered to Medicaid recipients, including homeless individuals, to encourage them to accept services they allegedly did not need.

• FALSIFIED RECORDS: Adding signatures of licensed professionals who had not participated in the treatment.

• FALSE WORK CLAIMS: Adding Noble's signature to treatment records for services she allegedly could not have provided because she was outside the country.

• MISLEADING AUDITORS: Giving false information to Medicaid insurance organizations reviewing the company's billing practices.

These are allegations made by federal prosecutors, not findings of guilt.

HOW MUCH MONEY WAS INVOLVED?

DOJ previously provided a more detailed financial breakdown when the case was first announced in June 2026.

According to those records:

• Approximately $49.6 million in allegedly fraudulent Medicaid claims were submitted.
• Approximately $38.6 million was actually paid by Medicaid.

That distinction matters.

The $49.6 million represents claims submitted, while $38.6 million represents payments reportedly issued.

Neither figure is a final court-confirmed fraud loss, and the records do not establish that Noble personally received the full amount.

WHAT CHANGED IN OCTOBER?

This investigation was already public before October.

• JUNE 23: DOJ announced that Noble had been charged with conspiracy to commit health care fraud.

• OCTOBER 20: A federal grand jury returned a new indictment charging Noble with one count of conspiracy and three counts of health care fraud.

• OCTOBER 28: Noble was arrested, and DOJ publicly announced the indictment.

Each charge carries a maximum possible sentence of 10 years in prison if she is convicted. Actual sentencing would depend on the court's findings.

WHAT HAS BEEN PROVEN?

The indictment establishes that federal prosecutors have formally brought charges.

It does NOT establish that:

• The alleged services were all fraudulent.
• Every dollar paid by Medicaid was improperly obtained.
• Noble personally received the full $38.6 million.
• Noble has been convicted of any of the charged offenses.

She is presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

The FBI and Virginia Attorney General's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit are investigating.

BOTTOM LINE

Federal prosecutors allege that a Virginia mental health provider submitted approximately $49.6 million in improper Medicaid claims, with about $38.6 million paid.

The allegations involve false treatment records, billing for professional teams that allegedly did not provide the claimed services, and hotel payments used to attract Medicaid recipients.

The October indictment and arrest are new developments in a case originally announced in June.

The amount of public funding involved is substantial, but the alleged fraud, individual responsibility, and any final financial losses must still be established through the legal process.

text:
📢Program Fit Analysis: Florida Gators (To add onto the article) @KamronRoberts9 

Kamron Roberts | CB/Nickel | 6'0/175 | 2028 | Brandon HS (MS):  Updated wingspan: 77.5 inches

Roberts’ verified length, 4.5 speed, and sticky man-coverage production align precisely with Brad White’s demand for defensive backs who can erase vertical threats while remaining assignment-sound against SEC route concepts. His high-volume PBUs and controlled leverage in trail technique address the secondary’s current liability in completion percentage and explosive plays, delivering immediate disruption in a unit that has shown growth but still yields too many clean windows. 

The competitive toughness reflected in 8.0 TFLs and urgent fill technique projects cleanly into White’s multiple-front philosophy, where boundary or nickel players must set edges and support the run without freelancing. High football IQ and coachable demeanor accelerate development inside a room already emphasizing process and confidence-building, creating early ROI while older veterans stabilize the perimeter. Multi-year value compounds as functional mass is added, turning an outlier athletic frame into a reliable coverage standard that elevates the entire secondary’s culture of accountability over flash.

Program Overview

Jon Sumrall’s first season has produced a 5-2 (3-2 SEC) record and top-20 ranking, powered by an explosive offense averaging nearly 40 points. Defensively, Brad White’s unit has generated pressure and limited the run more effectively than the secondary has limited the pass, allowing roughly 255 passing yards per game and a 65 percent completion rate through seven contests. 

White operates from a versatile 3-4 base that frequently morphs into four-down looks, relying on pre-snap movement, disguised pressures, and one-on-one opportunities rather than static alignments. The front seven has been the strength; the secondary, anchored by a mix of returning experience (and portal additions) has been a vulnerability, particularly against vertical and intermediate concepts. Culture markers center on process, physical pads, and “don’t miss the layup” execution. 

Recent improvement against Texas demonstrated the ceiling when confidence and technique align; sustained success against Georgia-caliber passing attacks will require longer, stickier coverage on the boundary and in the slot.

Roberts’ skill set matches this system through length that contests deep balls without sacrificing recovery speed, active hands that press and re-route at the line before transitioning into trail technique, and hip fluidity that mirrors vertical routes. His demonstrated ability to force incompletions and generate PBUs in man looks exploits White’s preference for creating isolated coverage matchups. Run-support urgency and TFL production further complement the multiple-front approach by allowing the secondary to play downhill without compromising gap integrity. 

The same traits that produced high-volume disruption against competitive high-school receivers translate directly into White’s emphasis on physical, disciplined coverage that forces offenses off schedule.

Prospect's Fit & Immediate Impact

Primary alignment is boundary corner in man or pattern-match looks, with secondary nickel/STAR utility that leverages his 77.5-inch wingspan and change-of-direction to erase slot threats. Day-one contributions arrive via rotational snaps in sub-packages and special-teams coverage, where length and competitive toughness produce early PBUs and tackles while the room continues developing. Long-term, Roberts projects as a multi-year starter who anchors the perimeter once functional mass improves anchor ability against physical run schemes. 

Film shows efficient hip flips and clean transitions that allow him to stay on vertical routes without false steps, finishing with controlled leverage rather than lunging—traits that scale immediately into White’s one-on-one coverage windows. Ball skills that high-point and track over the shoulder add a playmaking dimension currently missing from the secondary’s production profile, while WR upside offers package versatility without diluting defensive focus.

Scheme Alignment Breakdown

White’s philosophy centers on versatile fronts, pre-snap movement, and creating one-on-ones while demanding physical, assignment-sound play. Roberts’ sticky coverage and active hand usage directly exploit the isolated matchups White seeks, turning length into a mismatch advantage on deep balls that currently produce too many completions. 

Against outside-zone and gap schemes that stress edge setting, his urgency in filling and length to set the boundary align with White’s requirement that secondary players play with pads and maintain leverage. The same COD and twitch that allow him to close cushions late without false steps counter the route concepts that have stressed Florida’s current corners. Brandon Harris and Dae’one Wilkins, the primary contacts, emphasize ball skills, twitch, and instincts—precisely the traits Roberts has already shown in competitive settings. Continued refinement in off-man and zone drops will be accelerated by White’s process-oriented coaching and the existing secondary’s growing confidence, positioning Roberts to contribute in both man-heavy and hybrid looks from the outset.

Culture & ROI Projection

Roberts’ consistent gratitude, team-first focus, and multi-sport discipline match the maturity and resilience Sumrall and White have prioritized in building the program. Family athletic lineage and prior coaching exposure further reinforce a professional approach that raises daily standards without needing external motivation. 

Early production (10-plus PBUs, interceptions, and TFL volume) against tough competition signals locker-room impact as a high-character competitor who accelerates development for younger players while complementing veterans. Multi-year ROI is high: immediate rotational disruption in a secondary that needs length and ball production, followed by starter-level coverage as the frame matures. 

Programs investing in physical development gain a versatile piece who can also contribute on special teams or hybrid packages, delivering early wins and sustained cultural elevation. The offer and ongoing dialogue with the staff already validate scheme and character fit; continued production through the high-school season will only sharpen the trajectory toward early SEC contribution and long-term secondary leadership.

Micah Beckwith is dead wrong here. Every Hoosier must vote “YES” on Public Question 1 to deny bail to criminals.

Look at Illinois since passing the SAFE-T Act. Do Hoosiers really want their homes to become like the crime ridden ghettos we see metastasizing out of Chicago? I don’t think so.

“An accusation is not a conviction.” Obviously, Micah. Good thing a bail hearing isn’t a criminal trial, either.

The question is whether judges should have authority to detain defendants when the evidence is strong and the state proves that no conditions of release can protect the public. You can argue against those safeguards (you’d still be wrong), but you can't pretend they don't exist.

And spare us the suggestion that Christianity demands helplessness in the face of danger. Christian mercy and the protection of innocent families are not mutually exclusive.

In fact, your application of the former prevents the latter! Why are we fetishizing displays of Christian mercy to criminals but not the good, innocent families they destroy?

If the best your Church has to offer disillusioned young men is the same, feminized decline and anarcho-tyranny as Leftists, what good is your Church? At least DSA lets you sleep in on Sundays! 

Reducing Christianity to some weak, hippie caricature of unconditional passivity is not a serious theological argument. Neither is reciting the presumption of innocence while ignoring the actual legal standards at issue.

Vote “YES” on Public Question 1!

text:
Eleven years before Michael Jordan, Nike gave NBA star Spencer Haywood 10% of the company.

While Haywood was on a road trip, his agent sold the whole 10% stake for $100,000 in cash—just to collect his $10,000 fee.

In the video below, Haywood is asked if he is still friends with the man who sold it. His answer: "Yes."

In 1973, Haywood was 24 and averaging 29 points a game in Seattle. Phil Knight came to him and asked him to wear his new shoe.

Knight didn't have the cash to match Converse. So he offered Haywood stock instead.

"First of all, I was young, too, and I'm thinking: livestock? What are you talking about? Stocks," Haywood says.

Haywood took the stock.

His agent had a problem. An agent gets 10%. Ten percent of stock in a tiny shoe company couldn't pay his bills. Ten percent of $100,000 in cash was $10,000 in his pocket right away.

So the agent kept telling Haywood the shoe would never work. At the time, Nike only made running shoes for Steve Prefontaine. When Haywood ran down the court, defenders stepped on his heel and popped the shoe right off his foot.

Before leaving for a road trip, Haywood gave in.

"I said, 'Okay, man, I give you the power of attorney. Let me just go play. I got to really focus on this game now because this is my chance.'"

When Haywood came back, the stock was gone.

"He had sold that sh*t," Haywood says. "He said, 'Man, I got the cash right here — 100,000.'"

Matt Barnes asks him what that 10% of Nike would be worth.

"It was up around 2.7 billion," Haywood says. "Years ago." At Nike's peak, 10% was worth over $8.6 billion.

The case for the agent: in 1973, Nike was a tiny Oregon running-shoe company, and the shoes literally fell off Haywood's feet during games.

Could you stay friends with a man who cost you $2.7 billion?

There are mornings I wake up feeling ok emotionally, somewhat relaxed, determined, and ready to take on what falls in front of me. Then there are days like today, Angry, tired, worried, frightened, and no sure of my decisions. These days are rough but today I find myself fixated on one phrase, my doctor stated to me when we were discussing the surgery that I haven’t disclosed to anyone, except a couple of people. Mostly because I haven’t finished processing it yet. “Discuss your options”

What does that mean? It sounds so ominous, final, abrupt, and limiting. He said during our discussion that he would stop the surgery if things were too bad inside and then we would have to discuss your options. Again, what does that really mean for me. We never went any further because we both hand an understanding to a point what it meant, but not entirely until he was performing the surgery.

Either way, to me it is frightening. It is kind of hard to discuss specifics. Those three words carry quite a bit with them good and bad. When I get like this, I try to look on the better side of those words, maybe it opens up my options. Despite the situation, it offers directions to treat and better answers. I do my best to stay focused on that end of it, but the dark side of that statement is always looming around the corner waiting for that one moment to step in to remind me, “don’t forget about me”.

I am working on that today and it has been a battle for me all morning, hopefully the good outcomes, if there really are any in this, win out. November 16th can’t come soon enough. We will see……
