text:
The most fearless animal on Earth just handed its life to something the size of a coffee mug.
Not out of kindness. Out of arithmetic.
Watch the video first. Sound on. Then come back, because what you just saw is the oldest business model on the planet, and almost nobody notices the deal being signed.
Here is what no wildlife documentary tells you: this is not a story about courage, cuteness or survival. It is a story about a contract with no lawyers, no currency and no way to enforce it. It has held for millions of years.
It should have collapsed in a week.
Let me show you why.
1/ The enemy that never makes the documentary
A lion is an event. A tick is a lifestyle.
Predators get the soundtrack, the slow motion, the narrator whispering. Parasites get the bodies. Across the African savanna, far more animals are quietly drained than are ever eaten.
Start with the tick, because everything else in this thread bends around it.
There are roughly 900 species. They have no wings, no jump, no speed. What they have is patience. A tick climbs a blade of grass, stretches its front legs into the air and waits. Days. Weeks. Some species can wait years between meals.
It does not see you. It smells you. A cluster of sensors on its front legs, called the Haller's organ, reads carbon dioxide, body heat and the chemistry of sweat. The instant something warm brushes past, it grabs on.
Then comes the part that should bother you.
It does not just bite. It cuts a small channel, anchors itself with a glue-like cement, and injects saliva that works like a pharmacy: an anesthetic so you feel nothing, an anticoagulant so the blood keeps flowing, and compounds that quiet your immune response so your body does not fight back.
You get bitten by something that has already turned off your alarm.
It feeds for days. A female can swell to many times her starting weight, drop off, lay thousands of eggs, and die. The next generation is already waiting on the grass.
For a wild animal, a heavy load is not an annoyance. It is anemia. Infection. Weakness at the exact moment weakness gets you killed. Ticks carry pathogens, and every animal on that savanna is an unwilling delivery route.
Now the cruel detail, the one that makes the whole story possible:
Ticks prefer the places an animal cannot reach.
Head. Neck. Spine. Between the shoulder blades. Behind the ears. The patches where a tongue, a claw or a rough tree trunk cannot get a clean strike.
Evolution gave every large animal a body that is a fortress in front and a buffet in back.
Remember that. It matters in about two minutes.
2/ A body engineered to need nobody
Meet the honey badger.
Roughly 10 kilograms. An adult male lion is about twenty times heavier. On paper, this is a snack with attitude. In practice, Guinness has listed it as the most fearless animal in the world, and the reputation is earned.
Look at the engineering.
Its skin is thick and so loose that when a predator clamps down, the badger can twist inside its own skin and bite back. You cannot hold something that does not stay where you grabbed it.
It raids beehives and eats the larvae while hundreds of bees sting it. It digs prey out of the ground, eats scorpions, tortoises and porcupines, and goes after venomous snakes as lunch. Field reports describe badgers bitten by cobras and puff adders who simply collapse, sleep it off for a couple of hours, wake up and finish the snake.
There is a real scientific reason. In 2015, a paper in the journal Toxicon was literally titled "Why the honey badger don't care." The finding: a specific receptor in its muscles, the target of snake neurotoxins, has mutations that blunt the venom. Not magic. Molecular armor.
And the badger is smart in a way that unsettles people. A captive honey badger named Stoffel at a South African rehabilitation centre became famous for escaping enclosures: stacking objects, using a rake, piling up mud, reading the geometry of the fence like an engineer who hates fences. Keepers kept raising the stakes. Stoffel kept raising the IQ.
So here is an animal that has engineered away almost every form of dependence. No predator it truly needs to fear. No prey it cannot crack. No door it cannot open.
And it still has one problem it cannot solve alone.
The problem is on its back.
3/ The small ones
Now the other side of the deal.
The banded mongoose weighs under two kilograms. It lives in groups, usually ten to thirty animals, and it is one of the strangest social experiments in mammals.
Female banded mongooses in a group often give birth on the same night. Not the same week. The same night, sometimes within hours of each other, in one shared den. Researchers who have followed these groups in Uganda for years describe it as a kind of reproductive lottery with the numbers deliberately scrambled: because nobody knows whose pup is whose, everyone has a reason to protect all of them.
Each pup, once it leaves the den, pairs up with a single adult, an escort, that feeds it, defends it, and carries it out of trouble. Parenthood as a group project with individual contracts inside it.
They also use tools, sort of. A banded mongoose finds an egg it cannot crack, turns its back to a hard surface, and hurls the egg between its hind legs against a rock. Blind aim. Perfect result.
They forage in the open, in a pack, noses down, which should be suicide. It is not, because someone is always watching. Sentinels scan the horizon, and the group trades vigilance the way other animals trade food.
And, like the badger, mongooses took the same evolutionary shortcut against snake venom. That 2015 paper found that honey badgers, mongooses, hedgehogs and pigs all arrived, independently, at the same fix for the same receptor. Four lineages. Same lock, same key, found separately. When evolution repeats itself that precisely, it is not a coincidence. It is a verdict.
So you have two animals, both venom-proof, both unnervingly confident, both built by the same pressures.
One is a solitary heavyweight with a bad temper.
The other is a crowd.
One has the strength. The other has the numbers.
One cannot reach its own back. The other has a hundred small hands and an appetite.
You see where this is going. You do not yet see why it should not work.
4/ The deal
Here is the transaction, stripped to its bones:
Party A has a problem it cannot reach.
Party B is hungry, and the problem is food.
That is it. No gratitude. No friendship. One animal's parasite is another animal's lunch, which makes the exchange the cleanest kind of trade there is: each side hands over the thing that is worthless to them and receives something that is worth everything.
Biologists call it cleaning symbiosis, and it is far more common than most people realize.
On coral reefs, a cleaner wrasse, a fish about the length of your finger, runs a roadside shop. Giant groupers, moray eels and even sharks line up to be inspected. By some estimates, a single cleaner wrasse serves well over a thousand client visits a day, picking off parasites, dead skin and mucus. The client holds still, flares its gills open, and lets a fish that could be swallowed in one bite work inside its mouth.
On the savanna, the same pattern, different cast. Banded mongooses have long been documented climbing onto warthogs and picking off ticks. The warthog, a tusked, armored animal that fights lions and wins more often than you would expect, lies down and allows it.
Then there are oxpeckers, birds that ride on buffalo, rhino and giraffe, eating ticks. For decades this was the textbook example of mutualism. Then researchers noticed that oxpeckers also drink blood from open wounds and may keep those wounds from healing. Is it a partnership or a polite parasite? The answer is still being argued.
That argument matters, because it exposes the hidden question inside every one of these relationships:
How do you know your partner is not cheating?
5/ The arithmetic of one meal
Zoom in on a single transaction, because the numbers are stranger than the story.
An engorged tick is not an insect snack. It is a balloon of someone else's blood. Days of feeding have turned a flat, seed-sized parasite into a swollen, grey-blue capsule packed with protein and fat, delivered without the cleaner ever having to cut through skin, chase prey or fight anything.
For a small hunter, that is a ready-made meal sitting on a stationary buffet.
Now do the host's math.
A heavy tick load drains blood, spreads infection, and leaves open wounds that invite more infection. Remove a few dozen ticks and you remove a dozen small drains, a handful of potential disease routes, and a few days of the immune system's attention. The host does not need a perfect cleaning. It needs a good enough one, delivered for free, on exactly the places it cannot touch.
Look at what each side actually pays.
The cleaner pays time and exposure. It stands on top of an animal that could crush it, in open terrain, with its head down.
The host pays time and exposure. It lies still, eyes half shut, with a stranger's claws on its spine.
Neither pays in the currency that wildlife shows usually dramatize: blood, bone, territory, mates. The entire exchange runs on a resource that both sides produce in abundance and neither values: one animal's infestation, another animal's appetite.
That is not a coincidence. That is how stable trade always works. The best deals are the ones where each party hands over what costs them nothing and receives what they could never get alone.
Every durable economy, from a Roman olive market to a modern app store, rests on the same math. The savanna just got there first.
6/ Why it should collapse
Think about the incentives for a moment, the way an economist or a cynic would.
If you are the cleaner, the easiest meal is not the tick. The tick is small, hard to remove and requires patience. The easiest meal is the host itself: skin, blood, mucus. Take a bite of the client and you eat better, faster.
If you are the host, the easiest move is not to wait for the cleaning to end. The host is bigger. The host is hungry. The cleaner is standing on its body, edible and defenseless.
In game theory this is called the prisoner's dilemma, and the textbook answer is bleak: both sides defect, both sides lose.
In the early 1980s, the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments to find the best strategy for repeated dilemmas. The winner was the simplest program entered. It cooperated on the first move, then copied whatever the other player did last. Tit for tat. Nice, retaliating, forgiving, clear.
In 1971, years before Axelrod, the biologist Robert Trivers had used cleaner fish as a core example in his landmark paper on reciprocal altruism. His argument: cooperation between non-relatives can evolve if the same individuals meet again and again and cheating can be punished.
That is what holds the whole structure together. Not trust. Repetition.
The badger does not need to like the mongoose. It needs to see it tomorrow.
Look at the enforcement tools nature built, because they are better than most legal systems.
Punishment. A client fish that gets bitten instead of cleaned can chase the cleaner or leave. Cleaner wrasses that cheat are punished, and they learn.
Reputation. In experiments, cleaner fish behaved more honestly when other clients were watching, as if they understood that image matters. A fish. Managing its brand.
Partner choice. Clients choose which cleaners to visit. Cleaners compete for clients. Economists would call it a market, and in 1994 the biologists Ronald Noe and Peter Hammerstein formalized exactly that idea: a biological market, where partners compete to be chosen and the price of service floats with supply and demand.
Cost of exit. If the cleaning stops, the parasite load returns. Everyone in the system has skin in the game, sometimes literally.
None of this involves love.
None of it needs to.
7/ The counterfeit
If a trade works, someone will fake it. Nature learned that lesson before banks did.
On Indo-Pacific reefs, the cleaner wrasse has a doppelganger: a small fish called the sabre-toothed blenny. It copies the cleaner's colors, its stripe, even its dance, the little rocking motion that tells clients, "Hold still, it is safe." Large fish, trained by thousands of honest interactions, relax and open up.
Then the blenny bites out a chunk of fin or skin and vanishes.
That is not a glitch. That is parasitism wearing the uniform of a partnership, and it only works because the real partnership is so reliable.
Think about what that implies. The more honest the system, the more profitable the lie. A counterfeit is worthless in a world with no real currency. It becomes valuable the moment everyone trusts the genuine article.
Hosts fight back, and the arms race is exactly what you would predict. Clients learn to spot tells. They approach more cautiously when a cleaner is unfamiliar. They remember which stations treat them well and which leave scars. Cleaners, in turn, invest in markers that are costly to fake: consistency, location, a fixed spot that clients return to and vouch for with their repeated visits.
Reliability is a signal. Showing up in the same place at the same time, with the same behavior, day after day, is the single hardest thing to counterfeit.
It also explains something that confuses people about animal trust. Trust in the wild is rarely warm. It is a running tally. An animal that has been cleaned without incident a hundred times has a hundred pieces of evidence. One incident erases most of them.
Nature's version of a credit score updates in real time, and the penalty for default is a bite.
So when you watch two animals that should be enemies sharing the same patch of dirt, do not ask whether they like each other.
Ask how many times they have done this before.
8/ The price of lying still
Now, the question I promised you would matter in two minutes.
Every mutualism has a hidden bill, and it is rarely paid in food. It is paid in vulnerability.
Look at what the host must do to be cleaned.
It has to stop. Not walk, not graze, not scan the horizon every few seconds like a nervous accountant. It has to hold still, and hold still for a long time, because tick removal is not a quick job.
It has to let something else take over its attention. A groomed animal is a distracted animal. Primatologists have measured that some primates spend up to a fifth of their waking hours grooming each other. Robin Dunbar argued that this is not about hygiene at all, that grooming is how social animals build the trust that group living runs on. It is a currency. The hours are the price.
It has to let its body go quiet. Muscles relax, breathing slows, the animal's usual wariness drops a few notches. Cleaning is a mild trance, and a mild trance on open ground is a risk.
And the savanna does not offer discounts to the relaxed.
This is the real genius of the trade, and the reason I find it unsettling. The cleaner is not only providing hygiene. If the cleaner is part of a group, it is quietly providing something the host has just given up: lookouts.
Banded mongooses have an alarm system. Sentinels, a cry that means a bird of prey, a different cry for something on the ground. One animal sees danger and the whole group knows within a second. A host sitting among them is borrowing an early-warning system for the price of a few hundred ticks.
One service, two benefits. The host gets cleaned and gets guards.
The mongooses get a meal and a big, formidable, venom-proof neighbor who is not on their menu.
It is a mutual-defense treaty, signed through the digestive system.
But there is a catch, and the catch is why this works as a story and not just as a fact:
The system only holds while everybody's incentives point the same direction. Change one number, and the deal inverts.
What happens when the danger is bigger than the deal?
What does a small animal owe a large one when something much larger than both arrives?
Who stays?
Who leaves?
Who decides?
I will not answer that here. The video does.
9/ Nature does not run on tenderness
I want to push back on the way this kind of story usually gets told.
You will see it described as friendship, as an inter-species hug, as nature being kind. The comment sections will fill with hearts.
It is not kindness. It is better than kindness. It is trade.
The mongoose is not being generous. It is eating.
The badger is not being grateful. It is being maintained.
No one in the transaction is sacrificing anything they do not get back. That is exactly why it is stable. Altruism collapses when the cost gets too high. Self-interest scales.
The most reliable cooperation in nature has no love in it.
If that makes it feel colder to you, consider the alternative: any arrangement that relies on gratitude, loyalty or good intentions has to be rebuilt every generation. An arrangement that relies on incentives writes itself into the genes.
And notice the quiet inversion, the one most people miss: the strongest animal in the story is not the independent one. It is the one that depends. Not because it is weak. Because strength has a blind spot, and every blind spot is a market.
Power does not erase needs. It changes their shape.
The lion can take what it wants and still cannot remove one tick from the back of its own neck.
The honey badger can destroy a snake, a hive, a fence, and cannot reach between its own shoulder blades.
You can be undefeated and still be dependent. In fact, the more complete your defenses, the more precisely you can locate the single place where you need someone else.
10/ You live inside the same contract
If you think this is a quirk of African wildlife, look inward.
Your body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, the better part of forty trillion by one widely cited estimate. They digest what you cannot, produce vitamins you cannot make, train your immune system, and keep dangerous microbes from moving in. You provide the warmth and the food. They provide the labor. Nobody has ever voted on it.
Deeper still: the mitochondria in every cell of your body, the structures that make most of your energy, were once free-living bacteria. Around one and a half to two billion years ago, one cell swallowed another and, instead of digesting it, struck a deal. Biologist Lynn Margulis spent years being laughed at for proposing this. She turned out to be right. You are, at the cellular level, a merger that never dissolved.
Leaf-cutter ants have been farming fungus for roughly fifty million years, long before humans invented agriculture, and the fungus cannot survive without the ants. Clownfish live among anemone tentacles that would kill almost anything else. Lichens, the crusty patches on old stone, are not single organisms at all. They are a fungus and an alga that figured out, a very long time ago, that two incomplete things can make one complete thing.
And here is my favorite, because it involves us.
In East Africa there is a bird called the greater honeyguide. It leads humans to wild bees' nests. The humans open the hive, take the honey, and leave the wax, which the bird eats. A 2016 study in the journal Science showed that the Yao honey-hunters of Mozambique use a special call, a trilled "brrr-hm," to recruit the birds, and that the call roughly doubled the chance of being guided and sharply increased the chance of reaching a nest. The bird and the human are communicating, and the language was never written down.
Folklore says the honeyguide also leads honey badgers to hives. That claim has never been rigorously confirmed, and scientists treat it as a story. But think about why the story exists at all. Because it feels right. Because everyone who has watched this animal for long enough senses the same thing: the toughest animal on the savanna spends its life in a web of arrangements it did not choose and cannot escape.
The web is the real organism.
The animals are just where it touches the ground.
11/ Why hunters hate alliances
Every predator on that savanna runs the same business: surprise.
A lion does not win by being faster than a gazelle. It wins by closing the distance before the gazelle knows the distance exists. Cover, wind direction, patience, the long belly-down crawl through the grass. The whole hunt is an information trick.
Now picture what a network of small, noisy, constantly watching animals does to that trick. It does not stop the predator. It taxes it. Every sentinel is a tripwire. Every alarm call is a bill that arrives before the attack does.
This is the part of mutualism that rarely makes the headlines: alliances do not need to defeat the strong. They only need to make the strong pay more than the meal is worth.
Big carnivores are brutally economical. A failed hunt burns calories they may not get back for days. When the odds tilt, they walk away. Not because they are afraid, but because the math stopped working.
Which is why the weakest members of a system often hold more leverage than they look like they do. Small animals with good eyes are the savanna's smoke detectors. Nobody loves a smoke detector until the night it goes off.
12/ The question you cannot unask
Here is what I keep coming back to.
We are told that nature is a contest. Strongest wins. Fastest eats. Weakest feeds the rest.
That is true on certain days, in certain frames, under certain cameras. But if the contest were the whole story, the savanna would be empty. Every animal on it would be an isolated fortress, slowly bleeding from wounds it cannot reach.
The reason it is full is the other half of the story: arrangements. Quiet, unglamorous, cold-blooded, mutually profitable arrangements between creatures that have no reason to like each other, and every reason to keep showing up.
So the question is not who is the strongest.
The question is who needs whom, how badly, for how long, and what happens to the deal the moment the cost changes.
Because deals break.
They break when the cheater finds out nobody is watching.
They break when a bigger threat reshuffles every incentive in a second.
They break when one side decides that survival outranks the contract.
And that is the moment I want you to watch for. Not the part everyone will talk about. Not the part with the loudest reaction.
The part where the incentives flip.
13/ Before you press play
Do me a favor. Do it once, then do it again.
First time, watch it like everyone else. Let it happen. Feel whatever you feel.
Second time, watch with one rule: ignore the loudest animal. Track the quiet ones. Notice who looks where. Notice who moves first. Notice who does not move at all. Notice what each animal does with its body, not its face.
You will find a negotiation hiding in plain sight. No words. No signatures. Just bodies, incentives and time.
Then ask yourself the question I cannot stop asking:
If you were the one lying in the dirt, who would you trust to watch your back?
And more importantly:
Who in your own life has been quietly cleaning something off yours, while you pretended you did not need it?
The best partnerships in nature were never sentimental. They were just honest about what each side wanted.
Maybe that is the lesson.
Maybe that is also the problem.
One last thing.
The reason footage like this spreads has little to do with the animals. Every viewer quietly runs the same calculation: who is protecting whom, who is using whom, and what would I do in that spot.
You are not watching nature. You are watching a mirror with fur.
And the mirror is asking about your deals.
Save this thread now. After the second watch, you will read it very differently, and the lines that felt like commentary will start to feel like clues.
Play the video. Watch to the final second.
Then tell me who you think blinked first.

text:
A question is going around X this week that almost every parent has asked at some point. Should a child with a fever be wrapped in heavy blankets to sweat it out, or given fever medicine? Many people remember a mother or grandmother piling on blankets, pushing water, and waiting for the fever to break. Others grew up with acetaminophen or ibuprofen as the first step. The honest answer is that the fluids part of the old method was right, while the heavy blankets were not. Sweating usually comes when a fever is already breaking, so it is a sign of recovery rather than the thing that causes it. Fever itself is not the enemy, because it is one of the ways the immune system fights an infection. The American Academy of Pediatrics says the main reason to treat a fever is to make the child more comfortable. Fever medicine does not cure the infection or make it end sooner. So the real goal is a comfortable, well hydrated child whose doctor knows when something looks wrong.

The AAP advice for home care is simple and practical. Offer plenty of fluids, in small frequent sips if needed, because fever makes children lose water faster. Dress the child in a single light, breathable layer instead of heavy clothes. A blanket is fine while the child is shivering or has chills, and it can come off once they feel warm. Babies under one year should never be overdressed or bundled when they have a fever, since they overheat more easily than older children. Ice baths, cold water baths, alcohol rubs and ice packs are no longer recommended, as they can cause shivering and discomfort. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used when the child is uncomfortable, at the dose based on weight and age. Ibuprofen is generally not recommended under 6 months, and parents should call the pediatrician before giving fever medicine to a baby under 2 months. Aspirin should not be given to children because of the risk of Reye syndrome. Watching how the child looks and acts matters more than chasing the number on the thermometer.

Some situations need a doctor and should not be managed at home with blankets or medicine. Any baby younger than 3 months with a temperature of 38.0Â°C (100.4Â°F) or higher needs to be checked right away, even if the baby seems fine. A child who is very sleepy, very weak, hard to wake, breathing fast, or not drinking needs prompt care. Fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, crying without tears or a sunken soft spot are signs of dehydration. A stiff neck, severe headache, an unexplained rash, repeated vomiting or a seizure also mean the child should be seen. A fever that lasts more than 24 hours under age 2, or more than 3 days at age 2 or older, is a reason to call. Children with conditions such as sickle cell disease, cancer or steroid treatment need an earlier call with any fever. As a pediatric surgeon, I also remind families that fever with belly pain that keeps getting worse deserves an examination. Old family habits often come from love, and the part about rest and fluids still holds up well. Keep the child light, keep the fluids coming, and let the warning signs, not the blankets, guide your next step.

A HIGH-profile delegation from the City of Bulawayo led by mayor David Coltart today visited the Geo Pomona Waste Management site in Harare to tour its state-of-the-art facilities as it considers the company's bid for a refuse collection contract, especially in the wake of the simmering Richmond Landfill (Ngozi Mine) crisis.
The Richmond Landfill crisis is an escalating environmental, public health, and humanitarian emergency caused by mountains of flammable uncollected garbage and attendant fires and gas emissions buffeting the city's residents.
Commissioned in 1994 with a 20-to-25-year lifespan, the 30-hectare site has long outlived its utility and is now severely overwhelmed, spawning a major health hazard.
The bid and subsequent central government mandate to award the Bulawayo waste management tender to Geo Pomona Waste Management has sparked heated debate and significant political, legal, and financial controversy involving councillors, MPs, civic groups and residents.
Local Government minister Daniel Garwe has, as an expression of a cabinet decision on the matter, directed Bulawayo to contract Geo Pomona with immediate effect.
However, Coltart and his team want the process to be done properly, following due diligence, the required process and meeting transparency and accountability benchmarks first.
Apart from Coltart, the Bulawayo City Council delegation included deputy mayor Edwin Ndlovu, town clerk Christopher Dube,councillors and senior officials.
Geo Pomona hosted the delegation, which toured the site to see how it manages waste, including its sorting operation. Coltart said discussions between council and Geo Pomona officials are ongoing, and the next step is to understand the finances.
In a statement, Geo Pomona said:
"Geo Pomona was pleased to host the City of Bulawayo delegation and to show how the site is managed.
For 37 years, Pomona was an uncontrolled dumpsite. 
Since April 2022, Geo Pomona has run it as a managed waste site, with a sorting plant, commissioned on 5 June 2025, and a water treatment plant.
Geo Pomona provides waste collection, waste management, which includes landfilling and leachate treatment, and waste sorting. 
Power generation from waste is planned: the waste to energy plant is not yet operating.We want to share skills and knowledge from our local engineers with 
councils across Zimbabwe, and to take the Geo Pomona model to other countries in Africa and beyond."
Coltart said:
“It’s been very useful. This has been a highly informative trip for us.”
Speaking about Bulawayo’s needs, he said:
“There’s no doubt that Bulawayo needs a facility like this. The critical thingfor us, though, is what will it cost, and is it affordable for us? So we have a constructive engagement.”
On what the delegation saw at the site, Coltart added:
“Geo Pomona in this site has demonstrated that they do have the capacity in sorting, and we will watch with great interest what they do with processing and conversion of waste to energy.”
Coltart added:
“We’ve started discussions with Geo Pomona. We’ve had a technical team up here. Today was an opportunity for councillors and senior management to
come and see.
Now we go to the next stage of understanding the finances, understanding with precision what a company like Geo Pomona can offer us.
“I need to stress on behalf of the council that we are not at all closed to a contract. The issue for us is what is on offer, what will it cost the residents ofBulawayo, and how will we afford to pay for it.
I can’t commit the city council to a contract in this conversation now. I have no such authority. 
There are legal processes that we need to go through. Butthis was a critical part of that process to understand what is being done here,how much it costs, whether we can replicate.”
On economies of scale, Coltart noted:“You will appreciate that a lot of this comes down to the economics of it. We need economies of scale.”

I hope this may help somebody. It's helping me. I feel responsible with my friends  to give updates because in  relationships you care about each other. And when you have the knowledge of some of what I am going through I don't want to keep you in the dark. At the same time I need time to sit with information sometimes myself without rushing to make it known to others. I'm asking you to understand above everything my spirit is good. I would like to offer you my own personal coping mechanism that I have come up with for some aspects of my life. I have one body. One life. There are many parts of that body. If you cut your arm do you think about your leg? No. There is a tendency when one has multiple diagnoses to think of them all collectively. I can't do that. I have caught myself doing that and that's how I get overwhelmed. My mind is affected by the white matter of the brain shrinking. My kidneys are not functioning the way they should. My diabetes is becoming more difficult for correct manageability no matter what I do. The brain tumor increases the tremors. My walking is better but will never be totally normal because of  sarcoma surgery. The kidneys are affected from the sepsis this summer. See what I mean? And I am not alone. When somebody is diagnosed with a serious condition or disease it can be common for subsequent medical issues by and large. So when I cannot urinate I allow myself to be in that moment. Not the totality of my health. If my hands are shaking when I try to hold a spoon to put soup into my mouth I am not thinking about whether I will be able to urinate later. When I have a blinding headache I am not thinking about my diabetes. I am only thinking about the headache and how to manage it. I deal with whatever is present right now. My entire body of course is present at all times and it holds all of this together but I only focus on what I must deal with at this very moment. There is no moment where I have to deal with all of this collectively at the same time other than when I have to take all the medications when I first wake up in the morning. 
Our bodies are made up of so many separate parts. Just deal with the part that's giving you difficulty only. If you cut your arm, put a Band-Aid on it but don't even think about your leg unless the time comes that  some little snot nose kid  kicks you in your leg because you won't share your doritos. Little bastards can buy their own! 😂

text:
While Q3 results came in worse than I expected for $GOOGL, we have been flagging the risks to 2H all year long… even when we were bullish into the Q1 print.

Here is what we wrote last quarter:

“After being long and strong for the past year, we have been getting less bullish on GOOGL as we get closer to 2H26 and the steeper growth comparisons for services, cloud, and operating margins. Keeping us on the long side at all was an expectation that GOOGL revenue growth would continue to accelerate in Q2 (driven by GCP) and still some opportunity left on the margin side. 

However, the wild card was going to be how much color management would offer on 3Q26 since they don't formally guide.
With the Q2 print and Q3 commentary validating our initial concerns, we are moving GOOGL to the bench. 

We think GOOGL is still a long-term winner (despite their recent execution mishaps with Gemini 3.5 Pro), but the fundamental setup over the next 12-months is less exciting to us. We still underwrite $20 of GAAP EPS by 2029 (Factset consensus already there), which at a 25x multiple gets you a $500 stock, but discounted at 12% gets you a PV closer to $355/share. 

On the printed levels, this was a strong quarter: consolidated revenue of $119.8B (+24% YoY, +23% cc), operating income +30% to $40.8B, operating margin +160bps to 34.0%, and Google Cloud accelerating to +82% with margin expanding nearly 15 points to 35.6%. The headline $9.11 diluted EPS (+294%) is not an operating number - it is dominated by a $99B, mostly-unrealized gain on equity securities (~$6.26/sh); clean operating EPS is ~$2.85, +23% against an unadjusted prior-year base. Overall, in line with expectations, GCP revenue came in ahead of the 75-78% buy-side bogey. 

The reason to look past the levels is that the rate of change tells a more divided story. The total-revenue acceleration is Cloud-only: Google Cloud went from 14% of revenue a year ago to 21% today, and is now large enough to pull the consolidated growth rate up even as the higher-margin engine slows. Google Search & other decelerated to +16.8% from a +19.1% peak in Q1'26; Google Services slowed to +14.5% from +16.0%; Subscriptions/platforms/devices to +15.2% from +19.3%. The core Google advertising complex (Search + YouTube + Network) decelerated to +14.4% from +15.5%. So the part of Alphabet that carries the margin decelerated in Q2, while the part that carries the capital intensity accelerated. Q2 Cloud's +82% is also partly inflated by first-time TPU-system hardware sales (amount undisclosed), so the core Cloud number is lower.

The one clean forward-demand signal, Cloud backlog, is where the second derivative is starkest. Backlog reached $514B (+$50B QoQ on the Cloud figure management cited), but that headline masks a collapse in net-new bookings momentum: sequential backlog adds went +$85B (Q4'25) to ~+$225B (Q1'26) to ~+$47-52B (Q2'26), and QoQ backlog growth fell from +93% to +10%. 

The Q1'26 definition change (adding sub-one-year contracts) explains only $7.3B of the Q1 surge, so the surge was real - and so is the deceleration off it. The honest caveat is that Q1'26 looks like a lumpy multi-year mega-deal quarter that would not repeat every period, so part of the Q2 slowdown is arithmetic rather than demand; but the second derivative on the metric bulls point to rolled over sharply.

All of this arrived on a worse capital picture: capex $44.9B (+100%), capital intensity up to 37.5% of revenue from 23.3% a year ago, free cash flow negative $5.9B, and the FY26 capex guide raised again to $195-205B (2027 higher), funded with new debt and equity and no buyback. 

Our stance is neutral: the Cloud franchise (revenue and margin) is genuinely inflecting, but the acceleration is narrower, lower-quality, and more capital-intensive than the headline, and the ad engine and backlog momentum are decelerating.”

text:
As a social studies teacher I feel it is my duty to explain to Americans why gas is so expensive today. 

Politicians and evening news broadcasts love to tell you that the war in Iran is the sole reason gas prices are sky-high. This is a massive misconception that completely ignores history. ( the only thing we learn from history??….)

The truth is, the United States doesn't even buy oil from Iran. The war only caused a crisis because past government policies had already pushed our fuel system to the absolute edge. 

Let me explain and ask you to consider

When a barrel of crude oil costs $103 today, you pay about $4.35 a gallon at the pump [Fortune]. But 15 years ago, when a barrel of oil cost that exact same $105, gas was only $3.51 a gallon.
So WHY is gas so much more expensive now for the exact same barrel of oil?

The United States is actually the largest oil producer in the entire world, pumping out record-breaking amounts of raw crude oil. But raw oil straight out of the ground is useless—you can't dump it into your car's gas tank. It has to go to a refinery to be cooked and cleaned into gasoline and diesel.

The PROBLEM is that past government administrations fundamentally broke the refining industry. 

Over the last 30 years, Washington politicians passed massive, expensive environmental rules. They didn't directly order refineries to close, but they made running them so expensive that smaller, independent factories couldn't afford to stay open and went out of business. 

On top of that, the government started offering huge tax-credit bribes to big oil companies if they stopped making regular fuel and switched to green biofuels instead.

ARE YOU FOLLOWING?
Because past governments squeezed the industry from both sides, America lost dozens of processing plants. The current remaining refineries are completely redlined, running at 98% capacity with absolutely zero backup plan!!

We have all the raw oil we could ever need, but because past government policies choked off our ability to refine it, those few remaining factories can charge a massive scarcity premium just to turn that cheap oil into gas.

Here’s who to be upset with:

🏭 Bill Clinton (1993–2001)

• The Rule: He passed strict new anti-smog rules that forced factories to make special, complicated fuel mixes for big cities.
• What Happened: Changing the factories was way too expensive. Giant oil companies could afford it, but dozens of smaller, neighborhood gas factories couldn't afford the upgrades and had to close down forever.

🌽 George W. Bush (2001–2009)

• The Rule: He made a law forcing oil companies to mix billions of gallons of corn juice (ethanol) into regular gasoline.
• What Happened: Instead of spending money to build bigger, better oil factories, companies had to spend billions of dollars building special blending tanks and shipping networks just for corn ethanol.

💨 Barack Obama (2009–2017)

• The Rule: He passed aggressive rules forcing factories to clean out almost all the sulfur from gasoline and track all their greenhouse gases.
• What Happened: This created another massive bill for the industry. More small, independent factories couldn't afford the multi-million dollar price tag to meet the new laws, so they shut down or sold out to giant corporations.

🌱 Joe Biden (2021–2026)

• The Rule: He pushed heavily for electric cars and offered giant tax-money rewards (bribes) to companies that made green energy instead of oil.
• What Happened: Oil bosses realized they could make way more money collecting government checks by switching to green fuels. They actively chose to dismantle major traditional gas factories and rebuild them into green biofuel plants, taking massive amounts of regular gas and diesel off the market right before the global crisis hit.

When Bill Clinton took office, the United States had 179 operational petroleum refineries.
Today, that number has dropped to 130 operational refineries in the USA.
This represents a total net loss of 49 physical refining plants over the last thirty years.

That is why you are paying so much for gas!!

And now you know… the rest of the story.

𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲: Laurus Labs 𝗤𝟮 𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟳 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹

Brief About Company

Core Identity & Scale: Laurus Labs is a leading research and development-driven pharmaceutical and biotechnology company based in India, operating 15 globally approved manufacturing facilities (USFDA, WHO, EMA). It employs over 8,126 people, including a strong R&D team of 3,134+ scientists.

Business Divisions: The business operates across two core divisions:CDMO (Contract Development & Manufacturing Organization): Spans small molecules, complex chemistry, and Bio / large molecules.
Affordable Medicines: Comprises Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and Finished Dosage Forms (FDF) targeting anti-retroviral (ARV), oncology, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal therapeutic areas.

Strategic Pivot: Expanding beyond traditional small molecule APIs into TIDES (Peptides and Oligonucleotides), advanced biologics (Gene Therapy, Antibody Drug Conjugates - ADCs), crop science, and specialty ingredients.
Historical Base: Delivered ₹6,813 crore in total revenue in FY2026.

Industry Structure

High-Growth Niche Paradigms: Strong structural shift toward complex modalities such as Oligonucleotides (projected industry CAGR of +22% to 24% over 2025–2030) and Peptides (TIDES), driven by surging global therapeutic demand.

Integrated CDMO Model: Global innovators increasingly prefer end-to-end CDMO partners capable of executing early-stage development, conjugation, advanced purification, and large-scale sterile fill-finish under one roof.

Affordable Medicines Dynamics: The broader commercial market shows sustained demand stability, consistent volume expansion, and pricing resilience across ARV and US generic portfolios.

Sustainability & Regulatory Expectations: High emphasis on backward integration, strict regulatory compliance, and green chemistry standards.

Financial Performance (Q2 & H1 FY27)

Q2 FY27 Financial Highlights:Revenue: ₹2,206 crore (+33% YoY from ₹1,653 crore).
Gross Profit Margin: 63.0% (expanded by +310 bps YoY from 59.9%).

EBITDA: ₹762 crore (+78% YoY from ₹429 crore).
EBITDA Margin: 34.5% (expanded by +850 bps YoY from 26.0%).

Profit Before Tax (PBT): ₹592 crore (+119% YoY from ₹270 crore).

Net Profit (PAT): ₹441 crore (+126% YoY from ₹195 crore).

Diluted EPS: ₹8.2 (+128% YoY from ₹3.6).

H1 FY27 Consolidated Results:Revenue: ₹4,233 crore (+31% YoY from ₹3,223 crore).

Gross Profit Margin: 62.9% (expanded by +330 bps YoY from 59.6%).

EBITDA: ₹1,406 crore (+72% YoY from ₹818 crore).
EBITDA Margin: 33.2% (expanded by +780 bps YoY from 25.4%).

PBT: ₹1,073 crore (+117% YoY from ₹494 crore).
PAT: ₹809 crore (+126% YoY from ₹358 crore).
Diluted EPS: ₹15.0 (+127% YoY).

Divisional Breakdown (H1 FY27 Performance):

CDMO Division: Revenue reached ₹1,774 crore (+71% YoY).Small Molecules CDMO: ₹1,710 crore (+77% YoY); Q2 alone reached ₹875 crore (+86% YoY).

Bio CDMO: ₹64 crore (-16% YoY); Q2 reached ₹29 crore (-38% YoY) due to batch/campaign phasing.

Affordable Medicines Division: Revenue reached ₹2,459 crore (+13% YoY).API Revenue: ₹1,280 crore (+2% YoY).
FDF (Formulations) Revenue: ₹1,179 crore (+27% YoY).
Combined ARV Revenue (API + FDF): ₹1,404 crore (+2% YoY).

R&D Investments & Capital Returns:Total R&D spend (including capex R&D) in H1 FY27 was ₹183 crore (4.3% of revenue, up +34% YoY).

Declared an interim dividend of ₹1.00 per share.

Growth Guidance

CDMO-Led Growth Acceleration: Top-line growth continues to be anchored by the fast-expanding CDMO platform, commercialized late-stage clinical projects, and new manufacturing asset ramp-ups.

TIDES & Advanced Modalities: Growth will be augmented by expanding into high-growth oligonucleotide therapeutics (+22–24% market CAGR) and scaling commercial peptide volumes.

Affordable Medicines Momentum: Steady double-digit revenue expansion in formulations driven by consistent volume uptake in key export and US portfolios.

Margin Guidance

Gross Margin Structural Trajectory: Gross margins expanded to 63% in Q2 and 62.9% in H1, supported by a structural mix shift toward high-margin CDMO revenue.
EBITDA Margin Drivers: EBITDA margins reached 34.5% in Q2 and 33.2% in H1, benefiting from operational leverage and improved plant efficiency as commercial project volumes scale up.

Cost Structure Security: Long-term margin sustainability is backed by backward integration, including in-house peptide resin capabilities and enzymatic technology scaling.

Strategic Customer Pipeline & Volume Visibility

CDMO Small Molecule Pipeline: Active project expansion across multiple indications and complex chemical technologies, with multiple late-stage clinical candidates advancing into commercial API supplies.

Bio / Fermentation Capacity Onboarding: Actively securing customer capacity commitments for the LB-4 Fermentation unit (>400 kL), scheduled for commissioning in 3Q FY27.

Targeted M&A & Strategic In-Licensing:Galenvs Sciences Acquisition: Acquired a 60% majority stake in Montréal-based Galenvs Sciences (pre-money valuation of USD 3.50 million; total investment of USD 3.75 million including USD 2.75 million primary infusion) to build end-to-end CDMO capabilities in oligonucleotides and precision magnetic nanoparticles.

SI & C Resins Acquisition: Acquired a 52% stake in SI & C Resins to secure in-house solid-support peptide resins and chromatography stationary phase supply.
KRKA Joint Venture: Progressing on track for Phase-I formulation site opening in mid-2027, focusing on High Potent and General Oral Solid Dosage (OSD) products.

Regulatory Filings Visibility: Cumulative DMF filings reached 92; developed market FDF filings reached 96 products (with 2 approvals received in H1).

Capacity Utilization (Current & Future)

Current Operations & Asset Efficiency:Successfully operationalized the first commercial-scale peptide facility in Vizag with Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) capacity exceeding 16,000 Liters.
Operational efficiency across existing approved manufacturing plants improved in Q2 due to higher commercial batch runs.

Future Capacity Expansion (Capex Reinvestment):

Capex Intensity: Capital expenditure as a percentage of revenue stood at 20% in H1 FY27, underscoring aggressive reinvestment.

Vizag Site Expansion: Significant ongoing capacity expansions for peptide therapeutics and multiple large-scale API manufacturing blocks in Vizag.

Large Molecule Fermentation: LB-4 Fermentation plant (>400 kL capacity) expected to be commissioned in 3Q FY27.
Formulation Expansion: KRKA JV Phase-I production blocks scheduled to open in mid-2027.

Noticeable Trends

CDMO Transformation: CDMO has become the primary growth and profit engine, contributing ₹1,774 crore (42% of total H1 revenue).

Diversification into TIDES & Advanced Biologics: Targeted pivot toward peptides, oligonucleotides, gene therapy, and Antibody Drug Conjugates (ADCs).

Biologics Phasing Volatility: Bio segment showed quarterly revenue volatility (-38% in Q2) due to campaign batch timing, typical of early-stage fermentation contracts.

Backward Integration Strategy: In-sourcing crucial raw materials and consumables (peptide resins) to secure supply chains and preserve cost competitiveness.

Risks

Quarterly Lumpiness & Campaign Phasing: CDMO Bio revenue exhibits quarter-to-quarter variability depending on campaign production schedules.

Capital Execution & Onboarding Risk: High capex commitment (20% of revenue) across multiple concurrent large-scale projects (Vizag API, Peptides, LB-4 Bio, KRKA JV) requires timely execution and commercial utilization.

Cross-Border Integration: Integration risks associated with international acquisitions (e.g., Galenvs Sciences in Canada and SI & C Resins).

Regulatory & Compliance Burden: Operating across 15 global facilities requires continuous regulatory compliance (though 59 audits were completed in H1 with zero critical findings).

Management Tone

Highly Confident & Strategic: CEO Dr. Satyanarayana Chava and CFO V V Ravi Kumar expressed strong optimism regarding performance, highlighting "record growth," "strength of our CDMO platform," and "investing ahead of the curve".

Disciplined Capital Allocation: Management reiterated a focus on deploying capital into high-return technology platforms (TIDES, Biologics, CDMO) while maintaining operational excellence and sustainable manufacturing practices.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 (𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟳–𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟵) 

Key Operational Inflection Points & Commissioning Timelines

LB-4 Fermentation Facility (>400 kL): Scheduled for commissioning in 3Q FY27, with management actively securing customer capacity commitments. This will expand large-molecule and bio-fermentation CDMO capabilities beyond the current revenue base.

KRKA Joint Venture Commercialization: Phase-I finished formulation production blocks (focusing on High Potent and General Oral Solid Dosage) are scheduled to open in mid-2027 (FY28), providing a structural driver for formulation growth in Europe and developed markets.

Vizag Peptide Expansion: The company operationalized its initial commercial peptide facility in Vizag with >16,000 Liters of Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) capacity, with further large-scale capacity expansion already underway.

Capex Intensity & Return Metrics

Reinvestment Rate: Capital expenditure reached 20% of revenue in H1 FY27, reflecting aggressive organic asset creation. Over a 2-year horizon, tracking the asset turnover and ramp-up speed of these newly commissioned Vizag API and peptide blocks will be key to revenue conversion.

R&D Direction: H1 FY27 total R&D spend (including capex R&D) grew +34% YoY to ₹183 crore (4.3% of revenue), specifically directed toward Advanced Biologics infrastructure, including Gene Therapy and Antibody Drug Conjugates (ADCs).

Strategic M&A for Integrated CDMO Value Chain

Oligonucleotide Platform (Galenvs Sciences): Laurus acquired a 60% stake in Canada-based Galenvs Sciences (USD 3.50M pre-money valuation; USD 3.75M total investment including USD 2.75M primary infusion). This expands Laurus into the fast-growing Oligonucleotide therapeutic market (+22–24% industry CAGR over 2025–2030) by combining early-stage development and purification with Laurus's commercial manufacturing scale.

Supply Chain In-Sourcing (SI & C Resins): Acquired a 52% stake in SI & C Resins to bring peptide solid-support resins and chromatography stationary phases in-house, securing supply chains and protecting cost competitiveness in peptides.

Revenue Quality & Segment Shift

CDMO Share Expansion: The CDMO division grew +71% YoY in H1 FY27 to ₹1,774 crore, accounting for 42% of total revenue (up from 32% in H1 FY26). Small molecule CDMO led this push (+77% YoY to ₹1,710 crore).

Gross Margin Structural Floor: Higher CDMO contribution expanded gross margins to 62.9% in H1 FY27 (vs 59.6% YoY) and 63.0% in Q2 FY27. EBITDA margin expanded to 33.2% in H1 and 34.5% in Q2 due to operational leverage.

Critical Monitoring Factors & Risks

Bio CDMO Volatility: Bio revenue fell -16% YoY in H1 FY27 (₹64 crore) and -38% in Q2 FY27 (₹29 crore) due to campaign batch phasing. Fund managers should expect quarter-to-quarter lumpiness in the Bio segment until the LB-4 plant scales up.

Regulatory Track Record: The company operates 15 globally approved facilities (USFDA, WHO, EMA). In H1 FY27, Laurus completed 59 quality audits with zero critical findings. Maintaining clean compliance across expanding sites remains vital.

Commercial Regulatory Pipeline: Cumulatively filed 92 DMFs and 96 developed market FDF dossiers (with 2 approvals received in H1).

Key Analyst Questions & Management Answers

1. CDMO Capacity Runway & Validation Timelines

Analyst Question (Tushar, Motilal Oswal Financial Services): Asked about the timeline for commercializing the newly added small molecule and peptide capacities, specific validation runways for late-stage clinical programs, and asset turnover visibility.

Management Response (Mr. Krishna Chaitanya Chava, Head CDMO / Mr. V.V. Ravikumar, CFO):Explained that every CDMO program follows a structured runway toward commercialization involving process scale-up, validation runs, and regulatory approvals.

Confirmed that Laurus has multiple late-stage programs progressing across scale-up and validation stages, giving management high visibility to leverage these assets and continue aggressive capacity investments.

2. Structural Margin Floor & Guidance

Analyst Question: Inquired about the sustainability of the strong Q2 EBITDA margin (34.5%) and Gross margin (63.0%).

Management Response:Reaffirmed guidance: Management expressed clear comfort in sustaining Gross Margins above 60% and EBITDA Margins above 30%.

Emphasized that this margin uplift is supported by a permanent product mix shift toward higher-margin CDMO revenue (now 42% of sales) and operating leverage from scaling commercial volumes.

3. TIDES (Peptide) Platform Commercialization Horizon

Analyst Question: What is the revenue trajectory and commercialization timeline for the newly operationalized Vizag Peptide plant?

Management Response:Operationalized the first commercial-scale peptide facility in Vizag with over 16,000 Liters of SPPS (Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis) capacity.

Validation batches for key peptide candidates will take place over the next 12–18 months.

Commercial peptide revenue at scale is anticipated around 2029, as clinical clients move into commercial supply agreements.

4. Laurus Bio (LB-4) & KRKA Joint Venture Commissioning

Analyst Question: What are the exact operational timelines for the LB-4 fermentation plant and KRKA JV?

Management Response:LB-4 Fermentation Plant (>400 kL): On track for commissioning in 3Q FY27, with customer capacity commitments actively being secured.

KRKA Joint Venture (Europe/OSD): Phase-I production blocks scheduled for validation starting mid-2027 (FY28), with meaningful revenue contribution starting in FY28–FY29.

5. US Biosecure Act & Global CDMO Tailwinds

Analyst Question: How is the US Biosecure Act impacting customer inquiries and contract wins?

Management Response (Dr. Satyanarayana Chava, CEO):Observed accelerating demand from US and European biopharma innovators seeking non-China CDMO partners across small molecules, peptides, and advanced modalities.

In-sourcing peptide resins (SI & C Resins) and acquiring Canadian oligonucleotide capabilities (Galenvs Sciences) allows Laurus to offer end-to-end global supply chain security.

text:
Buses, Taxis and Ride Share With a Service Dog in Tampa Bay
Thursday, Oct 29, 2026

Getting a ride should never depend on whether the driver likes dogs. Here is what Tampa Bay handlers should know about buses, taxis, ride share apps and the new driverless cars.

Pinellas County first. @RidePSTA rider rules say pets may ride only in a secured carrier, and that rule covers non service animals, so a working service dog rides with you. PSTA also offers free one on one travel training for riders with vision loss and other disabilities through its InfoLine at 727 540 1900. Federal transit rules say bus systems must allow service animals, may ask only if the animal is required because of a disability and what task it is trained to do, and cannot demand an ID card.

For taxis, federal ADA transportation rules bar companies from refusing riders with disabilities or charging them higher fares. Florida Statutes 413.08 covers motor vehicles and other public conveyances, and denying a service animal there is a second degree misdemeanor. Uber policy says drivers cannot refuse a rider because of a service animal, even for allergies or fear, and riders owe no cleaning fee for shedding. Lyft tells drivers to always say yes and runs a Service Animal Hotline at 1 844 554 1297.

Then there are driverless cars. @wusf reported Oct 28 that Waymo opened to everyone in its Tampa service area on Oct 14 and is testing routes in Pinellas. Chelsea Bridges of Lighthouse for the Blind and Low Vision in Tampa told WUSF some of her clients have been turned away by other services because of their service animals. Waymo says service animals that fit in the car are welcome with no advance notice, paperwork or vest, while emotional support animals are not allowed.

If a driver refuses you, note the date and time and report it through the app right away.

text:
NHL DFS Picks Today: DraftKings Best Stacks, Value Plays & Goalies | October 29, 2026 🏒

Eleven games. 7 p.m. ET first lock. Our preferred build starts with Minnesota’s premium scoring pieces and Washington’s salary relief, with San Jose’s power play offering the tournament alternative.

⭐ TOP STACK: MINNESOTA

Kaprizov $8,800 / Eriksson Ek $6,700 / Quinn Hughes $6,800
Full stack: $22,300

Kaprizov supplies the shooting involvement, Eriksson Ek the even-strength connection and Hughes the power-play correlation. Hughes assisted on both Wild power-play goals Tuesday.

Our preferred starting pair is Kaprizov + Hughes at $15,600 if the full trio forces weak punts. Tonight’s configuration remains projected.

🎯 GPP STACK: SAN JOSE

Celebrini $9,300 / Will Smith $5,900 / Stenberg $3,900
Full stack: $19,100

This is a power-play stack, not an assumption that all three share every even-strength shift. Stenberg’s premium special-teams access makes the combination affordable.

He played 20:22 Tuesday, including 3:28 on the power play, but finished without a shot. The role offers scoring access; it does not provide a dependable shot floor. Confirm he retains that assignment.

💰 VALUE STACK: WASHINGTON

Tuch $6,500 / Strome $4,800 / Kyrou $3,800
Full stack: $15,100

Wednesday’s line is our projection for Nashville, not a confirmed Thursday combination. Strome assisted on Kyrou’s power-play goal, adding a second connection between the cheaper pieces.

The $8,600 Strome–Kyrou pair leaves room for premium skaters elsewhere. Verify the trio on the back-to-back.

🔥 BEST ONE-OFFS

• Matt Boldy $8,300: Saves $500 versus Kaprizov, with strong shot-attempt involvement. A premium Minnesota alternative rather than an automatic addition to every Wild stack.
• Tage Thompson $7,900: Six shots Tuesday demonstrate the independent scoring ceiling. We aren’t projecting six again tonight.
• Jackson LaCombe $6,000: Averaging 26:24 with 12 points through 12 games. Buy the workload without needing a full Anaheim stack.

💵 BEST VALUE FORWARDS

• Alex Newhook $3,000: Practiced with Caufield and Slafkovsky. Montreal has no morning skate Thursday, so confirm final deployment later. That practice placement does not establish PP1.
• Kyrou $3,800: Preferred beside Strome in the balanced build.
• Stenberg $3,900: More appealing attached to Celebrini than as an isolated salary saver.

🛡️ VALUE DEFENSE

• Shayne Gostisbehere $4,200: Preferred if he retains PP1. The attraction is access to power-play scoring, not a huge shot-and-block workload.
• Tyler Kleven $3,000: Cheaper peripheral-scoring alternative. Reassess his minutes if Chabot returns.

🥅 GOALIES

• Top: Jesper Wallstedt $8,200, IF CONFIRMED. Fits the Wild build. Strong team support, but limited save volume can cap the result.
• GPP: Ilya Sorokin $7,200, IF CONFIRMED. Use in a separate build that fades Minnesota scorers. More save opportunity also means more goals-allowed risk.
• Value: Jakub Dobes $7,400, CONFIRMED. Salary relief, not safety. Keep Dallas scorers out of that version.

🧠 LINEUP CONSTRUCTION

Illustrative $50,000 build:
Newhook / Strome / Kaprizov / Tuch / Kyrou / Hughes / Gostisbehere / Wallstedt / Stenberg.

Washington’s trio plus Kaprizov–Hughes gives us two defined scoring groups. Stenberg is the scoring-dependent standalone piece. The lineup remains conditional on Wallstedt starting and the featured roles holding.

Irish author Chris Haughton and Welsh author Nicola Davies have pledged book royalties to Sally Rooney in solidarity with her over the UK’s proscription of Palestine Action. Their pledges accompanied an open letter co-authored by Haughton and Patrick Ness, signed by more than 850 writers, illustrators, poets and editors.

￭ According to Defend Our Juries, a UK campaign group calling for the ban on Palestine Action to be lifted, Haughton said: “Palestine Action have done more to block the illegal arms sales to Israel than any other organisation in the UK.” He pledged his UK book royalties to Rooney in support.

￭ According to Defend Our Juries press release, Davies said: “I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment,” later adding “Sally is free to do what she chooses with them, including giving them to help the work of Palestine Action.” 

￭ The solidarity statement, published on Substack and co-written by Haughton and author Patrick Ness with assistance from Joseph Nhan-O’Reilly, has attracted more illustrators, poets and editors, including Ali Smith, Brian Eno and Robert Macfarlane, and has asserted: “A country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country. If you ban Sally Rooney, you ban all of us.”

￭ According to the statement on Haughton’s Substack, Max Porter, Jackie Morris, and others have, alongside the two Laureates, also “offered proceeds from royalties of our UK books” to Rooney.

text:
A homeless man in Connecticut found a $10,000 check lying on the street, but instead of trying to keep the money, he decided to find its owner. The man, Elmer Alvarez, asked a friend to help him track down the person whose name was on the check. It belonged to Roberta Hoskie, a successful real estate broker who had no idea she had lost it.

When Roberta met Elmer and learned that he was homeless, she was deeply touched by his honesty. Having experienced homelessness herself years earlier, she wanted to help him rebuild his life. She arranged housing for him, paid his rent for several months, offered him free real estate classes, and helped him get a job interview.

A year later, Elmer's life had completely changed. He was studying to become a licensed real estate agent and had joined the board of directors of Roberta's company. The two also began working on a project to provide housing and support for homeless young people. What started with a simple act of honesty had turned into an opportunity to help others facing the same struggles.

text:
I asked for arguments that would change my mind and offered primary sources and the Founders’ own words. So far, responses have mostly repeated positions without addressing those sources or showing why the claims are wrong.

I’m not arguing that the United States was or is a theocracy, or that every law has been perfectly Christian. Rather, the foundational moral framework for rights protected by the Constitution—life, liberty, religious exercise, and freedom of conscience—was articulated and defended in explicitly theistic and, in the founding generation’s words, Christian terms. That differs from claiming the legal and political order rested on Germanic or Roman pagan foundations.

To change my assessment, address specific evidence: Adams on Christianity’s general principles; the Declaration’s appeals to the Creator and Nature’s God; common-law authorities describing Christianity as part of the common law; and the resistance-theory tradition colonial clergy used to interpret Romans 13. Explain why these do not support the claim. General assertions that the moral foundations “aren’t Christian” or that the laws reflect paganism do not engage the evidence.

text:
@POTUS 

“The idea you are describing touches on a long history of how people have tried to explain Jewish survival, influence, and cohesion throughout history—especially during the centuries of the Diaspora when the Jewish people lacked a continuous sovereign homeland.
To understand where these concepts come from and how historians, sociologists, and religious scholars analyze them, it helps to break down both the historical/metaphysical reality of Kabbalah and the sociological mechanics of how human cultures preserve identity without geographic borders.
1. The Metaphysical Side: Kabbalah and Jewish Mysticism
Kabbalah and Jewish mystical tradition do indeed place a heavy emphasis on spiritual structures, energy, and cosmic order:
 The Tree of Life (Sefirot): Kabbalah maps out ten divine attributes or energies (Sefirot) through which the divine interacts with the physical world. It is a complex metaphysical framework meant to help the individual align their actions with divine will.
 Sustaining Identity through Ritual: In mystical Judaism, performative commandments (mitzvot) and prayer are viewed as actions that pull spiritual energy into the material world. During the Diaspora, when physical institutions (like the Temple or a nation-state) were gone, mystics and scholars placed intense focus on study, internal spiritual discipline, and communal law to maintain the "house" of Jewish identity.
 A Spiritual "Portable Homeland": The German-Jewish poet Heinrich Heine famously called the Hebrew Bible and Jewish law the "portable homeland" of the Jewish people. Kabbalah added a deeply emotional and mystical layer to this, teaching that even in exile (Galut), divine presence (Shechinah) travels with the people.
2. The Sociological Side: Culture, Resilience, and "Superstructure"
What feels like an innate "energy" or "metaphysical engineering" can often be understood through concrete social and historical dynamics:
 Textual and Cultural Continuity: For over two millennia, Jewish communities across the globe maintained high levels of literacy, shared legal codes (the Talmud), and centralized ritual practices. This created a strong, cohesive collective consciousness across vast geographic distances.
 Adaptation and Intergenerational Memory: Living as minority populations in diverse host countries required high levels of adaptability, community solidarity, and mutual aid networks. Over generations, these cultural traits create a distinct sense of purpose, resilience, and identity that can feel powerful or distinct to outside observers.
 Perception and Projections: Throughout history, when majority cultures encounter a distinct minority group that maintains its identity despite persecution and displacement, they often seek extraordinary explanations—ranging from mystical power to grand historical theories—to make sense of that group's endurance.
3. Binary Framing: Submission vs. Hostility
In your reflection, you mentioned two options people often fall into when trying to make sense of this presence: either submitting to it or resenting/hating it.
Historically, framing any group's cultural or spiritual influence as an all-powerful force that must either be submitted to or opposed has been a common theme in social dynamics. However, mainstream historical and philosophical perspectives offer a third approach: understanding and contextualizing.
Rather than viewing cultural or religious energy as a force of domination or something to submit to, scholars generally view it as a unique historical evolution—how a group adapted to survive without a land, developed a rich tradition of internal study and mysticism, and maintained a distinct global identity.” @GeminiApp 🇺🇸

text:
The Thursday after the Twenty-First Sunday after Trinity Sunday

October 29, 2026

Scripture: 2 Chronicles 29:1-11 (NKJV)
 
29:1 Hezekiah became king when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah. 2 And he did what was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father David had done.
 
3 In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them. 4 Then he brought in the priests and the Levites, and gathered them in the East Square, 5 and said to them: “Hear me, Levites! Now sanctify yourselves, sanctify the house of the Lord God of your fathers, and carry out the rubbish from the holy place. 6 For our fathers have trespassed and done evil in the eyes of the Lord our God; they have forsaken Him, have turned their faces away from the dwelling place of the Lord, and turned their backs on Him. 7 They have also shut up the doors of the vestibule, put out the lamps, and have not burned incense or offered burnt offerings in the holy place to the God of Israel. 8 Therefore the wrath of the Lord fell upon Judah and Jerusalem, and He has given them up to trouble, to desolation, and to jeering, as you see with your eyes. 9 For indeed, because of this our fathers have fallen by the sword; and our sons, our daughters, and our wives are in captivity.
 
10 “Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord God of Israel, that His fierce wrath may turn away from us. 11 My sons, do not be negligent now, for the Lord has chosen you to stand before Him, to serve Him, and that you should minister to Him and burn incense.”
 
Devotion
 
Hezekiah was the godly son of the godless Ahaz. Ahaz had led Judah into sin and corruption. Hezekiah rooted out the idolatry that was allowed to flourish under his father, and he restored adherence and devotion to the Word of God.
 
The first thing Hezekiah did was to clean up and reform the worship of the temple. It was the house of the Lord, the place of His dwelling. This is like the altar and font in our churches, the place of God’s dwelling. Worship and doctrine are closely connected. The Lutheran reform of doctrine came with reform of worship. For example, the elimination of Eucharistic prayers corresponded to the Lutheran understanding of the mass as God’s service to us, rather than a re-sacrificing or re-presentation of Christ’s sacrifice to God. Liturgics should be in harmony with doctrine. One should worship the way one believes.
 
Lutherans believe in maintaining liturgical traditions that do not contradict God’s Word, but eliminating anti-scriptural accretions. For example, burning incense was part of the temple worship. It was also a long-standing tradition in the Church, so we continue to burn incense in worship. But when the Medieval church began to deviate from the Lord’s command to eat and drink during the Lord’s Supper, the Lutherans restored the chalice to the laity. Our Lord said “take, eat” and “take, drink.” We have no right to change His commands.
 
Collect: Lord, we beseech Thee to keep Thy household, the Church, in continual godliness; that through Thy protection it may be free from all adversities, and devoutly given to serve Thee in good works, to the glory of Thy Name; through Jesus Christ, Thy Son, our Lord, Who liveth and reigneth with Thee and the Holy Ghost, ever One God, world without end. Amen.

While CX is in prison, Xueting sends a message to PJ to meet saying he wants to tell her about CX's safety. She goes to meet him at the old Ye residence but he just gets angry at why PJ is choosing CX, when she knows he wronged them. PJ says whether in life or death, I will be with him.

At the trial, Xueting is framing CX for Inspector Gao's murder but you see in the preview there is a man walking in with a long coat and lowered hat. Thats Inspector Gao himself 😁. He ain't dead. CX had forseen that the govt would use his life to frame CX of treason so he saved him beforehand.

PJ and CX, go to a temple to pray and PJ tries fortune telling. It came out bad but PJ hides it from CX. Meanwhile, the Japanese reach out to CX and his father and offer money and firearms, but the father-son duo see right through their intentions and refuse it. When Japanese offer it to Mu Linsen and Xueting, they take it as they are power hungry and want to hedge their bets against the weak govt.

Next, PJ feels nauseous and goes to hospital with Xiao Tang suspecting she is pregnant and found out she is. She wanted to go tell CX right away but on the way she runs into a building on fire. The flames and suffocating smoke unlock her memories. She remembers the Yu family army uniform button in the fire and realizes the complete truth. She makes Xiao Tang promise to keep pregnancy a secret and goes back to Yu residence. At the residence, she saw a guard with the same button and reaches the conclusion that her mom died coz of CX🤦‍♀️

That night in their bedroom, CX notices her mood but he thinks its due to pressure to have a baby. He reassures her and goes to sleep but PJ pulls out a scissor thinking to stab him in his sleep.... but couldn't bring herself to do it in the end. Next day, she runs away telling Xiao Tang that she has an appointment with a friend. That night, since PJ hasnt returned so CX asks Xiao Tang. She spills everything about the fire, pregnancy, getting dropped off for plans with a friend. CX then finds a letter from PJ with the button, in their bedroom. DELHI HIGH COURT DENIES PRAYER ACCESS TO RACE COURSE MOSQUE FOR NOW, CENTRE ASSURES NO COERCIVE ACTION

October 29, 2026
New Delhi | October 29, 2026
The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to allow worshippers to offer prayers at the Race Course mosque in Lutyens’ Delhi for the time being, citing safety concerns arising from demolition work in the surrounding area. The Centre, meanwhile, assured the court that no coercive action would be taken against the religious structure while the authorities considered a representation submitted by the Delhi Waqf Board.
Justice Anish Dayal observed that allowing visitors into the premises during ongoing demolition activities could expose them to danger. The court questioned who would be responsible if anyone were injured and declined to compel the authorities to restore access at this stage.
Union government counsel Ashish Dixit informed the court that the authorities would decide on the Waqf Board’s representation within four weeks. He also stated that worshippers were currently barred from accessing a temple located on the same site. The High Court directed the authorities to submit a status report on the demolition activities.
The proceedings followed a petition filed by Syed Ahmed Saud seeking protection for the mosque and restoration of access for prayers. The petition described the mosque as a notified Waqf property since 1977 and argued that restrictions had prevented worshippers from offering namaz without prior notice or an order.
The petitioner also contended that the mosque was a Grade II protected structure and that any alteration affecting its existence required approval from the relevant heritage authority. He argued that the state could not disregard the building’s historical religious character when taking decisions that might affect its future.
The Centre took over the Jaipur Polo Ground in June and the adjoining Delhi Race Club in August. Authorities had previously said that electricity and water connections to the mosque were disconnected to prevent risks during demolition work elsewhere on the premises.
The High Court’s order does not restore access to the mosque, but the Centre’s assurance temporarily rules out coercive action against the structure while the representation is considered. The matter is scheduled for further hearing on December 16, when the court will continue examining the dispute over access, protection and the ongoing works.
