Pamela: “in the situation room is inviting democratic and republican state party chairs as we come down to the midterms, and right now, we're joined by texas democratic party chair, kendall scudder. hi, kendall, great to have you on. so our new poll is out, we've been talking about it. how are you feeling about your party's chances here?”

Kendall Scudder: “you know, cautiously optimistic. things look like they're going pretty well here, but we're just keeping our heads down, working really hard every day, trying to turn every democrat out to vote that we can. the chips are gonna fall where they fall on election day, and the day after, no matter what happens, i'm gonna be loading signs and t-posts in the back of my pickup truck and recruiting candidates for the next one. democrats didn't lose texas overnight. i don't think we're gonna win it overnight. this is a long-term game that we're playing here, and so we're just really excited to be in this and excited for the opportunity that looks like it's ahead of us on election day next tuesday.”

Pamela: “so how much is support for talarico about his message versus being against ken paxton or president trump, in your view?”

Kendall Scudder: “well, i think the democrats are in the middle of a perfect storm right now. james talarico is a very positive candidate that i think offers a lot for this state. you know, the first bill he wants to file is sweeping anti-corruption reform, which is a big deal to texans who feel like their entire government has just been bought on a giant grift. but comparatively, you also see on the other side particularly bad candidates, not just in ken paxton, but up and down their slate. i mean, greg abbott has been governor for 12 years in this state, yet he says that if you give him another four years, he's gonna make all your dreams come true. the guy's raised our property taxes 85% since he's been in office. you have dan patrick, who's trying to lock people up for 99 years for having thc. and then you have an overt racist that's running on the ticket. i mean, the republicans have nominated some real, real special choices there. and democrats have a fantastic slate of problem solvers, ready to make life better for regular people. i think it's all kind of this perfect storm. i think both of those items can be true.”

Pamela: “so in cnn's poll, talarico has the support of 63% of latino likely voters in the state. now this is a group, as you well know, president trump carried in 2024. how much of this do you think has to do with immigration and tactics used by the trump administration?”

Kendall Scudder: “well, i think certainly is a large player there. i mean, those communities, particularly in south texas, have just been demonized and ripped apart by federal agents who are masked and their citizens have no recourse down there for what's happening in their communities. but i also think that it plays into all of the failed economics of the trump administration. donald trump sold everyone a false bill of goods. he lied to them to become president. he did what billionaires do. he exploited their labor. he preyed on their fears. he used them as a means to an end and then discarded them. he said he was gonna make life more affordable on day one. life's more expensive. he said that he was gonna end the ukraine war on day one. he's gotten us into more international entanglements. he's a liar. and the people in hispanic communities across texas know that. and so certainly the immigration issues are prevalent. but i think the economic issues are very salient here as well.”

Pamela: “so talarico, for his part, committed to spending $25 million on turning out black voters. democratic state rep jones says black voters are not feeling the force of that investment. they're not seeing where it's being spent. and this includes harris county, which, as you know, has a large black population. it's a county where democrats need to over-perform. did talarico actually make this investment for black voters? and if so, where did that money go? why aren't these voters feeling it?”

Kendall Scudder: “well, i'm sorry to hear that rep jones feels that way. i know that she's a fantastic advocate for the houston community, and we're lucky to have her. on questions of direct expenditures from the campaign, you'll have to reach out to the campaign on that. but what i do know is that they've been investing very heavily in turnout in all communities across texas at a 254-county strategy. we've seen record levels of investments that have happened throughout dallas, throughout houston, and i have no doubt that those funds have actually been spent in black communities. the exact dollar amount, i don't know what that is, but here's the thing. i'm hoping that the results of this speaks for itself, that when we get past election day, we'll see that these surges that are happening in communities, including minority communities across texas, are a consequence of the investments that the candidate and that the party have been making for the last year and a half.”

Pamela: “as we wrap up, i just wanna ask this final question. we've been asking all the state chairs, will you commit to accepting the certified results of next tuesday's elections, regardless of the outcome?”

Kendall Scudder: “of course. we get knocked down and we pop right back up. we're used to fighting back, even in really tough territories. sometimes elections don't go your way. i think we have great opportunity ahead of us on tuesday, but regardless, we're gonna be working really hard for the next one because this movement for working class people all across texas to get back control of this government, it's not something that happens overnight. it's something that we're gonna do over extended election cycles. and we'll see what that result is, but we'll certainly accept the result of that. and we'll be very aware of any dirty church republicans may be playing leading up to and beyond election day.”

text:
Crypto and the American Dream. Is it still too soon, or have we been asking the wrong question?

Before the millionaires, the memes, the influencers, and the market crashes, crypto represented something much bigger.

text:
Rebecca Solnit recently returned from Japan, where she felt wonderfully safe. Back in America, she was reminded of the dangers women face by something a stranger was watching on an airplane.

I wish she'd written more about Japan. It's a country with low violent crime, strong cultural traditions, a distinctive sense of public order, and historically restrictive immigration policies. I don't know exactly how much each of those things contributes to public safety, but I'd be curious to hear her thoughts. She'd just spent time somewhere she felt unusually secure. Surely the reasons are worth exploring.

Instead, she noticed a program involving the murder of a young woman and remembered David Lynch's Twin Peaks, which she refused to watch in 1990 because the story revolved around the murder of a teenage girl.

I've loved Twin Peaks for decades. So have countless liberals in Los Angeles, where Lynch's work has been admired, studied, and celebrated. Laura Palmer's murder exposes the corruption, sexual violence, hypocrisy, and cruelty concealed beneath the picture-perfect surface of American life. It's difficult to imagine a more misguided reading of Lynch than treating his depiction of violence as evidence that he was somehow celebrating it.

Now I can picture half of Los Angeles quietly reconsidering its admiration for him. After thirty-six years, Rebecca Solnit has apparently discovered something objectionable about Twin Peaks. The progressive faithful may have to surrender their box sets. Someone should probably notify the Criterion Collection.

There's a certain comedy in condemning a television series you refused to watch and then invoking it decades later to explain the moral condition of America.

Solnit's October 28 essay, Rape Culture on the Ballot, travels from that airplane to Harvey Weinstein, Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, Cornell University, an Ohio campaign advertisement, and eventually the Republican electorate. It's an ambitious itinerary. By the time she's finished, fictional violence, criminal convictions, disputed allegations, and political disagreements have all become illustrations of the same national disease.

I kept wondering why the particulars seemed to interest her so little.

The October 26 congressional report concerning Trump and Epstein is a good example. Democratic staff on the House Judiciary Committee included a new rape allegation from Beatrice Keul about an encounter in 1993. In her earlier public account, Keul described resisting Trump's sexual advances and getting him to stop. Her later account alleges that he raped her.

That's a considerable difference, and the report acknowledges the earlier account in footnote 49. The new details came from interviews with Keul. Photographs and other supporting material establish aspects of the circumstances, including her presence at the pageant, but don't independently establish the alleged rape.

The report appeared eight days before the midterm elections.

I'd have thought that combination would invite some serious questions. Why did the account change? What explains the discrepancy? What independent evidence supports the newer allegation? What did the investigators do to reconcile the two versions?

Solnit seems considerably more interested in what the allegation says about Trump than in examining the evidence behind it. I don't expect her to like the man. I would, however, expect a writer discussing an allegation of rape to read the footnotes and ask the obvious questions.

The report's timing is worth mentioning, too. Releasing a politically explosive accusation eight days before an election doesn't make the accusation false. It does make the circumstances of its release relevant. Congressional investigators and journalists ought to be prepared for scrutiny, particularly when the accusation concerns an event more than thirty years old and the complainant's earlier public account was materially different.

A congressional committee doesn't confer credibility by attaching its letterhead to a claim. The work of establishing what happened still has to be done.

Harvey Weinstein is another subject where the details become considerably more interesting once you move beyond the familiar headlines.

Solnit celebrates Megan Twohey's and Jodi Kantor's investigation and the film She Said. Their reporting was enormously influential. But the subsequent trials produced testimony and evidence that deserve attention, including material that complicated the original public narrative.

In Jessica Mann's case, Weinstein's defense introduced correspondence documenting continued personal and professional contact, meetings, and requests concerning her career. Mann's former roommate, Talita Maia, testified in ways that supported the defense's account of the relationship. Mann disputed that interpretation, maintained that Weinstein raped her, and described the complicated circumstances in which she continued interacting with him.

Weinstein's original New York conviction was overturned in 2024 because the trial had improperly admitted prejudicial testimony concerning allegations outside the charges. Later juries couldn't reach a verdict on Mann's rape allegation, and prosecutors dropped that charge in June 2026 at her request.

Miriam Haley's case produced a conviction in 2025. The defense introduced communications showing continued contact, professional requests, and affectionate language after the alleged assault. Haley gave her account of those interactions, and the jury convicted Weinstein. His separate California conviction also remained in place.

I find the differences among these cases more illuminating than the familiar shorthand about Weinstein. Mann's allegation ended without a surviving conviction. Haley's resulted in one. The defense evidence was part of the proceedings in both cases, and the outcomes weren't the same.

Why should discussing that history be controversial? It happened in court. The witnesses testified. The correspondence was introduced. The juries reached their respective outcomes.

A Pulitzer Prize is a tremendous achievement, but journalism doesn't end when the prizes are handed out. Trials can reveal things that weren't known when the original stories appeared. Surely the public is entitled to hear about those developments without being made to feel that examining the defense is an act of disloyalty to women.

I also remember Ashley Judd's performance at the 2017 Women's March. She delivered Nina Donovan's Nasty Woman, a poem featuring Hitler, gas chambers, menstrual blood, erections, and a sexual reference to Trump and his daughter.

I thought it was grotesque. Not daring, not especially clever, and certainly not profound. Just an escalating collection of outrageous images delivered with the theatrical conviction that political anger automatically transforms vulgarity into art.

The performance was widely celebrated. Apparently the difference between offensive and empowering sometimes depends on whether the audience agrees with the politics.

That episode has stayed with me because it reflects something I find increasingly strange about contemporary feminism. We've spent decades celebrating sexual liberation, personal autonomy, experimentation, and freedom from traditional expectations. Those freedoms are worth defending. But the accompanying conversation about responsibility often seems far less enthusiastic.

Cornell University offers a particularly interesting example.

Cornell has a long history of explicit sexual education and campus programming. There was an Anal Sex 101 presentation in 2007, and its 2014 Sex Week included discussions of pornography and sex toys. Student organizations have explored kink, BDSM, pleasure, and other aspects of sexual experimentation.

I have no objection to adults discussing any of this. What interests me is whether universities that encourage such frank conversations are equally serious about the complicated realities of consent, intoxication, coercion, and sexual encounters that later become disputed.

In her October 3 Guardian essay, Solnit used allegations involving seven Cornell fraternity members to argue that America is a rape-prone society. She drew on anthropologist Peggy Reeves Sanday's research into fraternity culture and male domination.

I understand why that framework appeals to her. It supplies a ready explanation for the entire controversy before anyone has to wrestle with the separate cases.

Cornell's disciplinary outcomes, however, were quite different. Two students were expelled, two received substantial suspensions, a former student was barred from campus, and two others received lesser sanctions.

Those differences caught my attention immediately. Seven accused men, seven sets of circumstances, and several different outcomes. I wanted to know what distinguished them.

What evidence did the university rely upon in each case? How did it assess the disputed communications and chronology? What did the investigation establish about intoxication, alleged drugging, and the complainant's ability to consent? What did each respondent actually do, and how did the evidence support the sanction imposed?

These are the questions that determine whether an investigation has been fair and thorough. An anthropological theory about fraternity culture cannot answer them.

More than two hundred Cornell professors signed a letter criticizing the university's response and campus culture. I wonder how many examined the individual disciplinary findings before signing. I'd be interested in hearing what they thought about the different sanctions, the evidence, and the university's reasoning.

Professors are supposed to be curious about complicated facts. I'd hope that instinct survives even when a case touches a subject about which they feel strongly.

The Duke lacrosse prosecution comes to mind. So does Rolling Stone's retracted University of Virginia fraternity rape story. In both instances, the public was given an account that became a powerful cultural symbol before the underlying allegations had been adequately tested. The Duke players were ultimately declared innocent, and the Rolling Stone story collapsed under scrutiny.

Those failures don't tell us what happened at Cornell. They do explain why I become uneasy when a university controversy is immediately presented as proof of a national social pathology.

Some of the conduct described in the Cornell case sounds reckless, disturbing, and deeply unpleasant. I'd have serious questions about the judgment of people involved in the circumstances described. But those reactions are different from determining whether a particular person committed a particular violation.

And I find the broader question of responsibility impossible to ignore.

For generations, women fought for the freedom to make their own choices, including sexual choices, without being governed by paternalistic expectations. Yet parts of contemporary discourse seem remarkably quick to return to a picture of women as people whose agency becomes secondary whenever the circumstances are emotionally or politically charged.

Adults can make poor decisions. They can behave irresponsibly. They can misread situations. They can also be coerced, assaulted, or rendered incapable of consent. These possibilities have to be distinguished rather than collapsed into a single story about male power and female vulnerability.

Men aren't automatically predators, and women aren't automatically helpless. Neither sex benefits from a culture that treats those assumptions as enlightened thinking.

The Ohio campaign advertisement Solnit discusses is another revealing example of how readily she turns a particular incident into a judgment about an entire political population.

Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign attacked Amy Acton's account of childhood abuse by featuring her estranged mother. It was ugly politics, and Republicans criticized it too. But Solnit uses the episode as part of a much larger argument about misogyny and the Republican Party.

I don't see how the behavior of one campaign establishes the moral character of millions of people who vote Republican. Nor does the existence of sexism in politics explain every disagreement over economic policy, immigration, crime, education, or government.

Solnit also cites Nicole Hemmer's argument that misogyny can help attract male voters across racial groups. I found myself thinking about how casually that interpretation diminishes Black and Latino men who have moved toward the Republican Party.

Perhaps they have opinions about wages, inflation, housing, immigration, public safety, or the Democratic Party's performance. Perhaps they don't appreciate being treated as though their political decisions are primarily expressions of hostility toward women.

It would be interesting to hear them explain their own choices. They are, after all, capable of doing so.

There's something deeply condescending about celebrating the political voice of a demographic group until some of its members begin voting differently. Then, suddenly, commentators discover that their choices require a psychological explanation.

I notice a similar tendency in Solnit's broader writing about feminism and transgender rights. She writes movingly about dignity and inclusion, yet there seems to be little patience for women who support transgender civil rights while raising questions about privacy, safeguarding, competitive sports, or sex-based protections.

These aren't imaginary disagreements. They involve real questions about how different rights and interests should be accommodated. Women can approach them in good faith without being motivated by hatred.

A movement that celebrates diversity ought to be able to tolerate disagreement among the very people it claims to represent.

Jonathan Haidt's work on moral reasoning has helped me understand some of what bothers me about this style of commentary. People often reach their moral conclusions intuitively and then assemble the reasoning afterward. Being intelligent doesn't necessarily prevent it. Sometimes intelligence simply gives people more elaborate ways to defend what they already believe.

Solnit is a gifted writer. She can take a disturbing image, connect it to a historical pattern, introduce a political controversy, and make the whole thing feel like one continuous moral revelation.
It's impressive until you begin looking closely at the individual examples.

The television series she refused to watch becomes evidence of America's fascination with violence against women. The congressional report becomes another chapter in Trump's history. Weinstein's trials are recalled primarily through the original journalistic triumph. The Cornell allegations illustrate an established theory about fraternity culture. An Ohio campaign advertisement helps explain the Republican electorate.

I kept returning to the details she left unexplored. The earlier account in footnote 49. The testimony in Weinstein's trials. The different Cornell sanctions. The Republicans who criticized the Ohio advertisement. The possibility that voters have reasons for their political choices that don't fit the diagnosis being offered.

Those aren't obscure distractions. They're the very things that make these stories worth investigating.

I've spent my life on the Democratic side of American politics. I know the arguments, the assumptions, the language, and the temptation to believe that our political opponents must be morally defective rather than simply wrong about particular issues.

I also know how exhausting it can become when every discussion requires a declaration of loyalty before anyone is permitted to examine the evidence.

I don't want to be told that questioning a congressional report means defending Trump, or that discussing Weinstein's trial evidence means dismissing sexual assault. I don't want seven separate university disciplinary cases treated as interchangeable because they fit a fashionable theory. And I don't want millions of voters, including Black and Latino men, reduced to psychological specimens because they cast ballots that disappoint progressive commentators.

I want to know what happened. I want to understand why people think what they think. And I'd like writers who make sweeping moral claims to show the same curiosity about evidence that challenges their conclusions as they do about evidence that supports them.

That doesn't strike me as an unreasonable expectation.

As for Twin Peaks, I'm keeping my admiration for David Lynch. If Rebecca Solnit ever gets around to watching the series she condemned in 1990, she might discover that it has quite a lot to say about cruelty, hypocrisy, and the ugly secrets hidden beneath respectable appearances.

She might even enjoy it.

Although I imagine that would be terribly inconvenient.

text:
For nearly 600 years the most exclusive honour in Europe has been a golden sheep hung round the necks of emperors, and the animal it celebrates is now worth less in Britain than its own haircut.

The Order of the Golden Fleece was founded in Bruges on 10 January 1430 by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, to mark his wedding to Isabella of Portugal. Bruges had grown rich weaving English wool, and the Burgundian court was the most lavish in Europe on the back of the Flemish cloth trade. The badge Philip chose was a whole sheepskin in gold, hanging by its middle from a collar of flints and fire-steels, head and hooves dangling.

The clergy were uneasy about naming a Christian order after Jason, a pagan who stole his fleece and abandoned his wife, so the order's chancellor found a more respectable sheep in the Bible: Gideon's fleece, which God soaked with dew.

It began with 24 knights and never grew much past 50. It passed by marriage to the Habsburgs and then to the kings of Spain, and the war over the Spanish throne after 1700 split it in two. Both halves still exist. The King of Spain grants one, and the head of the House of Habsburg grants the other.

Getting one has always mattered. The Duke of Wellington became the first Protestant to wear the sheep, in 1812. Louis XVIII sent his back in protest when Napoleon was given one. Franco was offered it in 1972 and turned it down, on the grounds that only a reigning king could give it. In 2015 King Felipe gave it to his nine-year-old daughter Leonor, the heir to the throne.

So the highest honour in the gift of the Spanish crown, the one a dictator thought was above his station, is a gold model of a fleece.

In Britain a fleece now often fetches less than it costs to shear the sheep. Six hundred years ago the richest duke in Europe hung one round his neck. Today the farmer pays to have it taken off.

text:
【Is This Gym Café an Add-On or Its Own Business?】

A family-run gym in a major Irish city has steady footfall but a café that refuses to grow. The gym once reached about 550 members, now sits near 420, and around 100 people still pass through the doors on a typical day.

The café serves healthy meals, shakes and protein snacks, with discounted food for members. The owners are considering a narrower macro-friendly identity, timed shake discounts and workout bundles, while wondering whether flyers delivered to nearby businesses would work better than email offers. They also recently opened a second company, which used some of the gym’s capital and attention.

A commenter said the first question is whether the café is meant to be an add-on for gym customers or an independent business. That choice should shape the pricing and menu. Someone who is not a gym member might even feel awkward eating in a place where everyone else is working out.

If gym members are the target, the commenter suggested testing lunch boxes and grab-and-go options instead of trying to make the whole menu appeal to everyone. The point is not to guess at a new identity before checking what people already want.

The basic analysis is simple: how many gym members actually buy from the café, and how much of the café’s total traffic or volume comes from gym members? That tells you who the current standard customer is and how much value you are really extracting from the existing gym base.

Before cutting the menu or discounting everything, separate the two businesses clearly, measure the overlap, and test a convenient offer for the audience you decide to serve. The 100 daily visitors may be an opportunity, but only if you know who they are and why they are not buying.

The café may not need more ideas yet. It may need a clearer customer, a simpler test, and enough attention from the owners to see whether the gym and café are genuinely supporting each other.

text:
Alabama receiver Noah Rogers’ eye for quarterback talent never looked sharper than in the 2026 season. Long ago, he spotted the talent the rest of the nation now views as the NCAA's leading passer, Oregon State’s Braden Atkinson.

Back in 2022, Rogers entered his senior season at Rolesville High as one of the nation’s top recruits. But quarterback Byrum Brown graduated and was at South Florida (he’s now at Auburn, where he led the Tigers to an upset of then-No. 1-ranked Georgia). Rogers was without an experienced quarterback to get him the ball.

He was asked about Rolesville turning to Atkinson for his first varsity season as a sophomore.

“Don’t worry about Braden,” Rogers said. “He’s going to be good.”

Atkinson is now a sophomore at Oregon State and, through seven games, has thrown for 2,604 yards (372.0 per game) and 24 touchdowns with only two interceptions. He’s completing 69 percent of his passes (189 of 273) and is on a 12-game pace for 4,464 yards. The Rolesville alum leads all NCAA Division I quarterbacks in passing yards and passing touchdowns.

In three varsity seasons at Rolesville (2022-24), Atkinson totaled 9,472 yards, 121 touchdowns and 14 interceptions. As a senior in 2024, he led the Rams to the N.C. High School Athletics Association title game in the large school 4A Division.

So, where did Atkinson rank coming out of Rolesville among the Class of 2024? He was the No. 1,307 player in the nation. He had offers from Boston College and Miami of Ohio, but no other FBS schools, including the Triangle schools with Rolesville in their backyard. The only North Carolina-based college to make a verbal offer was Elon.

HSOT Insiders can read more in this feature on Tom Shanahan, which includes perspective from Atkinson on his quiet in-state recruiting on HighSchoolOT.

🇺🇸🇺🇦🇷🇺 WASHINGTON OFFERS PUTIN ECONOMIC DEALS AS RUSSIA DEMANDS MORE OF UKRAINE

New details have emerged about a proposed US peace framework that would combine territorial arrangements in Ukraine with potentially lucrative economic cooperation between Washington and Moscow.

The American proposal would freeze fighting along parts of the current front line and establish extensive demilitarized zones, including areas near the Kinburn Spit in southern Ukraine and contested territory in Donbas.

These zones could be monitored by international military personnel or private security operators, with a preference for retaining Ukrainian control over the affected territory.

The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, currently under Russian occupation, would be transferred to independent or Ukrainian administration.

But the proposal goes beyond Ukraine's borders.

Washington is offering Moscow the prospect of renewed economic cooperation, including American involvement in oil extraction in Russia's Far East through the Sakhalin-1 project and the possible restoration of Russian oil exports to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline.

Russia's demands, however, remain far more extensive.

Moscow wants full control of Donbas, major reductions in the size of Ukraine's armed forces, permanent exclusion from NATO and no postwar security guarantees from NATO member states.

That last demand is particularly consequential. Russia is seeking restrictions not only on Ukraine's military capabilities but also on the international security arrangements intended to deter another invasion.

The emerging framework exposes a fundamental disagreement over what ending the war should mean.

Washington is exploring territorial compromises and economic incentives to secure an agreement. Moscow continues to demand concessions that would substantially limit Ukraine's sovereignty and future defense capabilities.

The proposals remain under discussion, with no final agreement announced.

For Kyiv, the stakes extend well beyond where the front line is drawn. Any settlement would determine whether Ukraine emerges with the military strength and security arrangements needed to prevent another Russian attack.

text:
🚨MELANIA’S UKRAINE TRUCE HOLDS AS HUMANITARIAN MISSION PREPARES TO MOVE

Diplomacy deserves credit when it creates a real opening to help people trapped by war.

The Associated Press reported Thursday that the localized ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky had entered its third day, with military units clearing mines and humanitarian supplies poised to enter. Both sides thanked First Lady Melania Trump for her involvement in securing the pause. Aid preparations are progress, but completed deliveries and safe evacuations remain the essential tests.

This is a meaningful development for the Trump administration’s diplomatic efforts. Getting enemies to cooperate on a specific humanitarian mission deserves recognition—even while their broader disagreements remain unresolved.

The limits are equally clear. Reuters reported that a drone strike killed 13 people at a railway station in Dnipro, according to local officials. That city is outside the ceasefire area. The wider war continues.

My view: Washington should build on this opening while keeping its demands practical and measurable.

Can relief workers reach civilians safely? Can residents who want to leave do so voluntarily? Can the parties maintain the pause long enough to complete the mission?

Those questions matter more than competing declarations of diplomatic victory.

For Americans, the value of this approach is straightforward. Negotiating specific protections can help save lives and test whether commitments will be honored before Washington considers broader obligations. Any larger agreement should clearly explain America’s responsibilities, costs and limits.

Melania deserves credit for pursuing a concrete humanitarian objective. The administration should now press both sides to turn that opening into verified results.

A successful mission would offer a reason to pursue further agreements. It would also establish a standard that future negotiations should meet: promises followed by action.

text:
She stepped to the mic like the room was her stage,
Smiling as if virtue had granted her wage.
A campus applause for the cleverest line—
Celebrating a bullet, then calling it fine.

She framed murder as verse, anniversary cheer,
A neck-shot remembered as something to hear.
No pause for the man, or the wife, or the child—
Just glee in the cadence, self-righteous and wild.

Entitled enough to demand that we nod,
To treat death as content, and silence as fraud.
She warned of the neck left uncovered and bare,
Then basked in the spotlight for daring to care—

About nothing but her own glittering spite,
A poem of blood for a late-evening light.
Houston-raised, campus-trained, fluent in sneer,
She offered the crowd what it wanted to hear:

That some lives are punchlines, some deaths are the point,
And arrogance dressed as the voice of the joint.
The verse was the tell, not the venue or name—
The pleasure she took in the killing’s acclaim.

No sorrow, no weight, just the performance of hate,
Recited with pride on the Kirkiversary date.

text:
Why is October-November considered one of the most dangerous periods for cyclones in India?

Cyclone Arnab has once again brought attention to the Bay of Bengal and India’s vulnerability to tropical cyclones.

But why does the Bay of Bengal witness more cyclonic activity than the Arabian Sea?

1. Warm Ocean Waters: High sea-surface temperatures provide the energy required for cyclone formation and intensification.
2. High Moisture Availability: Moisture-rich air supports the development of powerful thunderstorms and cyclonic systems.
3. Post-Monsoon Conditions: October-November offers favourable atmospheric conditions for cyclone development as the southwest monsoon withdraws.
4. Geographical Features: The funnel-shaped northern Bay of Bengal can amplify storm surges, increasing the risk of coastal flooding.
5. Coastal Vulnerability: The densely populated coastal regions of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal face significant risks from cyclonic winds, heavy rainfall and storm surges.

Important distinction: The frequency of cyclones and their intensity are two different concepts. While the Bay of Bengal has historically experienced more cyclones, the Arabian Sea has also witnessed intense cyclonic storms in recent years.

text:
164 years ago today, in a Missouri cornfield, Black soldiers went into combat for the first time in the Civil War, months before the Emancipation Proclamation officially authorized them to fight, and they won. It is a milestone that deserves to be far better known.

Long before the famous charge of the 54th Massachusetts at Fort Wagner, before the War Department had even formally agreed to accept Black men as soldiers, a regiment was raised on the Kansas frontier called the 1st Kansas Colored Volunteers. Many of its men were formerly enslaved people who had escaped bondage, now carrying rifles. In the autumn of 1862 their very existence was legally ahead of its time, so much so that they had not yet been officially mustered into the United States Army, because the government was not ready to accept Black troops. They were, in effect, soldiers before the nation was willing to call them soldiers.

In late October 1862, this regiment moved into Bates County, Missouri, to deal with Confederate guerrillas, the bushwhackers who terrorized the border. They built a rough camp they nicknamed Fort Africa and went looking for the enemy. On October 29, near a place called Island Mound, several hundred of these Black soldiers clashed with a larger force of Confederate guerrillas.

The fight was sharp and, for a time, desperate, with the outnumbered Kansans facing mounted guerrillas in the open fields. But the Black troops fought with discipline and courage, holding their ground and then driving the guerrillas off. They had passed the test of combat, and they had won.

The significance was immediate and national. Island Mound was the first time an organized unit of Black soldiers engaged in combat in the Civil War, and Northern newspapers took notice. At a moment when much of white America, North and South, openly doubted whether Black men would or could fight, these soldiers on a Missouri farm provided an early, concrete answer. They fought, and they prevailed.

It was a small skirmish by the numbers, but it was a crack in a wall. The 1st Kansas Colored would be formally mustered into United States service a few months later, after the Emancipation Proclamation opened the door, and would go on to fight hard at battles like Honey Springs. And the proof they offered at Island Mound, that Black men would stand and fight for their own freedom, would be written far larger, in blood and valor, at Fort Wagner, New Market Heights, and on a hundred other fields before the war was done. It began here, on this day, on the Missouri border.

text:
I see all the examples you say wow you've done lots of research haven't you?
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

text:
CHRISTINE LAGARDE: WHEN THE ECB BECOMES THE ANTECCHAMBER TO THE ÉLYSÉE
By @BPartisans 

It really seems that in “Macronia,” even retirements look like political rescue operations. Christine Lagarde will leave the ECB in February 2027, nine months before the end of her term. Officially, it’s to regain her freedom of speech. What a touching calling! After leading the IMF and then the European Central Bank, our high priestess of financial orthodoxy is suddenly seized by an irrepressible desire to participate in democratic debate.

Chance, that eternal Macronist activist, certainly works things out well.

For this departure comes just a few weeks before a presidential election in which Emmanuel Macron’s heirs are struggling to convince the French that they still deserve the keys to the shop. Attal dreams of a European empire, Philippe cultivates his image as a fallback option, and Macronism is desperately seeking a future without Macron. A succession that resembles a judicial liquidation more than a transfer of power.

And here comes Christine Lagarde, descending from her monetary Olympus.

A candidate? She insists she isn’t. But why burden oneself with an election campaign when one can try to influence the outcome? Votes are fickle, voters ungrateful, and debates exhausting. Might as well let the contenders get their hands dirty while the guardians of the temple hand out certificates of European respectability.

Above all, the timeline offers a delightful advantage: it allows Macron to influence the succession at the ECB before the French permanently strip him of the keys to the Élysée. One last chance to have a say in the distribution of seats in Brussels and Frankfurt. The independence of institutions, of course. That marvelous invention that consists of proclaiming their neutrality while carefully negotiating the identity of those who lead them.

Mind you, there is no evidence of a coordinated operation. But one would have to be remarkably naive not to see the political convenience of this timing.

As for Lagarde, she could become the economic guarantor of a Macronist candidate in dire straits. The banking guarantee for an electoral product that the French are no longer necessarily eager to renew their subscription to.

One can already imagine the sermons on stability, the markets, the euro, and the dangers of populism—the usual arsenal of those who confuse democracy with a credit rating agency: citizens vote, but the markets are supposedly tasked with explaining to them whether they voted correctly.

The most amusing part is this sudden passion for freedom of expression. After years spent at the helm of institutions shielded from electoral shifts, Christine Lagarde seems to be discovering the virtues of politics precisely when her former camp risks losing power.

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence. Perhaps Macronism, unable to convince voters, still hopes to impress them with the accolades of its former dignitaries.

When a regime no longer has a credible successor, it ends up recycling its vault guardians into guardians of democracy.

text:
Consoling Jesus’ Sorrowful Heart
“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how many times I yearned to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, but you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be abandoned. But I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Luke 13:34–35
In today’s Gospel, Jesus laments Jerusalem’s tragic history of persecuting the prophets sent by God to call His people back to fidelity. The deaths of Zechariah and Isaiah stand out, but the broader implication is that Jerusalem—the city of the Temple and the seat of divine worship—had often become the very place where divine truth was violently rejected. In lamenting this, Jesus reveals His deep love for His people and foreshadows His own death at their hands, which would also take place in Jerusalem.
Of note, Jesus’ words drip with holy sorrow and compassion, but also resolute clarity. Though He offers a condemnation in the form of a prophetic warning—that the Temple would ultimately be destroyed and the city overtaken by the Romans in AD 70—His tone is one of loving lament, not vengeful retribution.
In many ways, Jesus’ lament is that of a loving father mourning a wayward son: “How many times I yearned to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings.” Understanding this compassion in His Sacred Heart is especially helpful to us as we examine our own struggles with sin. Though God is perfectly just, His judgments are issued with a broken heart, not a violent one.
When you consider your sins, examine them through this lens. See Jesus’ Sacred Heart pierced with a sword of profound sorrow. When we turn back to Him, we console Him and relieve Him of that sorrow. Though we can add nothing to God’s greatness and glory on our own, we do have the capacity to fill Him with joy when we repent and diligently strive to overcome sin in our lives.
Recognizing this spiritual reality is the highest form of the spiritual Gift of Fear of the Lord. This gift of the Holy Spirit manifests itself in two ways. First, Fear of the Lord begins with what we traditionally call servile fear—that is, fear of punishment. Consider again a son who obeys his father because he fears being punished. This is a good beginning, but it is not the ideal.

John the Baptist Prepares the Way

3 In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, 2 and saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand!” 3 For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah, saying:

“The voice of one crying in the wilderness:
‘Prepare the way of the Lord;
Make His paths straight.’ ”

4 Now John himself was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist; and his food was locusts and wild honey. 5 Then Jerusalem, all Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him 6 and were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

7 But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? 8 Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance, 9 and do not think to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I say to you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones. 10 And even now the ax is laid to the root of the trees. Therefore every tree which does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. 11 I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance, but He who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. 12 His winnowing fan is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clean out His threshing floor, and gather His wheat into the barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

(The early church was called Followers of The Way)

Malachi 3
The Coming Messenger

3 “Behold, I send My messenger,
And he will prepare the way before Me.
And the Lord, whom you seek,
Will suddenly come to His temple,
Even the Messenger of the covenant,
In whom you delight.
Behold, He is coming,”
Says the Lord of hosts.

2 “But who can endure the day of His coming?
And who can stand when He appears?
For He is like a refiner’s fire
And like launderers’ soap.
3 He will sit as a refiner and a purifier of silver;
He will purify the sons of Levi,
And purge them as gold and silver,
That they may offer to the Lord
An offering in righteousness.

1 Peter 2:4
The Chosen Stone and His Chosen People

4 Coming to Him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and precious, 5 you also, as living stones, are being built up a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. 6 Therefore it is also contained in the Scripture,

“Behold, I lay in Zion
A chief cornerstone, elect, precious,
And he who believes on Him will by no means be put to shame.”

text:
Lamentations was written in the aftermath of Jerusalem's destruction, when the consequences of Judah's rebellion against God could no longer be ignored. The city lay in ruins, the temple had been destroyed, and many of its people had been carried into captivity. Yet amid this devastation, the author expressed a profound truth about God's character:

“For the Lord will not cast off for ever: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men” (Lamentations 3:31–33).

The Lord does not delight in our suffering. The Hebrew expression translated “willingly” can be understood as “from his heart,” suggesting that affliction is not His fundamental desire for His children. God’s underlying disposition is toward love. He may correct us or allow us to experience the consequences of our choices, but His purpose is our redemption, and His compassion outlasts our afflictions.

Sometimes suffering follows directly from our sins. We may damage relationships through selfishness or experience the consequences of turning away from God. Repentance does not always remove those consequences immediately; we may need to repair what we have broken and acknowledge the harm we have caused. Yet repentance turns us toward the Savior, whose Atonement makes forgiveness and spiritual renewal possible.

The writer of Hebrews compares the Lord's correction to the discipline of a loving father: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth” (Hebrews 12:6). Although chastening is painful in the moment, it can yield “the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby” (verse 11). We should not, however, assume that illness, tragedy, or loss is punishment for sin. Some trials arise from other people's choices or the conditions of mortality, and we may not know why a particular hardship has come.

Isaiah gives us the clearest reason to trust God's love. Prophesying of the Savior, he wrote: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3).

Christ did not stand at a distance from human suffering. He entered into it. Isaiah continues, “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows” (verse 4). He then explains the purpose of the Savior's suffering: “He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (verse 5).

The Atonement reveals both the seriousness of sin and the depth of God's love for sinners. We cannot redeem ourselves from sin and death, so Heavenly Father sent His Son to do what we could never do alone. Jesus Christ willingly bore our sins and sorrows, opening the way for forgiveness, healing, resurrection, and eternal life. His suffering was the means by which God offers us redemption.

We will not understand every trial, and not every wound will heal according to our preferred timetable. The gospel does not require us to invent explanations God has not given us. Instead, it invites us to turn to Jesus Christ. When we need to repent, He offers forgiveness and strength to change. When we face trials we cannot explain, we can seek His sustaining grace and trust in the hope of resurrection.

Lamentations assures us that our present circumstances do not define the limits of God's mercy: “Yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies” (Lamentations 3:32). Even what seems irreparably broken can be redeemed through Jesus Christ.

When correction is painful, we can seek what the Lord would have us learn. When we face the consequences of our choices, we can trust that repentance remains possible. And when we cannot discern the reason for our trials, we can remember that our circumstances alone do not determine how God feels about us.

The Lord does not afflict us willingly. He seeks our redemption, not our misery. We may not understand every sorrow in this life, but we can look to Jesus Christ, who bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and trust in the love of the Father who sent Him.

text:
A conditional loan commitment is not a megawatt.

The Department of Energy has offered Constellation up to $5 billion for uprates at eight nuclear plants in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania. Nearly 1.1 GW, per POWER Magazine. The easy read: more supply, softer capacity prices down the road.

Maybe. But a capacity charge is a price times your tag. New supply can move the price. Only your load during the system peak hours moves the tag.

Two plants, same product, same rate class. The one that curtailed at the right hours pays less. The headline never mentions that.

Do you know which hours set your tag?

To Brazil’s Victor Goes Political Revenge
Lula’s government targets losing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.
The Editorial BoardByOct. 28, 2026
Political victors are supposed to be gracious to the vanquished, but in Brazil they prosecute the losers. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva won re-election on Sunday, and within minutes his government ordered opposition leader Flávio Bolsonaro to give up his passport.

Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, a Lula ally, signed off on a federal police request to seize Mr. Bolsonaro’s travel documents. On Tuesday Mr. Bolsonaro secretly fled Brazil with his wife and daughters across the Argentine border. On Wednesday they arrived in Miami. The U.S. said it issued visas for the family, a justifiable offer of political protection.

text:
Let me analyze this for everyone ✅🔥

🏒 1. Andrei Svechnikov — 1+ Point
Confidence: 7/10 🟢

• Needs one goal or assist.
• Has scoring and playmaking upside in Carolina’s offense.
• Risk: Even an active offensive game can end without a point.

🎯 Verdict: Reasonable leg, but still dependent on direct scoring involvement.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 2. Jake Guentzel — 1+ Point
Confidence: 7.5/10 🟢

• A productive offensive forward with the ability to score or assist.
• Tampa Bay’s offensive opportunities can help create point chances.
• Risk: A quiet night from his line could leave him without a point.

🎯 Verdict: One of the more appealing point props on the slip.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 3. Erik Karlsson — 1+ Point
Confidence: 6.5/10 🟡

• His offensive contributions and power-play involvement offer a path to a point.
• Assists can cash this leg without needing a goal.
• Risk: His production depends on Pittsburgh generating quality chances and converting them.

🎯 Verdict: Playable, but not a guaranteed point.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 4. Connor Bedard — 1+ Point
Confidence: 7/10 🟢

• Bedard has the offensive skill to create scoring opportunities.
• One goal or assist is enough to cash.
• Risk: Chicago’s overall scoring output can limit his opportunities.

🎯 Verdict: Solid upside for a one-point requirement.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 5. Kirill Kaprizov — 3+ Shots on Goal
Confidence: 7.5/10 🟢

• Needs at least three shots on target.
• His offensive role gives him opportunities to shoot regularly.
• Risk: Missed attempts, blocked shots, or limited offensive-zone time can prevent the over from hitting.

🎯 Verdict: One of my favorite legs on the card, provided his usual shooting role is intact.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 6. Elias Lindholm — 1+ Point
Confidence: 6/10 🟡

• Can cash through either a goal or an assist.
• Boston’s offensive production and line deployment will be important.
• Risk: His point production can fluctuate, especially if his line struggles to generate chances.

🎯 Verdict: Moderate confidence. Not a leg I’d treat as a lock.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 7. Roope Hintz — 1+ Point
Confidence: 7/10 🟢

• Has the offensive ability to contribute a goal or assist.
• Dallas can provide scoring opportunities when its attack is clicking.
• Risk: A low-event game or limited production from his line could hurt this leg.

🎯 Verdict: A reasonable selection at 1+ point.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 8. Dylan Strome — 1+ Point
Confidence: 6.5/10 🟡

• Can cash through a goal or assist.
• His playmaking gives him another route to the target.
• Risk: Washington’s scoring opportunities and his involvement in them are key variables.

🎯 Verdict: Decent upside, but there is meaningful scoring variance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏒 9. Ivar Stenberg — 1+ Point
Confidence: 5/10 🟡

• Needs only one point, which is attractive in isolation.
• The key question is his role, expected ice time, and involvement in Vancouver’s scoring.
• Risk: If his minutes or power-play opportunities are limited, his path to a point becomes much harder.

🎯 Verdict: My biggest concern on this slip until his role and lineup status are confirmed.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 FINAL RISK CHECK

🔥 Strongest legs by initial assessment

* Jake Guentzel 1+ point
* Kirill Kaprizov 3+ shots on goal
* Andrei Svechnikov 1+ point
* Connor Bedard 1+ point

⚠️ Biggest concerns

* Ivar Stenberg 1+ point
* Elias Lindholm 1+ point
* Erik Karlsson 1+ point

text:
Brazil’s election delivered a surprise to investors. After Flávio Bolsonaro’s strong first-round showing, prediction markets favored him in the runoff, and Brazilian assets rallied on expectations of his victory. Luiz Lula da Silva won instead, with 51 percent of the vote. Israel’s election has produced a different kind of uncertainty: neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition appears to have enough seats to form a government, leaving coalition negotiations ahead.

These elections do not predict what will happen in the United States. They do offer a reason to keep an open mind. Political expectations can shift quickly, and the result that matters most to markets is often the one that differs from what investors already expect.

Heading into next week’s midterms, Democrats are favored to win the House and have the edge in the Senate. Prediction markets put their chance of taking the Senate around 64–68 percent, up more than 20 percentage points since July. Polls also show a Democratic advantage, though its size varies. Rasmussen’s latest generic-ballot poll has Democrats ahead by five points, compared with roughly eight points in broader averages.

The Senate remains close enough for a different result. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and the path runs through a handful of competitive races. Texas is one to watch. Rasmussen has Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico tied, while other polls and prediction markets give Talarico a narrow lead. A Talarico win would be a striking result in a state that has long voted Republican in Senate races; a Paxton win would strengthen the GOP’s chances of holding the chamber.

The possibility of a Democratic sweep is already on investors’ minds. Barron’s latest magazine cover asks what a “blue wave” would mean for Wall Street, with its cover story looking at the effects on AI, healthcare and other industries. That shows how firmly the scenario has entered the investment conversation.

For the AI trade, the concern is that Democratic control could bring more scrutiny of technology companies and data centers. Investors could worry about hearings, new rules or pressure on data centers to address their electricity use. Those concerns matter because the market’s expectations for AI depend in part on companies continuing to spend heavily on computing capacity and the infrastructure needed to support it.

But a Democratic win would arrive after months of discussion about these risks. A Republican president would also limit what a Democratic Congress could accomplish through legislation. Hearings and critical headlines could still weigh on stocks, especially in the short term, but the election result alone would not tell us whether the AI buildout will continue. Those fundamentals would continue to matter more to the long-term outlook.

This creates an asymmetry for markets. Democrats are favored to win the Senate, so a Democratic victory would largely confirm the expected outcome. It could still cause volatility, but investors have had months to consider the policy risks, and a Republican president would constrain major legislative changes. The result may be less damaging than feared.

A Republican Senate hold would be less expected and could bring a more positive market reaction. Democrats may still win the House, leaving Congress divided. That would make new federal restrictions on AI and data-center investment harder to enact, easing one concern around the buildout. The benefit could extend beyond technology stocks to the companies supplying data centers with power, equipment and infrastructure.

The point is to stay open to both outcomes: a Democratic win may be less disruptive than feared, while a Republican hold could be better than expected.
