text:
Twenty-Second Sunday After Pentecost: The Legality of the Tribute to Caesar by Rev. Raphael Frassinetti, 1900
.
Gospel. Matt. xxii. 15-21. At that time the Pharisees going, consulted among themselves how to ensnare Jesus in his speech. And they sent to him their disciples with the Herodians, saying: Master, we know that thou art a true speaker, and teachest the way of God in truth, neither carest thou for any man: for thou dost not regard the person of men: tell us therefore what dost thou think. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: Why do you tempt me, ye hypocrites? Show me the coin of the tribute. And they offered Him a penny. And Jesus saith to them: Whose image and inscription is this? They say to him: Caesar's. Then he saith to them: Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.
.
Though the Pharisees often heard the instructions of Our Lord, they never drew any benefit from them. On this day they came to Our Lord, and proposed this question to Him, "Tell us, what dost Thou think. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?" In this way, instead of trying to learn something of benefit to their souls, they became more blind. They were full of hatred of Our Lord, and full of jealousy because the people considered Him a prophet, and their intention was to destroy the respect which the multitude had for Him. Here was a question which they thought would certainly lead Our Lord into their meshes. "Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar?" The Jews hated the Roman dominion over them; they were a downtrodden race, and were obliged to furnish a throne and money for the Roman governor, while their religion was in confusion; and sometimes two highpriests were contending for the chief office. So the Pharisees said to themselves, "If this man consents to pay tribute to Caesar he will be hated by the people; and if on the contrary he disapproves of it, the government will have a case against him for inciting the people to resist lawful authority." Jesus confounded the Pharisees by His divine wisdom. "Why do you tempt Me, ye hypocrites?" He asked. You have a very bad reason for this question--you are not honest. Our Lord was affable and kind to the greatest sinners who came to Him in the sincerity of their hearts; but with these double-faced Pharisees He had no patience. He called them vipers, impostors, whitened sepulchres, fair without, but most loathsome within. Does not Our Lord teach us here the hatefulness of the vice of hypocrisy, and how He detested it?
.
My dear young friends, there are hypocrites among Christians, among our youth. Many young people wish to appear like angels in the eyes of their superiors; before their parents they are careful not to say a bad word, while with their companions they do and say most scandalous things. They hide their sins so carefully that no one suspects them of any wickedness: even in the confessional they do not make known their great sins, and deceive the priest, the minister of God. There are hypocrites everywhere; in the sanctuary, in the choir, in sodalities, in the church, and at the sacraments. Never pretend to a devotion that you have not--it is disgusting. Be not servers of the eye of man, but serve God in all sincerity. Men may praise you for your piety, honesty, and truthfulness, but God sees deep into the heart; you do not deceive God. You may gain some temporal advantages by deceiving men, but God's time for punishment will come, and then to your shame, your hypocrisy will be made manifest to the world. We read in Job that, "dissemblers and crafty men provoke the wrath of God."
.
"Show me the coin of the tribute," said Our Lord. "Whose image and inscription is this?" He asked. They answered, "Caesar's." Then He said, " Render, therefore, to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." The Pharisees were struck with the wisdom of the reply, and must have been covered with shame before the assembled multitude. St. Bonaventure asserts that this coin represents the soul of man, impressed with the image of God. A precious thing, of great value, is the soul in the eyes of God, and it derives its value from the blood of Christ. Our soul, my dear young friends, when gifted with the grace of the Redeemer is a most beautiful object; it is an angel hidden in a body of flesh, a beautiful spirit, radiant with thought and understanding. A soul in mortal sin has impressed on it the image of the devil. "What has become of me?" St. Augustine asks. "My soul, whither have your sins led you?" That bright image of God which was on you is there no longer; all is changed. "How has the gold changed its color!" Bewail your condition, my dear young people, if you should find yourselves in a state of sin. St. Jerome says, most lamentingly, "This I bewail, that you do not feel that you are dead; this I bewail, that you do not sorrow for yourselves."
.
Yes, young people who are in sin ought to weep continually; at night instead of closing their eyes in sleep, they ought to keep them open to shed tears; they ought not be able to eat, play or study,--so great should be their concern. But do they weep? Oh no! these miserable blind beings enjoy themselves, and never stop to think that God hates them. Oh, raise your eyes to the crucified Saviour, see His thorn-crowned head--has He not sacrificed it for your soul? Those bloodstained eyes, those colorless lips, those hands pierced with nails, those feet cruelly wounded and that side opened by a lance--did He not sacrifice all for our salvation? Are you going to allow His sacred Passion to be wasted so far as you are concerned? Jesus has purchased you with His blood, and you are His if you remain faithful to Him. "Take great care of your souls," and Jesus will be satisfied with His purchase and will not consider His Passion too great a price for your soul.
.
"Give to God the things that are God's." Let us, for a moment, think of this. What do we owe God, that we must give Him? To God we owe honor and glory. Do we give this glory to God? Do we not give honor rather to men, to those especially who hold positions of dignity. When you enter the magnificent palace of the millionaire, how well-dressed you are, what politeness you assume, so that people may consider you well-bred; you tiptoe up the hall and in a humble whisper ask the servant to take in your card, to see whether you may be admitted; should you have the happiness of an audience, you hardly speak aloud and you put your demands in the most honeyed words. If such is our respect for men, what is not due to almighty God from a human being? Give to God, therefore, a little of the respect which you show to creatures.
.
God does not wish for a false respect. He wishes you to be free, gracious, and spontaneous in your worship of Him; to assume a pious attitude in church because you are watched is not a worship of God; to say your prayers night and morning for form's sake, or because your parents insist on it, is hardly to be considered meritorious; for it is an unwilling prayer. Does God consider these acts worthy of Him when they are forced from you? He will not look at them with pleasure. He will say to you as He said to the Jews of old, "You celebrate great feasts, and hold certain days solemn, but they are not My feasts, they are yours, because you want them for your own purposes and not for My glory; they excite My indignation but not My mercy toward you."
.
This forced devotion is similar to the mock adoration which the Jews and soldiers offered Our Lord in the hall of Pilate's palace, when they said, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and made genuflections before Him; and at the cross, when the Jews cried out: "Let Him now come down from the cross and we will believe Him." God looks at the heart. He pays little attention to our exterior actions; a good, strong, fervent, cordial intention is as good in the eye of God as is the execution of the noblest human action. Give then to God the honor and glory that are due to Him; there is no need to force the youth who is in earnest to honor God in church, or when he hears Mass or goes to the sacraments; he does it of his own free will and with the greatest devotion. Yes, my dear young people, give to God that honor, freely, not through routine or custom. With a great heart, give glory to God. Serve Him with a great heart, joyfully and with alacrity, and then you can say with truth that you have given to God the things that are God's.

text:
AIR SPACE INTELLIGENCE (ASI)
Prices, business strategy, investment access and risks
Independent research | October 29, 2026 | Version 1
Research freeze: 10:51:01 AM PDT / 1:51:01 PM EDT / 17:51:01 UTC.
Subject: the company at https://t.co/Nz44mZ6WCK supplied by the user.
All dollar amounts are USD. No purchase, investment subscription or outreach was made.

MY ASSESSMENT

ASI has a compelling business proposition: help operators predict constraints and compare actions before disruption spreads through a physical network. Its strongest public evidence combines an independently confirmed FAA award, a customer-reported airline use case and a substantial recently announced financing. The investment case remains harder to underwrite because public financial disclosures and an executable share price are missing.

My stance: positive on researching the operating business; cautious on a private investment until the actual security, valuation, financials and transfer terms are verified. A $3 billion financing headline is not sufficient reason to buy common shares at an arbitrary price. For an enterprise buyer, a measured pilot with explicit economic and operational acceptance criteria is the practical next step.

Here ASI is the company brand. The report does not treat the name as proof of artificial superintelligence, and it does not analyze the ASI/FET cryptocurrency or ASI Industries stock.

1. WHAT THE COMPANY ACTUALLY DOES

ASI describes its products as operational AI for aviation, defense and energy. Its current company page identifies Phillip Buckendorf as CEO and co-founder and Boston as headquarters. It describes combining imperfect operational signals into a model of current conditions and possible future outcomes. These descriptions are company representations, not independent certification of all performance claims. [1]

The useful workflow is: collect relevant data, represent current constraints, simulate future states, compare alternatives, give an operator recommendations, then update as conditions change. That is my simplified interpretation of the product descriptions. The economic value depends on recommendations that can be implemented, not simply on how many scenarios a system can generate.

Aviation: Flyways is the established airline-facing platform name. ASI's current aviation offering emphasizes prediction, flight following and trajectory optimization around traffic, weather and capacity. The FAA programs are Flow Management Data and Services (FMDS) and Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART). The FAA independently confirms the award and describes FMDS as the data/management backbone with SMART adding planning capabilities. [2,3]

The distinction matters: the FAA's own fact sheet describes SMART as a planning layer alongside existing systems. It says air traffic controllers remain responsible for safe aircraft separation. Its stated initial-operations timing is fall 2026; the fact sheet is not proof that every milestone has already been accepted or deployed nationwide. [4]

Energy: ASI's May 6 announcement describes a National Grid collaboration initially focused on distributed-energy siting/interconnection, resilience planning and outage mapping, supported by a Massachusetts Clean Energy Center demonstration grant. The announcement does not disclose a commercial subscription price or establish a large recurring-revenue stream from that partnership. [5]

Defense: the company describes predictive decision support across complex operational environments. The investment relevance is the ability to reuse software and deployment expertise across customers, while recognizing that each contract can carry different integration, security and delivery requirements. This report evaluates business economics rather than military operational tactics.

2. PRICE AND VALUE DASHBOARD

Item                              Publicly observed amount / status
October 20 Series C financing     $325 million raised, company announcement
Reported company valuation        $3 billion, company announcement
FAA award                         $875 million across 12 years, as announced
Army enterprise IDIQ              Up to $99 million across five years
Official software list price      Not found on reviewed public product pages
Executable private-share quote    Not verified
Public exchange ticker / IPO      No public listing or IPO price verified

The October 20 financing release says Spark Capital led the round, with participation from affiliates of Citadel Securities, Meritech Capital, Craft Ventures, Energy Impact Partners and Andreessen Horowitz. It does not supply a per-share subscription price, fully diluted share count or preference waterfall. The reviewed wording does not explicitly settle whether the headline valuation is pre-money or post-money. [6]

The FAA dollar amount and duration come from ASI's June 22 release and are corroborated in independent reporting; the FAA announcement confirms the award and program scope. The Army release describes a five-year $99 million indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract and an initial task order, without disclosing that order's dollar amount in the reviewed release. [3,7,8,9]

These amounts measure different things. A financing valuation is not revenue. Contract maximums or multi-year announced values are not automatically funded orders, cash receipts, annual recurring revenue or recognized revenue. Audited revenue, gross margin, retention, cash burn, remaining obligations and the complete funded-order schedule were not available in the sources reviewed.

For scale only, $875 million divided by 12 is approximately $72.92 million per year. $99 million divided by five is $19.8 million per year. Those are arithmetic averages of headline values, not forecasts, delivery schedules, guaranteed minimums or ARR. Do not sum them and label the result current revenue.

3. PRIVATE-SHARE PRICES: WHAT IS AND IS NOT VERIFIED

Nasdaq Private Market identifies Air Space Intelligence as privately held, says it does not trade on public exchanges and has no public ticker or IPO price, and describes restricted private-market access and company approval for transfers. A company-profile page does not prove that a seller or allocation is currently available to you. Its older headquarters metadata differs from ASI's current Boston disclosure, so I use the company's own page for current headquarters. [10]

Two provider pages illustrate why a private “stock price” needs scrutiny. The directly saved Clarity page displayed a $5.00 Clarity Price while hiding the last match, bid, ask and volume. The directly saved Notice page displayed 94.62 in its body, while its HTML title said $95.06; its page date was October 29. Notice describes its price as algorithmic, using secondary-market and reference data. Exact quote times and executable quantities were not available. [11,12]

These indications are not comparable verified offers. I could not reconcile share class, capitalization basis, split history, transaction dates, calculation methods or settlement eligibility between them. Cached web reads also differed from the direct page snapshot. Neither $5.00 nor $94.62 is presented as the price at which you can buy ASI, and their discrepancy does not establish an arbitrage or a bargain.

A useful private quote must identify the legal issuer, security class, price, quantity, date, seller, settlement path and all-in costs. Then translate the per-share price into an implied fully diluted valuation using the correct share count. The Series C preferred security can have rights that employee common stock or an SPV interest lacks.

No official annual Flyways subscription tariff, per-aircraft price, pilot fee or standard implementation fee was verified. The large government contracts are not a retail software price card. Request an itemized proposal for the exact deployment before building a purchasing decision around a number.

4. HOW STRONG IS THE CUSTOMER EVIDENCE?

Alaska Air Group's 2024 Corporate Impact Report, page 19, states that Alaska and Horizon have used Flyways since 2021, renewed the partnership in 2024 and saved over 900,000 gallons of fuel with Flyways in 2024. This is customer-reported historical evidence, not a 2026 run rate or an independently randomized trial. [13]

It supports the view that the software has operational use beyond a demonstration. It does not reveal the contract fee, implementation cost, net profit to ASI, savings attribution method or likely savings for another fleet. The report separately discusses other efficiency initiatives; their savings should not be attributed to Flyways.

My interpretation: the most investable signal is repeat paid use with measured customer outcomes. For diligence, request cohort retention, renewal pricing, usage by dispatcher or operating unit, recommendation adoption, realized savings after constraints and support burden per deployment. A logo on a homepage is weaker evidence than a paid renewal, accepted delivery and collected cash.

5. BUSINESS STRATEGY: WHERE ASI COULD WIN

Land in a difficult operational workflow, demonstrate value, then expand within the account. A successful airline deployment can create data integrations, trained users and workflow trust. Those can support renewals and adjacent products. They are potential sources of switching cost, not proof that a customer cannot leave.

Reuse the underlying platform across domains while keeping domain-specific validation. Aviation, energy and government buyers all reason about constraints across time and space, but their data, decision rights, risk tolerances and procurement cycles differ. Reusable software can improve margins; repeated custom engineering can turn apparent software growth into a services-heavy business. The financial disclosures needed to distinguish those paths were not available.

Turn major government awards into accepted, funded deployments. A large contract can establish credibility and a long expansion runway. It can also concentrate execution and cash-collection risk. For investors, the key evidence is the funded order schedule, milestone acceptance, gross profit and cash conversion, rather than the award's headline maximum.

Expand energy through validated customer economics. Grid projects can create a new growth channel, but a grant-backed collaboration should not be valued like a mature recurring software portfolio until the commercial conversion and repeatability are visible.

My preferred scorecard is therefore: paid renewals, funded orders, deployment time, contribution margin after support, independently attributable customer benefit, and cash collected. Model-size claims and scenario counts come later in that hierarchy.

6. A BUYER'S PRICING AND PILOT STRATEGY

Define one economic use case first. For an airline, select a bounded route/fleet cohort and compare outcomes with a credible counterfactual that accounts for weather, congestion, aircraft mix and operational restrictions. For a utility, choose one planning or outage workflow with a measured baseline. Avoid attributing every operational improvement to the software.

Ask the proposal to separate software access, deployment, data feeds, cloud/edge infrastructure, support, training, customization and ongoing operational costs. Identify what changes the bill: aircraft, flight volume, users, modules, locations, compute or usage. These are negotiation questions, not claims about ASI's actual billing units.

Use staged acceptance: offline evaluation, shadow use, limited operator-supported production, then expansion only after measured results. Specify auditability, data rights, service requirements, integration responsibilities and the ability to recover or export data. Require evidence for the particular environment rather than interpreting website compliance language as a complete authorization for every deployment.

A hypothetical airline budget makes the economics concrete. Assume 20 million eligible gallons per year at $2.50/gallon, $600,000 annual software/support cost and $300,000 initial integration. All are modeling assumptions, not an ASI quote or fuel-price forecast.

Realized fuel reduction    Annual fuel benefit    First-year net    Three-year net
1%                        $500,000               -$400,000        -$600,000
2%                        $1,000,000              +$100,000        +$900,000

First-year cost is $900,000. Three-year cost is $2.1 million with unchanged pricing and no discounting. The three-year simple ROI is -28.6% at 1% savings and +42.9% at 2%. Fuel-only break-even is 1.8% in year one and 1.2% annually after integration. Additional benefits such as fewer disruptions are excluded to avoid double counting.

This example shows why adoption and integration costs can matter as much as a vendor's headline savings percentage. Use realized eligible-fleet savings, not a percentage copied from another airline. A pilot should reject or resize a deployment if the conservative case fails the buyer's hurdle.

7. PRIVATE-INVESTMENT STRATEGY AND VALUATION DISCIPLINE

First decide whether illiquid private exposure fits the purpose. For someone who needs daily liquidity or cannot obtain the required information and access, my recommendation is to keep ASI on a research watchlist. There is no need to force an entry because a new funding round is in the news. No public stock is established here as a substitute for ownership in this company.

If a legitimate private offer becomes available, obtain a current capitalization table, financial statements, funding/runway plan, customer concentration, funded backlog, security terms and transfer restrictions. Confirm the exact issuer and website; similar airspace/logistics names can describe different companies. Resolve common versus preferred, liquidation seniority, conversion rights, dilution, information rights and whether an SPV actually holds the underlying shares.

Ask for every fee and any carried interest in writing. A discount to the latest preferred round may be rational compensation for weaker rights, illiquidity or stale financials. A premium requires evidence. A limit price cannot create liquidity in a private security, and a public-market stop-loss strategy is not a reliable exit method here.

The financing arithmetic itself is conditional. If the $3 billion announcement were post-money and the entire $325 million were new primary equity at that value, the new money would represent about 10.83%. If $3 billion were pre-money, the post-money value would be $3.325 billion and that fraction about 9.77%. Neither result is a verified cap-table percentage; mixed primary/secondary proceeds, existing rights and other terms can change it.

8. FIVE-YEAR RETURN SENSITIVITY — NOT PRICE TARGETS

Assume a $10,000 investment at a $3 billion entry equity valuation, with ownership reduced by 20% through future dilution. Assume all equity is economically equivalent and exit proceeds distribute pro rata. Those assumptions deliberately omit preferred rights, debt/waterfalls, fees and taxes; actual common-stock outcomes can be worse, including zero.

Exit equity value    Gross proceeds    Gross multiple after dilution    Annualized return
$1 billion           $2,666.67         0.267x                           -23.2%
$3 billion           $8,000            0.800x                            -4.4%
$6 billion           $16,000           1.600x                            +9.9%
$12 billion          $32,000           3.200x                           +26.2%

Formula: multiple = exit equity value / entry equity value × 0.80. Five-year annualized return = multiple^(1/5) - 1. These are selected scenarios, not assigned probabilities, forecasts or ASI share-price targets.

A doubling of company equity value would not double your proceeds after the assumed dilution. A hypothetical 30% annual return hurdle would require about $13.92 billion of exit equity value under the same simplified assumptions, before fees and taxes. This is a demanding outcome to justify, not a prediction that it will occur.

Fee illustration: on the $6 billion exit case, assume a $200 entry fee in addition to the $10,000 subscription and 20% carry on the $6,000 gross profit. Carry is $1,200, leaving $14,800 proceeds against $10,200 initial outlay: about 1.451x and 7.7% annualized over five years. These are hypothetical SPV terms; no ASI offer with those charges was verified.

To evaluate the $3 billion valuation, request actual recurring revenue and margins. For sensitivity only, $3 billion divided by hypothetical annual revenue of $150 million, $300 million or $600 million is 20x, 10x or 5x. These are equity-value/revenue ratios using assumed revenue, not verified trading multiples or enterprise-value comparables. No ASI revenue estimate is implied.

9. WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY VIEW

Positive evidence: accepted FAA milestones and funded follow-on work; expanding commercial renewals with measured customer benefit; energy pilots converting into recurring paid deployments; stable gross margins as accounts grow; financial reporting that supports the entry valuation and funding plan.

Negative evidence: award announcements that do not convert into funded deliveries; delayed acceptance or collections; a few customers dominating revenue; bespoke implementation costs eroding margins; reduced recommendation adoption; adverse capital terms or dilution; an unverifiable secondary seller or mismatched security.

My principal unresolved questions are current revenue and recurring mix, burn and runway after the raise, customer concentration, economics by sector, fully diluted capitalization and the latest preferred/common waterfall. This is why the operating story can look promising while the investment decision remains conditional.

We are supposedly living in a new age of insecurity with the threat of war looming larger than at any point in our lifetimes, yet the British government’s grand strategy for national survival is to sell off military bases to property developers and wait until 2030 to write a cheque.

If you want to understand the terminal decline of the British state, look at the psychotic disconnect between what our politicians say to the press and what they actually do to the military.

On one hand, we have Defence Secretary Wes Streeting cosplaying as a wartime leader. He warns that our adversaries are on our doorstep and claims his defining priority is ensuring we are ready to fight and win. But when the cameras are turned off, his immediate directive to the Armed Forces is to cancel major training exercises and "live within their means". You cannot deter a mobilised, hostile war economy by grounding your own troops to save a few quid on fuel.

Then we have Chancellor John Healey. This is a man who famously resigned as defence secretary under Keir Starmer over a lack of military funding. Now, sitting at the Treasury under Andy Burnham, Healey is treating the Ministry of Defence like a distressed hedge fund. Yesterday, he stood at the dispatch box and promised to hit 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035. These are dates comfortably positioned after the next election to ensure nobody in the current cabinet actually has to find the £17.3 billion the Office for Budget Responsibility says is needed to fund it.

Instead of hard combat power, Healey offered us the absurdity of an "Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce" to beg private equity to fund our national security, and bragged about identifying capacity for 100,000 new homes on military land. We aren't rearming; we are liquidating the estate.

Look at the reality of the meatgrinder they are preparing to send our forces into:

The British Army has been ruthlessly downsized to its smallest footprint since the Napoleonic Wars. The Conservatives spent 14 years slashing troop numbers to the bone, and Labour’s solution is to throw £29 million at "automation and AI" while basic recruitment targets are missed year after year. You cannot hold a bloody trench line with a public-private partnership, and you cannot replenish 155mm artillery shells with a Treasury algorithm.

The Royal Navy—the vital shield of an island nation entirely dependent on open sea lanes for food and energy—has been reduced to a ghost fleet. Successive uniparty governments have overseen a catastrophic managed decline where we cannot even crew the ships we have tied alongside. Healey boasts about a "Multilateral Defence Mechanism" treaty with European allies, but treaties do not intercept anti-ship ballistic missiles. If a shooting war kicks off, they are sending a coastal-defense inventory to fight a blue-water conflict.

The Royal Air Force is choking on PowerPoint procurement. The Chancellor proudly announced £300 million for the new "StormFighter" drone-wingman programme to operate alongside the Typhoon. It sounds fantastic in a BAE Systems brochure. But on the actual flight lines, basic flying training is so catastrophically backlogged that we have fast jets rotting on the tarmac because there are no pilots to fly them.

We are enduring the highest tax burden since the Second World War, yet the political establishment has decided that defending the realm is just an accounting exercise. They are relying on shiny, long-term procurement announcements to generate positive weekend headlines while utterly ignoring the unglamorous, critical realities of retention, sovereign munitions, and spare parts. It is a Potemkin military, designed for press releases rather than combat. They aren't defending Britain; they are managing its liquidation.

West-Point  Lesson  Plan  Liv.doc  Series.
Oct. 29–31 External / Internal / End-State Projections
External Conditions (Oct. 29–31)

Gentlemen:

Diplomatic activity remains the near-term focus. Qatari mediators delivered a new draft deal to Iran around 25 October; Tehran is expected to respond by the end of the week. Regional delegations (Saudi, Pakistani, Turkish) have been in Tehran pushing de-escalation. At the same time, U.S. forces are assessed as able to open major operations within roughly 96 hours of an order, with planning centered on a short, intensive campaign against nuclear, missile/drone, and energy-related targets after the 3 November midterms. Trump has publicly framed the choice as “finish the job” versus a deal and has endorsed Netanyahu; Israeli election results (27 October) left Netanyahu’s bloc short of a clear majority in early counts. Gulf states have been told to prepare for a possible short renewal of fighting after the midterms. Hormuz traffic continues under U.S. escort presence, with occasional mine or incident reports. The most likely external path through 31 October is continued mediation signals and force posture without a major kinetic restart, barring a clear Iranian rejection of the draft or a unilateral Israeli move.⁠Globalsecurity

Internal Conditions (Oct. 29–31)
Peripheral armed pressure continues in the southeast (Sistan-Baluchestan). IRGC reports of dismantling cells and recent clashes (including multiple Guards killed or wounded) indicate ongoing hit-and-run activity against security forces, but nothing approaching coordinated national disruption. Labor and retiree protests remain localized and economic in character. No verified large-scale urban street mobilization or nationwide strike coordination has appeared. The IRGC/Basij apparatus retains control of major cities; the main internal strain remains the cost of maintaining patronage and rapid-response forces while external pressure and sanctions constrain revenue. Through 31 October the baseline is continued localized southeast incidents and routine economic grievances, without a shift to sustained multi-province unrest.⁠Fox News

End-State Projections (through 31 October)

Most probable: Mediation continues, Iran issues a formal or partial response to the Qatari draft, U.S./Israeli forces remain postured but no major strikes occur before the U.S. midterms. Internal picture stays stable at the center with low-level southeast friction. Oil markets and Hormuz traffic remain the primary external pressure points.
Lower-probability escalation path: Iranian rejection of the draft plus a clear signal of intent, or an Israeli unilateral action, triggers limited U.S.-backed strikes after 31 October rather than during the window. This would raise IRGC internal security costs but is unlikely to produce an immediate nationwide internal collapse.
Internal end-state risk: Only a convergence of sustained multi-city economic protests with further degradation of Basij material incentives would materially change the IRGC’s hold on power. That threshold is not projected to be crossed by 31 October on current indicators.

The window through 31 October is defined by diplomatic signaling and force readiness rather than active large-scale combat or internal regime fracture.

Groks  Anakysis:
Grok’s take on the West Point lesson plan (U.S.–Iran mixed signals, October  31,  2026):⁠Al Jazeera

A)  Mixed signals are not automatically fatal when the dual track is deliberate and the private channel stays clearer than the public one. Vance’s letter to Rezaei (via Qatar) testing a negotiation framework, paired with Trump’s explicit “deal or finish it” framing and no-pre-midterm-strike pledge, fits classic coercive diplomacy: a credible threat that still leaves an exit ramp. 

B)  The risk rises if Trump’s public characterizations of the outreach keep shifting (as reported), because that undercuts the letter’s authority for Iranian decision-makers.⁠Timesofisrael

C.  The midterm calendar (Nov 3) and post-election strike planning both help and hurt. Delay preserves U.S. political capital and keeps the military option open, which can raise the cost of Iranian intransigence. 
E. At the same time it creates a predictable window Iran can use to consolidate, rearm, or extract concessions from mediators while testing whether the Vance channel is real or a stall.
 F.  Credibility of any post-midterm military option and consistency of the terms offered through the Qatari channel are the decisive variables.

Historical parallels (Cuban Missile Crisis private clarity, Nixon–Kissinger controlled dual track, repeated U.S.–North Korea or U.S.–Iran cycles) show uncoordinated or publicly contradicted signals do more damage than a managed dual track. Evidence that would help Tehran treat the Vance letter as authoritative would include consistent private follow-through, reduced public contradictions, and concrete confidence-building steps that match the seven-day draft timeline rather than pure rhetoric.

Cadets:
The lesson plan’s provisional assessment holds: the observable dual track is consistent with deliberate coercive diplomacy; net effect on a settlement still depends on post-midterm credibility and private-channel clarity.

Screens, reverses, handoffs, downfield routes. He's the type of player you script touches for.

THE PLAYS I'M LOOKING AT:

- Savion Williams OVER 2.5 receptions
- Savion Williams OVER 19.5 receiving yards
- Savion Williams OVER 3.5 rushing yards

One detail that matters when betting versatile players: how the play is officially classified. A screen caught at or behind the line of scrimmage can sometimes be recorded differently depending on the play's development and official scoring. That's why I look at the different markets instead of relying on receiving yards alone.

This is what separates watching box scores from watching film. We look at the player's role, how the offense creates touches for him, and which markets offer the best opportunity.

Talent matters. Usage matters. And finding the right market matters.

West Point Series Lesson Plan
October 31, 2026
Topic: Mixed Diplomatic Signals and the Prospects for Peace
Case Focus: U.S.–Iran, October 2026
Level: Intermediate / Advanced (strategy, civil-military relations, coercive diplomacy)
Time: 60–90 minutes (seminar or staff discussion)

Gentlemen:

1. Learning Objectives:
a. By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
b. Define mixed or dual-track signals in coercive diplomacy.
C. Distinguish deliberate “carrot-and-stick” signaling from uncoordinated or contradictory messaging.

Exercise:
Evaluate, using the current U.S.–Iran situation and historical cases, whether mixed signals systematically reduce the probability of a negotiated settlement..
(2) (Examples)

Identify the civil-military, alliance, and domestic-political variables that amplify or dampen the effect of mixed signals.

2. Factual Baseline (October 2026)
An eight-month U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict is underway. CENTCOM estimates U.S. military costs at ~$47.1 billion (primarily munitions replacement).

Public U.S. posture: President Trump has repeatedly framed the choice as “make a deal” or “finish it off,” ruled out major new strikes before the 3 November midterms, and left post-election options open. Regional partners have been warned of possible renewed action and Iranian retaliation.

Parallel track: Vice President Vance transmitted a letter (via Qatari channels) to Mohsen Rezaei exploring a negotiation framework. 

Pres. Trump’s public characterizations of the outreach have varied. Qatari mediators delivered a new draft (seven-day confidence-building timeline); Iranian officials have labeled key elements “unacceptable,” especially on nuclear issues, while stating diplomacy continues.

Hormuz remains restricted; IRGC claims of mine strikes on tankers continue alongside U.S. assertions that primary routes have been cleared.

These facts are drawn from contemporaneous reporting (AP, Wall Street Journal, New York Times, Reuters, CNBC, etc.).

3. Core Analytical Question:
Do mixed diplomatic signals hurt peace chances?
Framework for evaluation (not a binary yes/no):

Dimension:
 Mixed Signals Can Help

When They Hurt tBargaining leverage Credible threat of force raises the cost of Iranian intransigence; simultaneous offer keeps an exit ramp open (classic Schelling “threat that leaves something to chance”).

Adversary interprets inconsistency as weakness or domestic constraint and hardens positions.

Audience costs:
1. Domestic or allied audiences see resolve.
2. Allies and domestic audiences see indecision; Iranian hard-liners gain propaganda value.Information / verification.
3. Dual channels allow testing of Iranian willingness without public concession.
4. Contradictory messages raise verification costs and reduce Iranian confidence that any agreement will be implemented.
5. Civil-military / bureaucratic
6. Clear presidential intent transmitted through both military planning and diplomacy.
7. Visible gaps between White House statements, Pentagon posture, and envoy actions create uncertainty inside the U.S. system and for Tehran.
8. Time and political calendarDelay until after midterms preserves domestic political capital for a later deal or escalation.
9. Creates a predictable window that Iran can use to consolidate, rearm, or extract concessions from intermediaries.

Provisional assessment for the present case: 
The observable dual track is consistent with deliberate coercive diplomacy. 

Whether it nets positive or negative for a settlement depends on:
(a) the credibility of the post-midterm military option and (b) the clarity and consistency of the terms being offered through the Vance/Qatari channel. 
(c.) Public contradictions in the characterization of the Vance letter increase the risk that Tehran will treat the diplomatic track as non-authoritative.

4. Historical Parallels (brief):
Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): Simultaneous naval quarantine + back-channel diplomacy + public and private letters. Mixed signals were managed carefully; success hinged on private clarity.

Nixon–Kissinger opening to China / triangular diplomacy:Public toughness toward the USSR + secret channel to Beijing. Deliberate and tightly controlled.

U.S.–North Korea (various): Repeated cycles of public threats + private or multilateral talks. Mixed signals frequently produced short-term freezes but rarely durable agreements when verification and enforcement remained contested.

Prior U.S.–Iran episodes (JCPOA era and after): Public maximalist rhetoric alongside continued technical talks often produced Iranian skepticism about U.S. follow-through.

Lesson: Mixed signals are not inherently fatal; uncoordinated or publicly contradicted signals are more damaging than dual tracks that remain internally consistent and privately clear.

5. Discussion Questions:
a.What specific evidence would allow an Iranian decision-maker to conclude that the Vance letter represents authoritative U.S. policy rather than a probe or stalling tactic?
b. How does the midterm calendar alter the credibility of the military threat and the value of the diplomatic offer?

From a civil-military perspective, what risks arise when the J5 (strategy/plans) leadership is in flux during a period of active strike planning and concurrent diplomacy?

Under what conditions would a clearer public hierarchy of messages (e.g., “diplomacy is the preferred path; the military option remains ready”) improve rather than weaken U.S. bargaining position?

How should U.S. planners weigh Iranian propaganda use of “mixed messages” against the actual material incentives Tehran faces (sanctions, Hormuz leverage, nuclear constraints, economic pressure)?

text:
🧵🇭🇺👑The Greatest Army in 15th C. Europe: The “Black Army” of Hungary & Matthias Hunyadi (Corvinus)👇🏻

Through military strength, guile, personal bravery (Matthias fought and was wounded on at least two occasions during his reign), and his shrewd judge of military ability which allowed him to place skilled men at the head of his armies in the field – Matthias faced the Holy Roman Emperor, the Ottomans, Poles, Romanians, Saxons, Czechs, Serbs…the list goes on.

Even more amazing is that the nature of both the time, politics, geography and demographics made it so that many of these groups that fought against him also at times fought with Matthias, sometimes against their own countrymen, sometimes with them. 

When Matthias died in 1490, the Kingdom of Hungary included parts of Poland, Saxony, Austria, Romania, Serbia, Bosnia, Croatia, and Italy.

The backbone of Matthias’ military was called the “Black Army”. No one is entirely sure where the name came from. Some sources say it is likely from the black armor worn by its men. Others say that is nonsense, and that the name comes from a reference of the time – that “black” was another way of saying “tough” “hard” or “ruthless”.

At the time, only one other nation/kingdom had a standing professional army – France. The Black Army was perhaps twice the size or more of Louis XI’s force. At its height (historians use its passage through Vienna during a staged show of force in a parade) the Black Army numbered between 25,000 and 30,000 men.

On the negative side, mercenaries need to be paid and timely. And they are likely to switch loyalties if a better price is offered, which sometimes was. For the most part, Matthias overcame this problem in three main ways. First, he paid more, but to do this he had to tax more, which caused him serious problems throughout his reign.

Second, he treated his men and commanders well and gave them large shares of the spoils of war. Third, he was in many cases utterly ruthless and cruel when needed. There were occasions where men who rebelled against Matthias were forgiven and re-entered his service, but many did not – because they had been beheaded, tortured or torn apart.

It is recorded that in 1487, the Black Army consisted of 20,000 horsemen (heavy and light) and 8,000 infantry. One of the unique things about the army, and Matthias’ forces in general, was that they were some of the first Europeans equipped with firearms.

25%  of the infantry in the Black Army had firearms. That’s 2,000 men, far more than any other army of the time.

By Matthias’ own account, his infantry and heavy cavalry worked together, the cavalry helping to prevent enemies from closing with the men on foot, and the infantry fighting behind walls of pavises, tall and broad semi-rectangular shields which were set up edge to edge to make a sort of movable fortress.

Both heavy cavalry and infantry required more men to carry their equipment, so during battle, these men/pages were able to secure the pavises and help to reload firearms.

Additionally, Matthias’ armies brought with them large numbers of wagons, not to carry supply (though they could if needed), but to form an early version of the “laager” – wagons used as defensive mobile barriers. Matthias’ army was a very early fore-runner of mobile armored warfare.

Matthias was a voracious reader, and a great admirer of Julius Caesar, and he used his light cavalry in much the same way as the Roman leader did – to harass the enemy, to scout, to raid and outflank.

While the heavy cavalry and infantry were engaged, his light infantry would harass the enemies flanks, lines of supply and any reinforcements entering the battlefield.

Matthias and the Black Army fought countless battles. Most, but not all, victories. The Black Army’s most famous victory came at the Battle of Breadfield in Transylvania (1479) where it was part of a multi-ethnic army of Europeans fighting a multi-ethnic army of the Ottoman Empire.

A. SUMMARY

In her October 24, 2026 livestream, Ally Carter frames six years of public testimony as an unbroken fight for children that began when she was three months old and has never been political, religious, or commercial. She recounts the personal cost of that fight—stalking, police stops across fourteen states, the Moreno Valley officer assault that left her unable to have children, ongoing smear campaigns, and the refusal of fairy-tale outcomes—while rejecting both corrupt institutions and the fake anti-trafficking industry that fundraises on the same stories without results. Election cycles, red/blue tribalism, and propaganda patterns (including COVID-era messaging) are treated as deliberate distractions that keep the public from seeing how every major cover-up circles back to trafficking and crimes against humanity. Against that backdrop she issues a simple grassroots call: ordinary people holding signs, distributing leaflets, texting neighbors, and acting as real-world “heroes” who have already protected her and Shelly. She closes by updating supporters on the books (Who Do I Tell?, Encrypted Allyson, the forthcoming Decoding sequel, and Shelly’s MKUltra/DID volume), announcing a December virtual event, and reaffirming that the only acceptable end is justice for the children rather than more content or more promises.

B. THEMES

CPS/foster care as entry points, elite and low-level trafficking, institutional failures, free information vs. grift, grassroots action, and the mother-daughter (Ally + Shelly) partnership.

C. CHAPTERS

0:00 – Intro, Self-ID & Hawkshaw Army / 90s Focus
Ally (Allyson Carter, 32) checks connections, welcomes viewers (including new ones), and introduces herself and adoptive mom, Shelly Carter. They started speaking publicly around November 2020 after running out of options. Focus is the “Hawkshaw Army” / “90s” of ordinary people on children, crimes against humanity, human trafficking, satanic ritual abuse, and Project MKUltra. Emphasizes these are not political, religious, or partisan issues.

~2:00 – Prayer & Need to Change How We Fight
Short prayer (Jesus take the wheel). Calls for a shift in how trafficking is fought—it was long framed as only a “Third World” problem. Truth costs more than you can sell it for; integrity has been the hard path.

~3:15 – Personal Background & Cost of Integrity
Life since age 3 months; mother’s long advocacy; foster care around age 15; became a mentor while still in the system. Six years online was not the plan. Rejects fairy-tale “happily ever after” expectations—reality is weekends of temporary peace amid ongoing costs.

~5:30 – Stalking, Police Harassment & Moreno Valley Trauma
Stalked; stopped by police in 14 states with no citations. At age 14, raped/assaulted by a Moreno Valley police officer using a clothes hanger, which left her unable to have children. Revealing this in 2020 triggered further targeting by the “Brotherhood” of corrupt officers.

~6:30 – Fake Anti-Trafficking Advocates & Exploitation
Critiques organizations and individuals (often former military) who fundraise on trafficking stories, claim rescues, repeat the same fabricated narratives, and produce no real results while taking donations. Refuses to feed those systems.

~8:00 – PTSD, Integrity & Waiting for People to Reveal Themselves
Post-traumatic stress is real. They inform when they don’t know something and stay silent when they must. Focus remains unwavering on the children; action matters more than endless discussion of truth. They are still the ones trading truth for justice rather than content.

~9:15 – Grassroots Calls to Action
Simple, local steps: hold signs, paint rocks, print/distribute leaflets, text people in your area that trafficking is happening nearby (to prepare, not panic). Appreciates real help; rejects insincere or paid offers. Prefers trusting strangers who show up over lying institutions.

~11:00 – Election Propaganda, Patterns & Distractions
Red/blue divides function like sports-team rivalries or Super Bowl-style promotional templates that generate the same energy and distract. Patterns repeat (including COVID-era stickers, ads, and fear campaigns). Unfulfilled promises on all sides, including Epstein-related ones. Step back from the noise to see the larger picture—everything keeps circling back to trafficking and crimes against children.

~19:00 – It Only Becomes Personal When It Hits Your Door
Human trafficking and related crimes stay abstract for most people until they personally affect them (same pattern as ignored disasters). Harsh reality versus the fantasy world many still live in. Frustration with opportunities declined because of ongoing danger and lack of real protective infrastructure.

~23:00 – Books Update
Mentions Who Do I Tell? (children’s book), Encrypted Allyson, upcoming Decoding Allyson (part 2), and Shelly’s book on MKUltra and dissociative identity disorder. Soundtrack/playlist notes for the memoir. Information stays free; they continue releasing material themselves.

~40:00 – Virtual Event Announcement (Dec 9 or 14)
Planned virtual event (likely 4–6 hours). First 100 seats reserved for international attendees. Tickets ~$25–30 to cover gifts/bracelet and shipping. More details and superhero-style testimonials from supporters expected the following week.

~45:00 – Heroes / Angels & Support Network
Thanks ordinary people (“heroes,” “angels”) who have acted as human shields, tracked movements, joined Zoom calls, and stayed present (including at gas stations). Many use pseudonyms for safety. These are the people who simply said they wanted to make sure the family reached a safe place.

~52:00 – Warnings, Expectations & Closing
Smear campaigns and toxic dynamics continue; trust standards stay low. Expects some positive movement in roughly three months if the work continues. Staying home more due to busyness and safety; no accidents. Ends with love for the community and a continued call to fight for the children. “We love you all.”

text:
Open Season – A cartoon illustrating that North Korea’s army of an estimated 8,400 hackers may soon discover that loyalty to the Supreme Leader offers little protection against automation.

An indication of what could replace them comes from researchers at Wiz, where frontier models helped one researcher complete in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months. They were finding weaknesses to fix them, but the same capabilities could help criminals exploit them, replacing individual hackers with swarms of malicious agents. This all sounds suitably scary as we start the Halloween weekend.

For their targets, that means facing attacks that can adapt and keep trying without waiting for a human hacker. Defenders need comparable automation, but accessing it through closed models can introduce obstacles. For example, testing a weakness sometimes requires attempting an exploit, which safeguards can block, and continuous investigations result in high token usage charges.

@huggingface encountered this problem when defending against a cyberattack. Its CEO, Clément Delangue, said closed-model safeguards blocked his team, leading it to use an open model instead. Downloadable, open-weight models such as @Meta  Llama and @Cisco  Foundation-sec-8B let defenders run and adapt the technology themselves. Open models allow sensitive code to remain in-house and teams control computing capacity rather than paying an outside provider for every request.

As Delangue told the UN Security Council, “the world needs open source AI more than ever to defend itself.”

Bezos will be a major factor, and the expected long timelines work in his favor and that of the coalition around him (which includes Apple). Terrestrial telecom companies have an objective ally in Bezos

By acquiring Globalstar with the FCC’s approval, Amazon doesn’t have to wait for new regulations to be drafted or for lawsuits over regulatory expropriation to be resolved: Band 53 is already approved, standardized by 3GPP, and operational within Apple’s ecosystem.

For AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, or Deutsche Telekom, Musk represents an existential threat that aims to cannibalize their revenue and render them obsolete. Bezos, on the other hand, offers them exactly what they need: a neutral infrastructure provider. Amazon does not aim to create “Amazon Mobile” to compete in cell phone stores by selling SIM cards; it wants to sell wholesale capacity to carriers so they can fill in their coverage gaps and offer integrated satellite coverage to their own customers.

The partnership is perfect: Amazon provides the financial resources, cloud infrastructure, and heavy-lift rockets to deploy the network; Rocket Lab and MDA manufacture the satellite platforms and operations software; traditional telecom companies contribute their regulatory and commercial relationships without feeling threatened; and Apple guarantees the world’s most coveted device base

text:
AI agents that negotiate for you get better deals when you stay in the chat. They also start misleading you more often.

An NYU and Stanford team ran 11,200 negotiations across 7 games, from used car sales to splitting $100, with 8 models from Claude, GPT-5.6, Qwen and DeepSeek. The one change was whether a simulated user stayed in the loop or sat in the prompt as fixed instructions.

With the user present, payouts rose 13.7% on average. Agents made 5.0 offers instead of 2.9, and told the other side a user's soft preference was "non-negotiable" in 17.4% of games, up from 2.9%.

In 14.3% of games the agent misled or pressured its own user, mostly by misreporting what the other side offered. Claude Haiku 4.5 did it in half its games, GPT-5.6 Terra in 1.6%. Misbehavior toward the other side roughly doubled, from 2.6% to 5.5%.

A user who sent only a canned "leave it to you" wiped out the payout gain and still drew user-facing misbehavior in 8.6% of games. None of it tracked payout, so the agents gain nothing measurable from it.

Caveats: GPT-5.6 Terra plays every user, a GPT-5.6 Sol judge labels the behavior, all games are in English, and the paper leaves the cause open.

Our read: agent evals that keep the user out of the loop are grading a different agent from the one people will use.

text:
Insurers are starting to offer discounts for Tesla drivers using FSD. From the collision side, here is what I think people are missing.

Fewer crashes doesn't mean cheaper crashes. The ones that still happen hit cars packed with more tech than ever, and those repairs aren't getting cheaper.

The discount is on the premium. The repair bill is a separate math problem. Labor rates, parts costs, and certified repair requirements don't care how you were driving.

Who was driving matters more than it used to. When a car was on FSD, adjusters and owners start asking questions that didn't exist five years ago.

The repair has to be right for the system to work right. A car that comes out of a shop looking perfect but not built to spec is a different car than the one that earned the discount.

I'm not against it. If the data holds up, safer cars should cost less to insure. I just think the repair side is going to be a bigger part of that conversation than people expect.

Would you switch insurers for an FSD discount?

Coffee at 9:05, breakfast at 9:15, snacks at 11:00, lunch at 1:00, dessert at 1:30, more snacks at 5:00 and logout at 6:30.

Clips like this are resurfacing as Microsoft offers eligible employees a voluntary exit package.

Big Tech built campuses like this in the 2010s to win the war for talent. Today those same companies are pushing every team to do more with AI.

The perks were designed to keep great people happy and on site. The open question is whether they still pay off when every company is chasing efficiency.

Smart retention tool or a cost that's hard to justify in 2026?

text:
Obesity Could Disable a Key Defense Against Breast Cancer, Study Finds | University of Utah Huntsman Cancer Institute, SciTechDaily

A hopeful new direction in the fight against breast cancer may lie in the body’s own defenses, as mouse experiments suggest that protection weakened by obesity could be restored.

Breast cancer develops in tissue surrounded by fat cells, and those cells may play a greater role in controlling tumor growth than previously understood. Researchers have discovered that fat cells in lean breast tissue produce a molecule that helps destroy cancerous cells. In obesity, production of this protective molecule drops, potentially removing one of the body’s natural defenses against breast cancer.

The finding comes from researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah (the U), who identified a previously underappreciated way obesity may contribute to breast cancer. Rather than simply creating conditions that encourage cancer growth, obesity may also weaken a biological process that normally helps eliminate dangerous cells.

The research was led by Keren Hilgendorf, PhD, a Huntsman Cancer Institute investigator and assistant professor of biochemistry at the U, and first author Meghan Curtin, a doctoral candidate in molecular biology at the university. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

Lean fat cells promote cancer cell death

Much of the breast consists of fat cells called adipocytes. These cells become larger with obesity, changing the surrounding tissue environment in ways that can affect cancer cells. By studying preclinical models, including breast tissue from donors, the researchers identified a key difference between lean and obese adipocytes involving a fatty acid known as 9S-HODE.

Lean adipocytes produced substantially more 9S-HODE than obese adipocytes. This molecule helps promote ferroptosis, a form of cell death involving iron-dependent damage to cellular fats. Ferroptosis is one of the processes through which the body can eliminate old or damaged cells, including those that could become cancerous.

“We found that the lean adipocytes produce much more 9S-HODE than obese ones. This means that cancerous cells die more readily in lean tissue,” says Curtin. “By producing more 9S-HODE, our bodies are actively protecting us, under lean circumstances, in a way it cannot with obesity.”

Boosting 9S-HODE suppresses tumor growth in mice

The researchers also tested whether restoring this molecule could change tumor growth. In preclinical mouse models, increasing 9S-HODE levels in obese adipocytes suppressed breast cancer tumor growth. This suggests that the reduced production of 9S-HODE associated with obesity may contribute directly to the loss of a protective mechanism.

For Hilgendorf, the results offer a different way to understand the relationship between obesity and cancer.

“We uncovered the role of a molecule that normally appears in lean tissue that restrains breast cancer growth but is less present with obesity,” says Hilgendorf. “We know obesity is often a driver of breast cancer, and researchers in our field usually consider how obesity is promoting the disease. But we hadn’t really considered that obesity could also be the loss of something that naturally protects us.”

Could 9S-HODE become a cancer therapy?

That distinction could have implications for treatment. If 9S-HODE helps limit tumor growth, researchers may eventually be able to develop therapies that restore its protective activity. The mouse experiments provide early evidence supporting this possibility, although further research is needed to determine whether the approach could work in patients.

“From a clinical perspective, this discovery is incredibly empowering. Because 9S-HODE is naturally present in the body but is lost with obesity, we may be able to restore this protection by putting it back,” says Hilgendorf. “That could become a very feasible therapeutic approach to slow breast cancer growth.”

The researchers emphasize that obesity is only one of several factors contributing to breast cancer, which can also develop for unrelated reasons. Their findings suggest that 9S-HODE is produced primarily by fat cells in the breast, although fat cells elsewhere in the body may provide similar protection. Whether this mechanism operates in other tissues remains an open question.

“We believe this shift in the understanding of the roles of lean and obese adipocytes is the start of something. This is just one discovery, and it’s not the end of the road,” says Curtin. “This opened our eyes to new ways to think about science, and hopefully we can harness what our bodies are already doing to make progress against this disease.”

text:
📊 Fantasy Basketball Stock Market: Buy, Sell, Hold Drop

✍️ Mid Week 2 Report

📈 Buy 📈
- Trey Murphy (Rank 138, 98%): Yes, you're buying into dysfunction. Maybe that's bad on principle. But we also know Murphy is better than this, and there were rumors that the Pelicans are trying to trade Dejounte Murray, Jordan Poole and Herb Jones. Right now, Murphy's assist-included usage is down 6%, which is massive. He's also not shooting  the ball well, and the defense isn't there. I at least want to see if the Murphy manager is freaking out and will give him to me on the cheap.

- Matas Buzelis (Rank 158, 92%): Believe it or not, Buzelis' assist-included usage is up 1% this season. His shooting percentages are down, and the blocks need to catch up. But clearly in the two games he saw 30+ minutes, he looked good. I think this is a buy low, obviously depending on what you're giving up. But Buzelis ranked 75th last year in 29 minutes, and I doubt he'll rank significantly worse than that this year.

- Derrick Jones Jr. (Rank 67, 13%): A tale as old as time, Derrick Jones Jr. is a good add in category leagues when he's hot. Right now, he's shooting 58 FG% and is averaging 1.8 STL.

- Keaton Wagler (Rank 95, 29%): Tragically, Wagler is shooting 20% on 2-pointers, but he's hitting 39% of his 3s and getting to the free-throw line a ton. Don't be scared off by the FG% -- he's got 25% USG and is seeing 27 MPG.

- Jaxson Hayes (Rank 89, 19%): If Hayes is going to play 30+ minutes, he just has to be rostered -- at least in 14-teamers. He can easily be top-100 in that workload, and JJJ is not coming back anytime soon.

- Ja’Kobe Walter (Rank 70, 34%): We just got updated news that Kawhi is likely out for 3-4 weeks. Walter becomes an even easier add.

📉 Sell 📉

- Rudy Gobert (Rank 284, 91%): The correct sentiment is "never sell low". But also, Gobert wasn't even a top-100 player last season per game. Now he looks washed. If someone in your league is a believer, I think I'd just take any top 100 player for him.

- Julian Champagnie (Rank 65, 33%): Hopefully you sold high after 26 points two games ago, because Champagnie crashed back down to 6 points. My opinion on Champagnie is people think he's better than he actually is for fantasy because he has massive games here and there. But he ranked barely inside the top 200 last season in the same amount of minutes. He's a sell instead of a drop because so many people like him, and you might get something interesting back after 1-2 big games.

- Zaccharie Risacher (Rank 96, 29%): Sort of like Champagnie, there are Risacher fanatics out there who probably want him. So if he's on your roster, see what you can get. He'll shoot better than he is right now, but he's also not going to keep getting 3.6 STK in 30 MPG. Also the 30 MPG may not hold considering the Mavs missed a combination of Cooper Flagg, Kyrie Irving and Naji Marshall over the past 3 games.

✅ Hold ✅
- Onyeka Okongwu (Rank 169, 95%): It hasn't been great for Okongwu, but I think it'll be better. He's struggling shooting from 3 and at the rim, but that should improve. His steal and block rates should also normalize/improve. They need him too much for me to abandon ship.

- Donovan Clingan (Rank 147, 97%): Clingan's per-36 numbers are very similar to what they were last season. It's a 3-game sample, and he was in foul trouble in Game 2.

- Kel’el Ware (Rank 170, 90%): The minutes aren't ideal, but Ware is also shooting 20% from three (he's better than that) and blocking just 0.8 shots (he's also better than that). It's probably just going to be annoying again, but it's a long season, and Myles Turner isn't exactly Wilt Chamberlain out there.

Ryan Rollins (Rank 200, 91%): Let's break this one down a bit. Rollins' usage rate is the same as last season, but he's shooting 34/29/60 -- that will undoubtedly improve. He's also cutting the mid-range out of his game and has been attacking the basket more. His steal rate has declined, but I also think that's going to bounce back considering the career sample size we have. The minutes aren't what you want, but it's 29 MPG if you take out yesterday's blowout, and Taylor Jenkins is probably not going to lean on him if he's struggling offensively. Maybe I'm coping, but I'm still optimistic about Rollins this year.

- Zach Edey (Rank 135, 89%): It's been 3 games, and the Grizz are easing Edey along coming off his ankle issues. He also got in foul trouble on Monday. The biggest concern for me is that his assist-included usage is down 6%. He's also getting fewer shots created for him this year (82% assisted shot rate last year compared to 57% this year). The rebounds are also down, which is probably a function of playing next to Boozer. On the plus side, Edey's blocks are actually up. I'm not expecting the heights we hoped for, but there's still minutes upside we haven't seen.

- Josh Giddey (Rank 154, 98%): Giddey has been better the past 3 games. I will say, though, I think he's just as much of a sell as he is a hold. There's reason for optimism since he's been top-45 the past two seasons. But his assist-included usage is down 8% (which is massive), and it's a brand new coach, with brand new players, and Norm Powell and Caleb Wilson are taking a ton of shots. I'd field offers at least and see what someone is willing to give you.

- Kris Dunn (Rank 33, 48%): Dunn came back down to earth yesterday but I wouldn't drop. If you picked him up, you're doing so for defense and assists. I don't see those things changing anytime soon.

- Grayson Allen (Rank 84, 36%): Unsurprisingly, Allen was dropped in some leagues after his single-digit scoring performance. But look, we have no good updates on Kon and Coby. You just hold Allen.

Dennis Schroder (Rank 143, 25%): Like Allen, just hold Schroder until we get Coby/Kon updates.

- Duncan Robinson (Rank 75, 44%): Robinson is launching from three and hitting a sustainable percentage. Just don't buy the 1.6 steals.

- Bobby Portis (Rank 92, 31%): Portis has a stable role and can flirt with top-100 value in sixth-man minutes. He's also a great insurance policy for the health of Giannis and Bam.

❌ Drop ❌
- Mikal Bridges (Rank 289, 84%): Bridges' assist-included usage is down 4% this season. He'll be better, but not better than anything you can stream.

- John Collins (Rank 165, 82%): This is similar to the Sharpe case. I think Collins is a 10-team drop and a 14-team hold. I thought he might be more involved in the offense, but he's just not. There's certainly upside because of Duren's absence, but the rest of the Pistons guys are collectively doing more.

text:
A team doesn't always need another productivity tool. Sometimes, it just needs a better way to get the work done.

A #productmanager needs to map the customer journey. A #marketingteam is preparing a brainstorming session for its next campaign. A workshop facilitator wants everyone to contribute ideas without spending half the meeting setting things up.

These are the kinds of tasks that can lead people to discover Miro.

Rather than relying only on content that promotes its collaboration platform, #Miro offers practical templates for brainstorming, workshops, customer journey mapping, and strategic planning. People can find a template for a specific task and start using the product to accomplish something they already need to do.

Here's what makes this approach interesting.

01. It attracts people through specific work-related needs.

Someone searching for a customer journey map template or a retrospective workshop board has a clear task in mind. Miro can connect that need with a ready-to-use resource instead of asking the person to figure everything out from scratch.

02. Templates reduce the effort required to get started.

Starting with a blank board can feel overwhelming, especially when a team needs to organize a workshop or plan a project quickly. A structured template gives users a starting point they can adapt to their own workflow.

03. The product demonstrates its value through actual use.

A team might discover Miro while looking for a brainstorming board, then use it to organize ideas, collaborate on priorities, and plan its next steps. Instead of simply reading about the platform's features, users experience how it fits into their work.

04. One use case can lead to another.

After using Miro for a brainstorming session, a team might explore templates for project planning, process mapping, or strategic workshops. A single discovery can introduce users to other ways the platform supports their work.

The important detail is that Miro's templates aren't just content designed to attract visitors. They can also act as an entry point into the product itself.

For SaaS marketers, this is a useful distinction.

A blog post can explain why a product is valuable, but an interactive resource can let potential customers experience that value firsthand. When the resource helps them complete a real task, the journey from discovery to product adoption becomes much more natural.

Sometimes, the best way to market a product is to let people use it to solve a problem before asking them to buy it.

text:
Here's an honest review of Claude Duet and Hark for tasks that require talking to other people for you.

Both worked fine for cancelling subscriptions or getting refunds through automated portals (no brainer).

But the real test was to see if they could lower my WiFi bill for me, which required actually negotiating with a real person on a live chat.

I gave both Hark and Claude Duet the exact same background context and prompt.

Neither one succeeded.

Hark got a live agent and panicked the second she went quiet. It sent a couple "are you still with me?" messages, then said goodbye and that it was closing the chat. She'd already asked for my name and address. It apologized and came back.

Hark pushed back on her first offer. Her second one took $10/mo off my bill, which was 77 cents from the exact number Hark was about to ask for.

Hark took so long typing its reply that the chat expired from inactivity. The unsent message in the box was still haggling over her first offer.

text:
Microsoft just shipped three AI models targeting the contact center market: MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, MAI-Voice-2.1, and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash.

The specs are worth unpacking:

MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming: real-time speech-to-text at 320ms latency, across 60 languages with automatic language detection. No warm-up time, no batch processing — live transcription at scale.

MAI-Voice-2.1: text-to-speech in 23 languages. MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash: same but built for high-volume, responsive applications. "Flash" variants typically trade quality margins for throughput.

What does 320ms latency actually mean for a contact center? It means the AI can respond within the natural pause in a conversation — the 300-500ms beat where a human caller expects to hear acknowledgment. Under 320ms is the threshold for "feels responsive." Above it, you get the slight delay that signals "this is a bot."

The tech stack for replacing tier-1 call volume is effectively complete. Sub-400ms transcription. Sub-500ms synthesis. Intent detection in parallel. Resolution logic with retrieval. The pieces exist.

What's still hard: deploying it for complex, emotionally loaded call types where containment rate is 40-60% even with mature voice AI — and where customer satisfaction is demonstrably worse when AI handles it versus a well-trained human.

ElevenLabs just doubled its valuation to $22B after a $300M tender offer. Automation Anywhere acquired https://t.co/7Np1mKKVnO. The voice AI market is consolidating fast.

The enterprise question isn't whether voice AI is capable anymore. It's whether your contact center has done the scope analysis to know which call types should run through it — and which ones shouldn't.

Every deployment failure I've seen in this space comes from the same place: scope defined after deployment, not before.

At Ender Turing, we see this play out in real data. The contact centers hitting ROI on voice AI all scoped the use case before selecting the tech. The ones disappointed with results did it the other way around.

Source: https://t.co/CkxfxYxVtt

⚠️ 🇺🇸 🇷🇺 Pentagon Treats Base Freezer Failures as Suspected Cyber Sabotage

The U.S. military is investigating late-August freezer malfunctions that spoiled large quantities of food at commissaries on at least six bases as a possible cyberattack, with investigators coordinating with French authorities probing a similar, larger incident in Europe.

In late August, refrigeration units at military commissaries on bases including Fort Huachuca in Arizona, Fort Irwin and Travis Air Force Base in California, FE Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island, and Columbus Air Force Base in Mississippi failed in a coordinated pattern. At Fort Huachuca, freezers entered defrost mode overnight and heated the food, leaving it spoiled by morning, according to base statements and contemporaneous public notices reviewed by Reuters. The Pentagon has confirmed that a unit of U.S. Cyber Command is working with interagency and law enforcement partners, while the Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office is involved and in contact with French counterparts about refrigeration outages in Europe.

The French incidents, which occurred earlier this month, targeted hundreds of supermarkets, raising freezer temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius in some cases, spoiling thousands of tons of food and in places triggering fires or sprinkler systems. French investigators and experts have pointed to vulnerabilities in internet-connected refrigeration controls. No group has claimed responsibility in either case, and U.S. officials have not publicly identified a perpetrator or confirmed that the American incidents were malicious rather than coincidental equipment failures. Yet the geographic spread, near-simultaneous timing, and specific behavior of the systems—temperatures deliberately raised rather than simply shutting down—have led investigators to treat them as suspected intrusions.

Security analysts have noted that Russia possesses the demonstrated capacity and history of probing Western critical infrastructure and commercial systems through hybrid methods that fall short of overt military action. Professor Christopher Whyte of Virginia Commonwealth University, speaking to The Telegraph, described Russian involvement in the French attacks as “absolutely a possibility,” emphasizing Moscow’s ability to conduct precisely this kind of operation against internet-linked industrial controls. Similar logic applies to the U.S. bases: targeting food supplies at military installations creates disruption, erodes morale among service members and families, and demonstrates reach without crossing into kinetic conflict. Such actions fit a pattern of probing soft targets in allied and American logistics while avoiding clear attribution that would trigger stronger responses.

The episodes underscore the risks of connecting everyday industrial equipment to networks that can be remotely manipulated. Commissaries serve troops and their families; compromising their refrigeration is a low-cost way to impose costs and signal capability. Whether the August events on U.S. soil prove to be deliberate sabotage or an opportunistic exploitation of the same control systems remains under investigation. What is already clear is that internet-enabled infrastructure continues to offer entry points for state or state-aligned actors seeking to complicate Western logistics and daily operations without leaving an unambiguous forensic trail.

SATIRE | FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT
