text:
Potential new "preppers", hear me out. 
(Warning: long post)
Given the intensity of prepperdoomporn- vaguepostmaxxing-engagefarmclickbait posts on my For you tab side of X, one would think the Doomsday Prepper Industrial Complex, aka "Big Prepping", desperately needs to replenish the ranks with new blood and their cash.

Sales of temu crossbows, rapid radios, kitty litter pails of pancake mix, mystery metal folding saws, & chyneseium knives must have been way down...

All joking aside, it's a healthy normal human impulse to want to live, and to be able to maintain the general welfare of yourself, your family & friends, regardless of external circumstances. It's normal and mentally healthy for one to get the urge to put a little excess food or supplies away when "winter is coming". Winter for humans is universally understood to be uncertainty, lean times, hardship if things go wrong - if "preparations" aren't made.  As Ben Franklin said, "all in moderation".

I have no affiliate links. I have nothing to sell you. No Patreon account or email newsletter for you to sign up for. All I can offer you is my knowledge and wisdom for life experience. 

Many moons ago, I was involved with FEMA, and also my county level EMA Medical Reserve Corps on the communications side. I've trained for some wild shit that, thankfully, hasn't happened, and most likely won't. I'm the grandson to the grandsons of German farmers that were here before Illinois was a state. I currently repair complex, high level technologically laden machines for my income and table meat. I've hunted, fished, and helped to farm in my youth, and I've not forgotten the lessons serious men took time to tell & teach me. 

I've pulled guts into slop pails while butchering hogs. I've nicked the bladder on white tail deer when field dressing and been sprayed with piss. A live bluegill can slice open your hand with surprising ease with its fin. I've made mistakes, and learned the hard way at times. I can repair all kinds of machines and electrical devices. I can weld. I can tie all sorts of knots. I'm a decent rifle and pistol marksman. I've passed the dreaded "simulated catastrophic antenna damage" test, by ripping 14 gauge NM-B romex out of a abandoned crack house wall, and called Chicago on HF to land simulated helicopters loaded with medical supplies on simulated hospital landing pads. I can successfully grow food from out of the Earth. I've read, studied, and contemplated human psychology and human nature under stress, the nature of society in disasters.   

And I'm here to tell you that Doomsday maxxing, rugged individual/family unit "I got mine" type prepping is a flawed plan at best, and the mistake is sold to you at retail pricing. Most of this kind of "prepping", as it's commonly packaged & presented, is mostly shopping for and accumulating useless trinkets and gear, followed by useless and unhelpful LARPing.  Use your highly evolved brain, your costly gift of human reasoning given to you by your ancestors long passed, and run all the thought experiments for the potential situations you might realistically find yourself in if X or Y event should occur. 

Then, and only then, prepare realistically and accordingly within your skill set and within your means. 

The first step after that, is to know your people and your area. Communicate directly and sincerely to family, friends, and also very important, with your neighbors. Ask "if they have thought about...?" and "what do you think would happen if....?". Start making judgment calls about whom around you are NPCs, whom are fellow helpers, whom are dependents/ loads that can maybe be turned into helpers, and whom are pieces of shit. Then act appropriately with that information going forward.

No one wins in a realistic break down of society and the social contract from any event, whether natural or man made. Humans know this instinctively, and won't permit a mad max type world to last very long. Order will soon be restored, it may look different from what was remembered. Justice, possibly very swift and harsh justice will still be administered. The social order might get reshuffled. Mass deaths may occur. After the smoke clears, homes, hospitals, and schools will be rebuilt and re-staffed. Society may be even stronger than before. Wedding celebrations and children's birthday parties will happen again. Governments might actually be better institutions afterwards. Priorities in the mind of men and women might get sorted better afterwards, too. 

We, society, will reward and appreciate the good people, the honest and fair, the builders and skilled helpers, and the guardians of those that were vulnerable in a trying or dangerous time. 

And the "I got mine" selfish cowards that ran away and hid themselves, and the raiders or "wolves" that abused or harmed their fellow man in a time of disruption and vulnerability, will also be remembered, as the pieces of shit they are. Those types also will be shunned or dead in short order. 

Learn more skills. Be a helper for your family, friends, and community. Learn more skills. Put aside enough so you can help yourself, then the good neighbors. Learn more skills. Protect the innocent and those that are good, but may be weak or vulnerable at the time. 

Learn. more. skills. 
Be. a. helper. 

The society you feel tempted to hide from, is you.

Politicians Vs Businessmen. 

No intelligent person sees a career politician and calls him “rich”. 

Any career politicians that has become rich has done so with money that actually belongs to you, the citizen. 

The process of politicians becoming rich is achieved through a crime called converting public funds to private use. 

And the present crop of politicians in Nigeria are trying very hard to normalize that crime. 

The problem with this practice is that money was created to represent and exchange value. 

So whoever acquires money without adding value is essentially creating poverty. 

The greater the amount of  public money that is being converted to private use, the greater the poverty - creating effect on the entire populace. 

It is more intelligent to treat a businessman as rich because they create value by creating jobs with multiplier effects for poverty reduction and human dignity. 

As a rule of thumb, in any country where career politicians are richer than businessmen, you always find systemic rent-seeking (often leading to a state characterized by kleptocracy, plutocracy or crony capitalism).

Kleptocracy- a government or political system whose leaders—known as kleptocrats—use state power, laws, and public institutions to systematically steal their nation’s wealth and resources for personal enrichment. (Sounds familiar?)

Plutocracy- a system of governance where society is ruled, controlled, or governed directly or indirectly by the wealthiest individuals (who are usually kleptocrats or their associates). 

Crony capitalism- An economic system that appears to be a free market on the surface, but where business success depends primarily on close, mutually beneficial relationships between business executives and government officials rather than on fair competition, innovation, or efficiency.

Instead of succeeding by delivering superior products or lower prices to consumers, "crony" businesses thrive through legal favoritism, government-sanctioned monopolies, special tax breaks, state subsidies, and selective regulations designed to keep competitors out.

(have you noticed that your billionaires dare not speak out against bad governance? Most of them are crony capitalists). 

Crony capitalism operates as a quid pro quo (a exchange of favors) between politicians and business elites:

What Politicians Give: Tax loopholes, state contracts, cheap access to land or natural resources, bailouts, and regulations that create high entry barriers for competitors.

What Businesses Give: Campaign contributions, lobbying dollars, kickbacks, favorable media coverage, or lucrative post-government job offers (the "revolving door").

All these have become very evident in the Nigerian political landscape today, and they are destructive to the political and business climate, as a result of politicians committing the unpunished crimes of converting public wealth to private use. 

Politics, finance and the economy are more closely related than you may think.

text:
1887 photograph of Harriet Tubman, her husband Nelson Davis and adopted daughter Gertie.

This 1887 photograph offers a glimpse of Harriet Tubman that is often missing from the stories told about her: Harriet not as an Underground Railroad conductor or Civil War scout, but as a wife and mother figure surrounded by family.

Standing beside Tubman are her second husband, Nelson Davis, and their adopted daughter, Gertie. Tubman married Nelson in 1869, after her return to Auburn, New York. Their marriage lasted nearly two decades, until Nelson died from tuberculosis on October 14, 1888.

Nelson had his own history of service. During the Civil War, he served as a private in the 8th United States Colored Infantry, one of the Black regiments formed as African American men were finally permitted to serve in the Union Army. Tubman herself also served the Union during the war as a nurse, cook, scout and intelligence operative.

Her family life had also been shaped by slavery and separation. Before escaping to freedom, Tubman had married John Tubman in Maryland. When she escaped in 1849, John remained behind. Harriet later returned to Maryland intending to bring him north, but John had remarried and chose not to leave with her. Their marriage was effectively over, and Harriet eventually built a new life with Nelson.

Gertie became part of that new chapter. Tubman never had biological children of her own, but she and Nelson raised Gertie as their daughter. The family lived in Auburn, where Tubman spent her later years helping formerly enslaved people, supporting her community and working toward the establishment of a home for elderly African Americans.

Photographs of Tubman are relatively rare, which makes this image especially meaningful. It captures a woman whose life is often remembered through extraordinary acts of courage, while also showing the quieter family relationships that mattered to her.

text:
Am in flight to the New Orleans Investment Conference, where among my hosting duties, I'll be asked for my thoughts on macro & the markets

So as I organize my thoughts, I thought I'd share some here with you

1) The Time Is Now For Diversification

The AI trade is long in the tooth and has commanded sky-high valuations. I'm skittish about it, but...if you look at demand for compute and AI capex spending/building there's no sign of slowdown. This juggernaut could keep steamrolling on in 2027 & the opportunity cost of being out of the trade has been huge, so maintaining *some* exposure still makes sense. And be VERY careful with short bets against this megatrend.

Bonds are now an attractive alternative. They make more sense to hold in your portfolio at these yields than they have in over a decade. Plus, they should provide good cushion should stocks puke next year.

Capital has been skittishly rotating between growth and value all year. So if you're holding tech, you likely also want to hold some more defensive names, too, as a counterbalance.

Commodities are a wild card, IMO. Lots of reason to own them (structural scarcity, AI capex demand, inflation concerns, etc), but they are volatile. And if a market correction/economic slowdown happen next year, they're likely to whacked in the process. If Ukraine and/or Iran wars end, oil will prob get clobbered. Be good about harvesting any gains along the way, and seriously consider hedges.

And speaking of hedges, risk management in this environment should take high priority, IMO. Retain some cash as dry powder, consider stops/option hedges on large positions, rebalance often, etc -- remember, hogs get slaughtered.

2) It's Do Or Die Time for Precious Metals

Gold & silver prices have been weak all year after hitting blow-off tops in January, but the price action has been especially sick of late. They're now at new lows for the year. Technically, they seem a whisker away from breaking below key support. If they're going to stage a reversal rally, now is pretty much the time. Else it likely will get a lot harder for prices to recover anytime soon.

That said, there are lots of reasons why such a rally could happen (some would argue *should*). Several experts I interview now think that prices, especially of the PM mining stocks, offer ridiculous value.

In short, neither a breakdown or breakout would be surprising soon. Position yourself so that you aren't busted no matter which happens. IMO, this is a great environment for dollar-cost-averaging into new positions in the PM sector.

3) The Battle for the West Is Intensifying

Both domestically and abroad, the battle to control the identity & future of Western Civilization is heating up & will likely only get hotter next year. 

Socialism vs Capitalism. Immigration vs Protectionism. Globalization vs Nationalism. Traditionalism vs Wokeism.
Western values vs Eastern ones.

Expect topics like these to continue to push themselves front & center. And all have economic consequences which is why, like it or not, investors need to pay attention to where the momentum is heading.

IMO, this fight for the West's future will be one of the most dominant social & investing trends of the next several decades. Monitor it, understand it, place your bets accordingly....and beyond all that, stand fast for the outcomes you want. We won't get the ones we want if we don't fight for them.

OK, the plane is starting its descent. So that's it for now.

text:
October 29, 1913: Negro’s Statement Legal Evidence, He Says; State Closes

Reading Time: 22 minutes, [3728 words]

The Atlanta Georgian,

Wednesday, 29th October 1913,

PAGE 4, COLUMNS 1 & 7.

DORSEY DEFENDS CONLEY TESTIMONY

Making a determined stand in behalf of the admissibility bearing on that part of Jim Conley's testimony which had to do with Leo Frank's moral conduct, Solicitor Dorsey Tuesday afternoon neared the close of his argument in opposition to the motion for a new trial made by Frank's lawyers.

The Solicitor read numerous legal citations which enumerated cases where evidence of this nature had been admitted to show the likelihood of the defendant's guilt in respect to the charge for which he was on trial.

Mr. Dorsey touched briefly on Judge Roan's failure to charge the jury with the amount of credibility which might be given Conley's testimony, in view of the negro's admission that he repeatedly had sworn falsely.

He read the law to show that the mere failure of Judge Roan to make the impeachment charge, in the absence of a request by the defense, was not at all a sufficient ground for a new trial.

Dorsey closed his argument at 4:55 and the State's case rested.

Solicitor Dorsey startled the court by the declaration that if Judge Roan reversed the Frank verdict on the grounds of prejudice or bias, that Henslee and Johanning, the jurors accused of unfairness, should be given maximum sentences in the penitentiary.

"They deserve no better fate if it is true that their minds were warped with prejudice," declared the Solicitor.

"But no except my friends on the other side who are grasping at straws believe these charges on which Mr. Arnold dilated in three days of delirious rambling."

"Henslee is unimpeached; Johenning is unimpeached.

I do not believe that there is a man in Georgia from the Governor down who is a more conscientious and upright citizen that Johenning."

Dorsey continued his assault throughout the day on what he appeared to regard as the most important stronghold of the defense, the alleged bias of the two jurors.

In emphatic language he told the court that there was not a ground in the entire motion for a new trial that had a semblance of merit.

"The truth is, your honor," he said, "that they haven't any defense in this case, and haven't a tenable ground for this motion.

They are beating aimlessly around like a man snipe-hunting, hoping against hope that something will fly into their net."

Dorsey to Finish Wednesday.

"If your honor adopts the policy of taking the word of irresponsible persons against that of a man like Henslee or Johenning, you are taking every protection away from the State and making it easy for red-handed murderers to go free."

"The people were not aroused against Leo M. Frank because he is a Jew," the Solicitor said, "but because he is a criminal.

In the name of the Gentiles of Atlanta, in the name of a community which the learned counsel for the defense declares was carried away with malice and a thirst for blood,' I challenge anyone to show me where anyone cried, Hang Frank!

Lynch him!'

or made any remark that could be taken as an expression of personal hatred.

The counsel for the defense when they charge the jury with a display of mob spirit,' are not making personal accusations against any of these men. They are slandering the citizenship of the community."

As to Cheers for Dorsey.

"It is true that the people in the streets did holler for me, but that shows nothing. Because the people, for some reason or other, saw fit to cheer for me, the counsel for the defense has chosen to warp it and construe it into a demonstration against Frank."

They might as well contend that when some people applaud the hero in a melodrama, and hiss the villain, that they are applauding the man and not the part; that they are hissing the man and not the part.

The people have a right to come to the courthouse: they have a right to cheer whom they please.

If they want to cry that cheering for your me in persecution of Frank because he is a Jew, let them do it.

"Their changes are an attack upon your honor (Judge Roan) as much as they are an attack upon me and the members of the jury. They combatted your rulings all during the trial.

They said they would move for a mistrial, and they did. And your honor overruled them.

Your honor was sworn to give Leo Frank as impartial trial, and yet on every point up jumped Rube Arnold, like a chattering jack-in-the-box, like someone was working him on a string.

A. H. Henslee, your honor, was not attacked more as a man than your honor was as a judge."

Discusses Henslee Affidavit.

Content warning: this post includes a racial slur quoted in the newspaper record, shown censored, and talk of sexual accusations from the trial testimony.

On this day, Wednesday, October 29, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Georgian covered the Leo M. Frank new trial hearing under the headline "Negro's Statement Legal Evidence, He Says; State Closes." The Georgian printed several editions that day, and by the later ones the front page read "Rosser Begins Final Frank Plea," then "Rosser Bitter in Closing Frank Plea."

Six months earlier, on Saturday, April 26, 1913, 13 year old Mary Anne Phagan went to the National Pencil Company to collect her pay from Leo Max Frank, the factory superintendent, and she never came home. A Fulton County jury convicted Frank on August 25, 1913. Now Judge Leonard S. Roan, who had presided over the trial, was hearing the defense motion for a new trial.

Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, the prosecutor, finished first. The defense had said Atlanta was carried away with "a thirst for blood." Dorsey answered, "I challenge anyone to show me where anyone cried, 'Hang Frank! Lynch him!'" The people were not aroused against Frank "because he is a Jew," he said, "but because he is a criminal." As for the crowds that cheered him in the street, he compared them to a theater audience that applauds the hero of a melodrama and hisses the villain. They were cheering the part, not the man.

He also defended the two jurors the defense accused of prejudice, A. H. Henslee and Marcellus Johenning. Of one scene the defense placed at the Elks' Club, Dorsey said it was "highly improbable," because the club "has more Jewish members than any club in the city, with the exception of the solely Hebrew clubs."

On Wednesday Luther Z. Rosser, Frank's chief counsel, gave the last argument for the defense. The Georgian called him "ponderous and pugnacious." Near the end of his own argument, Dorsey had said he would assume Rosser did not plan to attack him too. "You needn't assume anything of the kind," Rosser said.

He did not. He said Dorsey had cringed and bowed to "that mob that howled about the courthouse." He said the crowd that cheered when Jim Conley's testimony was admitted were not the people but "the scum." He said the detectives locked up witnesses "until they are ready to tell the lies that are wanted," and that Detective John Starnes "should have been locked up" over the jailing of Minola McKnight. He denied any "slush fund" and said he and Reuben R. Arnold were "poorer to-day because we ever heard of this case."

Then he said this about his client: "If I had a hint of a doubt about it I'd take that brief book of mine and I'd depart forever out of this case." He stayed in the case.

The defense motion rested on one idea: that prejudice had kept Frank from a fair trial. In the same speech, according to the Georgian, Rosser described the cheering when "the filthy testimony oozed from that lousy n*****." The man he meant was Jim Conley, the factory sweeper and the state's main witness. The Georgian printed it without comment.

In the Night Edition, the Georgian reported a shift in Rosser's attack. He aimed his heaviest fire at Jim Conley's testimony that Frank had a sexual perversion. "You might as well have put the brand of Cain upon his forehead as to have introduced that revolting and maliciously false testimony," he told Dorsey. He called Conley a "dirty monster" and said that testimony alone had "tried and convicted the man." Dorsey had already answered that the law allowed the testimony, and he read cases where proof of one crime was let in to show that a man was likely guilty of the crime he was on trial for. Judge Roan had let the jury hear it, and the jury believed Conley.

Rosser also complained about how long Dorsey had talked. "There never was a dead shoat so full of maggots as is Dorsey full of words," he said, and he counted "five and a half hours of words" spent defending Henslee. He said it in the middle of a speech the Georgian expected to run into the afternoon.

The paper noted one quiet moment. "A 'peace conference' between Reuben Arnold and Solicitor Dorsey was the only sign of amity during the hearing."

Judge Roan said he would probably reserve his decision until Thursday or Friday. On Friday, October 31, 1913, he denied the motion. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed on February 17, 1914, and the United States Supreme Court left the verdict standing in Frank v. Mangum on April 19, 1915.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

"I do not regret that I am in this case. I never have regretted it. It has had its hardships, its heart-burnings and its drawbacks, but I do not regret that I am here."

"But so far from hordes of money coming from the four winds of the heavens, I assert that Mr. Arnold and myself are poorer to-day because we ever heard of this case.

For six long months it has absorbed our life and our time. I'll open my books to any honest, decent man to show that this case has been a financial loss to me."

"My friend Dorsey asserted, and it was so strange a thing to do, that Mr. Arnold had attacked the whole public of Atlanta. Is that what Dorsey meant? If so, it was not true. Did he mean that Arnold criticized that mob that howled about the courthouse on that last day of the trial? If so, then make the most of it!"

"Did he mean that mob that he so cringingly represented? Then thank God that I don't represent them."

Crowd Not Representative.

"There were some people there, but they were not the people, not the public. Those people were screaming with delight and gratification because they thought the blood of a human being was to be shed. Is that the 'people' my friend Dorsey so bows to?"

"When the question was up as to whether the revolting testimony of Jim Conley was to be admitted and when your honor permitted the filth to be poured into the record, there were some people who cheered and cheered that this filth was to cover the young man in the prisoner's chair. Is that the crowd that Dorsey so worships as every politician worships, I reckon."

"I say this: If Dorsey approves of all this, and he's my officer as well as yours, then he isn't fit for his job."

Praises Frank's Character.

Rosser reiterated his belief in Frank's innocence and said that he was as decent a man as the Solicitor ever was or as he himself and Arnold were.

He made vigorous attacks on affiants who swore against the jurors, and ridiculed the idea that either of them had possessed any deep-seated prejudice before the trial.

The Solicitor doubted that they had made the remarks credited to them, but read law citations to show that even if they had, the fact did not furnish sufficient ground on which to upset the verdict of the jury.

Dorsey also defended Jim Conley's testimony on Frank's alleged conduct with women as perfectly admissible, again citing cases in which evidence of one crime had been admitted in the record for the purpose of establishing the probability that the defendant was guilty of the crime for which he was on trial.

$WY Q3 2026 earnings: Weyerhaeuser's timber harvests rebound, but mill costs cut wood profit

Weyerhaeuser's wood manufacturing rebound stalled as mill costs rose, while land sales slowed from their first-half peak. Third-quarter sales of the timber and wood products group grew 8% from a year ago, and Adjusted EBITDA rose 14% against last year's weak base. However, compared with the second quarter, cash profit fell by a fifth as Wood Products and Strategic Land Solutions dropped, offsetting a weather-aided rebound in Southern logging.

• Revenue: $𝟏,𝟖𝟔𝟐𝐌 (+8.4% from a year ago)
• Adjusted EBITDA: $𝟐𝟒𝟖𝐌 (+14% from a year ago (-20% from Q2))
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟎𝟖 ($0.06 a year ago ($0.13 in Q2))
• Q4 Strategic Land Solutions EBITDA outlook: ~$𝟒𝟏𝐌 (down ~$45M from Q3 (-57% from a year ago))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because higher log, resin and maintenance costs wiped out the expected profit boost from lumber prices, and the fourth-quarter outlook points to a further drop in both Wood Products and land sales. By our math, the plan leaves fourth-quarter land cash profit near $41 million, down more than half from a year ago. On the bright side, Southern timber harvests recovered and Weyerhaeuser broke ground on its first biocarbon plant and two more solar sites.

The question now is whether Strategic Land Solutions can grow in 2027 without another giant conservation deal, and whether lumber mills can expand margins while housing demand stays sluggish. One camp sees a growing stream of solar, carbon and biocarbon income; the other sees lumpy land sales and oversupplied wood panels. Full-year Climate Solutions profit and the 2027 land outlook in January will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐋𝐨𝐠𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲
Timberlands, the division that grows and harvests trees, normally slows down in the third quarter. Instead, Weyerhaeuser lifted segment Adjusted EBITDA — operating cash profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and land basis — by 8.1% from the second quarter to $133 million. Drier weather in the US South let crews harvest significantly more timber, and per-unit logging and hauling costs fell in both the West and the South.

The fourth-quarter outlook keeps that gain in place. Management expects fourth-quarter Timberlands cash profit to match the third quarter at about $133 million, which by our math is up 16.7% from $114 million a year ago. Slightly higher export log volumes and lower seasonal road costs in the West will offset lower harvest volumes in the South.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Western export log volumes and Southern log prices. If export shipments recover without a drop in Western log prices, Timberlands will enter 2027 with expanding margins.

🟢 𝐁𝐢𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐛𝐨𝐧, 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐛𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞
Weyerhaeuser wants its land and climate projects to generate $250 million of yearly cash profit by 2030, and it hit three construction and sales targets ahead of schedule this quarter. The timber owner also agreed in October to sell 81,000 acres in Arkansas for $146 million ($1,802 per acre by our math) to "optimize the return profile of its timberlands portfolio".

• Biocarbon (wood fiber converted into a coal substitute): began building its first plant in McComb, Mississippi, and is picking sites for more
• Forest carbon credits: sold about 340,000 credits in the first nine months, on pace for the "highest annual sales volume since program’s inception"
• Renewable energy: started building two more solar sites (two operating, five under construction) and signed a 145,000-acre geothermal exploration deal in Oregon and Washington

What to watch: full-year 2026 Climate Solutions cash profit in the fourth-quarter report, which is the only time the company publishes the figure. A number above $135 million, up from $119 million in 2025, would show that solar leases and carbon credits can grow even when one-off conservation deals slow.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝
"Our teams delivered solid operating performance in the third quarter against an increasingly challenging macroeconomic backdrop," chief executive Devin W. Stockfish said. Six weeks ago, higher lumber prices and a restored profit formula pointed to a third-quarter jump in Wood Products, the manufacturing arm that makes lumber, oriented strand board (OSB, structural wood panels) and engineered wood beams.

Instead, Wood Products Adjusted EBITDA fell 29.5% from the second quarter to $91 million, even though lumber prices rose slightly and lumber sales volumes grew moderately. Company-wide cost of sales — the direct cost of harvesting timber and running the mills — rose 2.9 percentage points of revenue from last quarter to 86.2% by our math. In OSB, prices fell 2% while manufacturing costs climbed on "more extensive planned annual maintenance and elevated resin costs", and engineered wood prices fell.

The fourth-quarter plan offers no relief. The company expects Wood Products profit to be "moderately lower than the third quarter, excluding the effect of changes in average sales realizations for lumber and oriented strand board", as lumber and engineered wood volumes drop and log and raw material costs rise again.

What to watch: the third-quarter average lumber price per thousand board feet in the quarterly filing. If lumber prices rose more than $10 per thousand board feet while segment profit still fell $38 million, mill cost inflation is eating the commodity recovery.

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐛𝐲 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟
Strategic Land Solutions, which sells real estate and leases land for energy and climate projects, carried Weyerhaeuser's profit in the first half of 2026 thanks to a $94 million Florida conservation deal in the first quarter. In the third quarter, the segment's Adjusted EBITDA dropped 33.3% from the second quarter to $86 million as acres sold fell sharply and average prices per acre declined.

That $86 million beat the company's $84 million target by 2.4%, inside its usual beat range. However, management held the full-year segment outlook at about $450 million and guided fourth-quarter cash profit down another $45 million to about $41 million (or $42 million by our math from the $408 million nine-month total). That would be down 56.8% from $95 million in the fourth quarter of 2025.

What to watch: the initial 2027 full-year Strategic Land Solutions outlook in January. A target below $450 million would confirm that this year's record profit depended on one-off land sales that will not repeat.

🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝
Weyerhaeuser aims to return 75% to 80% of Adjusted Funds Available for Distribution (Adjusted FAD) — operating cash flow minus capital spending, with spending on its new Monticello, Arkansas engineered wood plant added back — to shareholders. In the third quarter, Adjusted FAD fell to $110 million from $323 million in the second quarter and $117 million a year ago.

• Nine-month Adjusted FAD: $375 million, even after adding back $147 million of Monticello construction spending
• Nine-month regular dividends ($0.63 per share): about $454 million by our math, or 121% of Adjusted FAD
• Net debt (total debt minus cash): $5,005 million by our math, up from $4,898 million in June and equal to 5.0 times trailing 12-month Adjusted EBITDA ($1,006 million)

Because operating cash flow does not cover both the dividend and the Monticello build, the forestry group is bridging the gap by selling timberlands, including the $146 million Arkansas sale closing next quarter.

What to watch: third-quarter share repurchases in the cash flow statement once the full quarterly filing arrives. Another $10 million quarter against the $1 billion buyback plan would confirm that high debt and tight cash flow have frozen buybacks.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing risks and cost questions were not updated in the preliminary earnings release and await the conference call or quarterly filing.

• Monticello total budget: the release shows $54 million spent in Q3 ($147 million year-to-date), but does not say whether the ~$500 million total budget still holds after labor, steel and tariff inflation.
• 2030 profit target gap: trailing 12-month Adjusted EBITDA sits at $1,006 million by our math, $543 million below the $1,549 million 2024 baseline from which the $1.5 billion 2030 growth target is measured.
• Canadian lumber duty cut: the release gives no read on whether lower US import duties on Canadian lumber (implemented between August and October) brought competing supply across the border.
• Cost savings and legal expenses: management gave no tally for its 53 internal cost projects, and the preliminary tables do not break out whether net litigation expense rose again from $20 million in the first half.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟑𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Capital spending rose 9.6% from $125 million a year ago and equaled 7.4% of sales by our math. That includes $54 million for the Monticello engineered wood facility, down from $63 million in the second quarter. Nine-month spending is $388 million ($147 million for Monticello), leaving a steep fourth-quarter ramp to reach the ~$300 million full-year Monticello plan.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟖𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money owed by customers rose 8.5% from $353 million a year ago and 2.7% from $373 million in the second quarter, tracking the 8.4% year-over-year rise in third-quarter revenue. Inventories moved the other way, dipping 2.0% from June to $592 million as the company worked down seasonal log and wood product stocks.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟕𝟐𝟏.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The diluted share count fell less than 0.1% from 722.0 million a year ago, and period-end common shares dipped by roughly 350,000 from June to 720.3 million. After buying back $100 million of stock in the second quarter of 2025, the timber group has barely reduced its share count over the past four quarters.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟒 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐐𝟑 ($𝟏𝟑𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇒ stable
New. Weyerhaeuser expects fourth-quarter Timberlands earnings before special items and Adjusted EBITDA to hold steady with the third quarter's $133 million. By our math, that represents a 16.7% increase from $114 million in the fourth quarter of 2025, as higher Western export log volumes and seasonally lower Western road costs offset moderately lower harvest volumes in the South.

𝐐𝟒 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: ~$𝟒𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐐𝟑 (~$𝟒𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from ~$44 million (implied at Q2)
Cut slightly. The outlook puts fourth-quarter segment cash profit about $45 million below the third quarter's $86 million, or near $41 million (and pretax earnings down about $35 million to ~$32 million). That is down 56.8% from $95 million a year ago and confirms the ~$44 million fourth-quarter slump that the full-year plan pointed to last quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: ~$𝟒𝟓𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from ~$450 million
Unchanged. Management kept the full-year segment cash profit plan at about $450 million, which it raised by $25 million last quarter from the initial $425 million target. With $408 million earned in the first nine months, the full-year figure leaves about $42 million for the fourth quarter by our math, matching the quarterly outlook.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐬 % 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝟏𝟓–𝟐𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 15–20%
Unchanged. The accounting cost basis of land sold is still planned at 15% to 20% of segment sales for the full year, after being lowered from 20%–30% in the second quarter. Through nine months, land basis of $70 million equals 15.7% of the $446 million in year-to-date segment sales by our math, right at the bottom of the target range.

𝐐𝟒 𝐖𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐐𝟑 ($𝟗𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧) 𝐞𝐱-𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞  ⇘ decelerating
New. The plan calls for fourth-quarter Wood Products earnings and Adjusted EBITDA to fall moderately below the third quarter's $91 million before counting any price changes in lumber and OSB. Slightly lower lumber and engineered wood volumes, slightly higher log costs, and moderately higher engineered wood raw material costs will weigh on the mills.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐖𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞?
Wood Products Adjusted EBITDA dropped $38 million from the second quarter even though lumber prices and volumes rose. How much of the squeeze came from OSB maintenance and resin costs versus higher log costs in lumber?

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨 𝐛𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝?
Weyerhaeuser spent $54 million on the Monticello facility in the third quarter and $147 million in nine months, less than half its ~$300 million 2026 plan. Will 2026 spending fall short, or has total project cost risen above $500 million?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬?
With fourth-quarter Strategic Land Solutions Adjusted EBITDA planned near $41 million, how much of that quarterly base comes from recurring solar leases, mineral royalties and carbon credits rather than one-off land sales?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬?
The preliminary analyst package omitted the usual segment tables showing exact prices and volumes for lumber, OSB, engineered wood and logs, as well as the full cash flow statement. What were third-quarter realizations per thousand board feet?

text:
GODADDY $GDDY Q3’26 — EPS BEATS, AIRO BOOKINGS DOUBLE, BUT REVENUE GROWTH REMAINS AT 6%.
GoDaddy delivered stronger-than-expected earnings, with its AI-powered Airo platform emerging as an increasingly important part of the growth story.
THE NUMBERS
🔹 Revenue: $1.34B (Est. $1.33B) 🟢; +6% YoY
🔹 EPS: $2.08 (Est. $1.85) 🟢

The company is also generating substantial cash flow and returning capital through share repurchases.
MY TAKE
I'm constructive on GoDaddy's profitability and cash-generation profile.
Airo offers a potentially attractive opportunity to increase customer spending and improve retention.
But I'm not yet convinced AI is materially accelerating the overall business.
Revenue and bookings both grew 6%, while customer growth remains modest.
For me, the next test is whether Airo can translate its bookings momentum into faster Applications & Commerce revenue growth and higher spending per customer.
That's what would turn the AI narrative into a stronger fundamental growth story.

text:
a gym that charged per visit instead of per month would either go broke or get really good at getting customer to show up.

think about how most gyms work.

you pay monthly. the less you show up, the better for them. fewer people on the machines, same money coming in.

so there's no real reason to care if you come.

now flip it.

you only pay when you walk through the door.

suddenly the gym cares about everything. the schedule, the text that says "class starts in an hour," the guy at the front who knows your name.

same gym. different thing being measured. completely different gym.

cold email works the same way.

most agencies get paid for something that happens early. emails sent. leads delivered. a monthly retainer.

and whatever gets measured is what gets built.

so campaigns end up built to look busy. volume goes up. the dashboard looks great. nobody's on the hook for whether anyone shows up.

(yes, "we sent 50,000 emails this month" is the cold email version of "look how many members we have.")

now picture getting paid only for qualified leads that actually show up in the call.

the paradigm shift:

the list matters more. a wrong-fit prospect who books never becomes a qualified call.

the offer has to be real. nobody shows up for a vague one.

replies get answered fast, because a warm reply that sits for two days goes cold.

reminders and follow-up stop being nice-to-haves. a booked call that no-shows pays nothing.

and "send more" stops being the default fix, because more sends only help if every stage before the call holds up.

none of that is magic. it's what happens when you measure the last step instead of the first.

whatever you pay for is what gets built.

pay for emails sent, get emails sent.

pay for calls that show up, get calls that show up.

10 things we're seeing with many leaders at incumbent brands:

1. They want to rethink their offer from the ground up, not just 'adding AI' to their existing product

2. Can't disrupt cashflow and existing biz, so they're thinking about an entirely new product offering outside of core product

3. Cash, trust, data, and distribution are the four superpowers incumbents have - most don't know how to capitalize on all (or any) of them. Cash is precious and still feels better in the bank. Trust is beginning to move. Data is messy. Distribution is great, but current customers don't know what they want or don't like AI.

4. Hire a few ambitious leaders at the VP level from 'big name' tech co's to drive change, but those leaders aren't equipped with the team to move fast and ship

5. Everyone wants durability, but none feel confident it's possible 

6. They want to 'invent something new', but then reference existing patterns and companies as what they think they want

7. Coordination and cooperation across the team - evolving the way they work while innovating and keeping the train on the tracks - is really hard

8. Staying up to date with what matters is not feasible. Many miss important developments or get on them late - the space moves fast

9. Few understand that if you're building a tool, you're building for an agent (not a human), and you will eventually become plumbing. Products, agents, and new offers cannot be pure utility if you want durability and humans using you everyday (it can if you decide to be a muse connector or ChatGPT plugin / MCP in to the dominant AI apps)

10. Everyone's figuring it out. Even those with the most conviction are still questioning and rethinking things daily.

text:
UTAH FILES 14 CRIMINAL CHARGES AGAINST KALSHI AS FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CHALLENGES STATE GAMBLING LAWS

On October 28, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges against prediction-market company Kalshi and its cofounders, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara.

Utah alleges the company illegally offered online sports gambling despite the state's restrictions.

Meanwhile, the federal government is suing Utah, arguing that these markets fall under federal financial regulations.

Here's what the records show.

WHAT IS KALSHI?

Kalshi is a federally regulated platform where people trade contracts based on future events, including sports, elections, and economic reports.

For example, someone can buy a contract predicting whether a football team will win. The contract pays based on the outcome.

Kalshi argues these are financial contracts regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Utah argues that contracts tied to sporting events are gambling and must follow state law.

WHAT ARE THE CRIMINAL CHARGES?

Utah filed 14 counts:

• 12 third-degree felony counts of online gambling promotion.
• 1 second-degree felony count of engaging in a pattern of unlawful activity.
• 1 Class A misdemeanor count of general gambling promotion.

According to prosecutors, an undercover investigator created a Kalshi account using Utah identification and payment information.

Between September 13 and 24, the investigator allegedly:

• Placed 12 sports-related transactions.
• Risked a total of $114.87.
• Used the platform while physically located in Utah.
• Paid fees collected by Kalshi.

The transactions involved sports including professional and college football, baseball, hockey, and soccer.

Prosecutors argue these activities violated Utah's gambling laws.

Mansour and Lopes Lara were issued summonses to appear in court, not arrested.

WHAT DID THE COURTS ALREADY DECIDE?

The legal dispute began before these charges.

• AUG. 4: Federal Judge Robert Shelby ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act did not prevent Utah from enforcing its gambling laws against Kalshi.

• SEPT. 8: The Tenth Circuit declined Kalshi's request to temporarily block Utah's enforcement while its appeal continued.

• OCT. 20: Utah filed a separate civil lawsuit seeking to stop Kalshi's operations in the state.

• OCT. 26: The United States and CFTC filed a federal lawsuit against Utah.

• OCT. 27: The CFTC publicly announced that lawsuit, arguing federal regulation takes priority.

• OCT. 28: Utah filed the new criminal charges.

The August ruling favored Utah on the question of federal versus state authority. It did NOT find Kalshi or its founders criminally guilty.

WHAT ARE BOTH SIDES ARGUING?

UTAH'S POSITION:

State officials argue that offering sports-related wagers violates Utah law, regardless of whether the company calls them financial contracts.

Utah maintains that federal registration does not automatically protect a company from state gambling restrictions.

KALSHI AND THE CFTC'S POSITION:

Kalshi argues its contracts fall under federal financial regulations.

The CFTC maintains that Congress gave it authority over federally registered derivatives exchanges and that states cannot override that authority through gambling laws.

Kalshi has called Utah's criminal charges political overreach and says it will challenge them in court.

WHY DOES THIS MATTER NATIONWIDE?

Other states have also challenged prediction markets, and federal courts have reached different conclusions.

For example, a federal judge blocked Arizona's earlier criminal prosecution of Kalshi, while the August ruling in Utah favored state enforcement authority.

The wider dispute could eventually reach the U.S. Supreme Court.

WHAT HAS BEEN PROVEN?

The new filing establishes that Utah has formally brought criminal charges.

It does NOT establish that:

• Kalshi or its founders have been convicted.
• All prediction-market contracts are illegal gambling.
• Utah's interpretation applies nationwide.
• Federal registration automatically blocks every state gambling law.

Those questions involve different laws, contracts, and court proceedings.

BOTTOM LINE

Utah alleges that Kalshi illegally offered sports-related gambling to state residents, while Kalshi and the federal government argue that its contracts fall under federal financial regulation.

The new criminal charges are a significant escalation in an existing dispute.

However, the criminal allegations remain unproven, and the broader question of state versus federal authority is still being fought in court.

The outcome could affect how prediction markets operate across the country.

DEEP DEMOCRAT CORRUPTION: A Massachusetts firm co-owned by Rep. Ayanna Pressley’s husband holds a stake in a nearly $2 billion Springfield courthouse lease that losing bidders have sued to challenge as conflicted.
⠀
The Division of Capital Asset Management awarded the contract in July 2026 to Liberty Junction. The partnership includes CoJo Partners, co-owned by Conan Harris and John Barros, who at the time was interim executive director of the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority.

Under the deal the state will lease the new Regional Justice Center at 125 Liberty Street for at least 40 years and never own the building. Total construction and rent costs are estimated near $2 billion.
⠀
Two losing bidders filed suit in Hampden Superior Court alleging the process was rife with conflicts of interest.

They pointed to Barros’s role and the timing of his ethics disclosure. They also cited meetings with Gov. Maura Healey’s staff shortly before the award became public.
⠀
A judge denied their request for an injunction. Barros later said he would divest. Harris has not. Pressley has said she and her husband keep their finances completely separate and that she has no unique insights into the deal.
⠀
Healey has defended the selection as the best value for taxpayers, roughly $300 million below the next-lowest offer. Outside a Springfield event this week Harris was asked how much he stands to receive. He replied, “I have no comment.”
⠀
Republican Mike Minogue has called the arrangement the most corrupt business deal in Massachusetts history. Mass Fiscal Alliance has urged a rebid. Discovery in the civil case continues.

text:
If I took over marketing for a $3M plumbing shop in Phoenix tomorrow, here is the exact 4-quadrant plan for Month 1.

1. Win the Game (Q1)
Cap Google Ads to emergency terms only. Audit the GBP: fix primary categories, clean NAP across directories, and turn on review requests via SMS. One dialed GBP pulled 643 direct calls in 5 months with $0 media. Stop overpaying for basic search volume.

2. Build a Brand (Q2)
Take 15% of the ad budget out of search and put it into Meta video ads targeted within 5 miles of your highest-margin zip codes. Show the techs, the trucks, and pricing transparency. Warm the 97% of homeowners who don't have a broken pipe today so they don't search Google when they do.

3. Return and Retain (Q3)
Export your past 5,000 customers from ServiceTitan. Segment everyone who hasn't had service in 10 months and send a 2-way SMS offer for a pre-season water heater flush. This fills your dispatch board for two weeks without buying another click.

4. Operations & Intake
Wire lead tracking directly to closed CRM revenue, not form fills. Retrain dispatch: replacement calls get routed to a senior sales tech within 60 seconds, not a general CSR script.

Single-channel guys buy more clicks. Operators build an engine that compounds.

text:
The funding rate is the new quiet tax.
 In a perpetual, the continuous funding payment between longs and shorts is not just a technical fix to keep the contract near spot. Over time it functions as a structural transfer. When retail (or one cohort) is systematically long and leveraged, they pay the other side a recurring fee for the privilege of staying exposed. In a 24/7 regulated equity or index perp, this becomes a slow, automated drain that most users never explicitly notice.

ICE is not “adopting” Hyperliquid’s tech so much as enclosing it.
 The deal structure (ICE operates the regulated U.S. market and clearing, takes a stake in TradeXYZ, uses HIP-3 as the engine) is less a merger of paradigms and more a classic enclosure. The performance and 24/7 product features come from the crypto side; the regulatory moat, customer access, and clearinghouse rents stay with the traditional exchange. The technology is being licensed into a structure that preserves the incumbent’s position rather than disintermediating it.

Druckenmiller’s dual role is the feature, not the bug.
 He is both an equity investor in the platform and a prospective user of the product. Sophisticated capital can benefit from both the growth of the venue and the superior risk management and information advantages that come with trading the instrument itself. Retail, by contrast, mostly supplies the other side of the leverage and the funding payments. The asymmetry is structural once these products are opened more widely.

This accelerates the shift from ownership to pure exposure.
 A stock or index perpetual lets someone express a view on price with leverage and no expiry, without ever owning the underlying shares, voting rights, or dividends. Scaled up under a regulated U.S. venue, this further decouples “being long the market” from actual capital formation or corporate governance. Over time it can increase the share of price discovery and volatility that is driven by leveraged derivatives rather than by fundamental buyers and sellers of the real assets.

24/7 + high leverage creates a new transmission channel for weekend and overnight shocks.
 Traditional equity markets close. A regulated 24/7 equity or index perp does not. Large moves that occur when the cash market is shut (geopolitical news, earnings surprises released after hours, etc.) can now force liquidations and funding adjustments in real time among U.S. participants. That feedback can then hit the cash market harder when it reopens. The product doesn’t just offer convenience; it shortens the time between an external shock and leveraged forced selling, which can amplify rather than dampen volatility.

These are the angles that feel under-discussed relative to the surface “Wall Street embraces crypto perps” framing.

text:
The Toronto Raptors may be without Kawhi Leonard for three to four weeks, but Wednesday's 129-99 victory over Orlando offered an encouraging look at how they can compete without their biggest offseason acquisition.

• Leonard is dealing with swelling in his left knee after appearing in just two games this season. Medical imaging revealed no acute injury, but Chris Haynes reports the seven-time All-Star could miss three to four weeks before Toronto determines the next steps in his recovery.

• Scottie Barnes scored 28 points and RJ Barrett added 25 against Orlando, combining for 53 points. Immanuel Quickley contributed 16 points and seven assists, while Ja'Kobe Walter scored 14 starting in Leonard's place.

• Toronto also received 13 points and seven assists from Jamal Shead, demonstrating the depth coach Darko Rajakovic believes can keep the Raptors competitive. The win followed a disappointing 117-94 loss to Minnesota in their first game without Leonard.

Leonard's return date remains uncertain, making continued production from Barnes, Barrett and Toronto's supporting cast essential over the coming weeks.

text:
Matthew McConaughey turned down $14.5 million to make one more romantic comedy.

A few years later, he won an Oscar for a movie made on $4.9 million.

In the video below, he tells Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO how the offer kept going up.

In the 2000s, he was Hollywood’s go-to rom-com guy. The movies paid well, and the scripts kept coming.

But he wanted dramas, and nobody would cast him in one.

So he moved to his ranch in Texas and told his agent: no more rom-coms. His wife Camila was pregnant with their first child.

For months, nothing came. He says he thought about becoming a teacher or going back to law school.

Then an offer came in. $8 million. He said no.

They came back with $12 million. No.

Then $14.5 million. “Let me read that again.”

He says it was the same script he had already turned down at $8 million. “But it was better written.”

He still said no. His brothers asked him: “What is your major malfunction, little brother?”

He believes that one “no” told Hollywood he was not bluffing. “He’s not for rent.”

About 20 months after he walked away, the offers he wanted started coming in. Mud. Magic Mike. True Detective.

Then Dallas Buyers Club. It was shot in 25 days on $4.9 million, and it won him the Oscar for best actor, a goal he says he had written down in 1992.

The case for the skeptics: he already had years of rom-com money in the bank. Saying no to $14.5 million is easier when you can afford 20 months without a paycheck. Most people can’t.

So was it courage, or a bet only a millionaire could afford to make?

text:
“I was lied to by my friend”: TikTok panelist “Baby Doll” claims Sandra Davis fabricated a drunk-driver story about the I-10 crash tied to missing Texas mother Christin Munn-Holliday.
In a recent TikTok livestream panel, a participant identifying as “Baby Doll” made a series of pointed claims about Sandra (also referred to as Sandria or Sandy) Davis and the Sept. 30, 2026, hit-and-run crash on Interstate 10’s Atchafalaya Basin Bridge in Iberville Parish, Louisiana—the same crash after which 22-year-old Christin “Chrissy” Munn-Holliday of Katy, Texas, vanished and has not been seen since.
Baby Doll repeatedly denied any personal involvement or direct knowledge of Munn-Holliday’s disappearance while asserting that Davis, with whom she claimed a prior friendship, had lied to her about the circumstances of the collision.
Core denials and limited knowledge
From the outset, Baby Doll sought to distance herself: “I was not there. I don’t know who did what. I don’t know nothing specifically. I only know what was told to me, which is what I posted on Instagram, these messages between me and Sandria.” She emphasized she had never met Munn-Holliday (“I have never seen the girl a day in my life. I’m way from BR. I don’t know her”) and rejected any suggestion that her social-media posts implied special knowledge of the missing woman’s whereabouts.
She framed her public comments as a response to perceived efforts to link her to the disappearance simply because she had shared private messages with Davis.
The alleged lie and the “drunk driver” account
The central allegation concerned what Davis told her. According to Baby Doll, Davis texted that she “got hit by a drunk driver and they almost killed her.” Baby Doll said this was the entirety of what she had been told and the reason she initially spoke out: “I spoke out about it because me and Sandy were friends, and she lied to me about the situation, basically… Why would you lie to me if me and you are supposed to be friends?”
She later sharpened the point: the lie was specifically the drunk-driver narrative and the claim that the other driver fled. When confronted with online assertions that the other vehicle’s driver was never drunk and may not even have been in a car in the way described, Baby Doll reacted with frustration (“What the fuck?”) and questioned how a driver could “flee if both cars is totaled.” She concluded that Davis’s account to her was false.
Pregnancy claim and implications of cover-up
A secondary but repeated thread involved pregnancy. Baby Doll stated that Davis “is pregnant actively… She ain’t lose the baby” and expressed surprise at any impression that a miscarriage had occurred in the crash. She used the alleged falsehood about the crash details to escalate her skepticism: “If she lied about that to her close friend… you could imagine what all being covered up.” She reiterated that the betrayal of friendship—and the gravity of a missing person—was why she continued to speak: “At the end of the day, this is somebody that has gone missing.”
Context around the “chased” narrative
Baby Doll also addressed earlier posts she made about Munn-Holliday being chased. She attributed that specific claim to “the girl Kashmir… which is Chrissy friend,” who had posted on Instagram that they chased her. Baby Doll said her own comments about being chased stemmed from that source, and that the resulting fallout with Davis (“Me and Sandy got into it because I spoke out”) prompted her further disclosures.
Analysis of the statements
Baby Doll’s remarks do not claim first-hand observation of the crash or of Munn-Holliday’s actions afterward. They rest on two pillars: (1) second-hand information from Davis that she now labels a lie, and (2) a sense of personal betrayal that she presents as justification for publicizing the messages and questioning the official and street-level narratives.
The statements introduce or amplify several contested elements already circulating in online discussion of the case—the precise sequence of the collision, whether alcohol was involved on either side, whether anyone fled, and the medical/pregnancy status of Davis—while stopping short of asserting knowledge of what ultimately happened to Munn-Holliday. Authorities have charged Davis with reckless operation in connection with the crash (crash-data evidence reportedly showed high speed), but have publicly separated that charge from the active missing-person investigation. Munn-Holliday’s family has consistently rejected the idea that she simply walked away from the remote bridge and has called for expanded scrutiny of cameras, witnesses, and possible foul play.
As with most social-media panel claims, Baby Doll’s account remains unverified by independent reporting or official confirmation. It adds another layer of personal allegation to an already opaque case in which a young mother left the scene of a nighttime crash on a long, isolated elevated highway and has not been located. The $20,000 reward offered by the family for information leading to her safe return remains in place, and the investigation continues.

text:
When a coach asks “where else are you visiting?” — what you say next decides whether he chases you or forgets you 👇🏼

Here’s the formula:

1️⃣ NAME SPECIFIC SCHOOLS AT OR ABOVE HIS LEVEL
Bonus points if it’s someone in his conference or a rival. Vague doesn’t work. “A few schools” tells him nothing.

2️⃣ BE HONEST ABOUT WHERE IT STANDS
Dates locked in? Say that — it shows you’re busy and in demand. Only have invites? Say that instead:

“I’ve been communicating with Wake Forest and Toledo, they invited me out this season but I’m still getting my schedule finalized.”

3️⃣ THEN TAKE THE EDGE OFF
“But I love what you’re building at Louisville.”

That last line is what keeps it from sounding like bragging. You just showed demand and interest in the same breath.

That’s how a DM turns into a phone call — and phone calls are where real recruiting happens.

text:
The delivery man who had been bringing packages to our home for five years suddenly invited me to his wedding.

He had taped the wedding invitation to one of my packages.

Next to it was a small handwritten note:

"I've seen you almost every day for the past five years. It would mean so much to me if you could come to my wedding. But please don't feel obligated."

Honestly, this man had always been incredibly thoughtful.

Whenever I wasn't home, he would text me to let me know where he'd left my package.

On rainy days, he'd carefully wrap the boxes in plastic bags to keep them dry.

And whenever something was particularly heavy, he'd offer to carry it inside for me.

I'd never received a wedding invitation from a delivery driver before, so I was a little surprised.

But after thinking about it, I decided to go.

After all, I'd known him for five years.

Come to think of it, I'd probably seen him more often than some of my own relatives.

That Saturday, I got dressed, prepared a cash wedding gift, and arrived at the venue on time.

After checking in, a staff member showed me to the groom's side of the reception.

I'd barely sat down when an older man beside me smiled and asked:

"Which building are you from?"

"Sorry?"

"I'm from Building 103. What about you?"

I hesitated.

"Actually, I live in the apartment complex next door..."

His face immediately lit up.

"Oh! You're from the neighboring complex!"

Then he turned toward another table and called out:

"Hey! We've got someone from the neighboring complex over here!"

I followed his gaze.

And that's when I realized something extraordinary.

Almost everyone sitting on the groom's side was someone he'd delivered packages to over the years.

Some lived in Building 101.

Others lived in Building 103.

There was the owner of a nearby convenience store.

There was an elderly woman whose bags of rice he regularly helped carry inside.

Most of these people had never met one another.

Yet somehow, one delivery man had brought them all together at the same wedding.

But the biggest surprise was still waiting for me.

At the table closest to the groom sat the security guard from our apartment complex.

When he noticed me, he smiled and waved.

"Oh, you came too!"

I couldn't help laughing a little.

Without any of us realizing it, this ordinary man in his delivery uniform, pushing his cart through our neighborhood every day, had quietly become part of so many people's lives.

When the ceremony began, the groom stepped forward and picked up the microphone.

He looked a little embarrassed.

"I don't have any particularly successful friends," he began.

"And I don't know any important or influential people."

"For years, I've just been delivering packages every day."

"But people always say, 'Thank you for your hard work.'"

"Sometimes, when the weather is bad, someone offers me water or something to eat."

"I've always thought of myself as just an ordinary delivery man."

He paused.

"I never imagined that so many people would actually come to my wedding."

His voice began to tremble.

I looked down at the place card on our table.

There were no company names.

No job titles.

No impressive credentials.

Just a few simple words:

"The neighbors who have always been kind to me."

And in that moment, I realized something.

That wedding invitation, taped to a cardboard delivery box, might have been the most precious invitation I'd ever received.

Because sometimes, human connections aren't built through grand gestures or extraordinary moments.

Sometimes, they're built through five years of ordinary encounters.

A simple "Thank you."

A quiet "Take care."

A smile at the front door.

And somehow, those tiny moments become important enough that, on one of the biggest days of someone's life...

You're one of the people they want to have beside them.
